test: For every graph, list its non-data marks: enclosing box, gridlines, secondary axis ticks, background fill, drop shadows, and a legend that could be replaced by labelling two or three lines directly. Flag the graph if any of these is present and carries no information a reader needs.
cost: Ornament competes with the plotted data for the reader's attention at exactly the moment they are trying to read a value off the page, so the figure takes longer to read and its point lands less firmly.
suggestion: Delete the box and the gridlines, lighten the axes and the secondary ticks below the weight of the data marks, and move short legends onto the lines themselves.
mechanism: A graph is read by comparing marks, so every mark that is not data is a distractor the eye must reject. Zobel states the principle as a budget: ink is for data, not for dressing. Because the ornament is usually inserted by the plotting library rather than chosen, removing it costs the author nothing and is almost always an improvement.
counter_case: Gridlines earn their place when the reader is expected to recover absolute values rather than compare shapes, for example a calibration curve or a figure that stands in for a table of operating points. A legend must stay when lines are too dense or too short to label in place.
source: Justin Zobel, Writing for Computer Science, 2nd ed. (Springer, 2004), ch. 6 'Graphs, figures, and tables', p. 84: "Axes should be inconspicuous; ink should be used for data, not dressing. Gridlines and boxing are other forms of unnecessary ornamentation."

test: Flag any bar chart, pie chart or surface plot drawn with a depth or perspective effect when the underlying data has fewer dimensions than the rendering. A bar chart of one value per category rendered as 3D blocks always fails.
cost: Depth adds shading and foreshortening that scale non-linearly with the plotted value, so the reader's sense of the ratio between two bars is wrong in a direction the author did not choose.
suggestion: Redraw as a flat two-dimensional bar chart with a zero baseline, and if a third variable really exists, encode it as a second panel or a second bar group rather than as depth.
mechanism: A bar communicates through length, but a 3D bar communicates through a rendered volume whose apparent size grows faster than its height. Zobel notes that doubling a bar's height exaggerates the difference once depth is added. Nguyen and colleagues found size violations of this kind in 69.4% of the 363 published figures they audited, making it the single most common defect in their sample.
counter_case: A genuine surface over two independent variables, such as a loss landscape or a two-hyperparameter sweep, is legitimately three-dimensional, though a contour or heatmap panel is usually still easier to read off.
source: Justin Zobel, Writing for Computer Science, 2nd ed. (Springer, 2004), ch. 6, p. 85: "Graph-drawing tools allow bar graphs to be three-dimensional, but the addition of depth is deceptive; if one bar is twice the height of another, the use of depth exaggerates the difference." Corroborated by Nguyen, Jung & Gupta, 'Examining data visualization pitfalls in scientific publications', Visual Computing for Industry, Biomedicine, and Art 4:27 (2021), DOI 10.1186/s42492-021-00092-y, sections M2 and M3 and Table 4

test: Collect every graph that plots the same measured quantity. Compare their axis ranges, tick spacing, aspect ratio and physical size. Flag any set where the same quantity is drawn on different scales across panels that the reader is expected to compare.
cost: The reader compares panels by shape, so a scale change silently rescales the apparent effect and a method can be made to look better or worse than another purely by the choice of range.
suggestion: Fix one range per quantity across the whole set of comparable panels, render them at the same size, and if one panel genuinely needs a different range, break it out and say in the caption that its scale differs.
mechanism: Comparison across panels is done by remembered shape, not by re-reading the axis, so a reader who has just learned one panel's geometry applies it to the next. Zobel makes scale consistency an explicit requirement for the case where separate graphs illustrate several methods aimed at the same goal, and his editing checklist repeats it as a question about graph size and shared axis labels.
counter_case: Different ranges are correct when the panels are not meant to be compared, for example one panel showing a coarse sweep and another zooming into a region of interest. That case must be flagged in the caption so the reader does not read across.
source: Justin Zobel, Writing for Computer Science, 2nd ed. (Springer, 2004), ch. 6, p. 85: "Where several methods of achieving the same aim are being illustrated, the axes in each graph should have the same scale." and ch. 8 editing checklist, p. 135: "Are the graphs all the same size? Are the axis units always given? If, say, the x-axes on different graphs measure the same units, do the axes have the same label?"

test: Find every logarithmically scaled axis. For each, read the claim the surrounding text makes from that figure. Flag the figure if the claim is about a constant factor or a percentage difference rather than about growth order or about behaviour spanning several decades.
cost: A log axis compresses constant factors to near-invisibility, so a figure offered as evidence for a speedup shows two curves the reader cannot separate, and the claim ends up resting on the text alone.
suggestion: Plot the ratio of the two quantities on a linear axis, or plot the difference directly, so the constant factor becomes the thing the figure shows.
mechanism: Log scaling turns multiplication into addition, which is exactly what you want for growth order and exactly what you do not want for a fixed multiplier. Zobel gives the numbers: a uniform 30% advantage is almost indistinguishable on a log-log plot. The mismatch is between what the axis is good at and what the sentence next to it asserts.
counter_case: A log axis is right, and a linear axis would be wrong, when the data spans orders of magnitude or when the point is the asymptotic exponent. Keep the log axis and add a separate ratio panel rather than abandoning it.
source: Justin Zobel, Writing for Computer Science, 2nd ed. (Springer, 2004), ch. 6, p. 85: "Log scaling is not always appropriate. If one algorithm is 30% faster than another at all scales, then their performance will be almost indistinguishable on a log-log graph."

test: For every line drawn between two plotted points, ask whether a measurement could in principle exist between them. Flag any line joining categories that have no order, and any line spanning a region where the quantity on the x axis cannot take intermediate values.
cost: Joining points asserts that the two axes are related by a function and that the space between the points is populated, so the reader infers a trend the experiment never measured.
suggestion: Drop the connecting line and show the points alone, or switch to a bar chart when the x axis carries unordered categories.
mechanism: A line is a claim of interpolation. Zobel states it plainly: a line is an interpolation between two points, and if no data can validly be said to lie in that space, the line must go. Unordered categories fail the test outright, because there is no intermediate category for the line to pass through.
counter_case: A connecting line is legitimate, and often necessary for tracking a series, when the x axis is genuinely continuous and the sampling is dense enough that interpolation is a fair summary, such as a learning curve over training steps.
source: Justin Zobel, Writing for Computer Science, 2nd ed. (Springer, 2004), ch. 6, p. 94: "A line is an interpolation between two points; if no data can be validly said to lie in that space, omit the line." and p. 85 on unordered items: "(Such data should not be represented by joined points, which would imply that the axes were related by a function.)"

test: For each table, read the column heads and ask whether every entry below a head is the same kind of thing. Then read each row label and ask whether every entry to its right is a property of that label. Flag any table where a column mixes kinds, or where the top-left cell is used as a heading for the other column heads rather than left blank.
cost: A column that mixes kinds cannot be scanned, because the reader's guess about what the next cell means is wrong, and they fall back to reading the table cell by cell.
suggestion: Split the offending column into two columns of homogeneous kind, move any spanning label into a proper spanning header, and leave the stub corner empty.
mechanism: A table's efficiency comes entirely from the reader learning a column's type once and then scanning. Zobel states both halves of the contract, that items below a column head are of the same kind and that items right of a row label are properties of that label. A top-left cell that labels the other headings breaks the hierarchy, which is why he says to leave it blank.
counter_case: A deliberately heterogeneous summary column, such as a Notes or Configuration column holding short free text, is fine, provided it sits at the right-hand edge and is not something the reader is asked to compare down.
source: Justin Zobel, Writing for Computer Science, 2nd ed. (Springer, 2004), ch. 6, p. 106: "The items below a column head should be of the same kind or about the same thing. Items to the right of a row label should all be properties of that label... If there is no heading for the column of labels, leave the position blank."

test: For each table, ask whether any claim in the body text depends on the reader extracting and comparing numbers from it. If so, check that the text also states the comparison in words or that a graph shows it. A table that is the sole carrier of a headline result fails.
cost: Reading a table of any size is slow deliberate work that most readers will not do, so a result that lives only in a table reaches only the fraction of readers who stop and compute.
suggestion: State the comparison in a sentence with its numbers, or add a small figure that shows it, and keep the table as the reference a careful reader can check.
mechanism: Tables are precise and graphs are fast, and the two serve different readers. Zobel's position is unusually strong here: understanding a table of any complexity is hard work, so a table should be available for reference but must not be relied on to convey essential information. He also gives the degenerate case, where a table showing only a simple relationship should be replaced by the sentence stating it.
counter_case: A table is the right and only carrier when exact values matter more than the trend, as with dataset statistics, hyperparameter settings, or a results table whose whole purpose is to let others reproduce specific numbers.
source: Justin Zobel, Writing for Computer Science, 2nd ed. (Springer, 2004), ch. 6, p. 111: "Understanding a table of any complexity is hard work. For presentation of results, graphs or explanatory text are preferable; have a table to which the interested reader can refer, but don't rely on a table to convey essential information." The before/after pair is Zobel's own marked example, p. 106

test: Cover the body text and read each figure and table with its caption alone. Flag it if any line style, symbol, colour, abbreviation, column head or plus-minus term appearing in it is not defined in the caption or in the figure itself.
cost: Figures are the first thing a reader looks at and often the only thing a skimming reader looks at, so an undefined symbol turns the paper's most-viewed object into something that cannot be read without a hunt through the method section.
suggestion: Move the definitions of every visual encoding into the caption, and expand each abbreviation there even if it was expanded in the text.
mechanism: Readers enter a paper through its figures and read captions out of order, so a caption that depends on the body text has no reliable antecedent. Zobel requires that figures and tables be fairly self-contained and that the caption fully describe the figure's major elements, noting that computer science captions are habitually only a few words. The cost of the fix is a longer caption, which is not a cost readers pay.
counter_case: A caption should not restate the entire method, and in a venue with a hard caption length limit the right move is a compact key inside the figure panel plus a pointer to one named section, not an unreadable caption.
source: Justin Zobel, Writing for Computer Science, 2nd ed. (Springer, 2004), ch. 6, p. 111: "Captions and labels should be informative... it is preferable for captions to fully describe the figure's major elements." and "Since figures and tables should be fairly self-contained, the caption is an appropriate place to explain important details."

test: Count the figures and graphs. For each, name the claim in the paper it is the evidence for. Flag any figure whose information is already carried by another figure, and any figure that exists because a tool emitted it rather than because a claim needs it.
cost: Figures draw attention disproportionately, so a decorative or duplicated figure spends the reader's most valuable attention on something peripheral and pushes the figure that matters further from the argument.
suggestion: Delete the duplicate and the tool output, or move them to an appendix, and make sure each remaining figure is the unique evidence for one named claim.
mechanism: Zobel gives both halves. Each graph should convey interesting new information and the paper should not be flooded with statistics even in graphical form, and separately, because graphs and diagrams attract the attention of readers, they should be reserved for material that is central to the paper. He adds the diagnostic for the underlying cause: information should be presented because it is supporting evidence for a hypothesis, not because it is the output of some program.
counter_case: A deliberately redundant figure earns its place when it re-presents the same data in a form the argument needs separately, for example a per-language breakdown of an aggregate already shown, or a qualitative example illustrating a number.
source: Justin Zobel, Writing for Computer Science, 2nd ed. (Springer, 2004), ch. 6, p. 83: "Don't flood your paper with statistics, even in graphical form, and avoid repetition; each graph should convey interesting new information."; p. 84: "You should present information because it is supporting evidence for a hypothesis, not because it is an output of some program."; p. 93: "Graphs and diagrams attract the attention of readers, so should be reserved for material that is central to the paper."

test: For each schematic diagram, build a legend of every visual device it uses: each box shape, each line style, each arrowhead, each shade. Flag the diagram if any device carries two meanings anywhere in it, if components of primary interest are drawn identically to minor ones, or if it contains clip-art or hardware pictures that no label refers to.
cost: A diagram is read as a notation, so a box that means a module in one place and a data store in another makes the whole picture untrustworthy and the reader stops using it as a guide.
suggestion: Assign one meaning per shape and one per line style, write the mapping into the caption, give the components the paper is about a distinct visual weight, and delete the decorative art.
mechanism: Zobel's audit of system-structure diagrams is specific: symbolism used inconsistently, boxes with different meanings in different places, lines carrying both control flow and data flow, primary objects not distinguished from minor components, and irrelevant computer components included. He also gives two mechanical fixes, that lines should not touch unless separating them would create an unnatural break, so an arrowhead sits a small gap from its target, and that labels should be horizontal in a font close to the body text with no more than two or three fonts and sizes.
counter_case: A diagram drawn in an established formal notation, such as a UML class diagram, a plate diagram for a graphical model, or a circuit schematic, inherits its symbol meanings from the notation and should follow that standard even where it conflicts with the paper's internal scheme.
source: Justin Zobel, Writing for Computer Science, 2nd ed. (Springer, 2004), ch. 6, pp. 99-100: "Diagrams illustrating system structure often seem to be poor. In too many of these pictures the symbolism is used inconsistently: boxes have different meanings in different places, lines represent both control flow and data flow, objects of primary interest are not distinguished from minor components, and so on. Unnecessary elements are included, such as cheesy clip-art or computer components that are irrelevant to the system."

test: Extract every numeric mention of each headline quantity across the abstract, introduction, results, tables, figures and conclusion. Group them by quantity and flag any group whose members disagree, including disagreement between a rounded and an exact form that are not consistent with each other.
cost: A quantity that appears with four different values across one paper tells the reader that nobody checked, and a referee who notices it will distrust every other number in the paper.
suggestion: Fix one canonical value and one rounding per quantity, define it once, and propagate it to every mention including the abstract and the figure captions.
mechanism: Numbers drift because they are edited independently in several places, and no amount of reading catches it because each mention is locally plausible. Zobel reports a real paper that gave the same figure as 'almost 200,000', 'about 170,000', '173,000' and '173,255', calling it an entirely unnecessary inconsistency. The check is mechanical and finds a class of error that reading never does.
counter_case: Two different values for what looks like one quantity are correct when they genuinely measure different things, for instance the raw corpus size before deduplication and the size after. That case needs the two names to differ, not the numbers to be reconciled.
source: Justin Zobel, Writing for Computer Science, 2nd ed. (Springer, 2004), ch. 5, p. 79: "A paper gave the same figure in different places as \"almost 200,000\", \"about 170,000\", \"173,000\", and \"173,255\" -- an entirely unnecessary inconsistency."

test: For every percentage or rate in the paper, find its denominator. Flag the percentage if the denominator is not stated within one sentence, and flag it again if the denominator is small enough that the raw fraction would be more informative, which in practice means fewer than about twenty observations.
cost: A percentage over five trials borrows the authority of a large-sample statistic, so a reader who never sees the denominator takes a two-out-of-five result as a stable property of the method.
suggestion: Report the raw fraction for small samples, and for every percentage state the denominator in the same sentence.
mechanism: A percentage discards the sample size, which is exactly the information a reader needs to judge how much the number can move. Zobel puts it bluntly: do not use probabilities to describe small sets of observations, because success in two of five cases does not mean the method works 40% of the time, and the percentage gives the result an authority it does not deserve. Reporting the fraction restores what the percentage threw away.
counter_case: A percentage is the right form even for a modest denominator when the reader needs to compare against other percentages, for example per-language accuracy across a benchmark suite. In that case report the percentage and the denominator together rather than dropping to fractions.
source: Justin Zobel, Writing for Computer Science, 2nd ed. (Springer, 2004), ch. 5, pp. 79-81: "Don't use probabilities to describe small sets of observations. Success in two of five cases does not mean that the method \"works 40% of the time\". The percentage gives the result an authority it does not deserve."

test: After any terminology change, global rename, or notation revision, search the figure source files, plotting scripts, embedded image text, table headers and caption text for the old term. Flag every surviving occurrence.
cost: A rename that reaches the prose but not the figures leaves the paper using two vocabularies, and the figures are the part a reader trusts most because they look like data.
suggestion: Keep the label strings in one place in the plotting code, regenerate every figure after a rename, and grep the figure sources and captions for the retired term before submitting.
mechanism: Late renames happen by find-and-replace over the manuscript, which by construction does not touch binary images or separate plotting scripts. Zobel names the failure directly, that terminology sometimes gets changed at a late stage perhaps with a global substitution, and instructs that graphs and diagrams get updated too. This is invisible on screen because the author reads the figure as the thing it means rather than as the words it contains.
counter_case: An old term should survive deliberately where the figure reproduces a prior work's own labelling, or where the paper is explicitly discussing the earlier name. Both cases need a caption note saying so.
source: Justin Zobel, Writing for Computer Science, 2nd ed. (Springer, 2004), ch. 6, p. 113: "Sometimes the terminology of a paper gets changed at a late stage, perhaps with a global substitution. Ensure that graphs and diagrams get updated too."

test: List every dataset, condition, language, model size and hyperparameter setting named in the setup. Cross it against the reported results. Flag any that was run but whose outcome is absent, and check that stated failures appear at the same level of prominence as successes rather than only in an appendix or a footnote.
cost: Selective reporting makes the method look more general than it is, and because the omission is invisible the field builds on a capability that does not exist.
suggestion: Report every condition that was run, put the failures in the same table as the successes, and where a condition was dropped say so and say why.
mechanism: A results section is read as a census of what was tried, so an absence is read as nothing to report rather than as something withheld. Zobel sets the standard as prominence, not mere presence: reported results should be a fair reflection of the experiment's outcomes, and if a test fails on some data sets and succeeds on others it is unethical to conceal the failures, with the existence of failure stated as prominently as that of success. He adds the symmetric warning that reporting just one success invites the reader to suspect a fluke.
counter_case: Genuinely anomalous runs, the product of experimental error or a freak event, need not be reported as results, and preliminary experiments used only to choose between approaches can be sketched briefly rather than reported in full. Zobel allows both explicitly, so the test is whether the omitted run bears on the hypothesis.
source: Justin Zobel, Writing for Computer Science, 2nd ed. (Springer, 2004), ch. 11 'Experimentation', p. 191: "reported results should be a fair reflection of the experiment's outcomes. If a test fails on some data sets and succeeds on others, it is unethical to conceal the failures, and the existence of failure should be stated as prominently as that of success."

test: Find every claim that the contributed method is faster or cheaper than a baseline by less than roughly ten percent. For each, check the text rules out the seven rival explanations Zobel lists: unequal implementation effort, differing buffer or memory behaviour on this machine, unsupported floating-point operations, debug options left enabled in the baseline build, timing-mechanism inaccuracy, run-order and cache effects, and an input that happens to favour the new method.
cost: A few-percent timing win is within the range that implementation care and machine state produce on their own, so a claim resting on it can be wholly an artefact, and it will not survive anyone else's hardware.
suggestion: Report the timing method and its resolution, interleave and repeat the runs, state the compiler flags for both systems, and either name the confounds excluded or reframe the claim as parity rather than improvement.
mechanism: Both systems are externally indistinguishable, so the measured difference is attributable to the algorithm only after the alternatives are eliminated. Zobel enumerates them, noting among other things that the new system is your invention and it is reasonable to take the care necessary to ensure it runs well, care perhaps not taken with the baseline. He also caps the resolution: Unix-style timing mechanisms return nanoseconds but their accuracy below tenths of a second is often questionable.
counter_case: A small margin is defensible without the full elimination when the comparison is of operation counts, memory bytes, or another deterministic quantity that does not depend on machine state. There the measurement has no noise to explain away.
source: Justin Zobel, Writing for Computer Science, 2nd ed. (Springer, 2004), ch. 11, pp. 194-195, the NEW-versus-OLD list of rival conclusions, quoted in part: "NEW is better implemented than was OLD. After all, NEW is your invention... Inaccuracies in the timing mechanism randomly favoured NEW. Although, for example, Unix-style timing mechanisms can return values in nanoseconds, their accuracy below tenths of a second is often questionable."

test: For every mean reported as typical behaviour, check two conditions: that the quantity being averaged does not vary with an input parameter that also varies across the averaged runs, and that the distribution is not bimodal or heavy-tailed. Flag any mean of running time taken across differing input sizes, and any mean of a latency distribution containing effectively infinite values.
cost: A mean over a bimodal distribution lands in a gap where no observation occurred, so the number offered as typical describes nothing that ever happened, and a mean over mixed input sizes measures the input mix rather than the system.
suggestion: Report the mean per input size rather than pooled, and for heavy-tailed quantities report the fastest observed value with its variance, or a median with quantiles, and say which you are reporting.
mechanism: A mean is a good summary only when the distribution is unimodal and the population is homogeneous. Zobel gives both failures: it makes no sense to report average running time when input size varies, and for packet round-trip delay the average may well be meaningless because some delays are effectively infinite and the distribution is a large number of fast responses with a small number of extremely slow ones, so the average sits in a range where no values were observed at all. His analogy is averaging a flight and a car journey from Paris to Moscow and calling the middle value typical.
counter_case: A pooled mean is the right summary when the pooling is the question, for example expected cost under a stated production traffic mix, provided the mix is reported. Zobel's own counter-example is accuracy of noun detection over a document sample, where the mean is appropriate.
source: Justin Zobel, Writing for Computer Science, 2nd ed. (Springer, 2004), ch. 11, p. 200: "It makes no sense to report average running time when input size varies, for example... the distribution of such delays often consists of a large number of fast responses and a small number of extremely slow responses; the average is therefore somewhat slower than the fast times, but in a range where no values were observed at all... In such cases, it may be appropriate to report the fastest time observed, while noting the variance."

test: For every axis carrying a magnitude that a reader is asked to compare across categories, check whether the axis starts at zero. Flag any truncated or zoomed magnitude axis, and flag any axis whose direction is inverted relative to the convention that up means more.
cost: Truncating the baseline multiplies the apparent difference between bars by an arbitrary factor the author chose, and inverting an axis reverses the reader's conclusion outright.
suggestion: Extend a bar or area axis to zero. If the interesting variation is genuinely small, keep the full axis and add a separate panel or an inset showing the zoomed region, labelled as a zoom.
mechanism: A bar encodes value by length, so length must be proportional to value, which requires a zero origin. Rougier and colleagues list showing the full range of values among the ways not to mislead the reader, and Nguyen and colleagues group omitting data, truncating the axis and over-zooming as the popular techniques in their spatial-orientation category, with the inverted-axis case documented as a chart where readers infer a decline while the quantity rose.
counter_case: A non-zero origin is correct and often necessary for a line plot of a quantity whose meaningful variation is small relative to its level, such as accuracy between 0.90 and 0.94 across training steps, or a temperature series. The zero-baseline requirement binds on length encodings, not on position encodings.
source: Rougier, Droettboom & Bourne, 'Ten Simple Rules for Better Figures', PLoS Computational Biology 10(9):e1003833 (2014), DOI 10.1371/journal.pcbi.1003833, Rule 7 ('Do Not Mislead the Reader'). Corroborated by Nguyen, Jung & Gupta, 'Examining data visualization pitfalls in scientific publications', Visual Computing for Industry, Biomedicine, and Art 4:27 (2021), DOI 10.1186/s42492-021-00092-y, section M4: "Omitting data, truncating the axis (or non-zero-base axis), and over zooming to see the difference are popular techniques."

test: For each figure, name the visual channel each quantity is encoded in. Flag any quantity the reader is asked to compare precisely that is encoded in area, angle, volume, curvature, shading or colour saturation rather than in position along a common scale or in length.
cost: The reader's accuracy at reading a value depends on the channel, so a precise comparison asked of an area or an angle is answered wrongly, and the error is systematic rather than random.
suggestion: Re-encode the quantity as position along a common scale, which usually means replacing a pie with a bar chart, a bubble chart with a dot plot, and a heatmap cell with a small-multiple line panel where exact values matter.
mechanism: Cleveland and McGill ranked the elementary perceptual tasks by measured accuracy and found the order: position on a common scale, then position on a non-aligned scale, then length, direction and angle, then area, then volume and curvature, then shading and colour saturation. A figure is therefore not merely stylistically better or worse; the channel sets a ceiling on how accurately its numbers can be recovered. Nguyen and colleagues supply the arithmetic of the commonest instance, where a value 2.56 times larger is drawn so that the region seems 6.5 times larger.
counter_case: Skau and Kosara later found that for pie and donut charts arc and area encodings actually outperformed angle, so the ranking is not exact within its lower tiers. Area encoding is also the right choice when the quantity is genuinely an area, or when the reader is asked only for a rough ordering, as in a treemap or a cartogram.
source: Cleveland & McGill, 'Graphical Perception: Theory, Experimentation, and Application to the Development of Graphical Methods', Journal of the American Statistical Association 79(387):531-554 (1984), DOI 10.1080/01621459.1984.10478080, the ordered list of elementary perceptual tasks. Area arithmetic from Nguyen, Jung & Gupta, 'Examining data visualization pitfalls in scientific publications', Visual Computing for Industry, Biomedicine, and Art 4:27 (2021), DOI 10.1186/s42492-021-00092-y, section M3: "14.5 trillion is 2.56 times larger than 5.7 trillion, but the region seems to be 6.5 times larger." Counter-case from Skau & Kosara (2016) on arc, area and angle in pie and donut charts

test: Take each figure and ask what single sentence it is meant to make the reader believe. Write that sentence down. Flag the figure if the sentence cannot be written, if it takes more than one sentence, or if the figure was produced by accepting a plotting library's defaults without any setting being chosen deliberately.
cost: A figure with no single message spends a large block of page area and the reader's peak attention without moving the argument, and a defaults-only figure imports whatever emphasis the library happened to encode.
suggestion: Write the message as the caption's first clause, then remove or de-emphasise every element that does not serve it, and set the ranges, fonts, marker sizes and colours deliberately rather than accepting them.
mechanism: Rougier and colleagues put identifying the message before any design decision, on the grounds that the message drives the choices, and they warn separately that library defaults "are good enough for any plot but they are best for none", so a figure that has not been tuned has not been designed. Together the two rules give a procedure rather than an exhortation: derive the message first, then justify each element against it.
counter_case: An exploratory or diagnostic figure in an appendix, or a figure whose purpose is to let readers inspect raw data rather than to carry a claim, legitimately has no single message. It should be labelled as such and kept out of the main results.
source: Rougier, Droettboom & Bourne, 'Ten Simple Rules for Better Figures', PLoS Computational Biology 10(9):e1003833 (2014), DOI 10.1371/journal.pcbi.1003833, Rule 2 ('Identify Your Message'), Rule 5 ('Do Not Trust the Defaults': defaults "are good enough for any plot but they are best for none") and Rule 9 ('Message Trumps Beauty')

test: Check that every table's caption sits above the table and every figure's caption sits below the figure, consistently throughout. Then check each figure was generated at its final printed size rather than scaled, by comparing the label font size in the rendered figure against the body text size.
cost: A figure drawn large and scaled down arrives with labels smaller than the body text, which is the commonest reason a reader cannot read a figure at all, and inconsistent caption placement makes the reader hunt for the caption on every figure.
suggestion: Fix caption placement in the template once, and set the figure's output dimensions to the column width so no scaling is applied, letting the plotting library render text at the body point size.
mechanism: Scaling a figure scales its text, so a figure authored at twice the column width arrives with labels at half the intended size, and no amount of care in the plot itself survives it. The ANZIAM guidelines state the placement convention and the requirement to generate figures at reproduction size without overriding the default font size, which is the operational form of the rule. Zobel's editing checklist asks the matching consistency question about graph size.
counter_case: Caption placement is set by the venue's style file and some venues invert these conventions, so the house style wins. Deliberate scaling is also fine for a figure that contains no text, such as a qualitative image grid.
source: Proceedings of ANZIAM submission guidelines, Tables and Figures sections, https://journal.austms.org.au/ojs/index.php/ANZIAMJ/about/submissions (caption above for tables and below for figures; generate figures at reproduction size and do not override the default font size). Consistency check from Zobel, 2nd ed. (2004), ch. 8 checklist, p. 135

test: For each figure that combines several panels the reader is asked to read across, check that a shared axis is present and labelled, and that the panels are aligned on it. Flag any composite figure where panels are juxtaposed with no common axis, or where the time or category ordering differs between panels.
cost: Without a shared axis the reader cannot line up a position in one panel with the same position in another, so the comparison the composite figure exists to enable cannot be made and readers guess.
suggestion: Give the panels a single shared axis with one label, align them on it, and use the same category or time ordering in every panel.
mechanism: A composite figure is an implicit invitation to compare across panels, and comparison across non-aligned scales is measurably less accurate than comparison on a common scale. Nguyen and colleagues record the concrete failure as a figure 'missing axis to line up data' with contradictory data units and value locations, and separately the case where months appear in a random position rather than in chronological order. Their layout finding is that such tables and figures force at least two attempts to locate the absolute meaning.
counter_case: Panels that are not meant to be compared, such as a schematic beside a results plot, need no shared axis, and forcing one on them would misrepresent the relationship. Ordering may also legitimately differ when each panel is sorted by its own effect size and the caption says so.
source: Nguyen, Jung & Gupta, 'Examining data visualization pitfalls in scientific publications', Visual Computing for Industry, Biomedicine, and Art 4:27 (2021), DOI 10.1186/s42492-021-00092-y, section M4: figures 'missing axis to line up data' with "contradictory data unit and value location"; non-chronological ordering where "months appear to be in a random position"; Table 3 on layouts forcing "at least two attempts to locate the absolute meaning"

test: Find every sentence that reads significance or its absence off a figure, including phrases like 'the error bars do not overlap', 'the intervals overlap, so the difference is not significant', or 'clearly separated'. Flag each one unless the text names the bar type, names n, and applies the rule matching that pair.
cost: Overlap and significance are related by a rule that depends on both the bar type and n, so a claim read off the picture is wrong by a factor that changes with the experiment, and the direction of the error is not predictable.
suggestion: Replace the visual argument with the test result and its p value or interval, or state the correct correspondence for the bars actually plotted.
mechanism: The correspondences exist but are not interchangeable across bar types or sample sizes. For standard-error bars at n of 10 or more, a gap of one SE indicates p about 0.05 and a gap of two SE about 0.01, whereas at n = 3 it is doubled SE bars that must fail to overlap for p below 0.05, and for 95% intervals at n = 3 overlap of one full arm is already p about 0.05. Krzywinski and Altman give the errors in both directions with numbers: at n = 10, s.e.m. bars that just touch correspond to p = 0.17 rather than to significance, while 95% confidence intervals can overlap by as much as half their length and still mark a significant difference, and CI bars that just touch correspond to p = 0.005. Overlap therefore neither establishes significance nor rules it out, which is why the bar type and n have to be named before the picture can be read.
counter_case: A visual reading is legitimate as a supporting remark when the correct rule for the plotted bars and n is stated alongside it, and it is genuinely useful for guiding a reader across many panels where quoting every p value would be unreadable. The test is whether the rule is named, not whether the eye is used.
source: Cumming, Fidler & Vaux, 'Error bars in experimental biology', Journal of Cell Biology 177(1):7-11 (2007), DOI 10.1083/jcb.200611141, Rules 6 and 7: "a gap of SE indicates P ~ 0.05 and a gap of 2 SE indicates P ~ 0.01" (n >= 10); with 95% CIs at n = 3, "overlap of one full arm indicates P ~ 0.05, and overlap of half an arm indicates P ~ 0.01". Corroborated and extended by Krzywinski & Altman, 'Points of significance: Error bars', Nature Methods 10(10):921-922 (2013), doi:10.1038/nmeth.2659: "In general, a gap between bars does not ensure significance, nor does overlap rule it out -- it depends on the type of bar"; "when n = 10 and s.e.m. bars just touch, P = 0.17"; 95% CI bars "can overlap by as much as 50% and still indicate a significant difference. If 95% CI bars just touch, the result is highly significant (P = 0.005)"

test: For every error bar and every reported variance, identify what was varied to produce the spread. Flag the figure if the spread comes from repeated measurement of one artefact rather than from independently repeated runs. In an ML paper this means flagging bars computed over evaluation batches, over decoding samples from one checkpoint, or over bootstrap resamples of one test set, when the text presents them as run-to-run variability.
cost: Replicate spread is smaller than run spread, often much smaller, so the interval is too narrow, and a difference that would vanish across training seeds is reported as established.
suggestion: Compute the interval across independently repeated runs, with n the number of runs, and if only replicates are available say so explicitly and describe the interval as within-run measurement spread rather than as uncertainty about the method.
mechanism: The authors are categorical that bars and statistics belong only with independently repeated experiments "and never for replicates", and that for a single representative experiment no bars or p values should be shown because n equals 1. The reason is that an interval estimates how much the reported quantity would move if the whole study were redone, and only independent repetition samples that. In machine learning the analogue of the replicate is the second evaluation pass over one trained checkpoint, and the analogue of the independent experiment is the retrained run.
counter_case: Replicate-level intervals are the right thing to report when the question is measurement noise itself, for example characterising decoding variance at a fixed temperature, or quantifying test-set sampling error via a bootstrap. Both are legitimate as long as the caption says which source of variation the interval covers.
source: Cumming, Fidler & Vaux, 'Error bars in experimental biology', Journal of Cell Biology 177(1):7-11 (2007), DOI 10.1083/jcb.200611141, Rules 2 and 3: n is "the number of independently performed experiments" and must appear in the legend; bars and statistics are for independently repeated experiments "and never for replicates"

test: For every group summarised by a bar or a point with an error bar, read n from the caption. Where n is about 3 or fewer, flag the summary and require the individual observations to be shown instead.
cost: A bar plus an interval over three points hides the three points, so the reader cannot see whether the spread comes from a genuine distribution or from one outlier, and the summary looks more like a measurement than it is.
suggestion: Plot the individual runs as points, jittered if they collide, optionally with a line at the mean, and give n in the caption.
mechanism: Cumming, Fidler and Vaux advise that when n is very small, with n = 3 as their example, it is better to simply plot the individual data points. At that size the summary discards almost nothing in space while discarding most of what the reader needs, since three points shown are immediately interpretable and a three-point interval is not. They note they give n = 3 rules at all only because such small samples are common in practice.
counter_case: Summaries are still needed at small n when the figure has many groups and showing all points would be unreadable, for instance forty conditions at n = 3. There the fix is to show points for the conditions the argument turns on and summarise the rest.
source: Cumming, Fidler & Vaux, 'Error bars in experimental biology', Journal of Cell Biology 177(1):7-11 (2007), DOI 10.1083/jcb.200611141, Rule 4: when n is very small, the example being n = 3, it is "better to simply plot the individual data points"

test: Find any place a confidence interval is obtained by multiplying a standard error, or where standard-error bars are described as approximating a 95% interval. Check n. Flag the conversion if n is below 10 and the multiplier used was 2.
cost: At small n the correct multiplier is much larger than 2, so a doubled standard error understates the interval substantially and every comparison drawn from it is more confident than the data allows.
suggestion: Use the t critical value for the actual degrees of freedom rather than 2, and state the multiplier and n in the caption.
mechanism: The 95% interval is the mean plus or minus t(n-1) times the standard error, and t depends sharply on n at the small end. Cumming, Fidler and Vaux state that standard-error bars may be doubled to approximate the 95% interval only "provided n is 10 or more", and that at n = 3 the t critical value is about 4 rather than about 2. Doubling at n = 3 therefore produces an interval roughly half the width it should be, which is a systematic error in the direction that favours the author's claim.
counter_case: The factor of 2 is fine, and conventional, where n is comfortably large, and a normal-approximation interval is also acceptable for a bootstrap or a large-sample proportion where the t distribution is not the relevant reference. The rule binds on small-sample t intervals.
source: Cumming, Fidler & Vaux, 'Error bars in experimental biology', Journal of Cell Biology 177(1):7-11 (2007), DOI 10.1083/jcb.200611141, Rule 5 and Table I: SE bars may be doubled to approximate the 95% CI "provided n is 10 or more"; at n = 3 the multiplier is about 4; 95% CI = M +/- t(n-1) x SE. Corroborated by Krzywinski & Altman, Nature Methods 10(10):921-922 (2013), doi:10.1038/nmeth.2659: "two useful approximations for the CI are 95% CI ~ 4 x s.e.m (n = 3) and 95% CI ~ 2 x s.e.m. (n > 15)", and noting that in large samples an s.e.m. bar reads as a 67% confidence interval

test: Identify designs where every condition was run on the same units, meaning the same seeds, the same prompts, the same test items or the same checkpoints. Flag any comparison in such a design that is argued from separate per-condition error bars rather than from the distribution of per-unit differences.
cost: Per-condition bars include the between-unit variation that a paired design already controls, so they are wider than the comparison warrants and a real paired effect is reported as inconclusive.
suggestion: Compute the per-unit difference, plot its mean with its own confidence interval, and test it with a paired procedure, reporting whether the interval excludes zero.
mechanism: When the same units appear in both conditions, the between-unit spread is common to both and cancels in the difference. Cumming, Fidler and Vaux state that for repeated measurements on one group, confidence intervals and standard-error bars "are irrelevant to comparisons within the same group", and prescribe either a paired analysis or a plot of the mean of per-unit differences with its own interval, where an interval excluding zero indicates p below 0.05. This is the commonest way an ML paper understates its own result, because shared seeds and a shared test set make almost every ablation paired.
counter_case: Unpaired per-condition intervals are the correct display when the units genuinely differ across conditions, for instance comparing models trained on disjoint data shards, or when the reader's question is the absolute level of each condition rather than the contrast between them.
source: Cumming, Fidler & Vaux, 'Error bars in experimental biology', Journal of Cell Biology 177(1):7-11 (2007), DOI 10.1083/jcb.200611141, Rule 8: for repeated measurements on one group, CIs and SE bars "are irrelevant to comparisons within the same group"; use a paired analysis or plot the mean of differences with its own CI, where a 95% CI excluding 0 indicates P < 0.05

test: Before touching any number, recompute it. For each: re-add every table column and row that carries a total, redo every unit conversion, recompute every percentage from its stated numerator and denominator, and check every figure against the same figure elsewhere. Where the arithmetic fails, do not substitute your own value. Raise a query naming the inputs you used.
cost: An editor who silently corrects a total can be propagating a correct arithmetic operation over the wrong inputs, which converts a visible error into an invisible one and destroys the author's only chance to notice that the underlying data is wrong.
suggestion: Query with the arithmetic shown, in the form 'Column sums to 84.3, not 84.1 as printed. Which is correct, or has a row been dropped?' and change nothing until the author answers.
mechanism: Editors Canada makes numerals a query-or-correct category rather than a correct category, standard D7 covering material containing statistics, mathematics and numerals with incorrect totals in tables as its example, and D5 doing the same for calculations. The reason the choice matters is that an arithmetic mismatch has at least two causes, a typo in the printed total and a missing or wrong row, and only the author can tell which. Correcting the total picks one cause without evidence.
counter_case: Silent correction is right for an unambiguous typographical slip where the correct value is independently fixed elsewhere in the document and no interpretation is involved, for example a table cell reading '8..4' where every other mention of that quantity reads 8.4. Log it on the style sheet rather than querying.
source: Editors Canada, Professional Editorial Standards 2024, D3.1 (verified in the 2024 PDF); originally cited as PES 2016 D5; PES 2016 D7 — SUPERSEDED, no verified 2024 equivalent, re-verify before citing; https://editors.ca/wp-content/uploads/2024/04/PES-2024-Interior_V7-Approved-Version-April-15-2024.pdf

test: Fix the authorized level of edit in writing before starting. Then audit every change made against it. Flag any change that belongs to a higher level than authorized: a reordered section or deleted paragraph in a copy edit, a recast sentence in a proofread, a substituted term in a mechanical pass.
cost: An unauthorized deeper edit arrives without the author expecting it, so it is either reverted wholesale, taking the legitimate corrections with it, or accepted unread, which lets a meaning change enter the document with nobody having decided on it.
suggestion: Convert every out-of-scope improvement into a flag or a query, keep the pass itself inside its level, and if the material genuinely needs a deeper edit, say so once as a scope observation rather than performing it.
mechanism: Editors Canada draws the boundary twice. Standard A8.1 requires the editor to determine the stage and level of edit and to use judgment when deciding whether to intervene, leave as is, query, change, or recommend a change, and standard E5 is explicit for the final stage: flag or correct egregious errors but refrain from undertaking structural, stylistic, or copy editing tasks unless authorized to do so. The boundary exists because the author's review budget is allocated against an expected level, and exceeding it spends attention that was not offered.
counter_case: An egregious error is correctable at any level, and the standards say so, so a factual howler or a libel risk found during a proofread is fixed or flagged immediately rather than deferred on scope grounds. Scope also legitimately widens mid-project by agreement, which should be recorded.
source: Editors Canada, Professional Editorial Standards 2024, E1.7 (verified in the 2024 PDF); originally cited as PES 2016 E5; PES 2016 A8.1 — SUPERSEDED, no verified 2024 equivalent, re-verify before citing; https://editors.ca/wp-content/uploads/2024/04/PES-2024-Interior_V7-Approved-Version-April-15-2024.pdf

test: Confirm a style sheet exists for the document. Check it records a decision for each of these categories: spelling variety, capitalisation, hyphenation, abbreviations and italics; numbers including measurements, dates and percentages; symbols and equations; list structure, grammar and punctuation; heading hierarchy; names and technical terms; and alphabetical and numerical sequences. If no style sheet was supplied, create one and populate it as the edit proceeds.
cost: Without a written record the same decision is remade differently on page 40 than on page 4, and neither the editor nor the next person on the file can tell a deliberate choice from a slip, so consistency errors are undetectable rather than merely unfixed.
suggestion: Open the style sheet before the first change, add every decision to it as it is made with the page where it was first applied, and hand it on with the document.
mechanism: Editors Canada requires it twice, at D9 to develop a style sheet or follow one that is provided in order to track editorial style and apply it consistently, and at E2 to adhere to it and, if none is provided, to prepare one and update it as work progresses. IPEd supplies the contents list, an editing style sheet specific to the publication covering spelling, grammar, punctuation, capitalisation, hyphenation, abbreviations and italics; numbers including measurements, time, dates and percentages; symbols and equations; lists; heading hierarchy; chronology, descriptions, names and terms; and alphabetical and numerical sequences. Together they turn consistency from a memory task into a lookup.
counter_case: A very short document edited in one sitting by one person does not need a separate artefact, and forcing one is overhead. The threshold is whether any decision will need to be recalled later or by someone else, which for a multi-author paper with an appendix is always.
source: Editors Canada, Professional Editorial Standards 2024, D2.1 (verified in the 2024 PDF); originally cited as PES 2016 D9; PES 2016 E2, E2.2 — SUPERSEDED, no verified 2024 equivalent, re-verify before citing; https://editors.ca/wp-content/uploads/2024/04/PES-2024-Interior_V7-Approved-Version-April-15-2024.pdf

test: For every edit that is not the correction of an outright error, ask what would break if it were reverted. Flag the edit if nothing would, or if the only answer is that the editor prefers the new wording. Then check specifically for edits that flatten first-person stance, remove a hedge, replace a distinctive word with a common one, or convert the author's rhythm to a uniform sentence length.
cost: A document edited to the editor's ear reads as nobody's, and the author who no longer recognises their own prose stops trusting the edit and starts reverting changes that were necessary along with the ones that were not.
suggestion: Revert every change that only substitutes a preference, keep the ones that fix an error or a genuine ambiguity, and where a distinctive construction is merely unusual rather than wrong, leave it and query if you suspect it is unintended.
mechanism: Both standards bodies express the principle as a minimality constraint rather than as an attitude, which is what makes it checkable. Editors Canada standard C5 requires that in improving a sentence, paragraph or passage the editor change only what is required, while maintaining the authorial voice where appropriate, and C11 makes establishing or maintaining tone, mood, style and authorial voice a deliverable in its own right. IPEd standard D2 uses almost identical wording, that editors should change only what is necessary to establish and preserve consistency in reading level, register, voice, colour, tone and pace.
counter_case: Voice yields when it obstructs the document's purpose, and the standards allow this by conditioning on appropriateness. A hedge that makes a safety-critical instruction ambiguous, or a register that will not survive translation or a non-native readership, should be changed and the change explained.
source: PES 2016 C11, C5, D2 — SUPERSEDED, no verified 2024 equivalent, re-verify before citing; https://editors.ca/wp-content/uploads/2024/04/PES-2024-Interior_V7-Approved-Version-April-15-2024.pdf

test: Read each query with the manuscript covered. Flag it if it cannot be understood alone, if it does not say what is wrong, if it asks a yes-or-no question where a choice is needed, or if it reports a problem without offering at least one concrete resolution the author can accept as written.
cost: A query the author cannot answer without reconstructing the editor's reasoning costs them the work the editor was supposed to do, and an unanswerable query is usually dismissed, so the underlying problem ships.
suggestion: Write each query as three parts: the specific thing observed with its location, why it is a problem, and a drafted replacement the author can approve or overwrite.
mechanism: Editors Canada separates the judgment of whether to query, standards C14 and D18, from the craft of writing one, standards D19 and C15. D19 requires queries that are clear, coherent and diplomatic for the appropriate person, and C15 requires the editor to request clarification of meaning and intent, explain changes as appropriate, and propose or negotiate significant editorial changes. Proposing is the operative word: a query that only reports is incomplete under the standard, because the author is left to invent the fix.
counter_case: A genuine request for information the editor cannot supply has no drafted resolution to offer, for example asking which of two cited papers a claim came from. Those queries should still name what is missing and why it matters.
source: Editors Canada, Professional Editorial Standards 2024, A12.3 (verified in the 2024 PDF); originally cited as PES 2016 D19; PES 2016 C15 — SUPERSEDED, no verified 2024 equivalent, re-verify before citing; https://editors.ca/wp-content/uploads/2024/04/PES-2024-Interior_V7-Approved-Version-April-15-2024.pdf

test: Sweep for missing apparatus rather than for wrong apparatus. List every quotation without a source, every table or figure without a source line, every unsupported generalisation in a passage that otherwise cites, and every absent caption, heading, cross-reference target or link. Flag each; do not supply the source yourself.
cost: A missing citation is invisible to reading because nothing on the page looks wrong, so it survives every pass that checks what is present, and it is the author rather than the editor who knows where the claim came from.
suggestion: Flag each site with the specific sentence and what is missing, and supply only the mechanical elements you can derive from the document itself, such as a caption number or a cross-reference target.
mechanism: Editors Canada splits this into two standards with different verbs. D15 is flag-only, recognising and flagging places where citations are needed with quotations without sources, unsupported generalisations in academic work, and tables without sources as its examples. D14 permits supplying, ensuring material is complete and, as appropriate, querying or supplying missing elements such as captions and headings. The asymmetry tracks who holds the information: the editor can invent a caption, but only the author knows the source.
counter_case: An editor with access to the reference manager or the source material can and should supply a missing citation directly, and doing so is faster than a query. The rule binds when the editor would be guessing which source the author meant.
source: Editors Canada, Professional Editorial Standards 2024, D4.1, D4.2 (verified in the 2024 PDF); originally cited as PES 2016 D14, D15; https://editors.ca/wp-content/uploads/2024/04/PES-2024-Interior_V7-Approved-Version-April-15-2024.pdf

test: On every pass after the first, do not re-read the document. Instead work from the list of requested changes: confirm each landed, confirm each is correct, and check the consequences of each at the places a change propagates, meaning line and page breaks, text flow, figure and table placement, the table of contents, cross-reference numbers, and navigation.
cost: Re-reading the whole text on a later pass spends the budget on prose that is already settled while the errors introduced by the corrections themselves go unexamined, and a fix that reflowed a page is the commonest way a late error enters a document.
suggestion: Keep the change list as the checklist, verify each item at its site, then walk only the propagation points, and re-read continuously only where a change was large enough to alter the surrounding argument.
mechanism: Editors Canada distinguishes the first round from later ones. E3 requires reading word by word in the first round, comparing with previous copy if supplied, while E4 requires that in each subsequent round the editor refrain from reading the entire text unless instructed and instead check that all changes have been made as requested and that they do not introduce new problems, naming line and page breaks, text flow, visual elements, the table of contents and the navigation bar. The reasoning is that corrections are the only new material, so they carry all the new risk.
counter_case: A full re-read is required when the changes were structural rather than local, for instance a reordered results section or a substantially rewritten introduction, because the argument's continuity is exactly what local checking cannot see.
source: PES 2016 E3, E4 — SUPERSEDED, no verified 2024 equivalent, re-verify before citing; https://editors.ca/wp-content/uploads/2024/04/PES-2024-Interior_V7-Approved-Version-April-15-2024.pdf

test: For every figure, ask what surrounding data was available but not shown. Flag any plot whose window is cropped to a favourable region, any time series that begins or ends where the trend suits the claim, and any comparison that omits a condition the reader would need in order to judge it.
cost: A figure cropped to a favourable window is locally accurate and globally false, and because nothing on the page indicates the omission the reader has no way to detect it.
suggestion: Widen the window to the full run, or show the full range in a small inset alongside the zoom, and state in the caption what the full range shows.
mechanism: Tufte names this as the sixth principle of graphical integrity and gives the diagnostic: the emaciated, data-thin design should always provoke suspicion, for graphics often lie by omission, leaving out data sufficient for comparisons, so graphics must not quote data out of context. The check is a question about what is absent, which is why it cannot be automated from the figure alone and has to be asked against the run logs.
counter_case: A deliberate crop is right when the omitted region is genuinely uninformative and its omission is stated, for instance dropping the first few hundred steps of a loss curve where the scale would flatten everything after. The requirement is disclosure, not completeness.
source: Edward R. Tufte, The Visual Display of Quantitative Information, 2nd ed., p. 74: "The emaciated, data-thin design should always provoke suspicion, for graphics often lie by omission, leaving out data sufficient for comparisons. The principle: Graphics must not quote data out of context." Listed as the sixth principle of graphical integrity at p. 77

test: Apply the erasure test: ask of each element what fraction of the graphic could be erased without losing data-information. Then measure two things in the rendered figure. Flag any grid whose lines are not visibly lighter than the data marks, and any figure whose axis strokes are heavier than the data they frame.
cost: A grid drawn at the weight of the data competes with it, so the reader's eye has to separate structure from signal on every glance, and a dark grid measurably degrades how accurately values are recovered.
suggestion: Set the grid to a light grey with a delicate line, or remove it where the reader is not looking values up, hold axis strokes to about half a point, and drop redundant encodings of the same value.
mechanism: Tufte defines the data-ink ratio operationally as one minus the proportion of a graphic that can be erased without loss of data-information, which turns it into a test rather than an aesthetic. He then makes the grid case conditional rather than absolute: when a graphic serves as a look-up table a grid may help in reading and interpolating, but even then the grids should be muted relative to the data, and a gray grid with a delicate line may promote more accurate data reconstruction than a dark grid. Nature Methods supplies numbers for the same judgements, that axis weight of 0.5 pt is sufficient and grid line transparency is most effective in the range of 15% to 45% depending on data density.
counter_case: A prominent grid is correct where the figure is explicitly a look-up table and interpolation is the reader's task, and Tufte allows this. Redundant encoding is also defensible where the figure must survive greyscale reproduction, in which case the redundancy is doing accessibility work rather than decoration.
source: Edward R. Tufte, The Visual Display of Quantitative Information, 2nd ed., p. 93 ("Data-ink ratio = ... 1.0 - proportion of a graphic that can be erased without loss of data-information"), p. 96 ("Erase non-data-ink, within reason"), p. 116 ("the grids should be muted relative to the data. A gray grid works well and, with a delicate line, may promote more accurate data reconstruction than a dark grid"). Numeric thresholds from Krzywinski, 'Points of view: Data density', Nature Methods 10(3):183 (2013): "Axis weight should be modest -- 0.5 pt is sufficient"; "Grid line transparency is most effective in the range of 15%-45%"

test: Count the configurations actually run: every hyperparameter setting swept, every prompt variant tried, every seed trained, every checkpoint evaluated, every metric computed. Compare that count against what the paper reports. Flag the paper if the number of configurations explored is not recoverable from the text.
cost: A reader who cannot tell how many things were tried cannot discount the reported result for selection, so a number chosen as the best of forty is read as if it were the only one computed.
suggestion: State the size of the search, name the criterion used to select what is reported, and put the full sweep in an appendix or a log file rather than only the winner.
mechanism: The American Statistical Association makes disclosure a condition of valid inference rather than a courtesy, stating that proper inference requires full reporting and transparency and that researchers should disclose the number of hypotheses explored during the study, all data collection decisions, all statistical analyses conducted, and all p-values computed. Their name for the failure is data dredging, significance chasing, selective inference and p-hacking. In machine learning the sweep is the hypothesis set, so an undisclosed grid search is the same failure under a different vocabulary.
counter_case: A very large automated sweep cannot be reported configuration by configuration, and nobody expects it to be. The requirement is the count and the selection rule, not the enumeration, so 'best of 240 configurations selected on validation accuracy' satisfies it.
source: Wasserstein & Lazar, "The ASA's Statement on p-Values: Context, Process, and Purpose", The American Statistician 70(2):129-133 (2016), DOI 10.1080/00031305.2016.1154108, Principle 4: "Proper inference requires full reporting and transparency... Researchers should disclose the number of hypotheses explored during the study, all data collection decisions, all statistical analyses conducted, and all p-values computed."

test: Find every claim of significance or improvement. Check that each is accompanied by the size of the effect in the units the reader cares about, and flag any claim that rests on a threshold crossing alone. Then check that no claim treats a threshold as a decision boundary, and flag phrases such as 'highly significant', 'approached significance' or 'trended toward significance'.
cost: A significance claim without an effect size tells the reader that something is probably not zero while withholding whether it is large enough to matter, and at large n almost nothing is exactly zero.
suggestion: Report the effect with its uncertainty and its practical interpretation alongside any test result, drop the threshold language, and say plainly when a difference is real but too small to act on.
mechanism: The ASA statement makes three of its six principles bear on this. Scientific conclusions should not be based only on whether a p-value passes a specific threshold, because practices that reduce inference to bright-line rules can lead to erroneous beliefs and poor decision making; a p-value does not measure the size of an effect, since any effect, no matter how tiny, can produce a small p-value if the sample size or measurement precision is high enough; and a p-value near 0.05 taken by itself offers only weak evidence against the null. JAMA independently bans the hedge vocabulary, instructing authors not to use inappropriate hedge terms such as marginal significance or trend toward significance for results that are not statistically significant.
counter_case: A bare significance statement is acceptable where the effect size is already given immediately adjacent and repeating it would be redundant, and in a table note where space forbids. Threshold language is also legitimate when the paper is explicitly discussing a pre-registered decision rule.
source: Wasserstein & Lazar, "The ASA's Statement on p-Values: Context, Process, and Purpose", The American Statistician 70(2):129-133 (2016), DOI 10.1080/00031305.2016.1154108, Principles 3, 5 and 6: "Scientific conclusions and business or policy decisions should not be based only on whether a p-value passes a specific threshold"; "Any effect, no matter how tiny, can produce a small p-value if the sample size or measurement precision is high enough"; "a p-value near 0.05 taken by itself offers only weak evidence against the null hypothesis." Hedge-term ban from JAMA Instructions for Authors, 'Reporting Standards and Data Presentation', https://jamanetwork.com/journals/jama/pages/instructions-for-authors

test: For every panel that carries a statistical comparison, check that three things appear either in that panel's caption or in the main text discussing it: the value of n, the p value, and the name of the specific test used. Flag any panel missing one of the three.
cost: A reader evaluating a figure has the figure in front of them and the methods section elsewhere, so a test named only in the methods leaves the panel uninterpretable at the moment it is being read.
suggestion: Put n, the test name and the p value into each caption that reports a comparison, keeping the general description of the statistical approach in the methods.
mechanism: Science states the requirement as a location rule rather than a content rule, that the values for N, P, and the specific statistical test performed for each experiment should be included in the appropriate figure caption or main text, and separately that authors should mention methods in the materials and methods section and then provide the individual test name in the figure legend for each experiment. Nature imposes the matching requirement for uncertainty, that all error bars and statistics must be defined in the figure legend. The rule is checkable because all three items are short tokens with recognisable forms.
counter_case: A figure carrying no statistical comparison needs none of this, and a multi-panel figure where every panel uses the same test and n may state them once in the shared caption rather than repeating them per panel.
source: Science, Instructions for Preparing an Initial Manuscript, and Editorial Policies, 'Statistical Analysis', https://www.science.org/content/page/science-information-authors: "The values for N, P, and the specific statistical test(s) performed for each experiment should be included in the appropriate figure caption or main text" and "provide the individual test name in the figure legend for each experiment". Nature Portfolio formatting guide, 'Figure legends': "All error bars and statistics must be defined in the figure legend."

test: For every figure containing images rather than plots, check four things: that no panel is assembled from non-adjacent or separately captured images without a visible boundary line, that any brightness or contrast adjustment was applied uniformly across the whole image and to controls, that no content-aware or generative editing tool was used, and that no panel is duplicated elsewhere unless the duplication is labelled.
cost: A spliced or selectively adjusted panel presents as a single observation something that is not one, and because the manipulation is invisible in the rendered figure it survives every review that does not compare against the originals.
suggestion: Keep the unprocessed originals, mark every splice with a visible line or gap, apply adjustments globally and record them in the caption, and run a duplicate check across all panels before submitting.
mechanism: Nature states the boundary conditions concretely. Images gathered at different times or from different locations should not be combined into a single image, and if juxtaposing is essential the borders should be clearly demarcated in the figure and described in the legend; processing such as changing brightness and contrast is appropriate only when applied equally across the entire image and to controls, and contrast should not be adjusted so that data disappear; the use of touch-up tools such as cloning and healing tools is unacceptable, and the figure guide extends this to a named list including Content-Aware Move, Clone Stamp and Generative Fill, stating that the use of any sort of generative AI in figures is not permitted.
counter_case: Composite panels are entirely normal and expected in machine learning, where a qualitative grid of model outputs is deliberately assembled from many separate generations. The requirement there is that the grid reads as a grid, with visible cell boundaries and a caption saying what was selected and how.
source: Nature Portfolio, 'Image integrity and standards', https://www.nature.com/nature-portfolio/editorial-policies/image-integrity, and the Nature research figure guide, 'Image integrity', https://research-figure-guide.nature.com/figures/image-integrity/: "Images gathered at different times or from different locations should not be combined into a single image... the borders should be clearly demarcated"; "Processing (such as changing brightness and contrast) is appropriate only when it is applied equally across the entire image and is applied equally to controls"; "The use of any sort of generative AI in figures is not permitted. This includes content-aware editing tools in Photoshop." Science, 'Modification of figures', imposes the equivalent line-between-parts and linear-adjustment rules

test: Render each figure at its final printed width and measure the smallest text in it. Flag any text below about 5 point, any text larger than the body text, and any line thinner than about 0.25 point. Then confirm the figure is a vector format with fonts embedded rather than rasterised or outlined.
cost: Text below about 5 point is unreadable in print and vanishes at reviewer zoom levels, so the figure's labels are lost even though the figure itself survived, and a rasterised figure cannot be rescued after acceptance.
suggestion: Set the figure's output size to the target column width and let the plotting library render text at 5 to 7 point rather than scaling a large figure down, then export as PDF or EPS with fonts embedded as Type 42.
mechanism: Both publishers state numeric floors. Nature specifies a minimum of 5 pt and a maximum of 7 pt for figure text with panel labels at 8 pt bold, line weights between 0.25 and 1 pt at final size because lines thinner than 0.25 pt may vanish in print, and it lists .jpeg, .tiff and .png among formats it does not accept for line art. Science gives about 7 points and not smaller than 5 points, with line widths at a 0.5 pt minimum. Nature also gives the operational fix for Python users directly, to set the matplotlib PDF font type to 42, which embeds fonts as TrueType rather than as Type 3.
counter_case: Photographic panels, screenshots and rendered images are legitimately raster and cannot be vector, so the format half of the rule applies to plots and line art only. The floors also yield to a venue that specifies its own, which should be recorded on the style sheet.
source: Nature Portfolio figure guide, 'Preparing figures -- our specifications': minimum 5 pt and maximum 7 pt text, panel labels 8 pt bold, line weights "between 0.25 and 1 pt at the final size (lines thinner than 0.25 pt may vanish in print)", and "If you are using Python please use the following setting: Matplotlib.rcParams['pdf.fonttype']=42". Science, Instructions for Preparing an Initial Manuscript, and Editorial Policies, 'Statistical Analysis', https://www.science.org/content/page/science-information-authors, 'Typefaces and labels': text "about 7 points (2.5 mm) high, and not smaller than 5 points", line widths 0.5 pt minimum

test: For every figure, check whether the numbers it plots are available to a reader in machine-readable form, as a supplementary CSV, TSV, JSON or XML file or in a public repository. Flag any figure whose values exist only as rendered marks, and flag any availability statement that points at a location the authors can silently alter.
cost: A figure whose numbers are not published cannot be re-plotted, re-analysed or checked, so every later use of the result depends on reading values off a picture, which the picture is not accurate enough to support.
suggestion: Export the tabulated data behind each figure to a CSV alongside the submission, with a short note on the columns, and deposit it somewhere immutable rather than in a personal cloud folder.
mechanism: Science requires this at figure granularity, stating that at the very least the tabulated data underlying the figures should be archived in a standard machine-readable format such as csv, tsv, json or xml, either as a supplementary data file or at a public repository, accompanied by a brief explanation of their structure and meaning. It closes the two obvious evasions in the same section, that post-publication embargoes are not permitted, nor are stipulations for readers to contact the authors, and that sites such as Dropbox which give authors discretion to alter or remove files are not acceptable. This is a Science requirement specifically; Nature has no per-figure source-data mandate, so cite it accordingly.
counter_case: Data that cannot be released for licensing, privacy or safety reasons is a legitimate exception, and the right response is a statement of what is withheld and why plus release of whatever aggregate the restriction permits, not silence.
