source: Science, Instructions for Preparing an Initial Manuscript, and Editorial Policies, 'Statistical Analysis', https://www.science.org/content/page/science-information-authors, Editorial Policies on data availability: "at the very least the tabulated data underlying the figures should be archived in a standard machine-readable format (e.g., csv, tsv, json, or xml), either as a supplementary data file or at a public repository"; "Post-publication embargoes are not permitted, nor are stipulations for readers to contact the authors"; "Sites such as Dropbox that give authors discretion to alter or remove files are not acceptable"

test: A load-bearing claim (the problem, the central idea, the expected outcome) first appears after the first page, or appears only in a section a non-assigned panel member would skip.
cost: Panel members who did not read the full application still score it, and measured panel discussion runs 19-29 minutes per application, so a claim that surfaces late is scored by people who never reached it.
suggestion: Move the problem, the central idea and the expected outcome onto the first page in that order, and repeat each once in the section where it is developed.
mechanism: Gallo measured actual panel-discussion duration across 65 AIBS panels and found 19-29 minutes per application, with no correlation between discussion time and score. NIAID states officially that review meetings cover dozens to hundreds of applications and that all panel members score every application including those they did not read. The combination means the reading budget for a non-assigned reviewer is roughly the opening page plus the abstract.
counter_case: Schemes with a mandated structured summary that is itself scored, or two-stage schemes where Step 1 reviewers read only a short form, already force this and re-front-loading the body wastes space.
source: Gallo SA, Carpenter AS, Glisson SR. Teleconference versus face-to-face scientific peer review of grant application. PLoS ONE 2013;8(8):e71693. PMCID PMC3740535. https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3740535/ ; NIAID, Know Your Audience. https://www.niaid.nih.gov/grants-contracts/know-your-audience

test: A paragraph adds a further strength or benefit while an obvious objection to the design, the feasibility or the evidence base is left unaddressed anywhere in the document.
cost: Reviewer ratings track the absence of weaknesses rather than the count of strengths, so an unaddressed objection is not offset by adding strengths.
suggestion: Stop adding strengths and spend the space naming the objection and disposing of it. Hunt defects before adding merit.
mechanism: Pier had 43 experienced reviewers evaluate 25 real NIH R01 applications in four simulated study sections and coded every strength and weakness in the written critiques. Strength counts had no relationship to the numeric rating, while weakness counts predicted the rating within a reviewer. The authors concluded that a positive rating reflected an absence of weaknesses rather than a large number of strengths.
counter_case: In a first-page pitch or a scored lay summary the reader has not yet formed an objection, so pre-emptive defect discussion there reads as diffidence. Defect-first applies to the body, not the opening.
source: Pier EL, Brauer M, Filut A, Kaatz A, Raclaw J, Nathan MJ, Ford CE, Carnes M. Low agreement among reviewers evaluating the same NIH grant applications. PNAS 2018;115(12):2952-2957. PMCID PMC5866547. https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.1714379115

test: A preliminary-results or prior-work paragraph presents data and its implication without naming any limitation of that data.
cost: The limitation becomes the reviewer's own discovery, and it is discovered weaknesses that move ratings.
suggestion: Follow each data set with one sentence naming its clearest limitation and one sentence giving the mitigation the proposed work applies.
mechanism: Because ratings track weaknesses rather than strengths, an unnamed limitation is a weakness waiting to be found by a reader who then owns it. Naming it converts a discovered defect into a demonstrated awareness. The sentence also supplies the reviewer with the wording they need for their own critique.
counter_case: Where the limitation is fatal rather than mitigable, naming it does not repair the application and the data should be omitted or regenerated instead.
source: Pier EL et al. Low agreement among reviewers evaluating the same NIH grant applications. PNAS 2018;115(12):2952-2957. PMCID PMC5866547. https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.1714379115

test: Promotional terms (novel, critical, key, unprecedented, transformative, robust) run at well under roughly one per four sentences across the whole application, or the density falls away sharply after the opening page.
cost: Promotional density is positively associated with the probability of being funded at two independent funders, so unusually flat prose sits on the wrong side of a real if narrow margin.
suggestion: Raise promotional density toward roughly one validated term per four sentences and hold it steady across sections rather than spending it all on page one.
mechanism: Qiu analysed 2,439 NIH and 9,096 Novo Nordisk Foundation applications including rejected ones, with PI and year fixed effects and a 139-term validated dictionary. Density predicted funding at both funders with overlapping odds ratios. The absolute margin is thin, so this is a rule about the low tail and not a licence for florid prose.
counter_case: Above roughly twice the corpus mean the same dictionary describes hype that reviewers penalise as unsupported, and Reif-Lehrer's rule that every claim must be documentable still binds. Density is a floor, not a target to maximise.
source: Qiu HS, Peng H, Fosse HB, Woodruff TK, Uzzi B. Use of Promotional Language in Grant Applications and Grant Success. JAMA Network Open 2024;7(12):e2448696. PMCID PMC11635532. https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11635532/

test: A specific weak epistemic feature carries a claim the evidence actually supports. Check the named features one at a time - the modals may, might and should, the status verbs indicate and seem, and the adverbs possible, probable and perhaps.
cost: Successful applications have moved steadily away from these individual features and toward certainty verbs, so they now read as out of register for the genre. No outcome evidence attaches to them.
suggestion: Where the evidence supports the claim, replace the specific weak feature with a certainty status verb (demonstrate, establish, reveal) or with will. Where it does not, keep the hedge and fix the claim instead.
mechanism: Millar tracked 140 stance features across 901,717 NIH abstracts from 1985 to 2020 and found a consistent decline in weak possibility features and a rise in features conveying certainty, importance and empiricism. Wang replicated the direction on 12,187 Swedish Research Council abstracts. Millar's own conclusion is that these trends must be read feature by feature, because metadiscoursal categories average opposing movements into noise.
counter_case: Millar's explicit warning is that trends are better analysed at the level of individual features than at the level of metadiscoursal categories, so a rule keyed to a whole LIWC tentative block will fire on features that moved the other way. Wang also found a hard-versus-soft-science split, which matters across ERC panels.
source: Millar N, Mathis B, Batalo B, Budgell B. Trends in the Expression of Epistemic Stance in NIH Research Funding Applications 1985-2020. Applied Linguistics 2024;45(4):658-675. doi:10.1093/applin/amad050 ; Wang Y. Stance in successful grant application abstracts. JEAP 2026;81:101666

test: The case for significance or novelty rests on a hype adjective (novel, critical, key, sustainable, actionable, scalable) doing the work in place of a quantity, a comparison or a named consequence.
cost: These specific adjectives have inflated so far in the corpus that they no longer distinguish one application from another, so the sentence spends space without differentiating.
suggestion: Keep the adjective if you want the density, but put a number, a named comparator or a stated consequence in the same sentence so the claim carries information the adjective cannot.
mechanism: Millar measured 130 of 139 hype adjectives rising across 901,717 NIH abstracts, by 7,690 words per million in aggregate. Vinkers found the same inflation in the wider literature with negative controls that hold flat, so the rise is specific to promotional language rather than to writing generally. When a term is near-universal it stops carrying signal even while its presence still correlates with funding at the density level.
counter_case: Qiu shows density itself is associated with funding, so stripping these adjectives out to reduce inflation works against a measured association. Add information beside the adjective rather than deleting the adjective.
source: Millar N, Batalo B, Budgell B. Trends in the Use of Promotional Language (Hype) in Abstracts of Successful NIH Grant Applications 1985-2020. JAMA Network Open 2022;5(8):e2228676. PMCID PMC9412227 ; Vinkers CH, Tijdink JK, Otte WM. BMJ 2015;351:h6467. PMCID PMC4677695

test: The application describes its own team or approach using the praise vocabulary that appears in favourable reviewer critiques - standout adjectives, agentic words, ability words - on the assumption that mirroring reviewer language earns the score.
cost: There is no evidence in either direction for applicant use of these words. The measured association is between reviewer wording and reviewer scoring, and applying it to your own prose is a category error.
suggestion: Drop the mirroring. Spend the space on the two applicant-side signals that have been measured, which are promotional density and an absence of unaddressed weaknesses.
mechanism: Kaatz coded 454 critiques and found funded applications drew significantly more ability, agentic, standout and positive-evaluation words and fewer negative-evaluation words. The words are the reviewer's, written after the judgement. Achievement and research vocabulary carried no signal at all, and the word-to-score correlations reached significance only in the experienced-female-PI subsample with every male-subsample correlation null.
source: Kaatz A, Magua W, Zimmerman DR, Carnes M. A quantitative linguistic analysis of NIH R01 application critiques from investigators at one institution. Academic Medicine 2015;90(1):69-75. PMCID PMC4280285. https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4280285/

test: A specialised term or acronym appears in the title, the abstract, the lay summary or the first page, where the reader is least likely to share the specialism.
cost: Jargon proportion in the title and abstract is negatively associated with citations, and in lay-reader experiments jargon impairs processing and raises resistance to persuasion. Costs are measured for lay and general readers, not for expert panellists.
suggestion: Restrict specialised terms to the sections where they are unavoidable. Rewrite the title, the abstract and the first page in terms a reader outside the specialism can process, and let density rise in the methods.
mechanism: Martinez and Mammola analysed 21,486 articles and found a significant negative relationship between the proportion of jargon in the title and abstract and citation count, concluding that scientists should restrict jargon to sections where its use is unavoidable. The rule is positional rather than global, which is what distinguishes it from a flat instruction to reduce jargon. The reader profile changes by section, so the constraint should too.
counter_case: Vincent-Lamarre found the opposite for expert gatekeepers - across 12,364 AI conference submissions, higher jargon ratios were associated with higher acceptance and accepted papers scored lower on Flesch Reading Ease. Markowitz found NSF abstracts with fewer common words drew larger awards. Where the reader is an assigned specialist, the penalty may reverse.
source: Martinez A, Mammola S. Specialized terminology reduces the number of citations of scientific papers. Proc R Soc B 2021;288(1948):20202581. PMID 33823673. https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33823673/

test: An acronym is coined for a term used fewer than about ten times in the document, or for a term that is not already standard in the target readership.
cost: Reuse of acronyms has fallen while coinage has risen, so a locally coined acronym is very unlikely to be one a reader already holds. The reader carries a lookup cost with no compression benefit.
suggestion: Spell the term out every time unless it appears roughly ten or more times, or unless it is already standard for the panel you are writing to.
mechanism: Barnett and Doubleday analysed 24,873,372 titles and 18,249,091 abstracts from 1950 to 2019 and recovered 1,112,345 unique acronyms. Just over 2,000 of them, 0.2%, were used regularly, while 79% appeared fewer than ten times. Acronym density in abstracts rose from 0.4 to 4.1 per 100 words while reuse declined, which is the signature of coinage outrunning shared vocabulary.
counter_case: Strict page or character limits can make a long term genuinely unaffordable in repetition, and a few acronyms (DNA, MRI, PCR) are more legible than their expansions. The threshold is a heuristic on a continuum, not a boundary.
source: Barnett A, Doubleday Z. Meta-Research: The growth of acronyms in the scientific literature. eLife 2020;9:e60080. PMCID PMC7556863. https://elifesciences.org/articles/60080

test: An acronym or specialised term appears without its expansion at first use in the section where it first appears.
cost: The reader must either hold an unresolved token or search backwards, and in experiments the fluency cost of jargon persists even when definitions are supplied.
suggestion: Expand at first use in every major section, not once per document.
mechanism: Shulman found that the presence of jargon disrupts fluent processing of scientific information even when definitions for the jargon terms are provided. A definition therefore reduces but does not remove the cost, which means the placement of the expansion matters as much as its existence. Reviewers rarely read an application start to finish in one sitting, so per-section expansion matches the actual reading pattern.
source: Shulman HC, Dixon GN, Bullock OM, Colon Amill D. The Effects of Jargon on Processing Fluency, Self-Perceptions, and Scientific Engagement. Journal of Language and Social Psychology 2020;39(5-6):579-597. doi:10.1177/0261927X20902177

test: A sentence in the abstract or lay summary is long or multiply embedded, even though its individual words are ordinary.
cost: In the one grant genre where readability has been measured over time, structural complexity worsened while lexical difficulty stayed flat, so structure is where the damage accumulates.
suggestion: Split the sentence at its embedding boundaries and keep no more than one or two subordinate clauses. Do not attack the vocabulary first.
mechanism: Huang analysed lay summaries of Cancer Research Fund grant proposals from 2006 to 2024 and found readability measures related to structural complexity showing a significant upward trend while lexical difficulty remained stable. Jargon density averaged 8.0% per text, above the recommended threshold for a general readership, in summaries that all succeeded. Plaven-Sigray found the same structural signature in the wider literature, with sentence length rising steadily after 1960.
counter_case: Uniformly short sentences read as choppy and lose the connective work that transitions and subordination do, and Markowitz found longer NSF abstracts drew larger awards. Split for embedding depth, not for word count.
source: Huang Y, Li K, Li D. Writing for non-specialists? Investigating readability and jargon use in successful lay summaries of CRF grant proposals 2006-2024. Scientometrics 2025;130(11):6305-6321. doi:10.1007/s11192-025-05442-8

test: An abstract or first page scores below college-graduate readability, or general scientific jargon has crept into sentences whose function is to orient rather than to specify.
cost: More than a fifth of scientific abstracts now sit beyond college-graduate English, so the drift is the default and a document that has not been checked has probably followed it.
suggestion: Measure the abstract once and treat a Flesch Reading Ease near or below zero as a signal to reduce general scientific jargon and sentence length, in that order.
mechanism: Plaven-Sigray analysed 709,577 abstracts from 1881 to 2015 and found Flesch Reading Ease falling with r=-0.93 and New Dale-Chall difficulty rising with r=+0.93. The share of abstracts below Flesch Reading Ease zero rose from 14% in 1960 to 22% in 2015. General scientific jargon rose at r=0.96, which the authors identify as the main driver alongside sentence length.
counter_case: Readability formulas count syllables and clause length and cannot tell a necessary technical term from an avoidable one, so a score is a trigger to look rather than a target to optimise. No study links a readability score to funding outcome.
source: Plaven-Sigray P, Matheson GJ, Schiffler BC, Thompson WH. The readability of scientific texts is decreasing over time. eLife 2017;6:e27725. https://elifesciences.org/articles/27725

test: A sentence opens with information the reader has not met yet, separates its subject from its verb with intervening material, or buries the point it wants emphasised in the middle rather than at the end.
cost: The reader spends interpretive effort on structure instead of substance and may take the emphasis the structure implies rather than the one intended.
suggestion: Put known material in the topic position, follow the subject with its verb quickly, articulate the action in the verb, and place the new point in the stress position at the end of the sentence.
mechanism: Gopen and Swan derive seven structural principles from reader-expectation theory, including following a grammatical subject as soon as possible with its verb, placing old information in the topic position for linkage backward, and placing the new information you want emphasised in the stress position. Their claim is that structure carries interpretive cues independently of content. They state explicitly that these should not be treated as rules and that any expectation can be violated to good effect.
counter_case: The authors' own hedge is that no fixed algorithm for good writing exists because too many reader expectations operate at once and any one of them can be violated productively. A sentence that deliberately front-loads the new point for surprise is not broken.
source: Gopen GD, Swan JA. The Science of Scientific Writing. American Scientist 1990;78:550-558. https://www.usenix.org/sites/default/files/gopen_and_swan_science_of_scientific_writing.pdf

test: A passage is written in the dense traditional register when a more direct and accessible version would carry the same content.
cost: Readers report lower readability and lower confidence and answer fewer comprehension questions correctly, with small but measured effects.
suggestion: Rewrite toward the accessible end of the register, and expect a real but modest gain rather than a transformation.
mechanism: Ryba built abstracts of three real papers at four levels of difficulty from traditional to engaging and gave them to 170 readers, measuring reported readability, confidence and comprehension. All three improved with accessibility after accounting for topic and reader. The effects are small per unit, and style spanned roughly five units across the full range.
counter_case: Readers were third-year undergraduates rather than expert panellists, and the same accessibility push runs against Markowitz's finding that NSF abstracts with fewer common words drew larger awards. Effect sizes are small enough that accessibility should not be traded against accuracy.
source: Ryba R, Doubleday ZA, Dry MJ, Semmler C, Connell SD. Better Writing in Scientific Publications Builds Reader Confidence and Understanding. Frontiers in Psychology 2021;12:714321. https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/psychology/articles/10.3389/fpsyg.2021.714321/full

test: A summary or abstract states the territory, the gap, the aims and the methods but never states what results the work will produce or why the outcome matters.
cost: Unsuccessful summaries in the one funded-versus-unfunded comparison available omitted expected research outcomes far more often than successful ones.
suggestion: Add an explicit statement of the expected research outcomes, and a separate statement of why those outcomes matter, before the methods.
mechanism: Charles and Whiteside coded 27 funded and 75 unfunded proposal summaries against a ten-step move framework. Unsuccessful summaries underused the move Indicating the value of the research, specifically omitting the steps Importance and Research Outcomes. Territory, Niche, Proposed Research and Methods appeared at effectively identical rates in both groups, so the discriminating content is narrow and specific.
counter_case: Connor found Benefits, Importance Claim and Competence Claim to be optional moves in EU proposals rather than obligatory, so scheme conventions differ. Where a separate impact section is mandated and scored, duplicating outcomes in the summary may read as redundant.
source: Charles M, Whiteside K. Seeking research funding in a peripheral context - a learner corpus genre study of grant proposal summaries. JEAP 2024;71:101431. CC-BY. https://centaur.reading.ac.uk/121806/1/1-s2.0-S1475158524000997-main.pdf

test: An abstract has been cut to well under the scheme's allowance, or its factual claims have been softened, on the assumption that brevity and caution read as rigour.
cost: Among funded NSF proposals, longer abstracts with fewer common words and more verbal certainty were associated with larger awards, at roughly 372 dollars per additional word.
suggestion: Use the allowance. Where a claim is supported, state it with verbal certainty rather than trimming or hedging it to look modest.
mechanism: Markowitz analysed over 7.4 million words across 19,569 NSF proposals and found three directions associated with award amount - greater length, fewer common words, and more verbal certainty. He frames the result as contradicting the NSF's own call to communicate science plainly, which makes it a norm inconsistency rather than an endorsement of dense prose. The dollar figure is per one-word increase.
counter_case: The outcome is award amount among already funded proposals, so it cannot support any claim about being funded rather than rejected. The fewer-common-words direction also runs directly against every jargon-penalty study, so it must not be generalised into a licence for jargon.
source: Markowitz DM. What Words Are Worth - National Science Foundation Grant Abstracts Indicate Award Funding. Journal of Language and Social Psychology 2019;38(3):264-282. doi:10.1177/0261927X18824859. https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1177/0261927X18824859

test: A load-bearing claim is assembled across separated sections and depends on the panel pooling its readings to reconstruct it.
cost: Reviewer agreement on the same applications is near zero, so a claim that only survives aggregation may not survive any individual reading.
suggestion: Make each load-bearing claim complete and self-sufficient at its own location, and restate rather than cross-reference where the claim carries weight.
mechanism: Pier measured an intraclass correlation of 0 for ratings of the same applications, noting that although each application was evaluated by more than three reviewers the data had the same structure as if 83 different applications had been used. Fogelholm found kappa of 0.23 for panel scores after discussion, no better than averaging two independent reviewers. Graves estimated that 59% of 620 funded grants were sometimes not funded once random variability was taken into account.
counter_case: Restating a claim at every location inflates length against a hard page limit, and Russell and Morrison warn that redundancy between adjacent sections puts reviewers off. Restate where the claim is load-bearing, cross-reference elsewhere.
source: Pier EL et al. PNAS 2018;115(12):2952-2957. PMCID PMC5866547 ; Fogelholm M et al. J Clin Epidemiol 2012;65(1):47-52 ; Graves N, Barnett AG, Clarke P. BMJ 2011;343:d4797. https://www.bmj.com/content/343/bmj.d4797

test: A citation is attached to a specific factual claim and has not been checked against the cited source for that claim, or a text citation and its bibliography entry disagree on any detail.
cost: Measured quotation error rates in published medical articles run from 14.5% to 25.4%, and roughly two thirds of content errors are major, meaning the source fails to substantiate, is unrelated to, or contradicts the claim.
suggestion: Open every source attached to a load-bearing claim and confirm it states that claim. Reconcile years and details between text and bibliography.
mechanism: Jergas and Baethge ran a systematic review and meta-analysis of 28 studies and estimated total quotation errors at 25.4%, with major errors at 11.9%. Mogull recalculated against quotations examined rather than references selected and arrived at 14.5%, of which 64.8% were major. Both figures mean a substantial minority of citations do not support the sentence they are attached to, and the error is invisible to any check short of reading the source.
counter_case: Full verification does not scale to a hundred references under deadline. Triage to the citations that carry the argument, since Porter's interviewed reviewers reported checking references specifically in areas where they lacked expertise.
source: Jergas H, Baethge C. Quotation accuracy in medical journal articles - a systematic review and meta-analysis. PeerJ 2015;3:e1364. PMCID PMC4627914. https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4627914/ ; Mogull SA. PLoS ONE 2017;12(9):e0184727. https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0184727

test: Compare every publication entry in the CV and Track Record against the published record. Check that all authors appear in the published order and that co-first authorship, shared or multiple corresponding authorship is marked where it applies. Flag reordered, truncated or unmarked entries.
cost: ERC states applicants are expected to report outputs correctly with all authors in published order and joint authorships properly indicated. A panel member who spots a reordered author list stops assessing the science and starts assessing the applicant.
suggestion: Regenerate the list from the publisher record, keep the published order, and mark shared roles with an explicit legend rather than a symbol the reader must decode.
mechanism: The PI assessment is the half of ERC's criterion that turns on the record rather than the plan, so entries in it are read as testimony. Reordering authors to move yourself forward is the one editing move a reviewer can catch with a search engine and cannot unsee. Once one entry is wrong the reviewer discounts the rest of the list rather than checking it.
counter_case: Where a field's convention is alphabetical authorship, saying so in one clause is necessary context and is not a deviation from the published order.
source: ERC (European Research Council), Information for Applicants to the Starting and Consolidator Grant Calls, Version 11.0 (22 July 2026), section 2.2 Part B1, Curriculum Vitae and Track Record ('Applicants are expected to report their publications, patents and any other research outputs correctly, including all authors in the same order as published. Joint authorships (e.g. co-first author, multiple corresponding author) must also be properly indicated.'). URLs: ERC Information for Applicants V11.0 — https://ec.europa.eu/info/funding-tenders/opportunities/docs/2021-2027/horizon/guidance/information-for-applicants_he-erc-stg-cog_en.pdf

test: Diff the abstract in the Part B1 cover page against the abstract in the online submission form, character by character. Flag any difference.
cost: ERC requires the B1 abstract to be a copy-paste of the submission-form abstract, and admissibility requires the proposal be complete and readable. A divergence means the panel's reading copy and the administrative record state different projects.
suggestion: Paste once, in one direction, as the last edit before submission, and re-diff after any late change to either copy.
mechanism: The two abstracts are edited at different times by different tools, so they drift silently and nothing in the portal complains. A reviewer who notices a mismatch cannot tell which version is the project. The check costs one command and removes a class of finding entirely.
counter_case: A proposal submitted in an EU language other than English must additionally carry an English translation of the abstract, which is a required addition rather than a divergence.
source: ERC (European Research Council), Information for Applicants to the Starting and Consolidator Grant Calls, Version 11.0 (22 July 2026), section 2.2 Part B1 of the application form ('The abstract should be half a page and must be a copy/paste of the abstract from the submission form'). URLs: ERC Information for Applicants V11.0 — https://ec.europa.eu/info/funding-tenders/opportunities/docs/2021-2027/horizon/guidance/information-for-applicants_he-erc-stg-cog_en.pdf

test: Extract every number, staff month, equipment item and duration named in the scientific proposal's methodology and work plan, and match each against the dedicated Resources and Budget section. Flag any quantity that appears in one and not the other, or differs between them.
cost: ERC states Part II cannot deviate from the Resources section when describing the methodology and work plan. A mismatch is read as one of the two being untrue, and the Step-2 element asks whether timescales and resources are adequate and properly justified.
suggestion: Keep one table as the source and generate the prose numbers from it, then re-run the match after any late budget change.
mechanism: The prose and the budget are written weeks apart and usually by different people, so numbers drift. The Step-2 reviewer reads them together and the arithmetic is the easiest check available. Because the funder has stated the two must agree, the mismatch is a rule violation rather than a matter of judgement.
counter_case: A range in the prose against a point estimate in the budget is not a deviation when the prose says which end the budget assumes. State it rather than deleting the range.
source: ERC (European Research Council), Information for Applicants to the Starting and Consolidator Grant Calls, Version 11.0 (22 July 2026), section 2.2 Part B2 ('Part II of the Scientific Proposal cannot deviate from the Resources section when describing the methodology, workplan etc.'); ERC (European Research Council), ERC Work Programme 2027 (Commission Decision C(2026)4907), section 1.6.5 Step 2 ('To what extent are the timescales and resources adequate and properly justified?'). URLs: ERC Information for Applicants V11.0 — https://ec.europa.eu/info/funding-tenders/opportunities/docs/2021-2027/horizon/guidance/information-for-applicants_he-erc-stg-cog_en.pdf; ERC Work Programme 2027 — https://ec.europa.eu/info/funding-tenders/opportunities/docs/2021-2027/horizon/wp-call/2027/wp_horizon-erc-2027_en.pdf

test: For each objective, find the sentence that says why the chosen approach can reach it. Flag any objective whose approach text is only an inventory of methods, techniques, equipment or datasets.
cost: ERC's Step 1 element asks whether the proposed approach is scientifically convincing, and the Information for Applicants says the approach as laid out should be scientifically convincing. An inventory answers what will be used, which is a different question, and scores on the question it answers.
suggestion: Add the clause that links the method to the objective's difficulty, naming what about the method defeats the thing that made the objective hard.
mechanism: Listing methods is how researchers talk to peers who already know why those methods bite. A generalist reads the list as competence but cannot convert it into confidence, because the inference from method to result is the specialist knowledge they lack. One sentence supplies the inference and moves the paragraph from qualified to convincing.
counter_case: Where the approach is standard and the difficulty sits elsewhere, one sentence saying that the method is routine and naming the real obstacle is the argument. The fault is silence. Brevity is fine.
source: ERC (European Research Council), ERC Work Programme 2027 (Commission Decision C(2026)4907), section 1.6.5 Evaluation Elements, Step 1 ('is the proposed approach scientifically convincing?'); ERC (European Research Council), Information for Applicants to the Starting and Consolidator Grant Calls, Version 11.0 (22 July 2026), section 2.2 Part I ('the overall scientific approach or research strategy as laid out in the proposal should be scientifically convincing'). URLs: ERC Work Programme 2027 — https://ec.europa.eu/info/funding-tenders/opportunities/docs/2021-2027/horizon/wp-call/2027/wp_horizon-erc-2027_en.pdf; ERC Information for Applicants V11.0 — https://ec.europa.eu/info/funding-tenders/opportunities/docs/2021-2027/horizon/guidance/information-for-applicants_he-erc-stg-cog_en.pdf

test: Find every priority marker: first, first-ever, novel, unprecedented, paradigm, only, no one has, for the first time. Check that the same sentence or the next names the prior work being exceeded and the respect in which it is exceeded. Flag markers with neither.
cost: ERC requires each proposal be reviewed by at least three peer reviewers and lets the panel commission further specialist reviews, and every individual comment is reproduced in the Evaluation Report the applicant receives. An overreaching priority claim is checked by someone who knows the literature, and the correction arrives in writing.
suggestion: Name the closest prior attempt and the specific respect in which it falls short, or drop the priority marker and state the increment.
mechanism: Priority claims are cheap to write and expensive to defend, and they are the one kind of claim a reviewer can falsify from memory. A generalist panel member will not catch it, but the remote specialist reviewer the panel commissions exists precisely to catch it. Once one priority claim is shown false the reviewer treats the rest of the ambition as inflated.
counter_case: A genuinely first result should say so, with the closest attempt named and the reason it does not count. The fault is the unanchored marker. The claim of priority is allowed.
source: ERC (European Research Council), Guide for Peer Reviewers to the ERC Starting and Consolidator Grant Calls, Version 6.0 (30 September 2025, 2026 calls), section 2.2 How to Evaluate a Proposal ('each proposal shall be reviewed by at least three peer reviewers'; 'All the individual reviewers' comments are included in the Evaluation Report'); ERC (European Research Council), ERC Work Programme 2027 (Commission Decision C(2026)4907), section 1.6.5 (ambition). URLs: ERC Guide for Peer Reviewers V6.0 — https://ec.europa.eu/info/funding-tenders/opportunities/docs/2021-2027/experts/guide-for-peer-reviewers_he-erc-stg-cog_en.pdf; ERC Work Programme 2027 — https://ec.europa.eu/info/funding-tenders/opportunities/docs/2021-2027/horizon/wp-call/2027/wp_horizon-erc-2027_en.pdf

test: Locate the sentence stating why the research question matters. Check whether it names a consequence outside the project, meaning what becomes possible or what is currently blocked. Flag sentences that carry only an evaluative adjective: crucial, key, fundamental, pressing, important, timely.
cost: The first evaluation question at both ERC steps is the extent to which the research addresses important scientific questions. An adjective gives a generalist nothing to score, so the element is scored on whatever the reviewer can supply from their own field.
suggestion: Replace the adjective with the blocked consequence, naming who is blocked and what they cannot currently do.
mechanism: Importance adjectives are the applicant's own assessment of the thing the reviewer is being paid to assess, so they are read as filler at best. A generalist has no way to calibrate importance inside your subfield and needs the consequence stated in terms they share. Naming what is blocked also makes the claim falsifiable, which is what lets a reviewer credit it.
counter_case: Where the question is a famous standing problem, one clause citing it is enough and elaboration wastes strictly-applied page budget.
source: ERC (European Research Council), ERC Work Programme 2027 (Commission Decision C(2026)4907), section 1.6.5 Evaluation Elements; ERC (European Research Council), Guide for Peer Reviewers to the ERC Starting and Consolidator Grant Calls, Version 6.0 (30 September 2025, 2026 calls), Annex 1 Evaluation Form ('To what extent does the research address important scientific questions?'). URLs: ERC Work Programme 2027 — https://ec.europa.eu/info/funding-tenders/opportunities/docs/2021-2027/horizon/wp-call/2027/wp_horizon-erc-2027_en.pdf; ERC Guide for Peer Reviewers V6.0 — https://ec.europa.eu/info/funding-tenders/opportunities/docs/2021-2027/experts/guide-for-peer-reviewers_he-erc-stg-cog_en.pdf

test: Scan narrative prose for clipped informal forms: lab, math, temp, prep, config, stats, spec, demo, info. Flag each occurrence outside a quoted string or a proper name.
cost: NSF's proposal-writing guide says in general avoid abbreviations, naming laboratory over lab and mathematics over math. The register mismatch is the kind of finding a reviewer records as carelessness under an otherwise unrelated criterion.
suggestion: Expand each clipping to the full word, and keep only clippings that are the field's standard term of art.
mechanism: Clippings arrive from speech and from internal documents, and they cluster in the sections written last. A reviewer reading ten proposals uses register as a proxy for how much care the applicant took, because register is visible without expertise. The lexicon is closed, so a script settles it.
counter_case: A clipped form that is the field's standard name, such as RNA-seq, qPCR or e-print, is the correct term, and expanding it signals the writer is outside the field.
source: NSF, A Guide for Proposal Writing (NSF 04-016), Step 3, Little Things That Can Make a Difference ('In general avoid abbreviations. For example, use laboratory, not lab and mathematics, not math.'). URLs: NSF 04-016 — https://nsf-gov-resources.nsf.gov/pubs/2004/nsf04016/nsf04016.pdf?VersionId=_pFLVguJ41PzvWwyThPBaqnSFad20hao

test: Check that the project acronym is byte-identical on the cover page, in every page header, in the abstract, and at every mention in the body, and that its length is within the funder's maximum (20 characters at ERC). Flag any variant in case, hyphenation or spacing.
cost: ERC requires each proposal page to carry the PI's last name, the acronym and the part, and the acronym is the handle the panel and the Lead Reviewer use to introduce and discuss the proposal across two steps. A variant costs recognition at the moment your proposal is being argued for.
suggestion: Bind the acronym to a single macro or find-and-replace target, then grep for near-variants before submission.
mechanism: Each proposal is assigned to a Lead Reviewer who introduces it to the panel, so most of the panel meets your project as a name spoken once. A name that appears in three spellings is harder to hold and harder to search for in the evaluation system. This is the cheapest consistency check in the document and a script decides it.
counter_case: A funder-mandated prefix or suffix is not a variant: where a call requires the acronym to appear as part of a longer file name or header string, the surrounding text differs while the acronym itself stays identical.
source: ERC (European Research Council), Information for Applicants to the Starting and Consolidator Grant Calls, Version 11.0 (22 July 2026), section 2.2 layout ('Each proposal page shall carry a header presenting the Principal Investigator's last name, the acronym of the proposal, and the reference to the respective proposal section'); ERC (European Research Council), Guide for Peer Reviewers to the ERC Starting and Consolidator Grant Calls, Version 6.0 (30 September 2025, 2026 calls), section 1.3 ('Each proposal is assigned to a Lead Reviewer ... who introduces the proposal to the panel for discussion'). URLs: ERC Information for Applicants V11.0 — https://ec.europa.eu/info/funding-tenders/opportunities/docs/2021-2027/horizon/guidance/information-for-applicants_he-erc-stg-cog_en.pdf; ERC Guide for Peer Reviewers V6.0 — https://ec.europa.eu/info/funding-tenders/opportunities/docs/2021-2027/experts/guide-for-peer-reviewers_he-erc-stg-cog_en.pdf

test: Extract the ordered list of objective identifiers and their names from Part I and from Part II. Flag any identifier present in one and absent in the other, any renaming of the same objective, and any change of order.
cost: At Step 2 the panel and the external reviewers review Parts I and II together, and the Step-2 element asks whether the methodology and working arrangements are appropriate to achieve the goals. A drifted label makes the mapping from method to goal the reviewer's work.
suggestion: Keep one canonical list of objective identifiers and names, and generate both parts' headings from it.
mechanism: Part I and Part II are usually drafted separately and to different page limits, so objectives get merged, split and renamed on one side only. The Step-2 reviewer holds both documents and is explicitly asked whether the methods reach the goals, which requires a mapping the labels are supposed to supply. When the labels disagree the reviewer either builds the mapping or scores the element down.
counter_case: If a work package legitimately splits one objective into two, say so in one clause at the split. The fault is an unexplained mismatch. A many-to-one mapping is fine.
source: ERC (European Research Council), Information for Applicants to the Starting and Consolidator Grant Calls, Version 11.0 (22 July 2026), section 2.2 Part B2 ('The panel and the external reviewers will review Parts I and II together for the Step 2 evaluation.'); ERC (European Research Council), ERC Work Programme 2027 (Commission Decision C(2026)4907), section 1.6.5 Step 2. URLs: ERC Information for Applicants V11.0 — https://ec.europa.eu/info/funding-tenders/opportunities/docs/2021-2027/horizon/guidance/information-for-applicants_he-erc-stg-cog_en.pdf; ERC Work Programme 2027 — https://ec.europa.eu/info/funding-tenders/opportunities/docs/2021-2027/horizon/wp-call/2027/wp_horizon-erc-2027_en.pdf

test: Count words per sentence across the narrative. Flag every sentence over 20 words, and report the share of the document above that line.
cost: NIH states sentences of 20 words or less are easier to read, and gives the reason: reviewers must read quite a few applications in full detail. The average R01 discussion is about 15 minutes, so a sentence that needs re-reading is a sentence that does not get re-read.
suggestion: Split at the first coordinating conjunction or relative pronoun, and put the claim in the first half so the reader has it before the qualifications.
mechanism: A reviewer reading a stack of applications after their day job parses each sentence once. Past about twenty words the reader has to hold too many unresolved dependencies, and the failure mode is silent. They carry on with a partial reading rather than stopping. In a panel where most members only skim, a long sentence in the Aims or Significance is a sentence nobody scores.
counter_case: A sentence enumerating a matched set, such as four conditions in parallel, reads longer than twenty words and is still one parse. The count flags it and a human clears it.
source: NIH, General Grant Writing Tips (grants.nih.gov/grants-process/write-application/general-grant-writing-tips), Tip 3: Write in Clear, Concise Language ('Keep sentences as clear, simple, and short as possible. Sentences of 20 words or less are easier to read.'); NIH, Study Section Chair's Discussion Cheat Sheet (release date 1 July 2025), Step 9 ('The average discussion for an R01 application should be about 15 minutes.'). URLs: NIH General Grant Writing Tips — https://grants.nih.gov/grants-process/write-application/general-grant-writing-tips; NIH study section chair cheat sheet — https://grants.nih.gov/sites/default/files/Study-Section-Cheat-Sheet.pdf

test: For each aim or objective, count sentences and check the main verb of the first one. Flag aims longer than three sentences, and aims whose verb is not an outcome verb such as identify, define, quantify, establish, determine, measure.
cost: NIAID instructs applicants to describe each aim in one to three sentences and to state plans using strong verbs like identify, define, quantify, establish, determine. NIH advises against merely describing experiments as Specific Aims, and Factor 1 sets the ceiling on the overall impact score.
suggestion: Rewrite each aim as one outcome verb plus its object, then add at most two sentences of method, and move the rest into the Approach.
mechanism: Aims are the passage the whole panel skims while the assigned reviewers talk, so their first verb is doing most of the work. A verb like investigate or explore names an activity that any amount of effort discharges, which gives the skimming reader nothing to score. An outcome verb makes the aim a claim about the world that can be checked against the methods below it.
counter_case: An aim in an exploratory mechanism whose point is that the outcome is not predictable should say so and name what will be learned either way. NIH advises planning aims where a null result still contributes.
source: NIAID (NIH), Write Your Research Plan, Detail Your Aims ('State your plans using strong verbs like identify, define, quantify, establish, determine.'; 'Describe each aim in one to three sentences.'); NIH, Advice on Application Sections, Specific Aims ('we advise against merely describing your experiments as Specific Aims'); NIH, Simplified Review Framework: Scoring Guidance (release date March 14, 2025), Overall Impact Guidance. URLs: NIAID Write Your Research Plan — https://www.niaid.nih.gov/grants-contracts/write-research-plan; NIH advice on application sections — https://grants.nih.gov/grants-process/write-application/advice-on-application-sections; NIH SRF scoring guidance — https://grants.nih.gov/sites/default/files/Simplified-Review-Scoring-Guidance.pdf

test: Run a spelling and grammar pass over the final rendered PDF rather than the source, and count findings. Treat any non-zero count as a defect.
cost: NIH tells applicants to have zero tolerance for typographical errors, misspellings, grammatical mistakes or messy formatting, and states the consequence directly. If the application is sloppy or disorganized, reviewers may think your research could be conducted in the same manner.
suggestion: Proofread the rendered PDF, read the narrative aloud once to catch dropped and duplicated words, and re-run after the final reformat.
mechanism: Typos concentrate in the passages edited last, which are usually the aims and the closing paragraphs, and they survive because the source and the render differ. A reviewer with no way to audit your laboratory practice uses the artefact in front of them as the sample. The inference is unfair and it is also stated in NIH's own guidance, which makes it a predictable cost rather than a risk.
counter_case: A spell checker will flag domain terms and non-English names that are correct. The rule is zero unresolved findings, not zero flags.
source: NIH, General Grant Writing Tips (grants.nih.gov/grants-process/write-application/general-grant-writing-tips), Tip 5: Edit Yourself ('Have zero tolerance for typographical errors, misspellings, grammatical mistakes, or messy formatting. If the application is sloppy or disorganized, reviewers may think your research could be conducted in the same manner.'). URLs: NIH General Grant Writing Tips — https://grants.nih.gov/grants-process/write-application/general-grant-writing-tips

test: Read only the first sentence of every paragraph, in order. Flag the document if that sequence does not state the argument. Flag individual paragraphs whose first sentence carries background while the point arrives at the end.
cost: NIH states a clear topic sentence for each paragraph with one main point is key for readability, and that many reviewers will be scanning the application as they listen to the discussion. The score comes from the whole panel, including the members who only read your first sentences.
suggestion: Move the paragraph's claim to its first sentence and let the evidence follow, then re-read the first-sentence sequence as a standalone summary.
mechanism: Two readers score your proposal. The assigned reviewers who read it thoroughly and the rest of the panel who skim during a fifteen-minute discussion. The skimming reader's entire experience of a paragraph is its first sentence. A paragraph that builds to its point delivers nothing to that reader, and they vote.
counter_case: A paragraph whose point depends on a definition the reader does not yet have must supply the definition first. Put the claim in the second sentence rather than mangling the order.
source: NIH, General Grant Writing Tips (grants.nih.gov/grants-process/write-application/general-grant-writing-tips), Tip 3 ('Write a clear topic sentence for each paragraph with one main point or idea. This is key for readability.'); NIH, First Level: Peer Review (grants.nih.gov/grants-process/review/first-level), Meeting Overview and Roles ('many reviewers will be scanning it as they listen to the discussion. As you prepare your application, think about how to make it easy for someone scanning it to understand what you are proposing'). URLs: NIH General Grant Writing Tips — https://grants.nih.gov/grants-process/write-application/general-grant-writing-tips; NIH First Level: Peer Review — https://grants.nih.gov/grants-process/review/first-level

test: Read the summary or abstract with the rest of the application removed. List every term, number, acronym and claim that is unexplained or unsupported inside it. Flag each.
cost: NIH requires the project summary be able to stand on its own, separate from the application, informative to others in the same or related fields and understandable to a scientifically literate reader. ERC requires the equivalent of Part I to contain all essential information because it is the basis for the decision to read further.
suggestion: Resolve every dependency inside the summary: expand each acronym, name each dataset, and state each number's unit and comparison, cutting scope rather than leaving a pointer.
mechanism: The summary is written last, from the body, so it inherits the body's context without inheriting its explanations. It is also the part read first and by the largest number of people, including the staff who choose your reviewers. A dangling term in the summary costs you the reader before the argument starts.
counter_case: Where the funder caps the summary at one page or a fixed character count, cutting a claim is better than compressing it into an unreadable clause. Drop the claim rather than leaving it unresolved.
source: NIH, Application Guide FORMS-I, General Instructions for NIH and Other PHS Agencies, section 7 Project Summary/Abstract ('The project summary is a succinct and accurate description of the proposed work and should be able to stand on its own (separate from the application). This section should be informative to other persons working in the same or related fields and understandable to a scientifically literate reader.'). URLs: NIH Application Guide FORMS-I — https://grants.nih.gov/grants/how-to-apply-application-guide/forms-i/general-forms-i.pdf

test: Extract the noun phrases that carry the argument from the summary and from the aims. Flag any summary term absent from the body, and any body-central term absent from the summary.
cost: NSF Program Directors use the summary to choose reviewers, and NIH assigns applications to a study section on the same basis. A term mismatch routes the proposal to the wrong expertise, and the panel that scores you is then the wrong panel.
suggestion: Make the summary's vocabulary a strict subset of the body's, and ensure every term that determines which subfield should review you appears in it.
mechanism: Assignment happens before review and on the strength of the summary alone. Applicants tune the summary for accessibility, which often means replacing the field-identifying terms with general ones, and the proposal lands in front of generalists who cannot assess it. The check is a set comparison between two short lists.
counter_case: A deliberately cross-disciplinary proposal may need terms from two fields in the summary that the body treats unevenly. Name both and say which panel should lead, which ERC allows via an explicit second-panel request.
source: NSF, A Guide for Proposal Writing (NSF 04-016), Project Summary and Project Data Form ('Program Directors use the summary to choose reviewers for the proposal.'); NIAID (NIH), Know Your Audience, Investigate Committees and Members. URLs: NSF 04-016 — https://nsf-gov-resources.nsf.gov/pubs/2004/nsf04016/nsf04016.pdf?VersionId=_pFLVguJ41PzvWwyThPBaqnSFad20hao; NIAID Know Your Audience — https://www.niaid.nih.gov/grants-contracts/know-your-audience

test: For each aim, follow it through the Approach and check that it is addressed under its own label and in the same order. Flag any aim whose treatment is split across the document with no cross-reference, and any Approach section that does not name the aim it serves.
cost: NIH tells reviewers to provide sufficient context to orient their comments and asks whether the comment refers to a specific aim. Reviewers 1 to 3 speak for two to four minutes each, so an aim they cannot locate in the Approach is an aim they report as unaddressed.
suggestion: Head each Approach block with the aim identifier it delivers, keep the order of the aims, and add one cross-reference at any point where the treatment moves.
mechanism: The reviewer's critique template is organised by criterion, not by your document, so they must map your Approach back onto your aims themselves. When the mapping is implicit they build it from memory during a short discussion. Labelling it turns a reconstruction into a lookup, and NIH's own critique guidance shows that the lookup is what they are trying to do.
counter_case: Where two aims genuinely share one experimental platform, describe it once and reference it from both. Duplicating it to satisfy the labelling is worse.
source: NIH, Writing Effective Critiques for Research Applications (updated October 15, 2024), General Guidance ('Provide sufficient context to orient your comments (e.g., does the comment refer to a specific aim?)'); NIH, Reviewer Guide (Discussion Cheat Sheet, release date January 13, 2026), Step 2. URLs: NIH reviewer discussion cheat sheet — https://grants.nih.gov/sites/default/files/Cheat-Sheet-Reviewer-Guide.pdf

test: For every preliminary result, figure and dataset presented, find the clause that says whose work it is. Flag any item where the reader cannot tell whether the data are the applicant's, a collaborator's, or someone else's published work.
cost: NIAID's own checkpoint for the preliminary studies section is that it is clear which data are mine and which are not. Factor 3 asks whether the investigators have demonstrated the expertise to do the work, and unattributed data cannot count toward that.
suggestion: Attach provenance to each item in the sentence that introduces it: our unpublished data, our published work with a citation, or a named other group with a citation.
mechanism: Preliminary sections are assembled from slides and papers, and the attribution that was obvious in the talk vanishes on the page. A reviewer reading generously credits the applicant, then discovers a citation and re-reads the whole section sceptically. Stating provenance up front converts the same data into evidence of capability, which is what NIH is scoring it as.
counter_case: Where the point of a figure is that the phenomenon replicates across groups, showing several groups' data together is the argument; label the panels rather than splitting the figure.
source: NIAID (NIH), Write Your Research Plan, Preliminary Studies or Progress Report, Checkpoint ('It's clear which data are mine and which are not.'; 'focus on your preliminary data or unpublished data from your lab and the labs of your team members as much as you can'); NIH, Simplified Review Framework, Factor 3. URLs: NIAID Write Your Research Plan — https://www.niaid.nih.gov/grants-contracts/write-research-plan

test: Identify the prior results the proposal names as key support for the project. For each, find the sentence stating its strengths and its weaknesses or limits. Flag any key support presented without both.
cost: NIH requires applicants to describe the strengths and weaknesses in the rigor of the prior research that serves as the key support, and states that weaknesses or gaps in that rigor may affect overall impact scores. Silence transfers the weakness to your project rather than removing it.
suggestion: For each key result, state what it establishes, what it does not, and which part of the proposed work addresses the gap.
mechanism: Applicants present supporting literature as settled because that is how it reads in a paper's introduction, and reviewers are explicitly instructed to assess how strong that support actually is. A reviewer who finds the weakness themselves scores it against you and records that you either missed it or hid it. Naming it first turns the same fact into the rationale for an aim.
counter_case: Prior work cited only for orientation or definition is not key support and does not need a rigour assessment; over-applying the rule bloats the Significance section.
source: NIH, Guidance for Reviewers: Rigor and Transparency for the Simplified Review Framework (updated March 3, 2025), Rigor of Prior Research ('Applicants should discuss the strengths and weaknesses of the prior research used to support the project and describe how the proposed research will address weaknesses or gaps identified by the applicant.'; 'Weaknesses or gaps in the rigor of the prior research that serves as the key support for the proposed project may affect overall impact scores.'); NIH, Application Guide FORMS-I, General Instructions for NIH and Other PHS Agencies, Research Strategy, Significance. URLs: NIH rigor and transparency guidance — https://grants.nih.gov/sites/default/files/Guidance_for_Reviewers_Rigor_and_Transparency_SRF.pdf; NIH Application Guide FORMS-I — https://grants.nih.gov/grants/how-to-apply-application-guide/forms-i/general-forms-i.pdf

test: For every table, check that columns and rows are labelled and that units and n-values appear. For every chart, check each axis has a label and a unit scale and that colours and symbols have a key. Print the document in greyscale and flag any figure whose meaning depends on colour.
cost: NIH's figure guidance states these requirements and gives the reason for the greyscale check: readers may have limited colour vision or use a printer that alters contrast. A figure a reviewer cannot read is a claim with no evidence attached.
suggestion: Add the missing labels, units and n-values, and encode every distinction with a second channel such as line style, marker shape or direct labelling.
mechanism: Figures are lifted from talks and papers where the caption or the speaker supplied the missing labels. Reviewers read on printouts and on screens of unknown calibration, and NIH says so. Because the fix is per-figure and finite, an unlabelled axis reads as a choice not to make the evidence checkable.
counter_case: A schematic that carries no data has no axes or n-values to report. The greyscale and key requirements still apply to it.
source: NIH, Tips for Tables, Charts, and Figures, Focus on the Big Picture and Display Your Data ('Label columns and rows. Include units of measurement and n-values.'; 'Each axis should have a label and unit scale. Include a key for colors and symbols.'; 'Avoid relying solely on color to convey meaning. ... Try a test print in grayscale.'). URLs: NIH tips for tables, charts and figures — https://grants.nih.gov/grants-process/write-application/general-grant-writing-tips/tips-for-tables-charts-and-figures

test: List every method the proposal will use. For each, check that the text either describes it or cites the literature for it. Flag methods that are named and neither described nor cited.
cost: NIAID's checkpoint is that if a method is not described, a reference to the literature is added. NIH also asks applicants to cite a publication showing they can handle the method, and to state explicitly why they will succeed where they have no proven record. An unsupported method reads as a feasibility gap under Factor 2.
suggestion: For each named method, add either a two-line description or a citation, and where your team has no track record with it, add the sentence saying why you will succeed.
mechanism: Methods familiar inside a laboratory get named rather than explained, and the reviewer outside that laboratory cannot tell whether the method exists, works, or is yours. Factor 2 asks whether the studies can be done well, which is answered by the method's provenance rather than by its name. A citation costs one bracket and closes the question.
counter_case: A method the panel descriptor treats as standard needs neither description nor citation, and citing it wastes page budget. The rule bites on methods that are new, borrowed from another field, or the applicant's own.
source: NIAID (NIH), Write Your Research Plan, Referencing Publications, Checkpoint ('If I do not describe a method, I add a reference to the literature.'); Approach ('Cite a publication that shows you can handle the method where you can, but give more details if you and your team don't have a proven record using the method—and state explicitly why you think you will succeed.'). URLs: NIAID Write Your Research Plan — https://www.niaid.nih.gov/grants-contracts/write-research-plan

test: For every preliminary result the proposal interprets, check whether the text names at least one alternative reading of the same data. Flag results presented with a single interpretation.
cost: NIAID states the consequence plainly: give alternative interpretations to your data, and if you don't do this, the reviewers will. An alternative the reviewer supplies becomes a weakness in the critique the applicant later reads. One you supply becomes evidence of depth.
suggestion: After each interpretation, add the strongest competing reading and the observation that would separate them, then point at the aim that makes that observation.
mechanism: Applicants present preliminary data as confirming the hypothesis because that is what motivated the proposal. Reviewers are instructed to assess rigour and reproducibility, so generating alternatives is their job. Doing it first removes the reviewer's best line of attack and converts it into the rationale for an experiment.
counter_case: Where the data admit no serious alternative, saying so in one clause is honest and short. Manufacturing a straw alternative wastes space and signals that you cannot tell strong objections from weak ones.
source: NIAID (NIH), Write Your Research Plan, Describing Preliminary Studies ('Give alternative interpretations to your data to show reviewers you've thought through problems in-depth and are prepared to meet future challenges. If you don't do this, the reviewers will!'); Checkpoint ('I interpret my preliminary results critically.'). URLs: NIAID Write Your Research Plan — https://www.niaid.nih.gov/grants-contracts/write-research-plan

test: Locate the sentence stating the importance of the work. Check whether its subject is the proposed research or the disease, condition, or field it sits in. Flag sentences whose importance claim belongs to the field rather than to the project.
cost: NIH tells reviewers that Importance of the Research refers to the importance of the proposed research rather than to the importance of the research field or disease, and that the Factor 1 score sets a ceiling on the overall impact score. A field-level importance claim scores nothing and consumes the space where the project-level claim belonged.
suggestion: Rewrite so the subject is what this project will produce, and state what specifically will be learned and how valuable that knowledge is.
mechanism: Field-level importance is the easiest sentence to write and the one reviewers are trained to discount, because every application in the pile can write it. NIH's reviewer guide asks what specifically will be learned and how valuable that knowledge will be, and instructs reviewers to differentiate among applications on projected contribution. A sentence about the field cannot differentiate anything.
counter_case: One clause establishing that the field matters is legitimate orientation for a panel that does not work in it. The fault is when that clause is the whole importance argument.
source: NIH, Evaluating Applications Under NIH's Simplified Review Framework for Research Project Grants (reviewer guide, release date January 7, 2026), Factor 1: Importance of the Research ('Note that Importance of the Research refers to the importance of the proposed research rather than to the importance of the research field or disease.'; 'What specifically will be learned and how valuable will that knowledge be?'); NIH, Simplified Review Framework: Scoring Guidance (release date March 14, 2025), Overall Impact Guidance. URLs: NIH SRF reviewer guide — https://grants.nih.gov/sites/default/files/Simplified-Review-Reviewer-Guide-to-Evaluating-Applications.pdf; NIH SRF scoring guidance — https://grants.nih.gov/sites/default/files/Simplified-Review-Scoring-Guidance.pdf

test: Treat each narrative attachment as its own scope. Within each, check that every acronym is spelled out at its first use in that attachment. Flag acronyms that rely on an expansion in a different attachment.
cost: NIH's instruction is to spell out all acronyms on first use within each narrative section, because the attachments are read separately and in different orders. A reviewer who meets a bare acronym in the Approach cannot page back to the Aims to recover it during a fifteen-minute discussion.
suggestion: Maintain one acronym table and re-expand at the first use in every attachment, then re-run the check after any move between attachments.
mechanism: Multi-attachment applications are assembled from separately drafted files, and a reviewer may open the Approach before the Aims. The per-document check passes while the per-section check fails, which is why NIH states the rule at section granularity. The scan is cheap and the failure is invisible to the author, who always reads front to back.
counter_case: Acronyms that are the field's universal shorthand and appear in the panel descriptor need no expansion. Expanding DNA or GPU spends characters against a hard limit.
source: NIH, General Grant Writing Tips (grants.nih.gov/grants-process/write-application/general-grant-writing-tips), Tip 3 ('Spell out all acronyms on first use within each narrative section.'); NIH, Communicating Research Intent and Value in NIH Applications, Advice on Clear Technical Writing. URLs: NIH General Grant Writing Tips — https://grants.nih.gov/grants-process/write-application/general-grant-writing-tips; NIH communicating research intent and value — https://grants.nih.gov/grants-process/write-application/general-grant-writing-tips/communicating-research-intent-and-value-in-nih-applications

test: Scan for praise applied to your own work or team: outstanding, world-leading, excellent, pioneering, highly successful, internationally recognised, exceptional. Flag each occurrence that is not a verifiable fact.
cost: NIH instructs reviewers to evaluate progress without making general laudatory comments and states that specific comments praising the investigator or environment are not appropriate and can introduce bias. If Factor 3 is adequate, no comment at all is allowed. Praise you supply cannot be used and displaces the fact that could be.
suggestion: Replace each adjective with the fact a reviewer could verify: the result, the number, the named award and what it recognises.
mechanism: The reviewer is barred from writing the very sentence you are trying to plant, so self-praise cannot enter the record even if believed. It also occupies the position where a checkable fact would sit, and the reviewer reads the substitution as the fact being unavailable. ERC's parallel instruction is to explain the importance of an award rather than list it.
counter_case: A named honour is a fact rather than praise, and ERC explicitly asks applicants to explain the importance of listed peer recognition. The rule bites on adjectives, not on evidence.
source: NIH, Evaluating Applications Under NIH's Simplified Review Framework for Research Project Grants (reviewer guide, release date January 7, 2026), Additional Review Criteria and Overall Impact ('Evaluate progress made in the prior funding period without making general laudatory comments about the investigators.'; 'Specific comments praising the investigator/environment are not appropriate and can introduce bias.'); ERC, Information for Applicants to the Starting and Consolidator Grant Calls V11.0, section 2.2 ('the applicant should explain the importance of the award or recognition'). URLs: NIH SRF reviewer guide — https://grants.nih.gov/sites/default/files/Simplified-Review-Reviewer-Guide-to-Evaluating-Applications.pdf

test: Count acronyms and abbreviations defined in the narrative. Flag the document if the count exceeds what a reader can hold, and flag any acronym used fewer than three times after its definition.
cost: Wellcome instructs applicants to keep abbreviations and acronyms to a minimum and define them at first use. A reader who is holding twenty coined abbreviations is spending working memory on decoding rather than on the argument the panel scores.
suggestion: Delete any acronym used fewer than three times and write the words out. Keep the ones that recur and the ones the field already uses.
mechanism: Acronyms are coined to save space, and each one saves a few characters while adding a lookup the reader performs every time. Below about three uses the trade is negative even in pure character terms. Because the applicant defined the term, they never experience the lookup cost, which is why the count has to be checked rather than felt.
counter_case: A long compound that recurs in every paragraph earns an acronym even at moderate frequency, and abbreviations the field already reads fluently are not new load at all.
source: Wellcome Trust, How to write an application for funding, section 'Make your application easy to read and understand' and 'Make sure your proposal is competitive' ('Write in plain language and avoid technical jargon where possible. Keep abbreviations and acronyms to a minimum – define them when they're first used.'). URLs: Wellcome how to write an application — https://wellcome.org/research-funding/guidance/prepare-to-apply/how-to-write-wellcome-grant-application

test: Check whether the methodology or approach section is written as continuous prose or as a task list. Flag it if the majority of its content is bullets, task identifiers, or deliverable rows that the implementation section also carries.
cost: The Horizon Europe template instructs that the methodology section be presented as a narrative and that detailed tasks and work packages are described under Implementation. Excellence and Implementation are scored separately, so a task list under Excellence answers the wrong criterion and leaves the right one unanswered.
suggestion: Rewrite the methodology as narrative prose that argues from the research question to the design, and leave every task identifier, duration and deliverable in the implementation section.
mechanism: Work-package tables are easier to write than an argument and they look rigorous, so applicants substitute one for the other. The Excellence criterion asks about the soundness of the methodology, meaning the concepts, models and assumptions, which a table cannot express. An evaluator scoring Excellence from a task list has nothing to credit and will say so.
counter_case: One summary table of the methodology's stages can orient a reader before the narrative, and UKRI explicitly permits images, graphs and tables in the vision and approach attachment. The fault is the table replacing the argument.
source: European Commission, Horizon Europe Application Form (HE RIA and IA), Part B technical description template, V5.1 (22 January 2026), section 1.2 Methodology ('This section should be presented as a narrative. The detailed tasks and work packages are described below under "Implementation".'); European Commission, Horizon Europe Work Programme 2026-2027, 15. General Annexes (Commission Decision C(2025) 8493 of 11 December 2025), Annex A (admissibility) and Annex D (award criteria, scores and weighting), Annex D (Excellence and Implementation scored separately). URLs: Horizon Europe application form HE RIA/IA part B — https://ec.europa.eu/info/funding-tenders/opportunities/docs/2021-2027/horizon/temp-form/af/af_he-ria-ia_en.pdf; Horizon Europe general annexes — https://ec.europa.eu/info/funding-tenders/opportunities/docs/2021-2027/horizon/wp-call/2026-2027/wp-15-general-annexes_horizon-2026-2027_en.pdf

test: Compute the ratio of bullet points to prose sentences in the capability, track record, or team section. Flag the section if it reads as a formatted list of achievements rather than a narrative.
cost: UKRI instructs applicants to complete the capability section as a narrative and not to format it like a CV. The assessment question asks why you are the right individual or team, which is an argument rather than an inventory, and a list leaves the argument for the assessor to construct.
suggestion: Write the section as prose in which each achievement is followed by the clause saying which part of this project it makes deliverable.
mechanism: A CV-shaped section is faster to write and it also answers a question nobody asked, because the assessor already has the publication record elsewhere. UKRI asks assessors for evidence of relevant experience appropriate to career stage, which requires linking each item to the proposed work. Prose forces that link. A bullet list hides its absence.
counter_case: A short list is the right form for items whose relevance is self-evident and uniform, such as software releases the project will build on. UKRI also permits a narrative additions block for context such as career breaks.
source: UKRI/EPSRC, New Investigator Award (applicant-led mode) opportunity page, sections Vision and Approach, Applicant and team capability to deliver, and Summary, Applicant and team capability to deliver ('Complete this as a narrative. Do not format it like a CV.'; 'Why are you the right individual or team to successfully deliver the proposed work?'; 'Evidence of how you, and if relevant your team, have: the relevant experience (appropriate to career stage)'). URLs: EPSRC New Investigator Award opportunity — https://www.ukri.org/opportunity/epsrc-new-investigator-award-applicant-led-mode/

test: Find every claim that the work goes beyond the state of the art. For each, check whether the text names the search that established it, meaning a patent search, a publication search, or a named systematic sweep. Flag claims resting on the applicant's unaided recollection.
cost: The Horizon Europe template instructs applicants to refer to any patent or publication search carried out when arguing the advance beyond the state of the art. Excellence's first aspect is the extent to which the work goes beyond the state of the art, and a claim with no search behind it is scored as an assertion.
suggestion: Name the search: the databases, the query terms, the date, and the closest hit it returned, in one sentence attached to the advance claim.
mechanism: Beyond-the-state-of-the-art claims are written from what the applicant happens to know, and evaluators include people who know a different slice of the same literature. Naming the search converts an unfalsifiable claim about the world into a checkable claim about a procedure. It also pre-empts the evaluator's own recollection, which is the mechanism by which these claims usually die.
counter_case: In a field with no patent literature and no indexed venue, say what was searched and what could not be. An honest statement of coverage beats a claim of exhaustiveness.
source: European Commission, Horizon Europe Application Form (HE RIA and IA), Part B technical description template, V5.1 (22 January 2026), section 1.1 Objectives and ambition ('Describe how your project goes beyond the state-of-the-art ... Refer to any patent or publication search carried out.'); European Commission, Horizon Europe Work Programme 2026-2027, 15. General Annexes (Commission Decision C(2025) 8493 of 11 December 2025), Annex A (admissibility) and Annex D (award criteria, scores and weighting), Annex D Excellence. URLs: Horizon Europe application form HE RIA/IA part B — https://ec.europa.eu/info/funding-tenders/opportunities/docs/2021-2027/horizon/temp-form/af/af_he-ria-ia_en.pdf; Horizon Europe general annexes — https://ec.europa.eu/info/funding-tenders/opportunities/docs/2021-2027/horizon/wp-call/2026-2027/wp-15-general-annexes_horizon-2026-2027_en.pdf

test: For every image, chart and table, check that a descriptive legend sits immediately beneath it in the text, and check that the image conveys information that could not easily be put into words. Flag images with no legend and images that reproduce text.
cost: UKRI states the consequence in the strongest terms available: your response may not be considered by the panel if images are provided without a descriptive legend, or are used to replace text that could be input into the text box. It also states that legends count towards the word limit.
suggestion: Add a legend under each image saying what the reader should conclude from it, and convert any image that is really a block of text or a bullet list back into text.
mechanism: Images are used to smuggle content past a word limit, which is exactly what the funder has named and penalised. They also fail for assessors reading in accessibility modes, since an image of text is not text. Because the legend is charged to the word count, an image that carries no conclusion now costs words twice.
counter_case: A diagram of a mechanism, a pipeline, or a study design genuinely cannot be put into words at the same length, and UKRI permits images for exactly that. Keep it and write the legend.
