source: UKRI, How applicants use the UKRI Funding Service (updated 19 February 2026), What to include in the response ('use images sparingly and only to convey important information that cannot easily be put into words'; 'provide a descriptive legend for each image immediately underneath it (this counts towards your word limit)'; 'Your response may not be considered by the panel if images are provided without a descriptive legend in the text box, or are used to replace text that could be input into the text box.'). URLs: UKRI Funding Service guidance — https://www.ukri.org/apply-for-funding/develop-your-application/how-applicants-use-the-ukri-funding-service/

test: For each task or activity described, check that it is quantified, meaning a number of measurements, subjects, runs, protocols or outputs, and that the text names who will do it. Flag activities described without both.
cost: Horizon Europe instructs applicants to quantify all activities and to provide enough detail to clarify who will do this work and why it is needed. Implementation is scored on the appropriateness of the effort assigned to work packages, which cannot be judged against an unquantified activity.
suggestion: Attach a number and a named role to each activity in the sentence that introduces it, and state in the same sentence why the project needs it.
mechanism: Unquantified activities are readable and unfalsifiable, which is why they survive drafting. An evaluator asked whether the effort is appropriate has to compare the effort to the work, and with no quantity there is nothing to compare. Numbers also make the plan auditable later, which is why the funder asks for them.
counter_case: An exploratory activity whose scale genuinely depends on an earlier result should state the decision rule and the range rather than a false single number.
source: European Commission, Horizon Europe Application Form (HE RIA and IA), Part B technical description template, V5.1 (22 January 2026), section 3.1 Work plan and resources ('For each task or element of the work package, describe all activities to be carried out and quantify them (e.g., number of protocols, tests, measurements, combinations, study subjects, conferences, publications, etc.). Provide enough detail to clarify who will do this work and why it is needed for the project'); European Commission, Horizon Europe Work Programme 2026-2027, 15. General Annexes (Commission Decision C(2025) 8493 of 11 December 2025), Annex A (admissibility) and Annex D (award criteria, scores and weighting), Annex D Quality and efficiency of the implementation. URLs: Horizon Europe application form HE RIA/IA part B — https://ec.europa.eu/info/funding-tenders/opportunities/docs/2021-2027/horizon/temp-form/af/af_he-ria-ia_en.pdf; Horizon Europe general annexes — https://ec.europa.eu/info/funding-tenders/opportunities/docs/2021-2027/horizon/wp-call/2026-2027/wp-15-general-annexes_horizon-2026-2027_en.pdf

test: Establish whether the funder counts references inside or outside the limit, then measure the space the reference list actually consumes. Flag a reference list that is sized as if the other convention applied.
cost: The convention is inverted between funders and the loss is real either way. Horizon Europe RIA and IA count references against the 40-page limit. ERC excludes references from its page limits. UKRI counts references within the word count of the question section. A house style tuned to one funder silently spends or wastes argument space at the next.
suggestion: Look up the rule for the call in front of you before the final trim. Where references are counted, prioritise the most pertinent as UKRI instructs. Where they are not, cite completely.
mechanism: Reference lists are generated by a tool and their length is invisible until the render, by which time the page budget is already allocated. Applicants reuse the previous proposal's bibliography density without rechecking the rule. In a counted regime a long list eats the pages that carry the argument, and in an uncounted regime a trimmed list throws away free evidence.
counter_case: None on the rule itself, but where references are counted, deliberately citing fewer works is correct and UKRI explicitly asks for discretion. The fault is not knowing which regime you are in.
source: European Commission, Horizon Europe Application Form (HE RIA and IA), Part B technical description template, V5.1 (22 January 2026), Page limit ('All tables, figures, references and any other element pertaining to these sections must be included as an integral part of these sections and are thus counted against this page limit.'); ERC (European Research Council), Information for Applicants to the Starting and Consolidator Grant Calls, Version 11.0 (22 July 2026), section 2.2 ('References should be included (they do not count towards the page limits).'); UKRI, How applicants use the UKRI Funding Service (updated 19 February 2026), Use of references and hyperlinks ('References should be included within the word count of the appropriate question section. You should use your discretion when including references and prioritise those most pertinent to the application.'). URLs: Horizon Europe application form HE RIA/IA part B — https://ec.europa.eu/info/funding-tenders/opportunities/docs/2021-2027/horizon/temp-form/af/af_he-ria-ia_en.pdf; ERC Information for Applicants V11.0 — https://ec.europa.eu/info/funding-tenders/opportunities/docs/2021-2027/horizon/guidance/information-for-applicants_he-erc-stg-cog_en.pdf; UKRI Funding Service guidance — https://www.ukri.org/apply-for-funding/develop-your-application/how-applicants-use-the-ukri-funding-service/

test: Check that every reference is formatted in the style the call requests, that the style is uniform across the whole document, and that a persistent identifier such as a DOI is present wherever one exists. Flag mixed styles, missing identifiers and references not identifiable as references.
cost: Wellcome instructs applicants to list all references consistently using the format requested. UKRI states references should be easily identifiable by the assessors and that persistent identifiers should be used where possible. Horizon Europe makes readability an admissibility condition, so a reference list an assessor cannot parse is a compliance risk as well as an evidential one.
suggestion: Regenerate the whole list from one style file, add DOIs where they exist, and check that inline references are visually distinguishable from the surrounding prose.
mechanism: Bibliographies accumulate across proposal generations and across co-authors, so styles mix and identifiers are present for the recent entries only. An assessor deciding whether your claim is supported has to find the entry first, and an inline reference that looks like ordinary prose defeats that. Both halves are machine-checkable.
counter_case: Where the call requests a specific compact format to save counted space, that format wins over completeness; follow the requested style rather than your usual one.
source: Wellcome Trust, How to write an application for funding, section 'Make your application easy to read and understand' and 'Make sure your proposal is competitive' ('List all references consistently, using the format requested.'); UKRI, How applicants use the UKRI Funding Service (updated 19 February 2026), Use of references and hyperlinks ('references should be easily identifiable by the assessors'; 'persistent identifiers should be used where possible'); European Commission, Horizon Europe Work Programme 2026-2027, 15. General Annexes (Commission Decision C(2025) 8493 of 11 December 2025), Annex A (admissibility) and Annex D (award criteria, scores and weighting), Annex A ('Applications must be readable, accessible and printable.'). URLs: Wellcome how to write an application — https://wellcome.org/research-funding/guidance/prepare-to-apply/how-to-write-wellcome-grant-application; UKRI Funding Service guidance — https://www.ukri.org/apply-for-funding/develop-your-application/how-applicants-use-the-ukri-funding-service/; Horizon Europe general annexes — https://ec.europa.eu/info/funding-tenders/opportunities/docs/2021-2027/horizon/wp-call/2026-2027/wp-15-general-annexes_horizon-2026-2027_en.pdf

test: Search for language that defers a decision, a design choice, or a piece of evidence to after the award: will be determined, to be refined, subject to further work, we will decide once funded. Flag each instance that sits under a scored criterion.
cost: Horizon Europe states that proposals will be evaluated as they were submitted, rather than on their potential if certain changes were to be made, and that only proposals which successfully address all the required aspects have a chance of being funded. NIH tells reviewers to evaluate the application as it is presented and not to attempt to improve or redesign it.
suggestion: Make the decision now and state it, with the fallback named, or delete the claim that depended on the deferred choice.
mechanism: Deferring a decision feels like honesty and reads as an unaddressed aspect, because the reviewer is barred from crediting the version of the proposal you would write later. Two funders state this rule explicitly, so the discount is a procedure rather than a reviewer's mood. Naming a decision plus its fallback costs the same words and scores.
counter_case: A genuine decision gate is legitimate when the text states the criterion, the date and both branches. The fault is deferral with no rule for resolving it.
source: European Commission, Horizon Europe Application Form (HE RIA and IA), Part B technical description template, V5.1 (22 January 2026), Proposal template Part B preamble ('proposals will be evaluated as they were submitted, rather than on their potential if certain changes were to be made. This means that only proposals that successfully address all the required aspects will have a chance of being funded.'); NIH, Evaluating Applications Under NIH's Simplified Review Framework, Introduction ('Evaluate the application as it is presented. Do not attempt to improve or redesign the application.'). URLs: Horizon Europe application form HE RIA/IA part B — https://ec.europa.eu/info/funding-tenders/opportunities/docs/2021-2027/horizon/temp-form/af/af_he-ria-ia_en.pdf

test: List every consideration the application form or template asks applicants to address. For each one the proposal does not address, check that an explicit justification sentence is present. Flag silent omissions.
cost: The Horizon Europe template repeats the same instruction at every optional dimension. If you consider that this is unnecessary in the context of the proposed work, please provide a justification. Horizon Europe also states that only proposals which successfully address all the required aspects will have a chance of being funded, so silence is scored as a gap rather than read as a considered choice.
suggestion: Add one sentence per omitted dimension naming why it does not apply to this work, and put it where the template asks the question.
mechanism: Applicants skip a dimension when it seems irrelevant, which is indistinguishable on the page from not having considered it. The template's own wording shows the funder anticipates irrelevance and asks for the reasoning anyway. An evaluator with a checklist records an absence. The same evaluator reading one justifying sentence records the item as addressed.
counter_case: Where the call states a dimension is not applicable to the action type, adding a justification wastes counted space. Check the call rather than justifying everything.
source: European Commission, Horizon Europe Application Form (HE RIA and IA), Part B technical description template, V5.1 (22 January 2026), section 1.2 Methodology (repeated instruction: 'If you consider that an inter-disciplinary approach is unnecessary in the context of the proposed work, please provide a justification.'; 'If you do not consider such a gender dimension to be relevant in your project, please provide a justification.'; 'If you believe that none of these practices are appropriate for your project, please provide a justification here.'); Proposal template Part B preamble. URLs: Horizon Europe application form HE RIA/IA part B — https://ec.europa.eu/info/funding-tenders/opportunities/docs/2021-2027/horizon/temp-form/af/af_he-ria-ia_en.pdf

test: Check the title against the funder's character limit and give it to a researcher outside your subfield. Flag it if they cannot say what the project is about, or if it contains an unexpanded acronym, a coined term, or a formula.
cost: Horizon Europe states the requirement at the title field itself: maximum 200 characters with spaces, and it must be understandable for non-specialists in your field. NIH instructs reviewers to expect plain language in the title, and UKRI asks for a plain-English summary used to identify the most suitable experts.
suggestion: Rewrite the title as the question or the outcome in words the panel descriptor uses, keeping any coined name as a short prefix rather than as the content.
mechanism: Titles are written for colleagues and then reused unchanged, so they carry the subfield's shorthand. The title is read by the staff who route the proposal and by every panel member who never opens it, and it is the one string that appears in every list. A title only a specialist can parse routes the proposal to the wrong readers before anyone assesses anything.
counter_case: Where the coined name is already established in the literature and the panel will recognise it, leading with it is an advantage. The test is whether a non-specialist can state the subject, not whether the name is absent.
source: European Commission, Horizon Europe Application Form (HE RIA and IA), Part B technical description template, V5.1 (22 January 2026), Part A General information, Proposal title field ('Max 200 characters (with spaces). Must be understandable for non-specialists in your field.'); NIH, Communicating Research Intent and Value in NIH Applications ('We instruct peer reviewers to expect plain language in your application's title, Project Summary/Abstract and Project Narrative'); UKRI/EPSRC, New Investigator Award (applicant-led mode) opportunity page, sections Vision and Approach, Applicant and team capability to deliver, and Summary, Summary ('In plain English, provide a summary we can use to identify the most suitable experts to assess your application.'). URLs: Horizon Europe application form HE RIA/IA part B — https://ec.europa.eu/info/funding-tenders/opportunities/docs/2021-2027/horizon/temp-form/af/af_he-ria-ia_en.pdf; NIH communicating research intent and value — https://grants.nih.gov/grants-process/write-application/general-grant-writing-tips/communicating-research-intent-and-value-in-nih-applications; EPSRC New Investigator Award opportunity — https://www.ukri.org/opportunity/epsrc-new-investigator-award-applicant-led-mode/

test: Scan the abstract for formulas, mathematical notation, subscripts, superscripts, special characters and markup. Flag each.
cost: Horizon Europe instructs that the abstract be short and precise and use plain typed text, avoiding formulas and other special characters, because the abstract is reused as the short description of the proposal in the evaluation process and in communications to programme committees. Special characters are lost or mangled when the string is re-rendered downstream.
suggestion: Replace each formula with its verbal statement and each special character with an ASCII equivalent, and check the abstract survives a plain-text round trip.
mechanism: The abstract is not read only in your PDF. It is extracted into portals, committee papers and databases whose rendering you never see. A subscript that displays correctly for you arrives as a stray digit for the committee. Since the funder has said which characters are unsafe, the check is a character-class scan.
counter_case: Where a symbol is the object of study and no verbal form exists, name it in words and give the symbol once in parentheses. The rule targets notation used as shorthand, not notation as subject.
source: European Commission, Horizon Europe Application Form (HE RIA and IA), Part B technical description template, V5.1 (22 January 2026), Part A Abstract ('It must therefore be short and precise and should not contain confidential information. Use plain typed text, avoiding formulas and other special characters.'). URLs: Horizon Europe application form HE RIA/IA part B — https://ec.europa.eu/info/funding-tenders/opportunities/docs/2021-2027/horizon/temp-form/af/af_he-ria-ia_en.pdf

test: For each assessment question the funder publishes, find the passage that answers it and check the passage uses the question's own wording. Flag questions with no locatable passage, and passages that answer a question the form does not ask.
cost: UKRI states that applicants are given the criteria the assessors will be looking for with each question, and Horizon Europe's General Annexes tell applicants proposals should be designed to stay as close as possible to the award criteria. EPSRC states that where the majority of reviews are unsupportive the proposal is review rejected before the right to reply.
suggestion: Head each passage with the question's own noun phrases, in the order the form asks them, so the assessor can match answer to question without translating.
mechanism: Assessors fill a form whose fields are the published questions, and they do it under time pressure across a group of proposals. When your headings use your vocabulary and the form uses the funder's, every field becomes a search. The wording is published, so aligning it is a lookup rather than a judgement.
counter_case: Parroting the criteria without answering them is the failure mode this rule invites. The alignment is of vocabulary and order. It does not substitute for content.
source: UKRI, How applicants use the UKRI Funding Service (updated 19 February 2026), Complete your application ('You are given the guidance on what the assessors are looking for'); European Commission, Horizon Europe Work Programme 2026-2027, 15. General Annexes (Commission Decision C(2025) 8493 of 11 December 2025), Annex A (admissibility) and Annex D (award criteria, scores and weighting), Annex E ('Proposals should be designed to stay as close as possible to the award criteria'); UKRI/EPSRC, What happens after you submit your proposal (updated 8 May 2026), Applications with not enough support from reviewers. URLs: UKRI Funding Service guidance — https://www.ukri.org/apply-for-funding/develop-your-application/how-applicants-use-the-ukri-funding-service/; Horizon Europe general annexes — https://ec.europa.eu/info/funding-tenders/opportunities/docs/2021-2027/horizon/wp-call/2026-2027/wp-15-general-annexes_horizon-2026-2027_en.pdf; EPSRC what happens after you submit — https://www.ukri.org/councils/epsrc/guidance-for-applicants/what-happens-after-you-submit-your-proposal/

test: Identify the sentences that state the work's wider relevance. Count them and check each is intelligible to a reader outside the field. Flag relevance that exists only as an implication spread across a section.
cost: A Wellcome expert reviewer states the requirement as a shape. The relevance in a larger context should be highlighted in a few clear and concise statements that reviewers outside the field can pick up on. UKRI scores whether the work is of excellent quality and importance within or beyond the field and whether it is timely.
suggestion: Write two or three standalone sentences of wider relevance and place them where a skimming reader will meet them, rather than leaving the relevance to be inferred.
mechanism: Applicants establish relevance cumulatively, because that is how a paper's introduction works, and a reader who skims never accumulates it. The panel member who has to speak for your proposal needs a sentence they can quote. Wellcome and UKRI both describe the deliverable as a small number of portable statements, which makes the count checkable.
counter_case: Where the panel is entirely specialist, as with ERC remote reviewers at Step 2, a portable relevance statement spends space the specialist does not need; write it for the generalist reading and not for both.
source: Wellcome Trust, How to write an application for funding, section 'Make your application easy to read and understand' and 'Make sure your proposal is competitive', attributed reviewer comment from Professor Peter Robin Hiesinger, Cellular and Molecular Neuroscience Expert Review Group ('The relevance in a larger context should be highlighted in a few clear and concise statements that reviewers outside the field can pick up on.'); UKRI/EPSRC, New Investigator Award (applicant-led mode) opportunity page, sections Vision and Approach, Applicant and team capability to deliver, and Summary, Vision ('is of excellent quality and importance within or beyond the field(s) or area(s)'; 'is timely given current trends, context and needs'). URLs: Wellcome how to write an application — https://wellcome.org/research-funding/guidance/prepare-to-apply/how-to-write-wellcome-grant-application; EPSRC New Investigator Award opportunity — https://www.ukri.org/opportunity/epsrc-new-investigator-award-applicant-led-mode/

test: Check that font, size, paragraph justification, heading style and list style are identical throughout the document and across its attachments. Flag any inconsistency, and check the layout against the call's stated formatting requirements.
cost: EPSRC states that if the attachment does not meet its formatting requirements the application will be rejected. Horizon Europe makes readability, accessibility and printability admissibility conditions. A Wellcome grantholder names the reason it matters to a reviewer: reviewers have a lot of applications to read, so make it easy for them.
suggestion: Set the layout once from the call's requirements, apply it to every attachment, and check the rendered PDF rather than the source.
mechanism: Attachments are drafted in different tools by different people and merged late, so styles diverge exactly where the reader crosses from one section to the next. Some funders make this fatal rather than merely untidy. Because the requirements are published as numbers, this is the one check that a script settles completely.
counter_case: Horizon Europe permits a font other than the reference font where it is legible and gives no page-count advantage, and attachments a funder generates itself (portal-rendered forms, CV templates) carry their own house style; consistency is required within what you author, not against documents the system produces.
source: UKRI/EPSRC, New Investigator Award (applicant-led mode) opportunity page, sections Vision and Approach, Applicant and team capability to deliver, and Summary, Vision and Approach formatting ('The document should not be more than eight sides of A4, single spaced in paper in 11-point Arial (or equivalent sans serif font) with margins of at least 2cm. ... If the attachment does not meet these requirements, the application will be rejected.'); European Commission, Horizon Europe Work Programme 2026-2027, 15. General Annexes (Commission Decision C(2025) 8493 of 11 December 2025), Annex A (admissibility) and Annex D (award criteria, scores and weighting), Annex A ('Applications must be readable, accessible and printable.'); Wellcome Trust, How to write an application for funding, section 'Make your application easy to read and understand' and 'Make sure your proposal is competitive', attributed comment from Dr Alex Mold ('make sure it is clearly laid out using the same font, text size and paragraph justification throughout. Reviewers have a lot of applications to read'). URLs: EPSRC New Investigator Award opportunity — https://www.ukri.org/opportunity/epsrc-new-investigator-award-applicant-led-mode/; Horizon Europe general annexes — https://ec.europa.eu/info/funding-tenders/opportunities/docs/2021-2027/horizon/wp-call/2026-2027/wp-15-general-annexes_horizon-2026-2027_en.pdf; Wellcome how to write an application — https://wellcome.org/research-funding/guidance/prepare-to-apply/how-to-write-wellcome-grant-application

test: Read the proposal for the two audiences the funder names. First as a specialist, checking there is enough detail to judge feasibility; then as a researcher with broad experience outside the field, listing every sentence that cannot be parsed without subfield knowledge. Flag both an unparseable sentence and a section too thin for the specialist.
cost: Wellcome instructs applicants to aim the proposal at people with specific expertise in the field as well as those with broader research experience, and to give enough detail that reviewers can understand what is proposed, how it will be carried out and whether it is feasible. UKRI scores whether the methodology is clearly written and transparent.
suggestion: Keep the specialist detail and add the generalist's parse: put the plain statement first and the technical precision in the following clause, rather than choosing one audience.
mechanism: Applicants resolve the dual-audience problem by picking one, and both choices lose. Writing only for specialists loses the panel members who vote without reading closely. Writing only for generalists loses the specialist whose feasibility judgement the panel defers to. Leading with the plain form and following with the precise one serves both in the same sentence and is the only version UKRI can score as clearly written.
counter_case: Where a funder splits the document by audience, as ERC does with a generalist Part B1 and a specialist Part B2, write each part for its own reader; doubling up wastes the page limit in both.
source: Wellcome Trust, How to write an application for funding, section 'Make your application easy to read and understand' and 'Make sure your proposal is competitive' ('Aim your proposal at people who have specific expertise in your field as well as those who have broader research experience.'; 'Give enough detail that reviewers can understand what you're proposing, how it will be carried out and whether it's feasible.'); UKRI/EPSRC, New Investigator Award (applicant-led mode) opportunity page, sections Vision and Approach, Applicant and team capability to deliver, and Summary, Approach ('uses a clearly written and transparent methodology (if applicable)'). URLs: Wellcome how to write an application — https://wellcome.org/research-funding/guidance/prepare-to-apply/how-to-write-wellcome-grant-application; EPSRC New Investigator Award opportunity — https://www.ukri.org/opportunity/epsrc-new-investigator-award-applicant-led-mode/

test: Count words per paragraph and measure the longest unbroken block of text on each page. Flag paragraphs over about 150 words and any page with no heading, list or paragraph break in its upper half.
cost: NIH instructs applicants to use short paragraphs, bulleted or numbered lists, adequate white space and indents, and to establish a clear organised structure with headings. It gives the reason: many reviewers will be scanning the application while listening to the discussion, and a solid block gives a scanning reader no entry point.
suggestion: Split each long paragraph at its second claim, add the heading that names what the block argues, and convert any enumeration inside the prose into a numbered list.
mechanism: Long paragraphs come from drafting in one sitting and are never re-read as a stranger would meet them. The panel member scanning during a fifteen-minute discussion navigates by visual landmarks, not by sentences, so a page without landmarks is a page they skip. The measurement is a word count and a whitespace scan, so nothing here needs a judgement.
counter_case: A single sustained argument that would be falsified by splitting, such as a chain of inference where each step depends on the previous, should stay whole. Give it a heading instead of a break.
source: NIH, General Grant Writing Tips (grants.nih.gov/grants-process/write-application/general-grant-writing-tips), Tip 2: Be Organized ('Use short paragraphs, bulleted or numbered lists, adequate white space, and indents.'; 'Establish a clear, organized structure with headings.'; 'Make your application as easy to read as possible.'); NIH, First Level: Peer Review (grants.nih.gov/grants-process/review/first-level) ('many reviewers will be scanning it as they listen to the discussion'); NIH, Study Section Chair's Discussion Cheat Sheet (release date 1 July 2025), Step 9. URLs: NIH General Grant Writing Tips — https://grants.nih.gov/grants-process/write-application/general-grant-writing-tips; NIH First Level: Peer Review — https://grants.nih.gov/grants-process/review/first-level; NIH study section chair cheat sheet — https://grants.nih.gov/sites/default/files/Study-Section-Cheat-Sheet.pdf

test: For every field the funder caps by sentence count or character count rather than by pages, count sentences and characters. Flag any field over its cap and any field whose cap is met by running two claims into one sentence.
cost: NIH's Project Narrative instruction is to describe the relevance of this research to public health in at most three sentences, and the title is capped at 200 characters. These fields are extracted and reused, so an over-length or comma-spliced field is either truncated or read as non-compliant.
suggestion: Write to the cap as a budget of separate claims. One claim per sentence, and cut a claim rather than splicing two into one sentence.
mechanism: Sentence-capped fields invite writers to keep the content and lose the punctuation, which satisfies the counter and defeats the purpose of the cap. These are also the fields read by the largest number of people and reused outside the application, so their prose travels further than the rest. Both the count and the splice are mechanically detectable.
counter_case: Where a cap genuinely cannot hold the required content, say less rather than compressing. The fields NIH caps are summaries, and a missing nuance costs less than an unreadable sentence.
source: NIH, Application Guide FORMS-I, General Instructions for NIH and Other PHS Agencies, section 8 Project Narrative ('Describe the relevance of this research to public health in, at most, three sentences.'); NIAID (NIH), Write Your Research Plan, Craft a Title ('NIH gives you a 200 character limit, but don't feel obliged to use all of that allotment.'). URLs: NIH Application Guide FORMS-I — https://grants.nih.gov/grants/how-to-apply-application-guide/forms-i/general-forms-i.pdf; NIAID Write Your Research Plan — https://www.niaid.nih.gov/grants-contracts/write-research-plan

test: Identify the two or three sentences you intend the lead reviewer to quote when they introduce the proposal to the panel. Check each is self-contained, under about twenty-five words, and located where a reader will meet it. Flag the proposal if no such sentence exists.
cost: NIAID states the requirement directly: make explaining your research easy by including lines they can deliver to the rest of the study section. ERC assigns each proposal a Lead Reviewer who introduces it to the panel, and NIH gives assigned reviewers three to four minutes and tells them not to read their critiques.
suggestion: Write the quotable line as one sentence naming the question and what changes if it is answered, and place it at the head of the summary and again at the head of the objectives.
mechanism: Most of the panel meets your proposal through one person speaking for three minutes from memory and notes. If your proposal contains no sentence that survives being lifted out, that person paraphrases, and the paraphrase is what gets scored. Supplying the line is the only point in the process where the applicant controls what the panel hears.
counter_case: Where the whole panel reads the proposal itself, as with a small specialist panel or a single-reviewer scheme, the quotable line spends space that argument could use.
source: NIAID (NIH), Know Your Audience, Target Your Assigned Reviewers ('Make explaining your research easy by including lines they can deliver to the rest of the study section.'); ERC, Guide for Peer Reviewers to the ERC Starting and Consolidator Grant Calls, Version 6.0, section 1.3 ('Each proposal is assigned to a Lead Reviewer ... who introduces the proposal to the panel for discussion'); NIH, Reviewer Guide (Discussion Cheat Sheet, January 13, 2026), Step 2 ('Do not read your critiques.'). URLs: NIAID Know Your Audience — https://www.niaid.nih.gov/grants-contracts/know-your-audience

test: List every topic that gets a paragraph or more of discussion in the first third of the narrative. For each, search the remaining two thirds for a return to it. Flag any topic introduced at length and never taken up again.
cost: Introducing a topic early signals to the reader that it is central, so a topic that never returns has spent the reader's attention on a false lead and spent page budget the argument needed. The guide names the pattern and its remedy directly.
suggestion: Either connect the topic to a downstream objective in one explicit sentence, or cut the discussion to the single clause the argument actually uses.
mechanism: Early sections are drafted first and revised least, so topics that mattered to an earlier version of the project survive into the final one. A reviewer builds expectations from the order of introduction and reads the unreturned topic as either padding or a plan they were not told about. The check is a term-frequency comparison between the opening third and the rest, so it needs no judgement to produce the candidates.
counter_case: A topic introduced to be explicitly ruled out of scope belongs early and does not return. The fault is silent abandonment. A stated exclusion is fine.
source: Mike Cronan and Lucy Deckard (Academic Research Funding Strategies, formerly Texas A&M Office of Research Development and Grant Writing), New Faculty Guide to Competing for Research Funding, 2nd ed. 2022 (copy hosted by Loyola University New Orleans Office of Academic Affairs), 'Avoid Irritating Your Reviewer' ('The garden path proposal. Usually, when a topic is introduced early in a proposal, it's a signal to the reader that the topic is central to the proposed project. However, some PIs introduce a topic and discuss it at some length, and then never return to it in the rest of the proposal.'; 'If a topic is not really central to your proposal, don't discuss it at length early in the proposal.'). URLs: Cronan & Deckard, New Faculty Guide — https://academicaffairs.loyno.edu/sites/default/files/new_faculty_guide_to_competing_for_research_funding502_0.pdf

test: Read the narrative in five separated sittings, stopping at arbitrary points rather than at section boundaries. At each resumption, note whether you can carry on without paging back. Flag every point where you had to return to an earlier page to recover a term, a number or the thread.
cost: Kraicer states that reviewers often do their reading in bits and pieces and that the application should be organised so it can be read that way, because you do not want them to have to go back to the beginning after each break. Reid's handbook maps skimming, search reading and critical reading to different navigational features, so a document with none of them fails all three.
suggestion: Add a re-entry cue at each major transition, meaning a heading that names the claim and a first sentence that re-establishes the referent, and restate a load-bearing number rather than pointing back to it.
mechanism: Applicants write and read their proposal front to back in long sessions, which is the one reading pattern reviewers do not use. Volunteer reviewers read after hours, in fragments, across many applications, so every implicit back-reference becomes a page turn or a guess. Simulating the fragmented read is the only way to find the gaps, because a continuous read cannot expose them.
counter_case: Restating a number at every mention is noise in a short document a reader finishes in one sitting; scale the redundancy to the length and to how far apart the uses sit.
source: Jacob Kraicer (Director of Research Grants, Human Frontier Science Program), The Art of Grantsmanship, published by HFSP, section 3.1 General ('Reviewers often do their reading in bits-and-pieces. Have your application so organized so that it can be read in this way. You do not want them to have to go back to the beginning after each break.'); C.P. Patrick Reid (University of Arizona), Handbook for Preparing and Writing Research Proposals, IUFRO-SPDC, 2000 (ISBN 3-901347-23-2), chapter 8 'Types of Readers' (reading style to writing technique mapping). URLs: HFSP, The Art of Grantsmanship — https://www.hfsp.org/sites/default/files/webfm/Communications/The%20Art%20of%20Grantsmanship.pdf; IUFRO-SPDC proposal handbook — https://www.iufro.org/media/fileadmin/publications/manuals/research-proposal-writing-en.pdf

test: Find every direction word applied to an outcome: improve, increase, reduce, lower, raise, enhance, decrease, speed up, better. For each, check the same sentence carries a magnitude and the basis for that estimate. Flag direction claims with no number.
cost: Cronan and Deckard state the consequence. If you claim your research will improve efficiency or reduce cost without at least some estimate of magnitude and a rationale for it, reviewers will often disregard the claim altogether. Purdue makes the same point, that vague terms indicate a direction and not an amount.
suggestion: Attach a figure and its basis to each direction claim, or convert the claim into the measurement the project will make.
mechanism: Direction claims feel safe because they cannot be wrong, and that is exactly why a reviewer discounts them to zero. A reviewer weighing your proposal against others needs a quantity to compare, and an unquantified improvement supplies nothing to weigh. Adding the basis also protects the number, since an estimate with a stated derivation survives scrutiny that a bare figure does not.
counter_case: Where the magnitude is genuinely the unknown the project will establish, say so and give the range the work will distinguish. A fabricated point estimate is worse than an honest interval.
source: Mike Cronan and Lucy Deckard (Academic Research Funding Strategies, formerly Texas A&M Office of Research Development and Grant Writing), New Faculty Guide to Competing for Research Funding, 2nd ed. 2022 (copy hosted by Loyola University New Orleans Office of Academic Affairs), 'Avoid Irritating Your Reviewer' ('Vague claims. ... If you make claims that your research will "improve the efficiency" or "reduce the cost" of a step, the reviewer will want to know if you anticipate a 200% improvement in efficiency or a 0.02% improvement. If you don't give at least some estimate of the magnitude of the impact along with rationale for that estimation, reviewers will often disregard the claim altogether.'); Purdue University, Purdue OWL, Grant Writing in the Sciences and Specificity in Writing, Specificity in Writing ('vague terms such as, "improve, raise, lower, decease" indicate a direction not an amount'). URLs: Cronan & Deckard, New Faculty Guide — https://academicaffairs.loyno.edu/sites/default/files/new_faculty_guide_to_competing_for_research_funding502_0.pdf; Purdue OWL — https://owl.purdue.edu/owl/subject_specific_writing/professional_technical_writing/grant_writing/grant_writing_specificity_in_writing.html

test: Search for novelty used as the reason for doing the work: has never been done, no one has studied, there are no data on, this gap has not been addressed. For each, check whether the text also says why the result would matter. Flag novelty offered as its own justification.
cost: Kraicer states it directly: never state or imply that a study will be carried out because it has never been done or there are no data on something, because this may be so because it is trivial. The reviewer's own reading of an unexplained gap is that the field left it alone on purpose.
suggestion: Replace the absence claim with the consequence claim, saying what becomes decidable once the gap is filled, and separately state what is novel and what is merely confirmatory.
mechanism: Gap statements are the easiest justification to write and they invite the one inference the applicant cannot afford, which is that the gap is uninteresting. Reviewers who work in the field have a standing explanation for every gap they know about. Naming the consequence forecloses the trivial reading and is the same sentence the funder's importance criterion asks for.
counter_case: Where a gap exists because a method was previously unavailable and the proposal supplies it, the absence is the argument; say which barrier fell and when.
source: Jacob Kraicer (Director of Research Grants, Human Frontier Science Program), The Art of Grantsmanship, published by HFSP, section 3.6.1 General ('Never state or imply that a study will be carried out "because it has never been done" or "there are no data on ...". This may be so because it is trivial.'; 'State clearly what is novel, and what is merely confirmatory.'). URLs: HFSP, The Art of Grantsmanship — https://www.hfsp.org/sites/default/files/webfm/Communications/The%20Art%20of%20Grantsmanship.pdf

test: For every preliminary or progress claim, check whether the actual data appear, meaning a figure, a table or a stated number, rather than a summary assertion that the data exist. Flag claims supported only by an assertion or by a phrase such as data not shown or results available on request.
cost: Kraicer's instruction for both progress and preliminary sections is the same phrase twice: present the actual data, show the actual data, because this is what establishes experience, competence and credibility. A claim that the data exist establishes none of those, and the funder's feasibility judgement then rests on nothing.
suggestion: Show the number or the panel, in the page budget you have, and drop the claim rather than asserting evidence the reader cannot see.
mechanism: Preliminary sections are compressed last, and the first thing cut is the figure, leaving the sentence that referred to it. The reviewer is being asked to believe the applicant can do the work, and the only currency for that is data on the page. No grant funder in the sources reviewed prohibits 'data not shown' by name, so the rule here rests on the positive instruction to show the data rather than on a prohibition.
counter_case: Where the data are voluminous and the claim is a summary of many runs, one aggregate figure plus the count is the right showing. The fault is no showing at all.
source: Jacob Kraicer (Director of Research Grants, Human Frontier Science Program), The Art of Grantsmanship, published by HFSP, sections 3.6.2.4 Progress and 3.6.2.5 Preliminary Data ('Review your preliminary studies and results. Present the actual data. This will help establish your experience, competence and credibility.'; 'Describe preliminary data that are relevant and pertinent. Show the actual data.'). URLs: HFSP, The Art of Grantsmanship — https://www.hfsp.org/sites/default/files/webfm/Communications/The%20Art%20of%20Grantsmanship.pdf

test: Go through the methodology and mark each component as standard in the field or as introduced by this project. Check the text says which is which. Flag any component whose status the reader must infer.
cost: The Social Science Research Council states the requirement plainly. Help readers from other fields recognize what parts of your methodology are standard and which are innovative. Unmarked, a standard component reads as unwarranted novelty to a generalist and an innovative one reads as routine, so both the ambition and the feasibility judgements land wrong.
suggestion: Add a status clause to each component, citing the literature for the standard parts and naming the departure for the new ones.
mechanism: A specialist reads the status off the method names without noticing they are doing it, and the applicant writes for that reader. Panels mix specialists with generalists who cannot make the distinction, and the two errors run in opposite directions, so the section's credibility depends on which reader you get. One clause per component removes the dependence.
counter_case: In an entirely specialist review, such as ERC remote reviewers at Step 2, the status markers spend page budget on something the reader already knows; write them for the generalist pass.
source: [name] Przeworski and Frank Salomon, On the Art of Writing Proposals, Social Science Research Council, section 'Describe Your Methodology' ('help readers from other fields recognize what parts of your methodology are standard, which are innovative'). URLs: SSRC, On the Art of Writing Proposals — https://s3.amazonaws.com/ssrc-cdn1/crmuploads/new_publication_3/the-art-of-writing-proposals.pdf

test: Measure the length of every figure and table caption and check the font size against the body text. Flag captions longer than about 60 words and any caption set below the minimum font size the call specifies.
cost: Cronan and Deckard describe the pattern and the outcome: some applicants use the caption to get around font limitations by putting a lengthy discussion in 9 point type, and a grumpy reviewer will just skip the entire figure. Funders that specify a minimum font size condition their promise to read on that size being respected.
suggestion: Cut the caption to what the reader needs to interpret the panels, move any discussion into the body text at body size, and reset the caption to the minimum permitted size.
mechanism: Captions are the last refuge when a page limit bites, and they are the one place a reduced font looks conventional. The reviewer's response is not to read it more slowly but to skip the figure, which costs the applicant both the caption and the figure. Since both the word count and the font size are properties of the file, this is fully mechanical.
counter_case: A composite figure genuinely needs a longer caption to identify its panels; length spent on panel identification is different from length spent on argument.
source: Mike Cronan and Lucy Deckard (Academic Research Funding Strategies, formerly Texas A&M Office of Research Development and Grant Writing), New Faculty Guide to Competing for Research Funding, 2nd ed. 2022 (copy hosted by Loyola University New Orleans Office of Academic Affairs), 'Avoid Irritating Your Reviewer' ('Very lengthy figure captions. ... some PIs see it as a way to get around the font limitations by including a lengthy discussion of the figure in the caption in 9 point font. A grumpy reviewer will just skip the entire figure. If the figure merits a lengthy discussion, include that in your main text.'). URLs: Cronan & Deckard, New Faculty Guide — https://academicaffairs.loyno.edu/sites/default/files/new_faculty_guide_to_competing_for_research_funding502_0.pdf

test: Find every sentence that criticises named prior work or a named group. Check whether it states a limitation of the work or a judgement about the people who did it. Flag dismissive verbs and adjectives (naive, flawed, simplistic, fails to appreciate, misguided, crude).
cost: Reid's handbook gives the reason applicants most need to hear: be prudent and cautious in your criticism of specific work since it might be the work of one of your reviewers. ERC instructs its own reviewers to avoid dismissive statements about the applicant, the proposed science, or the field, which is the standard the ecosystem applies in both directions.
suggestion: State the limitation as a property of the study design rather than of its authors, and name what the study did establish before naming what it did not.
mechanism: Reviewers are selected for closeness to your topic, so the probability that a criticised paper belongs to a reader is high rather than negligible. A dismissive adjective also removes the applicant's ability to claim the limitation as an opening, because a reader defending their own work stops crediting the argument. The limitation itself is usually the load-bearing part and survives the rewrite intact.
counter_case: A genuine and material error in prior work must be stated, and softening it into vagueness costs the gap that motivates the project. State it precisely and impersonally, and cite the work fairly.
source: C.P. Patrick Reid (University of Arizona), Handbook for Preparing and Writing Research Proposals, IUFRO-SPDC, 2000 (ISBN 3-901347-23-2), chapter 7 Literature Cited ('When you discuss specific citations in the body of your proposal, be as objective as possible and not overly critical of existing literature ... Be prudent and cautious in your criticism of specific work since it might be the work of one of your reviewers!'); ERC (European Research Council), Guide for Peer Reviewers to the ERC Starting and Consolidator Grant Calls, Version 6.0 (30 September 2025, 2026 calls), section 2.2 General guidelines ('Avoid dismissive statements about the applicant, the proposed science, or the scientific field concerned.'). URLs: IUFRO-SPDC proposal handbook — https://www.iufro.org/media/fileadmin/publications/manuals/research-proposal-writing-en.pdf; ERC Guide for Peer Reviewers V6.0 — https://ec.europa.eu/info/funding-tenders/opportunities/docs/2021-2027/experts/guide-for-peer-reviewers_he-erc-stg-cog_en.pdf

test: Split the document into its objective technical parts and its significance or impact parts. Scan the technical parts for emotive and evaluative words (exciting, remarkable, dramatic, stunning, revolutionary, groundbreaking, tremendous). Flag every occurrence in a technical part, and flag the significance part if such words outnumber the concrete consequences it names.
cost: Adelaide's guide scopes the rule to proposal parts rather than banning emphasis outright. You must not use emotional words in the technical part, and in the subjective part you can get away with a few words that convey excitement but should not overdo it. Temple's NSF briefing states the same as show, don't tell, and avoid hyperbole.
suggestion: In the technical part, replace each emotive word with the property that made it feel that way. In the significance part, keep at most a couple and make each one carry a consequence.
mechanism: Applicants are pushed toward superlatives by funders' own language about transformative and ground-breaking work, and they apply it uniformly across the document. An emotive word in a methods paragraph reads as the writer supplying the reader's reaction, which a reviewer resists. Scoping by section makes the rule enforceable, because the same word is a fault in one part and permitted in another.
counter_case: The significance or broader-impacts part is partly subjective by design, and a small number of words conveying importance belong there. The technical part is where the ban is absolute.
source: Derek Abbott, Guide to technical writing, School of Electrical and Electronic Engineering, University of Adelaide, 'Dispassionate tone' ('A grant application has two parts: (a) a technical project description that is objective, and (b) a part that wants discussion about national benefit and significance ... You must not use emotional words in the technical part. But in the subjective part you can get away with a few words that convey excitement, but don't overdo it.'; 'Positive emotion: "This is an exciting development." Dispassionate version: "This is a significant development because..."'); Temple University Office of the Vice President for Research, Applying to NSF, 'Writing a Strong Project Description' ('Use plain language. Keep it simple and clear. "Show, don't tell." Avoid hyperbole.'). URLs: Abbott technical writing guide, Adelaide — https://www.eleceng.adelaide.edu.au/personal/dabbott/wiki/index.php/Guide_to_technical_writing; Temple University, applying to NSF — https://research.temple.edu/sites/research/files/Applying-to-NSF.pdf

test: Scan for complaints about the applicant's circumstances: previously inadequate funding, lack of equipment, a difficult department, unfair earlier reviews, limited institutional support. Flag each.
cost: Kraicer states it in four words plus a reason: don't complain about previously low or inadequate funding, this is self-defeating. Funders assess resources as a criterion, so a complaint reads as evidence against the resources element rather than as a case for support.
suggestion: Convert each complaint into a resource statement about what is now committed and what this grant supplies, and put context such as career breaks in the section the funder provides for it.
mechanism: Complaints are written from a sense of fairness and land as a feasibility risk, because the reviewer is asked whether adequate resources are available rather than whether they should have been. The same fact stated forward, as what the grant makes possible, answers the criterion instead of undermining it. Funders that want the context provide a named place for it, which is where it should go.
counter_case: Career breaks, caring responsibilities and major life events belong in the proposal, and ERC instructs panels to take them into account. State them as context in the section provided, not as grievance in the science.
source: Jacob Kraicer (Director of Research Grants, Human Frontier Science Program), The Art of Grantsmanship, published by HFSP, section 3.6.2.4 Progress ('Don't complain about previously low or inadequate funding. This is self-defeating.'); ERC, Information for Applicants to the Starting and Consolidator Grant Calls, Version 11.0, section 2.2 (career breaks and life events belong in the CV context block). URLs: HFSP, The Art of Grantsmanship — https://www.hfsp.org/sites/default/files/webfm/Communications/The%20Art%20of%20Grantsmanship.pdf

test: Scan for idioms, phrasal verbs, sporting and military metaphors, culture-bound references and humour (level playing field, low-hanging fruit, ballpark, home run, silver bullet, game changer, from scratch, tackle head-on). Flag each and check whether a plain equivalent exists.
cost: Kraicer states that many agencies, even national ones, send applications for review abroad, and instructs applicants to use language that will be easily understood by those for whom the language is foreign. An idiom a reviewer misparses costs the sentence, and they will not report that they missed it.
suggestion: Replace each idiom with its literal statement, and keep metaphors only where the vehicle is technical rather than cultural.
mechanism: Idioms feel like plain language to a native speaker precisely because they are processed without decomposition, so the writer cannot detect the cost. Panels are international by design at ERC, Horizon Europe and HFSP, and remote reviewers are drawn worldwide. Because the idiom lexicon is enumerable, this is one of the few register rules a script settles outright.
counter_case: A metaphor that has become the field's technical term, such as pipeline, bottleneck or pruning, is the correct name and replacing it obscures the meaning.
source: Jacob Kraicer (Director of Research Grants, Human Frontier Science Program), The Art of Grantsmanship, published by HFSP, section 3.1 General ('Remember that many agencies, even national ones, send applications for review abroad. Use language that will be easily understood by those for whom the language is foreign.'; 'Assume that you are writing for a reviewer in a somewhat related field, rather than for an expert directly in your area.'). URLs: HFSP, The Art of Grantsmanship — https://www.hfsp.org/sites/default/files/webfm/Communications/The%20Art%20of%20Grantsmanship.pdf

test: Search for the word proposal used where the referent is the research rather than the document. The goal of this proposal, this proposal will measure, the proposal's results. Flag each.
cost: Cronan and Deckard name the confusion and the correction. You should not say the goal of this proposal is to do the research, because that is the goal of your proposed project. The document has one goal, which is to be funded, and conflating it with the research reads as imprecision in the section where precision is being assessed.
suggestion: Use proposal for the document and project for the work, and check that each occurrence names the thing that actually has the property.
mechanism: The two words are interchangeable in speech about grants and diverge in writing, so the slip is invisible to the author. It is a small fault that accumulates, and Cronan and Deckard put it in a list of irritations they compare to a pebble in a shoe for a reviewer reading at two in the morning. The distinction is a fixed pair of words, so a script settles it.
counter_case: Statements genuinely about the document are correct with proposal: page counts, structure, the abstract, and what the proposal requests.
source: Mike Cronan and Lucy Deckard (Academic Research Funding Strategies, formerly Texas A&M Office of Research Development and Grant Writing), New Faculty Guide to Competing for Research Funding, 2nd ed. 2022 (copy hosted by Loyola University New Orleans Office of Academic Affairs), 'Avoid Irritating Your Reviewer' ('Using "proposal" when you mean "project." ... Therefore, you should not say, "the goal of this proposal is to [research goal here]." That's the goal of your proposed project.'). URLs: Cronan & Deckard, New Faculty Guide — https://academicaffairs.loyno.edu/sites/default/files/new_faculty_guide_to_competing_for_research_funding502_0.pdf

test: For each acronym, measure the distance in pages between its definition and each later use. Flag any acronym whose next use is more than about two pages after the definition, and any acronym used fewer than about three times in total.
cost: Cronan and Deckard put this first among reviewer irritants: nothing is more annoying than having to search for the definition of an acronym that was defined on page 2 and then used again on page 9. NIH's rule is per narrative section for the same reason, and a reviewer who cannot recall the expansion loses the sentence rather than pausing to search.
suggestion: Re-expand on first use in each major section, and delete acronyms that recur too rarely or too far apart to earn the abbreviation.
mechanism: Defining at first use satisfies the letter of every funder's rule while failing its purpose, because the rule assumes a continuous reader with a short memory. Reviewers read in fragments across weeks, so the definition is effectively lost after a page or two. The measurement is a page-distance computation over the rendered document, which no reader has to be asked to make.
counter_case: Acronyms the field uses universally and that appear in the panel descriptor need no re-expansion at any distance. The distance rule applies to terms the proposal itself coins.
source: Mike Cronan and Lucy Deckard (Academic Research Funding Strategies, formerly Texas A&M Office of Research Development and Grant Writing), New Faculty Guide to Competing for Research Funding, 2nd ed. 2022 (copy hosted by Loyola University New Orleans Office of Academic Affairs), 'Avoid Irritating Your Reviewer' ('Overuse of acronyms. Nothing is more annoying to a reviewer than having to search for the definition of an acronym that was defined on page 2 and then used again on page 9. Terms that are used just a few times in a proposal shouldn't be converted into acronyms unless the acronyms are universally used in your discipline and the reviewers all share your discipline.'); NIH, General Grant Writing Tips, Tip 3. URLs: Cronan & Deckard, New Faculty Guide — https://academicaffairs.loyno.edu/sites/default/files/new_faculty_guide_to_competing_for_research_funding502_0.pdf; NIH General Grant Writing Tips — https://grants.nih.gov/grants-process/write-application/general-grant-writing-tips

test: Search for references to a previous submission or to an earlier version of this work: as noted in our previous application, in response to the previous reviewers, this resubmission, our earlier proposal. Flag each occurrence in a document that will be read as new.
cost: Reid's checklist asks directly whether you have avoided reference to an earlier grant application that may otherwise confuse or frustrate a new reader. NIH tells reviewers to evaluate the full application as now presented rather than its responsiveness to the prior review, so the reference cannot be credited and only signals that a reader is missing context.
suggestion: Delete the back-reference and state the content it pointed at, and put any resubmission narrative only in the section the funder provides for it.
mechanism: Resubmissions are edited rather than rewritten, so pointers to the previous round survive into a document read by people who never saw it. A reader who meets one either goes looking for a document they do not have or concludes the proposal is not self-contained. Where a funder does provide an introduction-to-resubmission section, that is the only place the reference belongs.
counter_case: Where the funder asks for a response to previous reviews or an introduction to a resubmission, the reference is required. ERC's right-to-reply and NIH's resubmission introduction are both such places.
source: C.P. Patrick Reid (University of Arizona), Handbook for Preparing and Writing Research Proposals, IUFRO-SPDC, 2000 (ISBN 3-901347-23-2), Appendix III Preparation and Submission Checklist, category B Proposal Clarity ('Have you avoided reference to an earlier grant application that may otherwise confuse or frustrate a new reader?'); NIH, Evaluating Applications Under NIH's Simplified Review Framework, Additional Review Criteria ('Resubmissions: Evaluate the full application as now presented.'). URLs: IUFRO-SPDC proposal handbook — https://www.iufro.org/media/fileadmin/publications/manuals/research-proposal-writing-en.pdf

test: A rule or edit deletes, weakens, or replaces a hedge (may, might, appears, suggests, we argue, tentative modals), drops an intensifier from a graded absolute (almost all, fairly complete, largely), or removes a first-person stance marker (we find, in our view, as far as we can tell).
cost: Claim strength rises without the evidence rising with it. The author is left asserting something the results do not support, which is the defect reviewers punish hardest and the author is least likely to notice, because the sentence still reads fluently.
suggestion: Never apply automatically. Raise it as a query showing the before and after side by side, and state which claim would become stronger. Where the hedge really is empty filler, the query is still the correct output, because only the author knows whether the uncertainty is real.
mechanism: Hedges encode the distance between what was measured and what is being asserted. Deleting one is grammatical, meaning-preserving by every mechanical test, and semantically destructive. No free professional standard states this rule, which is why every source-derived rule that touches hedging arrived unguarded.
counter_case: None. A hedge deletion may turn out to be correct, but it is never correct to apply it without the author seeing it, because the editor cannot know the evidence behind the claim.
source: Local extension. Warrant: World Bank Publications Editorial Style Guide 2020 §A.1 requires unclear person and demonstrative reference to be pointed out rather than fixed at mechanical level; Editors Canada PES 2024 A13.1 forbids altering intended meaning, and claim strength is meaning. Empirical warrant: five rules across three provenances in this ledger were independently flagged unsafe for exactly this failure.

test: A rule's test covers two or more situations whose correct fixes differ, or point in opposite directions. Detect it by asking whether any single stated suggestion repairs every case the test matches.
cost: Applying the rule repairs one case and damages another. Because the test fires on both, the damage is invisible in the report, which shows only that the rule matched.
suggestion: Split the rule into one rule per situation before it is used at all, each with its own test and its own fix. A rule that cannot be split is a query-only rule.
mechanism: Bundling was the single most common cause of unsafe rules in this ledger. Prose advice from an authority routinely covers several cases in one paragraph, and compressing that paragraph into one test-and-fix pair silently merges them.
counter_case: A rule may cover several situations when the fix is genuinely identical across all of them, for example deleting a trailing space regardless of what precedes it.
source: Local extension, derived from the audit of this ledger: the majority of the 50 rules flagged unsafe as written were flagged for bundling.

test: A rounding, precision-harmonising, or number-normalising rule is about to touch a value that is exact rather than measured: a count, a random seed, a byte or parameter size, a hash, an identifier, a version number, or an epoch or step index.
cost: The value is destroyed rather than tidied. A rounded seed or step count cannot be recovered, and a reader can no longer reproduce the run.
suggestion: Restrict every precision rule to measured quantities. Before applying one, classify the number as measured or exact, and skip the exact ones.
mechanism: Precision rules exist because reporting more digits than the measurement error supports is misleading. That reasoning applies only to measurements. An exact integer has no measurement error, so there is no excess precision to trim.
counter_case: A very large exact count may be presented approximately in running prose for readability, provided the exact value appears in a table or the appendix.
source: Local extension. Empirical warrant: two rounding rules in this ledger, from Zobel and from the statistics-reporting standards, were independently flagged unsafe for exactly this, one naming counts, seeds and byte sizes explicitly.

test: A \cite key or bracketed reference names the work by description rather than by an author-year key (all-caps words, OUR, OWED, KEY).
cost: The reader cannot find the work, and the key survives into submission because it looks deliberate.
suggestion: Replace the descriptive stand-in with the real author-year key the moment the bib entry exists, and grep the file for remaining all-caps keys before every build.
mechanism: A descriptive stand-in reads as prose to a human and as a valid key to LaTeX, so neither the author nor the compiler flags it.
counter_case: A concurrently-submitted paper by the same authors under double-blind review must be cited as an anonymous descriptive reference ("(Anonymous, under review)" or a bracketed description), because a real author-year key would deanonymise the submission. Replacing the stand-in with the true key there breaks the venue's anonymity rule rather than fixing a placeholder.
source: erc-proposal 4db3b2197

test: A citation key's author segment does not match the paper's actual first author.
cost: Every in-text mention of the work carries the wrong name, and the error propagates to anyone who copies the key.
suggestion: Derive the key from the first author's surname at the moment the entry is created, and rename repo-wide with a single pass rather than fixing mentions one at a time.
mechanism: The same wrong key was renamed twice in this history, first to a wrong surname and then to the right one, so the cost of a late rename scales with the number of mentions.
counter_case: Large-consortium technical reports are conventionally keyed by the issuing organisation or the model, not the first listed author: openai2023gpt4, gemini2024, llama2, olmo2024. Renaming those to the first author's surname (achiam2023gpt4) makes the entry unrecognisable to every reader and co-author who knows it by the organisation.
source: erc-proposal 4be88b4cc

test: A citation key uses an ad-hoc short form where the venue publishes a canonical key.
cost: Two keys can point at one work, and the bibliography silently duplicates the entry.
suggestion: Take the key from the publisher's export instead of inventing a short form.
counter_case: A work with both a preprint and a later proceedings record has two records, and the numbers or section labels the paper quotes may come from the preprint. Swapping in the venue's canonical key silently redirects the reader to a different version whose tables and numbering may not match the quoted claim.
source: erc-proposal b623f0a70

test: One referent carries two labels in different sections (an abbreviation in one place, the spelled form in another).
cost: The reader has to work out that O2 and Objective~2 are the same thing, and cross-references stop being searchable.
suggestion: Pick the spelled form for body prose, and replace every abbreviated mention in one commit.
mechanism: The author's own review comment caught this before the prose did, which means the drift is invisible while writing a single section and only shows up when two sections are read together.
counter_case: Table headers, figure legends and axis labels where column width is the binding constraint are correctly abbreviated (O1, O2, O3) with the expansion given once in the caption. Spelling out "Objective~2" in every cell of a ten-column table forces a line break in each header and makes the table less readable, not more consistent.
source: erc-proposal c6ad377 -> 752032718

test: The same multi-token notation is typed out inline in several places instead of being bound to a macro.
cost: The forms drift apart, and one of them renders a hyphen as a minus sign.
suggestion: Define one macro for the notation and replace every inline occurrence.
mechanism: A reviewer note in this repo objected to the inline form on rendering grounds, and the macro conversion then fixed six sites at once.
counter_case: In a multi-file document whose sections are compiled standalone (a proposal where each part is built separately, or a shared preamble kept in another repo), a macro defined only in the main preamble makes the section fail to build or render as an undefined control sequence for a co-author. A notation that occurs twice inside one paragraph also gains nothing from a macro and costs an Overleaf co-author the ability to see what it renders as.
source: Multilingual-Knowledge-Transfer 6fc0e0947

test: A term is borrowed from a neighbouring field where it already means something else.
cost: Readers from that field read the wrong claim, and a reviewer spends the objection on vocabulary instead of the result.
suggestion: Either rename to a term the paper owns or define the local sense at first use, and do it throughout rather than at one site.
counter_case: When the borrowed term is the established name for this exact technique in the venue's own literature (attention, kernel, regret, distillation), renaming to a private coinage cuts the paper out of its own citation graph and makes it unfindable by people searching the familiar word. The correct move there is one sentence naming the analogy, which is what this repo ended up doing.
source: Multilingual-Knowledge-Transfer be896db31

test: A symbol's letters collide with a standard mathematical reading.
cost: The reader parses the symbol as an exponent or a different quantity before recovering.
suggestion: Rename the symbol to something with no standard reading in the surrounding notation.
source: Multilingual-Knowledge-Transfer ecbb81057
narrower_test: A multi-letter subscript or superscript is set in math italics rather than \mathrm/\text/\operatorname, so it renders as a product of single-letter variables ($x^{pos}$ rather than $x^{\mathrm{pos}}$). That is machine-checkable, has a unique repair, and carries its own counter-case (a genuine product of variables that only looks like a word).

test: A load-bearing term is used repeatedly without a definition anywhere in the paper.
cost: Each reader supplies a different definition, so disagreements about the result are really disagreements about the word.
suggestion: Define the term at first use in one sentence, or drop it for a narrower word the paper already defines.
counter_case: When the term is itself contested and the paper's point depends on that (semantics, reasoning, understanding, emergence), a one-sentence definition falsely settles a live disagreement and invites the objection that the authors have redefined the word to suit the result. The correct surface there is to name the disagreement and cite it, or to state which operational proxy is measured, not to legislate a definition.
source: Multilingual-Knowledge-Transfer 715783dfa

test: An abbreviation appears in a form that drops a letter of the thing it abbreviates.
cost: The short form looks like a different object, and search misses half the mentions.
suggestion: Expand the abbreviation at first use and make every later mention identical to that expansion's initials.
counter_case: LM and LLM are distinct established abbreviations. A paper that also judges with small or fine-tuned models correctly writes LM-judge for the general construct and reserves LLM-judge for the large-model instance; expanding every LM-judge to LLM-judge then asserts a scale property the experiments do not have.
source: do-llms-benefit-own-words 8171525ab

test: A section heading names a mechanism the section does not describe.
cost: The reader arrives with the wrong expectation and rereads the section to find the promised content.
suggestion: Rename the heading to the operation actually performed, and update the noun used for that operation in the body to match.
mechanism: The supervisor changed heading and body noun in the same commit, so the two have to move together or the mismatch just relocates.
counter_case: A paper organised by purpose rather than by pipeline correctly heads a section with what the step is for ("Making Responses Comparable") rather than with the operation it performs ("Response Filtering"). Renaming every such heading to the literal operation turns the table of contents into an implementation log and deletes the only place the reader learns why the step exists.
source: do-llms-benefit-own-words 796397703

test: Headings mix Title Case and sentence case within one document.
cost: The inconsistency reads as carelessness on the first page a reviewer sees.
suggestion: Choose one case convention and apply it to every heading in a single pass.
counter_case: Several venue style files mandate a mixture by level: Title Case for \section and sentence case for \subsection is required by common ACM and IEEE templates. Unifying to one convention there fights the class file and is reverted at camera-ready. Proper nouns, acronyms and defined terms also keep their capitals inside a sentence-case heading.
source: erc-proposal 3d331defc

test: A sectioning command has no \label while the text cross-references that section.
cost: Cross-references break or point at whatever label happens to be nearest.
suggestion: Add the \label on the same line as the heading when the heading is written, not when the first reference is added.
source: erc-proposal c18938ce7

test: Panels of a composite figure are referenced by digit while the figure itself is numbered.
cost: Figure~3(2) is ambiguous between panel two and figure two.
suggestion: Letter the panels and reference them by letter.
counter_case: When the artwork itself carries numbered callouts, as in a pipeline diagram with steps 1--3 or an annotated screenshot, the prose must match what is drawn. Lettering the references while the image still shows "2" sends the reader hunting for a panel (B) that does not exist in the figure.
source: Helix-Agent-Eval-ICML2026 094c39f6c

test: Two tables or figures share a \label because one was copied from the other.
cost: Both references resolve to one target and the reader is sent to the wrong table.
suggestion: Give the copy a distinct label at the moment of copying.
source: Do-LLMs-Play-Differently ea2f32484

test: A fitted or chosen hyperparameter is named in the method but its value appears nowhere.
cost: The result cannot be reproduced, and a reviewer reads the omission as a choice being hidden.
suggestion: State the values in the setup, or point to a table that carries them for a representative run.
mechanism: The same reviewer asked for these values in four separate commits before they were supplied, so the gap survives normal rereading.
counter_case: When the parameter is fitted per instance (per language pair, per seed, per fold) or deliberately swept because the claim is robustness across the sweep, there is no single value to state, and inserting one asserts a tuned choice that was never made. The correct surface is the range plus the fitting criterion, or a released config, not a number in the setup.
source: Multilingual-Knowledge-Transfer 95fd8135f

test: A number is reported with a plus-minus term whose meaning is never stated.
cost: The reader cannot tell a standard deviation from a range, so the number carries no weight.
suggestion: Say at first use what the plus-minus term measures and over what population.
source: Instructions-shape-Production 49ac72e6e

test: A figure shows deltas without the caption naming the baseline they are relative to.
cost: The reader cannot sign or scale the bars, and the panel is unusable on its own.
suggestion: Name the reference condition in the caption.
counter_case: When the axis title already names the reference condition ("$\Delta$ accuracy vs. instruction-first"), the caption need not repeat it, and adding the gloss to each panel's caption in a four-panel figure pushes the caption past the column while telling the reader what the axis already said. The requirement is that the baseline be stated where the reader is looking, not specifically in the caption.
source: Instructions-shape-Production 49ac72e6e

test: A correlation coefficient is reported without the unit being ranked, the number of points, or an interval.
cost: The coefficient cannot be judged, so the strongest sentence in the results is the least checkable one.
suggestion: State what was ranked, how many points entered, and attach an interval or p-value.
counter_case: When the correlation describes two complete populations rather than a sample, for instance the rank agreement between two full leaderboards over all of their entries, a p-value tests a sampling hypothesis nobody holds and dresses a description up as inference. Reporting n and what was ranked is right there; attaching an interval is not.
source: Instructions-shape-Production 49ac72e6e

test: An empty \citep{} or \cite{} sits in the text.
cost: The build emits a bare bracket and the claim ships with no support.
suggestion: Grep for cite commands with empty braces before every build and fill or cut them.
mechanism: Three separate repos in this corpus shipped an empty cite command through many commits, so the pattern is not one author's slip.
source: erc-proposal 8bcc088b1

test: A factual claim about prior work ends without a citation.
cost: The claim reads as the authors' assertion, and a reviewer who disagrees has nothing to check.
suggestion: Attach the citation to the clause that carries the claim rather than to the end of the paragraph.
counter_case: When a three-sentence passage is entirely attributable to one source cited at its end, moving a citation onto each clause implies three independent sources for one finding. Statements that are common ground in the venue (transformers use attention) also correctly carry no citation, and citing every clause makes the paragraph unreadable.
source: erc-proposal 175ded591
