test: A named dataset, model or benchmark is first mentioned with no citation.
cost: The reader cannot tell which version is meant, and comparison to other papers using the name becomes guesswork.
suggestion: Cite at the first mention of every named artifact.
counter_case: Most venues forbid citations in the abstract, so a benchmark's genuine first mention there correctly carries none and the citation belongs at the first body mention. Likewise, in a table that lists thirty model names, citations go in a single column or the caption; a \citep in each cell destroys the layout.
source: do-llms-benefit-own-words 667e926cb

test: The body asserts a result whose supporting table or figure lives only in the appendix.
cost: A reader who does not turn to the appendix has to take the claim on trust.
suggestion: Move the smallest sufficient evidence into the body, or state the number inline in the sentence that makes the claim.
mechanism: Two reviewers in this corpus raised appendix imbalance independently, and one of them raised it twice.
counter_case: In a page-limited submission whose main claim already has its own body figure, the appendix table is the twenty-language breakdown, and pulling the smallest sufficient piece of it into the body displaces the figure that carries the headline result. Robustness checks and negative controls also belong in the appendix by design, and promoting them buries the contribution.
source: Multilingual-Knowledge-Transfer a13e6b39e

test: A figure is included as a raster file (.png or .jpg) rather than vector.
cost: Axis text blurs at print size and the plot cannot be zoomed.
suggestion: Export plots as PDF and keep raster only for photographs or screenshots.
counter_case: Scatter plots, t-SNE projections and attention heatmaps with 10^5 or more marks produce vector PDFs of tens of megabytes that stall the viewer and can breach arXiv's size limit. A 600 dpi PNG is the correct export there, as it is for photographs and screenshots.
source: do-llms-benefit-own-words 89b20b3ef

test: The related-work section was written from memory with no record of a literature sweep.
cost: A missed closely-related paper becomes a reviewer's first objection.
suggestion: Run named searches before the section is finalised and note which were run.
source: Multilingual-Knowledge-Transfer 39a9d0688
narrower_test: The related-work section cites nothing from the last twelve months, or nothing from the two most recent proceedings of the target venue, in an area with active recent output. That is checkable from the .bib alone and carries its own counter-case (a section on a settled classical result).

test: A caption reports the paper's findings instead of describing what the panels show.
cost: The reader cannot decode the figure without the body text, so the figure stops standing alone.
suggestion: Open with one bottom-line sentence, then describe the axes, colours and panels, and leave interpretation to the body.
mechanism: The resolution in this repo followed the note's shape exactly, with a bottom line first and a panel-by-panel description after.
counter_case: A single-panel figure with two labelled bars needs no walkthrough of axes, colours and panels; adding one restates the graphic and pushes the caption past the column. Some journals also specify the caption as a findings statement with the description carried by the axis labels, and rewriting to a panel-by-panel description there fights the house style.
source: Multilingual-Knowledge-Transfer e3d2fd421

test: A qualitative claim about the data is made with no instance shown.
cost: The reader cannot calibrate what the category covers and the claim stays unfalsifiable.
suggestion: Insert one concrete instance where the claim is made rather than promising it in an appendix.
source: do-llms-benefit-own-words ab23c70b1
narrower_test: A category the paper coins for its own data (a failure mode, a prompt type, a taxonomy label) is used in a claim, and no instance of that category appears anywhere in the paper, appendix, or released artifact.

test: A paragraph runs a measured result and an explanation for it together without marking which is which.
cost: The reader inherits the explanation as a finding, and the paper claims more than it measured.
suggestion: Split the sentence so the measurement stands alone, then attribute the explanation as an assumption or tie it to the prior result that supports it.
counter_case: Where the paper measured the mechanism directly rather than inferring it, the fused sentence is one intervention result: 'accuracy drops 4 points when the shared tokens are removed, because removing them severs the shared representation' reports an ablation whose whole point was manipulating the cause. Splitting it into a measurement plus an attributed assumption demotes a causal finding to a guess.
source: Multilingual-Knowledge-Transfer 980e4b073

test: A section heading or opening sentence states the conclusion the section is about to test.
cost: The experiment reads as confirmation rather than a test, which invites the reviewer to look for the missing control.
suggestion: Set up the question in the heading and the opening, and let the result land where it is measured.
counter_case: Papers organised as a list of findings title each results subsection with its finding ('Finding 3: disjoint tokens do not transfer') so a reviewer can navigate eight subsections by skimming. Neutralising those headings into questions makes the results section unnavigable and hides the contribution from anyone who does not read linearly.
source: Multilingual-Knowledge-Transfer 4c26b7d71

test: A correlational or probing result is introduced with a proof verb (establish, prove, confirm).
cost: The claim outruns the design, and one reviewer objection removes the paper's headline.
suggestion: Use a verb that matches the evidence, such as demonstrate for a measured effect or find for an observation.
mechanism: This edit was made twice in one paper, first from establish to demonstrate and then further down to a plain verb.
counter_case: A declared replication legitimately uses 'confirm': 'we confirm the layer-wise pattern reported by Chen et al. on two further language pairs' is accurate, and downgrading it to 'demonstrate' erases the fact that the prediction existed before the experiment was run.
source: Instructions-shape-Production 2918d8778

test: A frequency adverb (often, frequently, typically) quantifies a result the paper measured on one setup.
cost: The reader generalises past the evidence, and the sentence cannot be defended if a second setup disagrees.
suggestion: Replace the frequency claim with a possibility claim, or state the setup the frequency was measured over.
counter_case: When the adverb reports a measured within-setup rate over many items ('the model often ignores the constraint' standing for 63% of 500 prompts), the frequency word is the result. Replacing it with 'may' throws away a measured rate and asserts something strictly weaker than the data.
source: do-llms-benefit-own-words 27fca0e8d

test: A hedged comparative names no baseline and no amount (better performance to an extent).
cost: The sentence cannot be checked in either direction, so it carries no information.
suggestion: Name the quantity recovered and what it is recovered against.
counter_case: Abstract and introduction sentences are conventionally qualitative, with baseline and amount supplied in the results table. Forcing 'recovers 4.2 of the 6.1 points lost relative to the monolingual baseline' into an abstract that already carries three such comparisons buries the claim in numbers the reader cannot yet interpret.
source: Do-LLMs-Play-Differently e8322eb9f

test: A single coefficient stands in for a range that varies across the models tested.
cost: The reader treats one model's number as the population value.
suggestion: Attach the axis the number varies along in the same clause.
counter_case: When the sentence is about one named model ('the strongest model reaches 0.92'), the single number is exact. Attaching 'depending on the model' converts a precise per-model figure into a vague range and suggests 0.92 was never actually observed.
source: Do-LLMs-Play-Differently e8322eb9f

test: An intensifier or minimiser sits next to a number that already carries the size (only minor deviations of 0.7).
cost: The word and the number make the same point twice, and the word is the one that can be disputed.
suggestion: Delete the qualifier and give the number its unit and its scale instead.
counter_case: A minimiser that carries a comparison the bare number cannot must stay: 'deviations of only 0.7 pp against a 12 pp effect' uses 'only' to relate two magnitudes, and deleting it hands the reader the size judgement the sentence was making. The mined edit itself kept 'only' and deleted only 'minor'.
source: Instructions-shape-Production 6fb5368a5

test: The discussion converts a measured effect into a deployment benefit the paper did not measure.
cost: The specific unmeasured benefits (memory, cost) are the easiest sentence in the paper to reject.
suggestion: State the measured effect and its scope, and leave the downstream benefit to future work.
counter_case: Where the deployment consequence is arithmetic rather than empirical, stating it is a derivation: halving the sequence length halves the KV cache at fixed batch and layer count. Deferring that to future work hides a consequence the reader can verify on the spot and makes the paper look unaware of it.
source: do-llms-benefit-own-words 27fca0e8d

test: A mechanism sentence proposes a cause in terms too vague to test.
cost: The sentence is both unsupported and unfalsifiable, so it costs credibility without buying anything.
suggestion: Either drop the sentence or restate the mechanism as the specific constraint it implies.
source: Multilingual-Knowledge-Transfer 5b46569ac
narrower_test: A causal sentence names its cause with an abstract noun (capacity, interference, pressure, competition), no quantity in the sentence could be measured or varied to test it, and the sentence does not sit in a paragraph labelled as hypothesis or speculation.

test: A hedge sits on a claim the paper's own numbers fully support.
cost: Under-claiming buries the contribution and reads as uncertainty about the result.
suggestion: Drop the hedge where the measurement is direct, and keep it only where the inference is indirect.
mechanism: Both directions occur in this corpus, twenty-one hedge removals against a smaller number of hedge additions, so the rule is to match the verb to the evidence rather than always to soften.
counter_case: A hedge that marks scope rather than confidence must survive: where the gain appears on three of five datasets, 'can improve' is the accurate form and 'improves' overclaims. The numbers fully supporting the claim on the subsets where it holds does not license the unhedged general form.
source: do-llms-benefit-own-words 5b2b2512b

test: Another paper's position is reported with a verb that grades it (assumes, merely).
cost: The reader cannot separate the cited claim from the authors' opinion of it.
suggestion: Use a neutral reporting verb and put the disagreement in its own sentence.
counter_case: When the cited paper itself labels the proposition an assumption, 'assumes' is the neutral report and 'posits' misdescribes it. Neutralising a verb that already matches the source's own framing introduces a factual error about the cited work.
source: Instructions-shape-Production e4e42ec3b

test: A cross-reference resolves to the section it sits inside.
cost: The reader follows the pointer, lands where they already are, and loses the thread.
suggestion: After any section move, resolve every \ref in the moved text and delete the ones that now point at their own home.
mechanism: This corpus records the failure arising specifically from moving a block between work packages, so the check belongs to the move, not to the prose pass.
counter_case: A float that names its own section is doing locating work, because floats drift pages from their home: a caption reading 'Overview of the pipeline of Section 3' can print on the page before Section 3 starts, and a reader who arrives at the figure first needs the pointer. Deleting it there strands them.
source: erc-proposal e33c79f

test: The same claim is stated in two sections in two voices.
cost: The reader cannot tell whether the second statement adds anything, and the weaker phrasing dilutes the stronger.
suggestion: Cut the duplicate, but first check whether any qualifying clause survives only in the copy being cut.
mechanism: The note in this repo flags exactly that hazard, a design constraint carried only by the redundant copy.
counter_case: In an ERC B2, or any document whose sections are read separately by different assessors, each work package must be independently readable, so the objective is restated in every package by design. Cutting the second statement leaves a reviewer who reads only WP2 without the claim that package exists to serve.
source: erc-proposal e33c79f

test: One paragraph carries two claims that the document's structure assigns to different sections.
cost: Neither section reads as complete, and the reader meets the second claim before its setup.
suggestion: Name the cut point sentence by sentence before splitting, and move each half under the heading that owns it.
counter_case: A paragraph whose content is the relation between the two claims is destroyed by the split, because neither half then carries the link that was the point. The signature is a topic sentence that names both limbs, as in a paragraph whose subject is the interface between a mechanism and its evaluation.
source: erc-proposal ff4896a

test: The last sentence of a section and the first sentence of the next share no term or consequence.
cost: The reader experiences a jump and rebuilds the argument themselves.
suggestion: Read consecutive boundaries as pairs, and where the step is real, name it in the opening clause rather than starting cold.
counter_case: A section that opens a genuinely independent question should start cold. The first sentence of a new experimental section following a completed argument must not be bridged, since a connective there falsely implies the new experiment continues the previous one rather than standing beside it.
source: Multilingual-Knowledge-Transfer 39a9d0688

test: Interpretation of results is interleaved with the results themselves instead of sitting in its own section.
cost: The reader cannot separate what was measured from what it is taken to mean, and the results section reads as argument.
suggestion: Collect the interpretation into a discussion section and leave the results section to the measurements.
mechanism: Three separate notes in one repo make this request, which makes it the most repeated structural complaint in the corpus.
counter_case: A chained multi-experiment section must interleave, when the design of experiment 2 is motivated by the interpretation of experiment 1. Deferring all interpretation to one discussion section forces the reader through three result sets before learning why any was run, and in an 8-page limit the separate section spends a page restating numbers.
source: Multilingual-Knowledge-Transfer 738df3bd8

test: A summarising paragraph sits mid-results rather than at a section boundary.
cost: The register shifts to textbook or blog and the reader loses the experimental thread.
suggestion: Move the summary to the discussion or the section close.
counter_case: In a long results section, a mid-section recap of what the first three subsections established is the waypoint that lets the reader follow the fourth. Moving it to the discussion leaves the later subsections resting on findings the reader has to reassemble from memory.
source: Multilingual-Knowledge-Transfer c6138ef91

test: A metrics or evaluation section precedes the benchmarks and systems whose properties it measures.
cost: Every metric is defined over objects the reader has not met.
suggestion: Order the sections so each one's objects are introduced before its operations.
counter_case: When the metric is the paper's contribution and the benchmarks are merely its instantiations, metrics belong first: a measurement paper defines the measure, then shows what it does on each system. The same holds when the metrics are standard (accuracy, macro-F1), where defining them up front keeps the benchmark description uninterrupted.
source: Helix-Agent-Eval-ICML2026 b5cc5586e

test: A paragraph becomes redundant after a reordering but stays in place.
cost: The reader reads a preview of material that now sits earlier in the paper.
suggestion: When sections are reordered, reread the paragraphs that bridged them and cut the ones whose work the new order already does.
counter_case: The paragraph flagged as redundant is often the only place a term or a design constraint is stated in full, the earlier occurrence being an instance rather than the definition; cutting on redundancy alone silently deletes the definition. In a document read non-linearly, such as a proposal's work packages, the recap is also load-bearing for a reader who entered at that section.
source: Helix-Agent-Eval-ICML2026 43e83b1bd

test: A forward reference points at a section without saying what the reader will find there.
cost: The reader cannot decide whether to jump, so the pointer costs attention and returns nothing.
suggestion: Say what the target section supplies, or cut the reference.
counter_case: A reference that prints a descriptive name needs no gloss, because the section title is the gloss ('we follow the evaluation protocol of the Framework section'). Likewise a compact deferral list at a section's end ('the remaining ablations are in A.3, A.4 and A.5') only needs to tell the reader the material is deferred; three glosses would run longer than the material.
source: Helix-Agent-Eval-ICML2026 b5cc5586e

test: A paragraph or sentence opens with a bare demonstrative whose referent is the previous paragraph as a whole.
cost: The reader guesses the antecedent, and a later edit to the previous paragraph silently changes the meaning.
suggestion: Name the referent at the opening, and use the bare demonstrative only inside a sentence whose subject is already fixed.
mechanism: Edits in both directions appear in this corpus, so the rule is about position rather than about avoiding demonstratives.
counter_case: After a display equation or an enumerated construction with no short name, a bare demonstrative is the natural resumption: 'This gives the bound in (4).' Naming the referent forces a restatement of the whole construction, which is both longer and less clear than the pronoun.
source: Multilingual-Knowledge-Transfer 5f9dd4b0d

test: A sentence explains the authors' writing decision rather than the subject.
cost: A slot that could carry a fact carries process commentary instead, and in a length-capped document that slot is expensive.
suggestion: Replace the remark about the writing with the content it was justifying.
counter_case: A paper that deliberately renames a contested concept needs the terminology note as content: stating which of several competing names in the literature it adopts, and against which, is what stops a reader mapping the term onto the wrong prior work. Replacing that sentence with subject matter removes the anchor.
source: erc-proposal 7cbba2cc1

test: A noun phrase repeats a subject the sentence has already fixed (the frontier itself, this same phenomenon).
cost: The repetition slows the sentence and adds nothing recoverable.
suggestion: Pronominalise once the referent is unambiguous in the clause.
counter_case: 'The frontier itself' is emphatic rather than redundant, since 'itself' contrasts the frontier with its neighbourhood and 'it' cannot carry that contrast. Pronominalisation also fails whenever another noun of the same number and gender intervenes between referent and pronoun, because the reader then has two candidates.
source: erc-proposal d8af5c31f

test: A verb is wrapped in an attributive frame that adds no attribution (is known to gain, has been shown to).
cost: Three words of frame buy nothing, and the passive frame hides who found it.
suggestion: Use the plain verb and put the attribution in the citation.
counter_case: 'Has been shown to' earns its words when it separates others' established finding from the authors' assertion in a sentence carrying no citation of its own, and 'is known to' is the honest marker for field folklore with no citable source. Flattening either makes the paper appear to assert the claim on its own evidence.
source: erc-proposal b623f0a70

test: The limitations passage apologises for the work rather than bounding it.
cost: The reader takes the register as a signal that the authors doubt the result.
suggestion: State the boundary as a scope condition and say what falls inside it.
counter_case: A limitations section that concedes a real defect found after the experiments (a leaked test split, a scoring bug in one baseline) is correctly written as a plain concession. Recasting it as a scope condition there reads as concealment to a reviewer who can see the defect, and in a venue with a responsible-research checklist the softened wording fails the checklist item.
source: Multilingual-Knowledge-Transfer 64025e5c6

test: The body carries a full replication dump (every training detail) rather than the details needed to follow the argument.
cost: The reader loses the argument in the parameters, and the space is unavailable for the result.
suggestion: Keep one paragraph of the details that change the interpretation and send the rest to an appendix pointer.
counter_case: A resource, dataset or reproducibility-track paper whose contribution is the artifact itself needs the full training and construction detail in the body, and a length-capped document with no appendix (an ERC B2, a 2-page extended abstract) has nowhere to send it. Moving the details out in either case deletes the contribution or the material.
source: Multilingual-Knowledge-Transfer dd60e89f8

test: A clause spells out a distinction the sentence's own words already carry (each with its own measure, over chunks rather than single words).
cost: The sentence gets longer without becoming more specific.
suggestion: Compress to the shorter phrasing and keep the distinction only where it does work.
mechanism: Compression of this shape is the single most frequent edit in the corpus at 215 occurrences, and it dominates in the length-capped proposal.
source: erc-proposal c5cf5293f
narrower_test: A sentence ends in a trailing appositive or a 'rather than' clause whose content words all already appear in the same sentence's head noun phrase. Flag only when deleting the trailing clause leaves every technical term and every quantifier in the sentence intact. The two mined examples do not share this shape, so they belong to different rules.

test: A nominalisation carries the verb of the clause (with no supervision of the, computation learned against).
cost: The agent disappears and the sentence takes longer to parse.
suggestion: Break to a new sentence with a finite verb and a named subject.
counter_case: A nominalisation that is the field's term of art ('with no supervision', 'gradient accumulation', 'ablation') must stay nominal, since the finite-verb rewrite invents an agent the setting does not have ('nobody supervises the objects'). A nominalisation in the opening slot also often repeats the previous sentence's topic, and breaking it into a new sentence with a fresh named subject snaps that given-new chain.
source: erc-proposal 9f38d3d37

test: Draft scaffolding (highlight boxes, italic review framing) is still around finished prose.
cost: The scaffolding reads as emphasis and misdirects the reviewer.
suggestion: Strip review-time markup in a dedicated pass before circulation.
counter_case: Some venues require a revision to mark its changes in colour, and some position papers use a boxed takeaway as final typography. Stripping \colorbox or the box environment in those two situations removes a required marking or a designed element that the author put there for the printed page.
source: do-llms-benefit-own-words 24fd6e455

test: A comma joins two clauses that each carry an independent claim.
cost: The reader has to work out which claim is subordinate, and the sentence's logical structure is lost.
suggestion: Split at the comma into two sentences and let the second open with its own subject.
mechanism: Twenty-six such splits occur in this corpus, all in the length-capped proposal, so the pressure that produces the splice is compression.
source: erc-proposal d8af5c31f
narrower_test: A comma joins two spans that each carry their own subject and finite verb with no coordinating conjunction and no subordinator between them. The mined example ('necessary, since even') fails this test, since 'since' subordinates the second clause, so the rule as written flags correct subordination and its suggested split would drop the causal link.

test: A space sits between a word and a following \footnote, \cite or \ref.
cost: The footnote mark can wrap to the next line, and the reference can break across lines.
suggestion: Bind footnotes directly to the word and tie references with a non-breaking space.
source: Open-human-feedback c4bbfcd87
narrower_test: Split into two rules with different fixes. First, a space precedes \footnote or \footnotemark, and the fix is to delete the space so the mark sits against the word or its punctuation. Second, a plain space precedes \cite, \citep, \ref or \cref, and the fix is to replace it with a tie. As written the rule says 'bind directly', which applied to \citep yields 'Argilla(Smith, 2020)' with no space at all.

test: A reference is preceded by a plain space where the convention is a tie.
cost: The number can start a line on its own.
suggestion: Use a tilde before every \ref, \cref and \cite.
source: Multilingual-Knowledge-Transfer 621180bfb

test: A verb does not agree with its subject after the subject was edited.
cost: The reader stumbles, and in a proposal the slip lands in a sentence a panel reads closely.
suggestion: Recheck the verb whenever the subject of a sentence is changed.
mechanism: Three such fixes in this corpus all follow an earlier edit to the same sentence's subject.
counter_case: Notional and collective agreement are correct English. 'A number of annotations were discarded' and, in British usage, 'the committee have agreed' both look like disagreement against the head noun, and forcing formal agreement ('a number ... was') makes the sentence wrong. The same applies to 'data' used as a plural in a paper that treats it that way throughout.
source: erc-proposal 505e5a859

test: A misspelling survives many commits in body prose.
cost: The reviewer reads the paper as unproofed, which colours every later judgement.
suggestion: Run a spellchecker over the .tex before every circulation, since these errors do not surface by rereading.
mechanism: Six independent misspellings in this corpus each survived multiple commits, including two inside review notes that were themselves being edited.
counter_case: Misspellings inside quoted material must be preserved. Verbatim model outputs, dataset examples, annotator comments and a cited paper's own title carry their errors as data, and a typo-robustness experiment needs its perturbed strings intact. A spellchecker pass that rewrites those destroys the evidence the sentence is presenting.
source: Open-human-feedback d7d349d45

test: A word is split or run together by a typing slip (occursin, difficuprioritisations).
cost: The sentence becomes unreadable at that point, and search for the intended word fails.
suggestion: Spellcheck catches these, and they cluster in text edited late.
counter_case: Code identifiers and product names look exactly like run-together slips. 'occursin' is a real Julia function, and 'argmax', 'softmax', 'GSM8k' and camel-cased model names are correct as written. Splitting any of them corrupts a reference a reader would try to run or look up.
source: Helix-Agent-Eval-ICML2026 3fe78e4d4

test: A negated modal is written as two words where the closed form is standard.
cost: Minor, but it is the kind of slip a close reader notices on page one.
suggestion: Use the closed form.
counter_case: 'can not' stays two words when 'not' scopes over a following phrase rather than the modal, as in 'the probe can not only detect the feature but also localise it', and in a contrastive pair such as 'a model can act or can not act'. Closing those to 'cannot' reverses the sentence.
source: Instructions-shape-Production a272a3c9c

test: A footnote is duplicated at each reuse instead of being labelled and referenced.
cost: The same URL appears several times and the footnote numbering misleads.
suggestion: Label the footnote once and reference the label at later mentions.
counter_case: When the two uses are pages apart in a two-column layout, a reader hitting 'see footnote 3' has to flip back, while a repeated URL costs one line. Several venue styles also disallow \ref into a footnote, and the numbering breaks silently when the footnote moves column. Repeating is also required when the second mention needs a different access date or a different anchor in the same page.
source: Helix-Agent-Eval-ICML2026 e2106cf5e

test: An identity field carries a template placeholder (XXXX for an ORCID, Prof. Name Surname, Coauthor / Affiliation).
cost: A submitted document asserts a false or empty fact about a person, which is the one class of error that cannot be explained away.
suggestion: Grep for placeholder shapes in every identity field before submission, and treat an unfilled one as a blocking defect.
mechanism: This corpus contains the pattern in two unrelated repos, one a grant CV and one a paper author block, so it is a property of template reuse rather than of one author.
source: erc-proposal 0f0951ae1

test: A CV line states an award in wording that hides whether it was taken up.
cost: The line reads as a held fellowship when it was declined, which a panel can check.
suggestion: Say the disposition explicitly for every award listed.
mechanism: The author's own query note raised this before the wording was fixed, which is what turned an ambiguous line into two precise ones.
counter_case: Awards with no take-up axis get worse under this rule. A best-paper award, a medal or a prize cannot be held or declined, so 'Best Paper Award (2024, held)' reads as though the author was unsure what the award was. Stating disposition for a competitive grant that was awarded and returned is right, applying it to every line is not.
source: erc-proposal 0a02767e9

test: The same quantity appears with different values in the table, the figure and the prose.
cost: Whichever number the reader checks first, one of the three is wrong, and the paper cannot be trusted on any number.
suggestion: After every rerun, update table, figure and prose in one commit and diff the three.
mechanism: Two independent notes in this repo report the mismatch, one across a table and a figure and one across two sections' baselines, so the failure is a rerun that touched one surface.
counter_case: The three surfaces sometimes report different quantities under the same name, for instance a table of test-set scores beside prose quoting the development set, or a figure showing per-seed values beside a prose mean. Unifying the values then overwrites a correct number with one measured on other data. The fix in that situation is to label each surface, not to make them agree.
source: Multilingual-Knowledge-Transfer aef267d58

test: A results table ships with placeholder cells (x.x, xx) inside real rows.
cost: A reader or co-author reads a placeholder as a measured value.
suggestion: Mark placeholder cells with a macro that renders visibly and check that no such macro survives the final build.
mechanism: This repo used a \temp macro for exactly this, which is why the placeholders were findable at all.
source: Multilingual-Knowledge-Transfer 852d30a4f

test: A number in the prose was superseded by a rerun and the prose still carries the old value.
cost: The paper states a result the current experiments do not produce.
suggestion: Keep reported numbers in one place the prose reads from, or diff every number against the run log before circulation.
source: Multilingual-Knowledge-Transfer 6fc0e0947

test: Prose drafted by an assistant is not distinguished from author-written prose in the working copy.
cost: Nobody can tell later which sentences a human vouched for.
suggestion: Label each block's provenance and word count in a comment, and update the label when the author revises.
mechanism: This repo tracks provenance and a word budget per block in comments, and the label flips from assistant-drafted to author-revised as the block is worked.
counter_case: arXiv and most camera-ready pipelines distribute the .tex source, so provenance and word-budget comments ship to every reader of the bundle, and an anonymised submission's supplementary source can leak workflow details about the authors. Labels also go stale on a heavily co-edited block, at which point a comment saying 'assistant-drafted' asserts something false about prose the author has since rewritten twice.
source: erc-proposal 06bc90219

test: An anonymised submission carries a placeholder where the de-anonymised link will go.
cost: The placeholder ships in the camera-ready and the artifact stays unreachable.
suggestion: Wrap every de-anonymisation edit in a macro that is visible in the camera-ready build and invisible under review.
counter_case: Under review the placeholder is the correct content. Filling it in the anonymous build breaks double-blind, and deleting it drops the artifact promise the reviewers are asked to weigh. The rule only holds for the camera-ready build, so applying it to the submission harms the submission.
source: Multilingual-Knowledge-Transfer 89123fa

test: A section carries an under-construction warning in prose rather than in a comment.
cost: A co-author or reviewer reading the shared draft cannot tell whether the warning is current, and it can compile into the PDF.
suggestion: Put draft status in a comment or a review macro and never in body text.
mechanism: The supervisor deleted this line rather than updating it, which is the usual fate of status text left in prose.
counter_case: A draft circulated to co-authors as a PDF is exactly the situation where the warning belongs in the body. Co-authors who read only the compiled document never see a .tex comment, so moving the notice into a comment hides the incompleteness from the readers it was written for. Body text is right until the draft stops being circulated as a PDF.
source: CUBE-position-paper 7f924160b

test: A word-budget or item-count comment states a number that the block no longer matches.
cost: The author trims against a stale target and either overshoots the cap or leaves space unused.
suggestion: Recompute the count in the same commit that edits the block.
mechanism: This proposal's own budget comments were corrected several times, so a stale count is the normal state unless the count is recomputed on every edit.
counter_case: Many of these comments state a target rather than a measurement, as in '182 words against a 165 target'. Recomputing overwrites the budget with the current length, after which the block has no target left and the author trims against nothing. Only the measured half of such a comment may be recomputed.
source: erc-proposal fbb56c1f4

test: A category sentence uses a grouping verb and a vague quantifier where a count would do (can be grouped into a small number of).
cost: The reader cannot tell how many categories there are, so the taxonomy carries no structure.
suggestion: Give the count and use a plain verb of observation.
counter_case: When the categories were not enumerated exhaustively, or when items fall into more than one, a stated count claims a completeness the annotation does not support. 'Fall into four categories' invites a reviewer to ask for the fifth, and the honest form is the open quantifier the mined fix itself kept ('one of a few').
source: do-llms-benefit-own-words 796397703

test: An orange or coloured placeholder stands where a count belongs.
cost: The draft shows a marker instead of a number and the marker can survive to submission.
suggestion: Fill the count and delete the colouring macro in the same edit.
source: Do-LLMs-Play-Differently e71975920

test: A results claim is qualified in the text but the qualifying comparison is never cited.
cost: The reader cannot place the result against the literature it partly contradicts.
suggestion: Add the citation that reports the contrasting finding in the same sentence.
counter_case: Sometimes no prior work reports the contrast, either because the qualification comes from the paper's own other experiment or because the contrasting result is unpublished. Adding the nearest plausible citation then attributes a finding to a paper that does not report it, which is worse than the missing reference. The fix there is a pointer to the paper's own section.
source: Multilingual-Knowledge-Transfer a3617f1a6

test: Count the admissible repairs for the problem. If exactly one correction is possible, the problem is a fixing case. If two or more defensible solutions exist, it is a flagging case.
cost: Editing where several repairs compete substitutes the editor's taste for the author's choice, and the author never learns a decision was made. Flagging where only one answer exists wastes the author's attention on a non-decision.
suggestion: Apply the cardinality test as the first gate on every finding. One admissible answer means edit silently. More than one means hand the decision back with the span quoted.
mechanism: SENSE separates 'fixing' from 'flagging' by whether more than one solution is possible. Cardinality is observable from the text itself, so it does not depend on guessing intent. It also aligns the two failure modes, since a single-answer fix cannot misrepresent the author and a multi-answer fix always can.
counter_case: A multi-answer problem that recurs on nearly every page can be settled once by a batched note stating the convention adopted, rather than by dozens of separate queries.
source: SENSE (Society of English-language professionals in the Netherlands), Guidelines for Proofreading Student Texts, Version August 2016, p.4, fixing versus flagging definition. https://www.sense-online.nl/files/esense/esense-public-files/759-sense-guidelines-for-proofreading-student-texts/file

test: The finding matches one of three triggers. The text is unclear so only the author can decide, or the issue sits outside the agreed remit, or the same issue recurs across the text.
cost: Without the three triggers, flagging degenerates into flagging whatever the editor happens to notice, and recurrent problems get repaired one instance at a time instead of being named as a pattern.
suggestion: Flag when the text is unclear, when the issue is out of remit, or when the issue is recurrent. State which of the three applies in the note itself.
mechanism: SENSE enumerates exactly these three grounds for flagging. Each names a limit on the editor rather than a defect in the writing, which is why the author has to be brought in. Recurrence is the one that most often gets mishandled, because the individually easy fix hides a decision the author should own.
counter_case: A recurrent problem with one admissible answer, such as a consistently misspelled technical term, can be fixed throughout and reported once instead of flagged.
source: Editors Canada is stricter here, but SENSE, Guidelines for Proofreading Student Texts, Version August 2016, p.2, three-category taxonomy. https://www.sense-online.nl/files/esense/esense-public-files/759-sense-guidelines-for-proofreading-student-texts/file

test: The change is a single-answer fix, but a reader looking at it would not immediately see why it was made.
cost: An unexplained correct change teaches the author nothing and invites a revert. On a student text it also removes the learning that was the point of the exercise.
suggestion: Fix and flag together. Make the correction and attach a one-line reason, so the author can accept it knowingly.
mechanism: SENSE keeps a third category for a correction plus explanation, used when the reason for the change may not be immediately clear. The change is safe on cardinality grounds, so it does not need permission. What it needs is legibility, which a short note supplies at almost no cost.
counter_case: Obvious typo repairs need no note, and annotating every one of them buries the notes that matter.
source: SENSE, Guidelines for Proofreading Student Texts, Version August 2016, p.2, 'fixing and flagging' used 'when the reason for the change may not be immediately clear'. https://www.sense-online.nl/files/esense/esense-public-files/759-sense-guidelines-for-proofreading-student-texts/file

test: Ask which norm the passage breaks. A correctness break means 'we don't say this in English' and covers spelling, grammar, vocabulary, punctuation and typing errors. A formulation break means 'we don't say this in academia' and covers style, expression, register, sentence construction and word order.
cost: Collapsing the two lets style preferences travel under the authority of correctness, which is how an editor ends up silently rewriting voice while claiming to fix errors.
suggestion: Fix correctness breaks silently. Route formulation breaks to the author, since academic norms vary by field, supervisor and venue.
mechanism: SENSE draws the line between the two questions explicitly and ties the fix-or-flag decision to it. Correctness is checkable against the language and has one answer. Formulation is checkable only against a target community the author knows better than the editor does.
counter_case: A house style sheet or an explicit brief can convert named formulation items into single-answer fixes, and then they are fixed silently like any correctness item.
source: SENSE, Guidelines for Proofreading Student Texts, Version August 2016, p.4, correctness versus formulation distinction. https://www.sense-online.nl/files/esense/esense-public-files/759-sense-guidelines-for-proofreading-student-texts/file

test: The text is a graduate student text and the finding is a mechanics problem, such as sentence combining, a comma splice, or subject-verb agreement.
cost: Fixing mechanics in a text that is being assessed transfers credit for the writing from the student to the editor, and the student never acquires the skill the assessment is testing.
suggestion: Err toward flagging rather than fixing, and leave the revision to the student.
mechanism: Editors Canada sets a deliberately stricter default for student work than commercial editing uses, because the text is evidence of the student's own ability. The same comma splice that is a silent fix in a trade book is a query in a thesis. Authorship integrity, not cardinality, is doing the work in this rule.
counter_case: Non-assessed writing, such as a commercial manuscript or a corporate report, inverts this default, and there mechanics are silent fixes.
source: Editors Canada, Guidelines for Ethical Editing of Graduate Student Texts, revised 2024-08-14, Part 1, p.2. https://editors.ca/wp-content/uploads/2023/07/Guidelines_Editing_GraduateStudentTexts_revised_08-14-2024.pdf

test: The draft query proposes the answer instead of asking for one, for example by offering a candidate reading of the sentence.
cost: A query that supplies the wording turns into dictation the author can only accept. On assessed work it also puts the editor's words into the student's text.
suggestion: Phrase the query so the onus stays with the author. Ask for clarification of the named span rather than proposing what it might mean.
mechanism: Editors Canada requires queries 'phrased to put the onus on the student' and warns against drafting alternatives. The asymmetry matters because authors accept suggestions under time pressure whether or not the suggestion is right. Asking for clarification produces the author's own repair, which is both more accurate and properly theirs.
counter_case: PES A12.3 asks the editor to offer a best solution where applicable, and outside assessed student work a query with one concrete option is usually faster for the author.
source: Editors Canada, Guidelines for Ethical Editing of Graduate Student Texts, revised 2024-08-14, Part 1, p.2, query phrasing. https://editors.ca/wp-content/uploads/2023/07/Guidelines_Editing_GraduateStudentTexts_revised_08-14-2024.pdf

test: A rewrite is needed only to make the problem visible, and the rewrite would replace wording the author chose.
cost: A demonstration rewrite that reads better than the original quietly becomes the new text, and new content smuggled into a query is content the author never wrote.
suggestion: Keep the author's own wording as far as possible in any illustrative rewrite, and introduce no new content in queries or changes.
mechanism: Editors Canada allows a rewrite that illuminates a problem while requiring the original wording be retained as much as possible. The purpose is diagnostic rather than stylistic, so anything beyond the minimum edit is scope creep. The no-new-content rule closes the remaining gap, since a query can inject material as effectively as an edit.
source: Editors Canada, Guidelines for Ethical Editing of Graduate Student Texts, revised 2024-08-14, Part 1, p.2, 'introduce no new content'. https://editors.ca/wp-content/uploads/2023/07/Guidelines_Editing_GraduateStudentTexts_revised_08-14-2024.pdf

test: The wording is wrong under the rules of grammar or fixed idiom, so no competent reader could take it as intended.
cost: Leaving an unambiguous grammar or idiom error in place while querying it spends the author's attention on a decision that has already been made by the language.
suggestion: Correct it as mechanical copy editing without a query.
mechanism: Editors Canada treats 'The cat sitted near the fire' and 'The cat sat on the fire' as clear errors in grammar and idiom respectively, and calls correcting them mechanical. The test is that the intended reading is recoverable and unique. That is the cardinality test resolving to one.
counter_case: On assessed student work the same errors may be flagged rather than fixed, because the mechanics are part of what is being assessed.
source: Editors Canada, Guidelines for Ethical Editing of Graduate Student Texts, revised 2024-08-14, Part 2, p.5, grammar and idiom examples. https://editors.ca/wp-content/uploads/2023/07/Guidelines_Editing_GraduateStudentTexts_revised_08-14-2024.pdf

test: The word is odd in its context but has a reading on which the author meant it. A near neighbour would be more expected.
cost: Correcting a possible diction error destroys a deliberate choice and leaves no trace that anything was decided. The author cannot recover what they wrote.
suggestion: Query the word rather than replacing it. Point at the word itself and ask the author to check it.
mechanism: Editors Canada contrasts 'The cat roared by the fire' with the grammar cases, calling it probably an error in diction that could be exactly what was intended. Two readings exist, so cardinality forbids a silent fix. Asking the author to check the dictionary keeps the choice with them and costs one line.
counter_case: When the surrounding text makes the intended word certain, such as an obvious keyboard slip, the repair is a single-answer fix.
source: Editors Canada, Guidelines for Ethical Editing of Graduate Student Texts, revised 2024-08-14, Part 2, p.5, diction query. https://editors.ca/wp-content/uploads/2023/07/Guidelines_Editing_GraduateStudentTexts_revised_08-14-2024.pdf

test: A citation is wrongly formed, is inconsistent with the rest of the text, or is missing where the claim plainly needs one.
cost: An editor who repairs or supplies citations takes over the part of scholarly work that establishes what the author actually read. Consistent citation errors also point to a misunderstanding that a silent fix hides.
suggestion: Query citation errors to draw attention to them, and do not correct them. Never supply a citation that is absent.
mechanism: Editors Canada makes both halves explicit, and singles out consistent errors as the case where the query matters most. Supplying a reference asserts on the author's behalf that a source was consulted. The pattern of errors is also information the author needs, which a clean repair would erase.
counter_case: PES D4.2 still expects the editor to recognize and flag where citations are needed, so silence is not the alternative to fixing.
source: Editors Canada, Guidelines for Ethical Editing of Graduate Student Texts, revised 2024-08-14, Part 2, p.4, citations. https://editors.ca/wp-content/uploads/2023/07/Guidelines_Editing_GraduateStudentTexts_revised_08-14-2024.pdf

test: Separate two kinds of finding. A statement of fact or a conclusion drawn in the argument is out of bounds. A silly error in an incidental remark, wrong on its face, is in bounds.
cost: Querying the argument makes the editor a second examiner and delays the work. Staying silent on a howler lets an obviously wrong detail reach print and damage the author's credibility.
suggestion: Do not question statements of fact or conclusions in the argument. Flag the incidental howler.
mechanism: Editors Canada draws this line and gives 'Edmonton is about 5,000 kilometres east of Halifax' as the flaggable kind. The distinction is whether the claim carries the argument or is scenery. Scenery errors are cheap for the author to fix and expensive to publish, and they need no subject expertise to spot.
counter_case: CIEP 5.4.5 asks the editor to raise any factual inaccuracy noticed, which reaches further into substantive claims than this rule does.
source: Editors Canada, Guidelines for Ethical Editing of Graduate Student Texts, revised 2024-08-14, Part 2, p.4, facts and howlers. https://editors.ca/wp-content/uploads/2023/07/Guidelines_Editing_GraduateStudentTexts_revised_08-14-2024.pdf

test: Before raising a query, ask whether the problem can be resolved from the material already available without consulting anyone.
cost: Every avoidable query spends reviewer time that the real questions need, and a long list trains the reviewer to skim.
suggestion: Use judgment about when to query and when to resolve without consultation. Do as much work as you can to minimize queries.
mechanism: PES A12.2 makes query volume itself a quality measure. A query is a transfer of work to someone with less context about the text and usually less time. Resolving what is resolvable protects the credibility of the queries that remain.
counter_case: Minimizing queries must not become resolving multi-answer problems by fiat, which the cardinality test forbids.
source: Editors Canada, Professional Editorial Standards 2024, approved 15 April 2024, A12.2. https://editors.ca/wp-content/uploads/2024/04/PES-2024-Interior_V7-Approved-Version-April-15-2024.pdf

test: Read the draft query as the reviewer will. It must be clear, tactful, succinct and actionable, and where a solution exists it should be offered.
cost: A vague or preachy query gets deferred rather than answered, and the problem returns at a later and more expensive stage.
suggestion: Rewrite the query until it names the span, states the issue in one line, and asks for a specific action. Offer your best solution where you have one.
mechanism: PES A12.3 sets four properties and adds the offer of a best solution. Actionable is the load-bearing one, because a reviewer can only respond to a request that names what to do. The offered solution converts an open question into a yes or no wherever that is honest.
counter_case: Editors Canada's student-text guidance forbids drafting alternatives, so the offered solution is withheld on assessed work.
source: Editors Canada, Professional Editorial Standards 2024, approved 15 April 2024, A12.3. https://editors.ca/wp-content/uploads/2024/04/PES-2024-Interior_V7-Approved-Version-April-15-2024.pdf

test: Compare the sentence before and after the edit. If the proposition, its strength, or its scope moved, the edit failed regardless of how much better it reads.
cost: A meaning-altering edit publishes a claim the author never made, under the author's name, with no record that anything changed.
suggestion: Make all changes without altering the intended meaning and without introducing errors of fact, style or formatting.
mechanism: PES A13.1 states this without exception, and every other permission in the standards sits underneath it. Meaning is the one property of the text that belongs entirely to the author. An edit that changes it is not an edit at all, so no efficiency gain can buy it.
source: Editors Canada, Professional Editorial Standards 2024, approved 15 April 2024, A13.1. https://editors.ca/wp-content/uploads/2024/04/PES-2024-Interior_V7-Approved-Version-April-15-2024.pdf

test: Locate the change in the agreed scope and the current stage of editing. A structural or stylistic change made at a mechanical stage is out of bounds even when it improves the text.
cost: Out-of-stage changes wreck the schedule they sit in, break work already signed off, and shift voice, tone and register without anyone deciding to.
suggestion: Keep changes inside the project scope and the stage, and hold voice, tone and register steady while making them.
mechanism: PES A2.5 binds scope, stage and voice together in one requirement. Stage discipline exists because later stages assume earlier decisions are settled. A change that is right in the abstract can still be wrong now, and the correct output for it is a note.
counter_case: An egregious error is corrected at any stage under E1.7, which overrides stage discipline for the narrow class of errors that would embarrass in print.
source: Editors Canada, Professional Editorial Standards 2024, approved 15 April 2024, A2.5. https://editors.ca/wp-content/uploads/2024/04/PES-2024-Interior_V7-Approved-Version-April-15-2024.pdf

test: Ask whether the change reverses a decision an earlier editor already made, or performs a task the next editor in the chain owns.
cost: Undoing earlier work reintroduces settled problems and destroys the audit trail. Doing later work duplicates effort and leaves the later editor auditing your judgment instead of doing their own job.
suggestion: Leave prior editorial decisions standing unless they are errors, and leave later-stage work to the editor who owns it.
mechanism: PES A1.3 states both halves of the boundary. An editorial chain works only if each link trusts the previous one. Where an earlier decision looks wrong, the honest output is a query naming it rather than a silent reversal.
counter_case: CIEP 5.6.3 confirms that errors and omissions in prior work are still corrected or queried, so the boundary is not a licence to pass on real mistakes.
source: Editors Canada, Professional Editorial Standards 2024, approved 15 April 2024, A1.3. https://editors.ca/wp-content/uploads/2024/04/PES-2024-Interior_V7-Approved-Version-April-15-2024.pdf

test: A spelling or grammar error sits inside quoted material.
cost: Silently correcting inside a quotation falsifies the source. Silently leaving it makes the author look careless when the error may be the source's.
suggestion: Query the error to establish whether it was present in the original before doing anything to it.
mechanism: PES D3.4 requires the query precisely because the editor cannot see the source. Two states of the world produce identical text on the page, and only the author can distinguish them. The answer also determines the repair, since an original error takes sic and a transcription slip takes a correction.
counter_case: Chicago allows a silent fix of one or two probable typos in an uncheckable quotation when the change follows the prevailing style of that quotation.
source: Editors Canada, Professional Editorial Standards 2024, approved 15 April 2024, D3.4. https://editors.ca/wp-content/uploads/2024/04/PES-2024-Interior_V7-Approved-Version-April-15-2024.pdf

test: A quotation appears without attribution, a generalization in academic work goes unsupported, or a table or figure carries no source.
cost: Unsourced material exposes the author to plagiarism findings and leaves readers unable to check the claim. These gaps are invisible to the author, who remembers where the material came from.
suggestion: Flag the place where the citation is needed, and leave the supply of it to the author.
mechanism: PES D4.2 names the three recognizable shapes of a missing citation. Each is detectable from the page without knowing the literature, which is what makes it the editor's job. Supplying the source is not, since only the author knows what was actually consulted.
counter_case: In heavily cited text a long list of individually obvious gaps is better delivered as one batched note than as a query per instance.
source: Editors Canada, Professional Editorial Standards 2024, approved 15 April 2024, D4.2. https://editors.ca/wp-content/uploads/2024/04/PES-2024-Interior_V7-Approved-Version-April-15-2024.pdf

test: The stage is proofreading. Sort each finding into egregious errors and everything else.
cost: Copy editing during proofreading resets pages, costs money, and introduces fresh errors at the stage that was meant to catch them. Passing over an egregious error defeats the stage.
suggestion: Flag or correct egregious errors at every round, and refrain from structural, stylistic or copy editing work unless it has been authorized.
mechanism: PES E1.7 keeps proofreading narrow while carving out the errors that must not survive. The asymmetry follows from the cost of change late in production. Anything short of egregious is recorded rather than acted on, which is what the batch tier is for.
counter_case: An explicit authorization from the client widens the remit, and then stylistic work at proof stage is in scope.
source: Editors Canada, Professional Editorial Standards 2024, approved 15 April 2024, E1.7. https://editors.ca/wp-content/uploads/2024/04/PES-2024-Interior_V7-Approved-Version-April-15-2024.pdf

test: Two or more repairs would each fix the problem. Compare their cost against the production process, schedule, medium, purpose and type of material.
cost: Choosing the expensive repair late in production can reflow pages and blow a schedule for a change no reader would notice.
suggestion: Pick the least costly appropriate change. Correct what must be right, such as contact details, and leave low-stakes inconsistency such as capitalization alone.
mechanism: PES E1.8 makes cost a first-class criterion at proof stage rather than an afterthought. It also supplies the graded example, since wrong contact information fails the reader while inconsistent capitalization merely annoys. Consequence, rather than tidiness, sets the threshold.
counter_case: Inconsistent capitalization in a heading hierarchy or a brand name can be consequential enough to fix even late.
source: Editors Canada, Professional Editorial Standards 2024, approved 15 April 2024, E1.8. https://editors.ca/wp-content/uploads/2024/04/PES-2024-Interior_V7-Approved-Version-April-15-2024.pdf

test: The change would alter a copyeditor's decision on grounds of improvement rather than error, and the client has not asked for that.
cost: Second-guessing a copyeditor produces churn, breaks a style the client approved, and puts two editors' preferences in one text.
suggestion: Follow the editorial style guide and leave the copyeditor's choices alone unless the client asks otherwise. Correct or query genuine errors and omissions.
mechanism: CIEP 5.6.3 separates improvement from error repair and licenses only the second. Improvement is by nature multi-answer, so the cardinality test already routes it away from silent editing. Errors and omissions stay actionable because they were never anyone's decision.
counter_case: Harnby's counterweight applies where the inherited choice is not a style preference but a readability failure, and then intervention is warranted.
source: CIEP Professional Practice Code, 5.6.3. https://www.ciep.uk/about-the-ciep/membership-codes/professional-practice-code.html

test: A name, date, event, place, person or reference to a visual element is internally inconsistent or looks factually wrong.
cost: Contradictory names and dates are the errors readers spot fastest and trust least. A figure reference pointing at the wrong element breaks the argument at the moment the reader needs it.
suggestion: Raise a question on the inaccuracy or the inconsistency. Do not pick a winner between two spellings or two dates on your own.
mechanism: CIEP 5.4.5 makes this an active duty of the editor. Internal inconsistency is fully decidable from the text, since two passages cannot both be right. Which one is correct is usually not decidable from the text, which is what makes it a query rather than a fix.
counter_case: Where one variant is demonstrably correct from an authoritative source in hand, the repair is a single-answer fix that only needs reporting.
source: CIEP Professional Practice Code, 5.4.5. https://www.ciep.uk/about-the-ciep/membership-codes/professional-practice-code.html

test: Grade each query by consequence. A major query blocks or changes downstream work. A minor one does not.
cost: Holding a major query until delivery lets the author build further work on a broken foundation. Sending minor queries one at a time interrupts everyone for no gain.
suggestion: Raise major queries without delay, and send minor queries in batches at times convenient to all concerned.
mechanism: CIEP 5.3.2(a) sets the timing rule by consequence rather than by discovery order. Urgency is a property of the effect, not of when the editor noticed. Batching the rest keeps the author's attention on the queries that actually block progress.
counter_case: A single very large batch delivered at the end can still overwhelm, so a mid-project instalment is sometimes kinder than strict end-loading.
source: CIEP Professional Practice Code, 5.3.2(a). https://www.ciep.uk/about-the-ciep/membership-codes/professional-practice-code.html

test: Check the passage against the eight triggers. More explanation needed, something apparently missing, too much assumed reader knowledge, material better shown as a table or diagram, the editor genuinely does not understand, inconsistency or ambiguity, an internal contradiction, or repetition where a preferred context must be chosen.
cost: Without a fixed trigger list, the query set drifts with the editor's mood, and the recurring comprehension failures that readers will also hit go unrecorded.
suggestion: Raise a query when any of the eight triggers fires, and name which one in the note.
mechanism: The CIEP article enumerates these eight as the standard grounds for querying an author. Each names a gap the editor cannot close without information only the author holds. The list is also a coverage check, since a review that raises none of the eight has probably not read for sense.
counter_case: The editor's own failure to understand is not always the text's fault, so an unfamiliar term should be looked up before it becomes a query.
source: CIEP free article, Philippa Tomlinson, 'What are queries, and how should an author respond?', 19 January 2024, eight query triggers. https://www.ciep.uk/resource/queries-author.html

test: Style inside a quotation is inconsistent and the source cannot be checked. Count the instances and judge how noticeable they are.
cost: Silently normalizing a quotation misrepresents the source. Flagging every trivial slip in a heavily quoted text buries the substantive problems.
suggestion: For a minor inconsistency or two, follow the prevailing style of that quotation and make the change silently. Where the inconsistencies are extensive or notable, use sic or comment on them instead.
mechanism: Chicago grades the response by extent rather than by kind. One or two probable typos carry no information about the source, so normalizing them to the quotation's own prevailing style loses nothing. Extensive inconsistency is itself evidence about the source, which sic preserves and a silent fix would delete.
counter_case: PES D3.4 asks the editor to query any error inside a quotation, which is the stricter default where the author can plausibly recheck the source.
source: Chicago Manual of Style Q&A, Manuscript Preparation, silent change inside quotations. https://www.chicagomanualofstyle.org/qanda/data/faq/topics/ManuscriptPreparation/faq0171.html

test: The word is unusual but correct. Before querying it, state the reason the plainer word would be better.
cost: A query the editor cannot justify costs the author a decision and returns nothing. Repeatedly overriding vocabulary flattens rhythm, humour, allusion and precision the author put there deliberately.
suggestion: Query it only if you are prepared to say why the alternative is better. Put that reason in the query.
mechanism: Chicago points out that an unusual word may serve rhythm, humour, allusion or precision, and then permits the query on condition that the editor can defend it. The condition is the whole rule, since a defensible query is one the author can weigh. An undefended one reads as a demand for plainness.
counter_case: Where the unusual word is also wrong in sense, the diction rule applies and the query needs no aesthetic justification.
source: Chicago Manual of Style Q&A, Usage, five-dollar words. https://www.chicagomanualofstyle.org/qanda/data/faq/topics/Usage/faq0137.html

test: The author has chosen between two equally acceptable variants. Check whether they applied it consistently.
cost: Overriding a consistent author risks leaving the text inconsistent where it was clean. Leaving an inconsistent author alone passes visible sloppiness to the reader.
suggestion: If the author is consistent, leave the choice alone. If the author is inconsistent, impose your preference throughout.
mechanism: Chicago frames this as two branches on one observable fact. Consistency is mechanically checkable, so the rule is fully decidable. The risk it manages is real, since a partial sweep by the editor is worse than either uniform state.
counter_case: A publisher house style that mandates one variant overrides the author's consistent choice, and then the sweep is required.
source: Chicago Manual of Style Q&A, Manuscript Preparation, equal variants and consistency. https://www.chicagomanualofstyle.org/qanda/data/faq/topics/ManuscriptPreparation/faq0070.html

test: Count how many instances of the small problem exist, how much else the author has to deal with, and how much the author would plausibly care.
cost: A query list dominated by trivia gets skimmed, and the important entries in it are the ones that get skipped.
suggestion: Weigh the volume before adding another minor query. Batch or drop the low-value ones so the list stays readable.
mechanism: Chicago's advice not to peck an author to death treats reviewer attention as a budget. Each marginal query lowers the expected response rate on every other query. Triage by count and by likely author interest keeps the whole set actionable.
counter_case: Systematic incompleteness, such as page ranges missing throughout, needs one clear note rather than silence, because the pattern matters even when each instance is trivial.
source: Chicago Manual of Style Q&A, Documentation, not pecking an author to death. https://www.chicagomanualofstyle.org/qanda/data/faq/topics/Documentation.html?page=30

test: Check the draft query for three parts. The exact span at issue is highlighted, the concern is sketched briefly and precisely, and a specific question names what the author should do.
cost: A query missing any of the three parts cannot be answered. The author has to reconstruct what the editor meant and often replies asking what was meant.
suggestion: Highlight exactly the text at issue, state the concern in a line, and ask a question that names the action wanted.
mechanism: The ACES guidance builds the query from these three parts and names the bare unanchored ask as the failure mode. Each part supplies something the author cannot infer, namely location, reason and requested action. A query with all three can be answered in one pass.
counter_case: For a query that spans the whole manuscript there is no single span to highlight, and the anchor becomes a description of the pattern with two or three located instances.
source: ACES, Erin Brenner, 'Writing effective author queries', 2019, three-part query structure. https://web.archive.org/web/20240708123911/https://aceseditors.org/news/2019/writing-effective-author-queries

test: Before raising a factual or reference query, spend five minutes trying to answer it yourself.
cost: Queries the editor could have answered erode trust in the query list and hand back work the editor was hired to do.
suggestion: Apply a five-minute research gate. Query only what survives it.
mechanism: The ACES beginner's guide sets an explicit time box on self-research. The box matters in both directions, since it stops both lazy querying and open-ended rabbit holes. Five minutes is enough to settle most spellings, dates and reference details without displacing the edit.
counter_case: PES A12.2 asks for as much work as you can do to minimize queries, which for a high-stakes fact can justify more than five minutes.
source: ACES, Erin Brenner, 'The beginner's guide to queries', 2019, five-minute research gate. https://web.archive.org/web/20240526094936/https://aceseditors.org/news/2019/the-beginners-guide-to-queries

test: Ask how much of the manuscript the query touches. A local query affects one passage. A global one affects the whole text or a large part of it.
cost: Holding a manuscript-wide question until the end means editing the whole text on an assumption that may be wrong, and then redoing it.
suggestion: Send local queries at the end of the edit. Send a query that pertains to the entire manuscript or a large portion of it immediately.
mechanism: The ACES guidance splits query timing by reach. A global question is a precondition for the rest of the work, so its answer changes what the edit should be. Local questions have no such dependency and are cheaper to answer in one batch.
counter_case: CIEP grades urgency by consequence rather than reach, so a local query with a blocking downstream effect also goes out at once.
source: ACES, Erin Brenner, 'The beginner's guide to queries', 2019, query timing. https://web.archive.org/web/20240526094936/https://aceseditors.org/news/2019/the-beginners-guide-to-queries

test: Read the draft query and ask whether a one-word brush-off would dispose of it.
cost: A dismissible query wastes the exchange and leaves the real confusion unrecorded, since the author has now formally answered it.
suggestion: Identify the point of confusion as precisely as you can, so the query cannot be waved away.
mechanism: The ACES piece uses 'Will readers understand this?' as the pattern, because 'Of course they will' ends it. Precision removes the escape route by naming what specifically is unclear. It also does the author a favour, since a located problem is far cheaper to fix than a diffuse worry.
counter_case: A genuine audience-level question sometimes has to be asked broadly, and there the fix is to supply the two readings you fear rather than to drop the query.
source: ACES, Adrienne Montgomerie, '10 ways to word a sensitive query', 2019, dismissibility. https://web.archive.org/web/20240412123826/https://aceseditors.org/news/2019/10-ways-to-word-a-sensitive-query

test: Scan the draft query for a pronoun standing in for the text at issue, such as this, that or it.
cost: The author cannot tell what to change, so either the wrong thing gets revised or the query gets ignored. Both outcomes cost a round.
suggestion: Quote the exact text in question inside the query instead of referring to it with a pronoun.
mechanism: ACES names the pronoun query as an anti-pattern, since 'Should this be expanded?' leaves the referent open. Quoting the span makes the query self-contained wherever it is read, including in a list detached from the page. It also forces the editor to check that a definite span really is the problem.
counter_case: In a comment anchored to a highlighted span the pronoun is unambiguous, though quoting still survives the move into a query list.
source: ACES, Berna Ozunal, 'Quills and Queries', 2020, pronoun anti-pattern. https://web.archive.org/web/20201104110117/https://aceseditors.org/news/2020/quills-and-queries

test: Check whether the query can be understood where it sits, or whether it sends the reader to another page.
cost: Cross-referenced queries force the author to navigate the document to reconstruct the point, which is slow and often abandoned.
suggestion: Make each query self-contained. Restate the relevant point rather than pointing at a note elsewhere.
mechanism: ACES lists asking reviewers to jump around the document among the practices to avoid. Restating costs the editor a sentence and saves the author a search. Repetition across queries is the correct trade here, because each query is read on its own.
counter_case: A genuinely global decision is better stated once in a cover note than repeated in fifty places, and then the individual queries can refer to it.
source: ACES, Berna Ozunal, 'Quills and Queries', 2020, cross-reference anti-pattern. https://web.archive.org/web/20201104110117/https://aceseditors.org/news/2020/quills-and-queries

test: Count the solutions offered in the query. Zero leaves the author with a problem. More than one turns the query into a menu.
cost: A bare complaint gives the author work with no starting point. A menu of options makes the author do the editor's comparison and slows the reply.
suggestion: State the issue briefly and provide one concrete solution.
mechanism: The ACES guidance pairs a brief statement of the issue with exactly one concrete solution. One option converts an open problem into a yes or no, which is the cheapest possible reply. It also shows the editor has thought the repair through rather than merely flagged discomfort.
counter_case: Editors Canada forbids drafting alternatives on assessed student work, where the onus must stay with the student, and there the query offers none.
source: ACES, Berna Ozunal, 'Quills and Queries', 2020, one concrete solution. https://web.archive.org/web/20201104110117/https://aceseditors.org/news/2020/quills-and-queries

test: Before writing the query, ask whether it is a valid query at all and whether it truly needs raising.
cost: Invalid queries dilute the list and cost the author time, and a list padded with them makes the editor's judgment harder to trust.
suggestion: Run a validity gate on each candidate query. Drop the ones that do not need raising.
mechanism: The validity gate sits upstream of every craft rule about phrasing, because a well-written query about a non-problem is still waste. Asking whether it needs raising forces the editor to name the consequence of leaving it. Where no consequence can be named, the query goes.
counter_case: A query that seems marginal alone can be worth raising as part of a named pattern, so validity is judged against the set and not only the instance.
source: Sue Littleford, '7 golden rules for author queries', live mirror, validity gate. https://aptwords.co.uk/7-golden-rules-author-queries/

test: The word is unfamiliar to the editor. Look it up before either changing it or querying it.
cost: Changing or querying a word that is simply outside the editor's vocabulary makes the editor the limit of the text, and repeated instances destroy credibility.
suggestion: Look the word up first. Act only if the dictionary does not support the usage.
mechanism: Not knowing a word is a fact about the editor rather than about the text. Checking converts the situation into a decidable one, since the dictionary either supports the usage or does not. The lookup is seconds of work against a query that would otherwise be both wrong and revealing.
counter_case: Where a term is correct but likely opaque to the target readership, a query about accessibility is still legitimate after the lookup.
source: Sue Littleford, '7 golden rules for author queries', live mirror, look it up first. https://aptwords.co.uk/7-golden-rules-author-queries/

test: Compare the two outcomes for the same finding. Work out what happens if you query and what happens if you change, in both the case where you are right and the case where you are wrong.
cost: Ignoring the asymmetry leads editors to change in cases where a wrong change does real damage to the text and the relationship.
suggestion: Default to the query wherever a wrong change would harm and a query merely costs a line.
mechanism: Harnby's comparison notes that querying looks diligent whichever way the uncertainty resolves, while changing looks harmful when the editor is wrong. The payoffs are not symmetric, so the risk-weighted choice is not a coin flip. The decision to query nearly always wins on that arithmetic.
counter_case: PES A12.2 caps this, since a habit of querying everything shifts the whole cost onto the reviewer and is its own failure.
source: Louise Harnby, 'How to query like a superhero', asymmetric payoff. https://www.louiseharnbyproofreader.com/blog/how-to-query-like-a-superhero-5-tips-for-new-fiction-copyeditors-and-proofreaders

test: Ask two questions. Are you unsure how to solve the problem, and do you think several solutions to it exist?
cost: Resolving an unsure or multi-solution case by editing installs a guess as the text, with no record that a choice was made.
suggestion: Let the query trump the amendment whenever either condition holds.
mechanism: Harnby states that the query trumps the amendment every time under uncertainty or multiplicity, which is the cardinality test arriving from the practitioner side. Uncertainty is added as a second trigger alongside multiplicity. Both describe states of the editor's knowledge that the author can resolve and the editor cannot.
counter_case: Uncertainty about a mechanical rule is resolved by looking the rule up, not by querying the author.
source: Louise Harnby, 'How do I deal with repetition while respecting authorial style?', the tie-breaker. https://www.louiseharnbyproofreader.com/blog/qa-with-louise-how-do-i-deal-with-repetition-while-respecting-authorial-style

test: Decide whether the pattern is a style choice or a readability problem. Ask whether a competent reader of the target audience loses the thread, not whether you would have written it differently.
cost: Deference applied to a readability failure leaves the reader stranded and makes the edit worthless. Treating a style choice as a failure overwrites the author's voice.
suggestion: Intervene where readability breaks down, even where the pattern is consistent and clearly deliberate. Leave genuine style choices alone.
mechanism: Harnby draws the line between a style choice and a readability problem and holds that readability trumps poor style. The counterweight matters because otherwise every finding can be dismissed as authorial style, which would make the editorial role empty. Consistency is evidence of intent rather than evidence of success.
counter_case: On assessed student work the intervention is a flag rather than a rewrite, because the prose has to remain the student's own.
