source: Louise Harnby, 'How do I deal with repetition while respecting authorial style?', readability trumps poor style. https://www.louiseharnbyproofreader.com/blog/qa-with-louise-how-do-i-deal-with-repetition-while-respecting-authorial-style

test: Check the finding against the proofreading checklist. In-scope items are fixed. Out-of-scope items are left alone unless the error would embarrass in print.
cost: Querying inside scope wastes the production editor's time on decisions already delegated. Changing outside scope at proof stage costs pages and reintroduces risk.
suggestion: Keep queries to a minimum. Make in-scope changes without querying, and make no other change unless a potentially embarrassing error turns up.
mechanism: The World Bank guide gives the publisher-side version of stage discipline, with a written checklist as the boundary. A checklist makes the boundary decidable rather than a matter of judgment. The embarrassment carve-out is the same narrow exception the standards call egregious error.
counter_case: The production editor can instruct otherwise, and the guide says so explicitly.
source: World Bank Group, Publications Editorial Style Guide 2020, section 2.48. https://documents1.worldbank.org/curated/en/318281583390046594/pdf/World-Bank-Group-Publications-Editorial-Style-Guide-2020.pdf

test: At a mechanical editing level, look for factual inconsistency, faulty logic, a particularly awkward or unclear passage, an incomplete comparison, or a vague time reference.
cost: These defects mislead readers in ways proofreading never catches, and repairing them at a mechanical level means rewriting argument the editor cannot verify.
suggestion: Point them out to the author. Do not repair them at this level.
mechanism: The World Bank Level C list is a duty to report rather than a licence to revise. Each item is detectable from the page while its correct resolution needs knowledge the editor lacks. Reporting therefore captures the value without the risk of inventing content.
counter_case: At a substantive level the same findings are in scope to fix, so the routing is set by the agreed level and not by the defect.
source: World Bank, Publications Editorial Style Guide 2020, Appendix A.1, Level C mechanical, point-out list. https://documents1.worldbank.org/curated/en/318281583390046594/pdf/World-Bank-Group-Publications-Editorial-Style-Guide-2020.pdf

test: Track every first-person and second-person pronoun and every demonstrative. Ask whether the referent or antecedent is unambiguous at that point in the text.
cost: An unresolved 'we', 'you' or 'this' lets each reader supply a different subject, and the sentence silently means several things. Guessing the referent for the author is how an editor changes a claim without touching a claim word.
suggestion: Point out pronouns whose referent is unclear and demonstratives whose antecedent is unclear, and let the author name the referent.
mechanism: The World Bank guide lists both pronoun classes as point-out items at the mechanical level. Ambiguity is decidable from the text, since more than one antecedent is available. The resolution is not decidable from the text, which is exactly why it goes to the author.
counter_case: Where the antecedent is unique and adjacent, spelling it out is a single-answer clarity fix that needs no query.
source: World Bank, Publications Editorial Style Guide 2020, Appendix A.1, Level C mechanical, pronoun and demonstrative items. https://documents1.worldbank.org/curated/en/318281583390046594/pdf/World-Bank-Group-Publications-Editorial-Style-Guide-2020.pdf

test: The defect is a dangling participle, a subject-verb disagreement, or an incorrect preposition choice.
cost: Flagging these spends the author's attention on repairs with one right answer, and a text full of such queries hides the ones that need thought.
suggestion: Fix them at the mechanical level without a query.
mechanism: The World Bank Level C list puts these among the fixes rather than the point-out items. Each has a unique correct form determined by the grammar, so cardinality resolves to one. Grouping them with silent fixes is what keeps the query list short enough to be read.
counter_case: On assessed student work Editors Canada routes subject-verb agreement to a flag, since the mechanics are part of what is being assessed.
source: World Bank, Publications Editorial Style Guide 2020, Appendix A.1, Level C mechanical, fix list. https://documents1.worldbank.org/curated/en/318281583390046594/pdf/World-Bank-Group-Publications-Editorial-Style-Guide-2020.pdf

test: The proposed change cuts a redundant passage, converts a passive construction to an active verb, or trims excess words. Check which editing level was agreed.
cost: Prose-tightening at a mechanical level rewrites voice under the cover of correctness, and it is the change authors most often experience as being edited out of their own text.
suggestion: Do not cut redundancy, flip passives, or trim wordiness unless the substantive level was agreed. Raise them as notes instead.
mechanism: The World Bank guide grants these three licences only at Level B, and their absence from Level C is the operative fact. All three are multi-answer changes, since the same passage can be tightened many ways. That is why they need an explicit mandate rather than editorial initiative.
counter_case: Harnby's counterweight applies where the wordiness has crossed into a readability failure, and then intervention is justified at any level.
source: World Bank, Publications Editorial Style Guide 2020, Appendix A.1, Level B licences absent from Level C. https://documents1.worldbank.org/curated/en/318281583390046594/pdf/World-Bank-Group-Publications-Editorial-Style-Guide-2020.pdf

test: Ask whether the change affects content. Significant changes are tracked. Minor changes that do not affect content need not be.
cost: Tracking every comma makes the revision unreadable and hides the changes the author must actually approve. Leaving a content change untracked removes the author's chance to refuse it.
suggestion: Use tracked changes selectively to surface significant changes, and make minor non-content changes silently.
mechanism: The Wesleyan guidance treats visibility as a scarce resource rather than a default. Marking everything and marking nothing both destroy the signal, so the split is by content effect. Content effect is also the same line the meaning-preservation rule draws, which keeps the two consistent.
counter_case: Some authors and some assessed contexts require every change tracked, and an explicit instruction overrides the default.
source: Wesleyan University Press, Manuscript and Art Preparation Guidelines, October 2020, selective track changes. https://dhjhkxawhe8q4.cloudfront.net/wespress-wp/wp-content/uploads/2021/06/18161111/manuscript-art-prep-guide.pdf

test: Reviewer names the paper's writing, presentation, clarity or readability itself as a weakness, separately from any technical objection.
cost: The reviewer stops evaluating the contribution and starts budgeting effort to decode the paper; clarity complaints migrate into the score justification.
suggestion: Do a dedicated presentation pass before submission: read only for whether a competent non-specialist can follow each section, and fix the worst three sections rather than polishing everywhere.
source: ICLR 2024, ICLR 2025
narrower_test: Fire only when the clarity complaint cites a locatable site (a line number, section, equation, or float). A bare global verdict on writing quality carries no site to repair, so the checkable replacement is the per-site union of the located rules in this ledger.

test: A core mechanism (method, algorithm, training procedure, derivation) cannot be reconstructed from the main text alone, so the reviewer says it is not described, convoluted, or hard to follow.
cost: The reviewer cannot check correctness or reimplement, so every downstream result becomes unverifiable and the paper is judged on trust.
suggestion: Write the method section as an executable recipe: inputs, each transformation with its symbols, outputs, then a worked pass over one concrete input.
counter_case: A dual-use method paper (jailbreak synthesis, malware generation, biosecurity uplift) where the reviewer's demand for an executable recipe plus a worked pass over one concrete input is exactly the artifact that should stay behind a gated release. The same inversion hits papers whose pipeline is an already-published standard (plain LoRA fine-tuning, vanilla PPO), where a full recipe spends the page budget the novel component needs.
source: ICLR 2024, ICLR 2025

test: Section order, paragraph order, or emphasis does not match the reading path, and the reviewer suggests reorganizing or says the structure is odd or confusing.
cost: The reader spends attention on navigation rather than content and may never find the contribution.
suggestion: Draft a one-line purpose per section, check each line depends only on lines above it, and move any section whose purpose repeats another.
counter_case: A submission bound to a mandated template (a datasets-and-benchmarks track requiring datasheet order, or a journal enforcing IMRaD) where resequencing to the reviewer's reading path breaks the required section order. The dependency check also mislabels papers with two genuinely parallel contributions, forcing one into false subordination under the other.
source: ICLR 2024, ICLR 2025

test: Content the reviewer needs to judge the paper (model details, assumptions, dataset construction, listed contributions) lives only in the appendix.
cost: The reviewer either misses the content entirely or has to reconstruct the paper by cross-referencing two documents, and reads the omission as hiding weakness.
suggestion: Every claim in the introduction must have its supporting detail in the main text; the appendix holds only proofs, extra ablations, and reproductions of what the main text already states.
counter_case: A paper already at the hard page limit where the appendix content the reviewer wants promoted is a forty-row settings table or a licensing datasheet the venue itself requires in supplementary form. Promoting it evicts the method description that the same reviewer flagged as underspecified, trading one complaint for a worse one.
source: ICLR 2024, ICLR 2025

test: A figure, table, or example sits pages away from the text that discusses it, or arrives much later than the point where the reader first needs it.
cost: Each reference forces a page jump, which breaks the argument the reviewer is trying to hold in mind.
suggestion: Place every float on the page of its first discussion, or restate the one number the reader needs inline so the jump is optional.
counter_case: A full-width or full-page float (a two-column architecture diagram) discussed in three separate sections. Pinning it to the page of first mention lengthens the other two jumps and ejects a page of body text, and a deliberate page-one teaser figure discussed in Section 4 is a convention reviewers expect rather than a defect.
source: ICLR 2024, ICLR 2025

test: A specific claim, hypothesis, or conclusion is stated without the figure, table, proof, or citation that would establish it, and the reviewer says it is not supported or no evidence is given.
cost: The reviewer must decide whether to take the claim on faith; the usual resolution is to discount it and everything built on it.
suggestion: For each claim sentence, name the exact artifact that proves it (Table 3, Thm 2, ref [7]) in the same sentence, or weaken the claim to what the artifact actually shows.
counter_case: A forward-looking sentence in the introduction that previews a result proved in Section 5, and a position paper whose contribution is an argument rather than a measurement. Bolting an artifact pointer onto every such sentence produces a citation stub for each promise, and weakening them to what a table already shows deletes the roadmap the paper needs.
source: ICLR 2024, ICLR 2025

test: Wording is stronger than the result: superlatives, promotional adjectives, or scope words the experiments do not reach, flagged as overclaiming, overstated, or too strong.
cost: The reviewer starts auditing every other claim for the same inflation, and the real contribution is discounted along with the inflated one.
suggestion: Rewrite each strong claim to the narrowest true version, naming the models, datasets, and regime tested; delete adjectives that add no measurable content.
counter_case: A result that genuinely wins on every tested benchmark. Rewriting 'outperforms all prior methods on all twelve benchmarks' into a hedged 'improves on some benchmarks' understates a table showing twelve of twelve, and reviewers then score the contribution as incremental on the strength of the authors' own hedge.
source: ICLR 2024, ICLR 2025

test: The abstract or title promises scope, objects, or findings that the body does not deliver, or omits the actual main result.
cost: Readers arrive with the wrong expectation and read the whole paper as a failure to deliver, which is worse than the paper being described accurately.
suggestion: Write the abstract last, from the results tables: every noun in it must appear in an experiment, and the headline sentence must name the strongest thing you actually measured.
counter_case: A dataset or benchmark release whose artifact deliberately covers more ground than the paper's experiments demonstrate. Narrowing the title and abstract to the experiments misdescribes what is being released. The same rule misfires on a negative-result paper, where taking the headline from the strongest measured number promotes a minor positive over the finding the paper exists to report.
source: ICLR 2024, ICLR 2025

test: Claims, descriptions, or experimental conditions are stated informally enough that the reviewer cannot tell what was actually done, and asks for precision or calls the writing vague or not rigorous.
cost: The claim cannot be verified or falsified, so it carries no evidential weight even when it is true.
suggestion: Replace every vague quantifier and unnamed component with the concrete value or name (which GNN, how many samples, what threshold), and state claims as testable propositions.
counter_case: A claim that holds for a stated class (any permutation-invariant encoder, any convex surrogate) where only one member was tested. Pinning the wording to the tested instance replaces a correct general proposition with a weaker one, and the honest repair is a proof or an explicit scope sentence rather than substituting the instance.
source: ICLR 2024, ICLR 2025

test: A symbol, variable, parameter, or term is used before (or without) its definition, including definitions that appear only many lines later.
cost: The reader stalls at the first use, and any equation containing the symbol becomes uncheckable.
suggestion: Introduce every symbol at first use in the same sentence, and keep a notation table; verify by reading the paper in order and flagging each symbol whose meaning you cannot state.
counter_case: Field-universal notation such as the gradient operator, expectation, a norm, or d for dimension. Defining each at first use adds a page of noise, and a notation table for a four-symbol paper reads as padding. Enforcement also breaks abstracts, where a symbol is often used once as shorthand and defining it there costs the abstract its only free sentence.
source: ICLR 2024, ICLR 2025

test: The same symbol denotes two different objects, or its meaning silently changes between sections or equations.
cost: The reviewer cannot tell which object an equation refers to and has to guess, which makes checking the math impossible.
suggestion: One symbol, one referent, paper-wide: rename the second use, and add a table mapping each symbol to exactly one object with its type and shape.
counter_case: Deliberate abuse of notation that the theory relies on, such as p(x) for both a density and a mass function, or a loss L applied to a single example and to a batch. Renaming the second use splits objects the derivation intends to identify and forces a duplicate statement of every lemma that ranges over both.
source: ICLR 2024, ICLR 2025

test: Reviewer describes the notation system as a whole as confusing, imprecise, heavy, or messy, and asks for revision rather than flagging one symbol.
cost: The reviewer cannot verify the theory at all, so theorems are read as unchecked assertions.
suggestion: Cut the symbol inventory: delete any symbol used fewer than three times, use consistent case and decoration conventions, and re-derive the key result to confirm it still reads.
source: ICLR 2024, ICLR 2025
narrower_test: Count the distinct symbols in display math and flag those used fewer than three times, then check case and decoration conventions for collisions (bold versus arrow for vectors, hat for both estimate and normalization). That is checkable, whereas a global verdict that notation 'seems to vary' names no symbol to change.

test: An acronym or abbreviation is used without being expanded at first use in the main text.
cost: Non-specialist reviewers lose the referent and skim past the section where it matters.
suggestion: Expand every acronym at first use in the main text (and again at first use in the abstract), then grep the PDF for all-caps tokens and check each one has an expansion before it.
counter_case: Acronyms whose expansion is dead weight because the short form is the field's actual name. Writing out Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers, Long Short-Term Memory, or Bilingual Evaluation Understudy at first use costs a line and tells a reader nothing the token did not already convey.
source: ICLR 2024, ICLR 2025

test: The same concept is named two or more different ways, or two concepts share a name, including spelling variants between title, text, and figures.
cost: The reader cannot tell whether two passages discuss the same thing, so apparent contradictions appear where there are none.
suggestion: Fix one canonical name per concept in a glossary before writing, then search-and-replace all variants; check the title, abstract, figure labels, and captions against the glossary.
counter_case: A global search-and-replace to the canonical name also rewrites strings that must not change, including cited paper titles, dataset and model identifiers, code symbols, and quoted prior-work phrasing. It also erases real distinctions where two names mark two things, such as the technique versus the deployed system built on it.
source: ICLR 2024, ICLR 2025

test: Symbols or labels in a figure do not match the symbols used for the same objects in the text.
cost: The reviewer cannot map the figure onto the argument and has to treat the figure as decoration.
suggestion: Generate figure labels from the same symbol list as the text, and proofread each panel against the paragraph that discusses it.
counter_case: A figure reproduced from prior work under permission, or a screenshot of a released tool's interface. Relabelling its panels to match this paper's symbols falsifies the source and breaks the correspondence a reader would find on checking the original.
source: ICLR 2024

test: Equations are unnumbered, or a single equation packs several steps into one unreadable line.
cost: Reviewers cannot cite the step they are questioning, which turns a specific objection into a vague one.
suggestion: Number every display equation and split any equation whose derivation needs more than one substitution to follow.
counter_case: A multi-line chain of inequalities whose whole point is transitivity from the left-hand side to the final bound. Splitting it into two or three numbered equations destroys the single object the reader needs to hold, and each fragment then needs its own restatement of the terms carried through.
source: ICLR 2024, ICLR 2025

test: Figure text, axis labels, tick labels, legends, or line widths are too small or too crowded to read at normal viewing size.
cost: The figure conveys nothing, so the evidence it was meant to carry does not reach the reviewer at all.
suggestion: Size every figure at final print width and check that the smallest text is no smaller than the caption font; drop panels rather than shrinking them.
counter_case: A grid of many small panels whose message is the aggregate pattern rather than any single trace, such as a per-layer heatmap array or a qualitative sample sheet. Dropping panels to enlarge the survivors deletes the pattern that is the evidence, and the repair is a zoomed inset alongside the full grid.
source: ICLR 2024, ICLR 2025

test: A table or figure is legible but its content is ambiguous: the reviewer cannot tell what rows, columns, bolding, or plotted elements mean.
cost: The reviewer cannot read off the comparison the table exists to make, so the result does not count.
suggestion: State in the caption what each column reports, what bold marks, and over what the aggregate is taken; make bolding rule-based and apply it consistently.
counter_case: Rule-based bolding of the best mean in every column, applied to results whose gaps sit inside the reported spread. The consistent rule then asserts a winner the error bars do not support, converting an ambiguity complaint into an overclaiming one, and the honest table bolds nothing or bolds every entry statistically tied with the best.
source: ICLR 2024, ICLR 2025

test: The caption does not carry the information needed to read the panel without hunting through the text, or asserts something the panel does not show.
cost: A reader skimming figures (which is how most reviewers first read) gets the wrong message or none.
suggestion: Make each caption self-contained: what is plotted, what the axes and series are, what varies across panels, and the one factual takeaway the panel supports.
counter_case: An exploratory figure with a mixed or null result. Adding the one factual takeaway the rule demands manufactures a claim the panel does not support, which is the failure the second quoted reviewer already caught. Self-contained captions also duplicate a shared legend across fifteen tables, where one reading-the-tables paragraph does the job.
source: ICLR 2024, ICLR 2025

test: A figure, table, or algorithm block is never referenced or explained in the running text.
cost: The artifact is skipped, and the reviewer reads the space it occupies as padding.
suggestion: Every float needs at least one sentence in the text that names it and states what it shows; grep for each label and confirm a text reference exists.
counter_case: An appendix gallery of qualitative samples, dozens of floats that exist to be browsed. A mandatory naming sentence per float produces boilerplate that repeats the gallery's one caption, which then trips the verbosity complaint the same reviewer pool raises.
source: ICLR 2024, ICLR 2025

test: Hyperparameters, training setup, or implementation details needed to reproduce a reported number are absent or only partly given.
cost: The reviewer cannot judge whether the gain comes from the method or the tuning, and reproducibility claims collapse.
suggestion: Add a settings table per experiment covering optimizer, learning rate, batch size, epochs, seeds, and hardware, and state which were tuned and over what grid.
counter_case: Experiments run entirely through a closed model API, where optimizer, learning rate, batch size, and epochs do not exist. A settings table full of not-applicable rows implies withheld detail rather than absent detail. The same applies to a production system under a licence that forbids publishing its training configuration, where stating the constraint beats a plausible-looking table.
source: ICLR 2024, ICLR 2025

test: Results are reported as point estimates with no error bars, standard deviations, seed count, or significance test, or with too few seeds.
cost: Differences between methods cannot be distinguished from run-to-run noise, so the headline comparison is unresolved.
suggestion: Report mean and spread over at least three to five seeds for every headline number, state the seed count in the caption, and say what the interval represents.
counter_case: Pretraining-scale runs where one seed costs thousands of GPU-hours. Demanding three to five seeds pushes authors to shrink the model until seeds are affordable, trading away the regime the paper is about for a variance estimate. Deterministic closed-form or full-batch methods have exactly zero run-to-run spread, and reporting an interval there is theatre.
source: ICLR 2024, ICLR 2025

test: A mechanism, format, or abstract concept is described only in prose where the reviewer asks for a concrete example, worked instance, diagram, or pseudocode.
cost: The reviewer cannot instantiate the description, so they cannot tell whether they have understood it correctly.
suggestion: Pair every abstract construct with one small worked example or a pseudocode block, positioned at the point of first definition.
counter_case: A construct whose smallest honest instance is large, such as a two-hundred-token prompt template or a full crystal structure. Dropping it in at the point of first definition displaces the method text, and the example belongs in an appendix with a pointer. Pseudocode for an object every reader knows, such as [name] or a transformer block, is pure filler.
source: ICLR 2024, ICLR 2025

test: The released code or supplement cannot be run as given: no README, no environment or run instructions, or the reviewer concludes reproduction is not possible.
cost: A reviewer who wanted to verify gives up, and the reproducibility claim becomes an assertion.
suggestion: Ship a README with exact environment, one command per reported table, and the seeds used; have someone outside the project run it from a clean checkout.
counter_case: Work whose pipeline is welded to internal infrastructure or licensed data. A stripped skeleton that installs cleanly but reproduces none of the tables is worse than a precise statement of what cannot be released. Under double-blind review, an exact-environment README also leaks cluster paths, internal package names, and organisation identifiers.
source: ICLR 2024, ICLR 2025

test: Typos, grammatical errors, misspellings, or missing punctuation and whitespace appear often enough that the reviewer lists them or asks for proofreading.
cost: Reviewers read density of surface errors as a proxy for care taken with the results, and it costs goodwill on every borderline judgement.
suggestion: Run a spellchecker and a grammar pass over the final PDF text, then read the paper aloud once; fix the classes of error, not only the instances found.
counter_case: A blanket spellchecker or grammar pass over a paper dense with domain identifiers silently corrupts gene symbols, dataset names, and code tokens such as argmax or nn.Linear. A heavy fluency rewrite of non-native prose also flips technical scope, turning 'we do not assume X' into 'we assume not X', so the pass must stop at surface errors.
source: ICLR 2024, ICLR 2025

test: Citation commands are used incorrectly: parenthetical where textual is needed or the reverse, missing brackets, or a nonstandard citation style.
cost: Sentences become ungrammatical and authorship attribution reads as sloppy, which invites scrutiny of the bibliography.
suggestion: Use textual citations when the authors are the sentence subject and parenthetical otherwise; grep for every citation command and check the surrounding sentence still parses.
counter_case: A venue whose style file uses numeric citations, where the textual command already renders as Smith et al. [1]. Adding the parentheses the reviewer asks for produces a double-bracketed citation and breaks the required format, so the complaint is an artifact of the style rather than a defect in the source.
source: ICLR 2024, ICLR 2025

test: Cross-references are broken: raw LaTeX label text in the output, a reference pointing at the wrong float, or numbering that does not resolve.
cost: The reviewer is sent to the wrong place or nowhere, and the error is visible evidence the PDF was never read end to end.
suggestion: Compile twice, then read the final PDF for stray label text and check every numbered reference points at the intended float.
source: ICLR 2024, ICLR 2025

test: A specific sentence cannot be parsed, so the reviewer quotes it back and asks what it means.
cost: The reviewer must guess the intended meaning; if the sentence carries a claim, the claim is lost.
suggestion: Split the sentence into one proposition each, name the subject explicitly, and define any term doing unusual work; re-read the quoted-back sentences reviewers flag.
counter_case: A sentence that is precise in a formalism the reviewer lacks, such as a measure-theoretic or type-theoretic statement. Splitting it into plain one-proposition prose drops the quantifier structure that made it correct, and the right response is a pointer to the definition plus an informal gloss beside the formal sentence.
source: ICLR 2024, ICLR 2025

test: The same point, paragraph, or formula is restated, or prose is verbose enough that the reviewer proposes condensing it.
cost: Page budget goes to repetition instead of the content reviewers say is missing, and the repetition itself signals the draft was not revised.
suggestion: Delete every sentence that adds no new proposition, then reinvest the recovered space in the method or settings detail reviewers ask for.
counter_case: Redundancy that saves a page jump, such as restating the loss at the point where the experiments use it or recapping the assumptions at the head of a long proof. Deleting every sentence with no new proposition forces the reader back across the paper, which is the cost the float-distance complaint measures.
source: ICLR 2024, ICLR 2025

test: Familiar background is explained at length while the paper's own novel content is compressed or deferred.
cost: The reviewer reads pages they already know and then hits the contribution with no room left to understand it.
suggestion: Budget space by novelty: cite standard background in one sentence, and give the space to whatever no reader could look up elsewhere.
counter_case: A cross-community submission, machine learning for clinical or chemistry data, or the first paper of a new subfield at a general venue. The assigned reviewers cannot look the background up in one citation, and compressing it to a single sentence strands exactly the readers who decide the paper.
source: ICLR 2024, ICLR 2025

test: The prose registers as promotional, showy, or as an engineering report rather than a research paper.
cost: The reviewer discounts the framing and looks for the substance behind it, which reads as adversarial rather than cooperative reading.
suggestion: State what was built and what was measured in plain declaratives; move product-style framing out and let the numbers carry the emphasis.
source: ICLR 2024, ICLR 2025
narrower_test: Check for the two things a research paper carries and an engineering report does not, a stated question or hypothesis the work could have falsified, and a controlled comparison isolating the claimed cause. Also count unmeasured evaluative adjectives per page. A verdict that the framing feels showy names no sentence to change.

test: Two passages of the paper (text vs figure, section vs section, text vs released code) assert incompatible things.
cost: The reviewer cannot tell which version is true and must assume the worst, and one found contradiction licenses a search for more.
suggestion: Before submitting, list every quantitative and structural claim with its location and check each pair for consistency, including the code and appendix.
counter_case: Two passages that differ because their settings differ, such as a derivation assuming full-batch gradients while the released script uses batches of 128 for a separate ablation. Editing one passage to match the other papers over a real difference, and the correct repair adds the scope qualifier that says which setting each passage describes.
source: ICLR 2024, ICLR 2025

test: The same quantity is reported with different values in different tables, figures, or the text, without explanation.
cost: The reviewer loses confidence in every number in the paper, not just the mismatched pair.
suggestion: Generate all reported numbers from one results file rather than transcribing, and diff every duplicated cell across tables before submission.
counter_case: A table that quotes a published number beside your own reproduction of the same setting. Generating both cells from one results file erases the reproduction gap, which is itself a finding, so the two values must stay and the caption must say which is quoted and which was rerun.
source: ICLR 2024, ICLR 2025

test: A factual statement, established result, standard loss, or named concept is asserted with no citation, or known prior work is not cited.
cost: The reviewer cannot separate the paper's contribution from inherited background, and uncited prior work reads as a novelty claim over work that exists.
suggestion: Attach a citation to every sentence stating a fact you did not establish in this paper, and cite a definition before its first use rather than after.
counter_case: Textbook facts such as the chain rule or the definition of softmax. Attaching a source to each reads as unfamiliarity with the field and inflates the bibliography, and under an open review cycle the demand to cite all prior work often resolves into padding with the reviewer's own loosely related papers.
source: ICLR 2024, ICLR 2025

test: Equations, derivations, or theorem statements contain errors, wrong (in)equalities, or symbols that do not match their surrounding definitions.
cost: The formal contribution cannot be trusted, and the reviewer must either redo the derivation or discount the theory.
suggestion: Have a co-author re-derive every displayed result from the stated assumptions, and check each equation's symbols against the notation table.
counter_case: A paper that reproduces a flawed derivation in order to critique it, where the displayed error is the object of study. Correcting the equation to match the surrounding definitions deletes the paper's point. The same trap catches a deliberately simplified expression flagged as an approximation in the line above it.
source: ICLR 2024, ICLR 2025

test: For each sentence in a paragraph, underline the words from the start up to the main verb. Read the underlined strings in order. Flag the paragraph if they do not form a small set of related ideas, or if more than roughly a third of them name something appearing in the discourse for the first time.
cost: The reader cannot tell whose story the paragraph is, so each sentence has to be re-anchored from scratch and the paragraph reads as a list of unrelated true statements.
suggestion: Pick the one character or concept the paragraph is about and move it into the opening slot of most sentences, recasting the sentence around it rather than deleting anything.
mechanism: Readers treat whatever arrives first as the thing the sentence is about. When that slot changes occupant every sentence, the reader has to rebuild the frame each time and never accumulates a through-line. The information may all be present and still fail to connect, which is why the paragraph feels disorganised without containing any identifiable error.
counter_case: A deliberately enumerative passage, such as a related-work paragraph that surveys four unrelated prior systems, or a limitations list, is correctly written with a shifting topic string because the shifts are the content.
source: Gopen & Swan, 'The Science of Scientific Writing', American Scientist 78(6), 1990, 'The Topic Position'; procedure as given in Williams (rev. Bizup), 'Style: Lessons in Clarity and Grace', 11th ed., Lesson 5, 'Diagnosis and Revision: Topics'

test: Take the last eight words of each sentence and the first eight of the next. Flag the join if no word, synonym, or pronoun from the closing span reappears in the opening span and no explicit connective bridges them.
cost: The reader has to supply the missing link, and different readers supply different ones, so the argument the author believes is on the page is not the argument being read.
suggestion: Either open the second sentence with the term the first sentence ended on, or add the connective that names the relation the author actually intends.
mechanism: Cohesion is judged locally, at the seam between one sentence ending and the next beginning. A seam with no shared material forces the reader to hold the previous sentence in memory while guessing at a relation. Adding the bridge word costs one phrase and removes the guess entirely.
counter_case: A deliberate hard break, such as the first sentence of a new subsection or a pivot after a long digression, should not be bridged. Forcing a link there falsely implies the new material continues the old.
source: Gopen & Swan, 'The Science of Scientific Writing', American Scientist 78(6), 1990, 'Perceiving Logical Gaps'

test: Check each sentence for whether the material at its end is already familiar from earlier in the discourse while the material at its start is new. Flag any sentence where that ordering is reversed.
cost: The reader carries unexplained new material forward before there is anywhere to attach it, and then arrives at a flat ending that gives the sentence no point.
suggestion: Invert the sentence so the familiar term opens it and the new term lands last, changing voice if that is what the inversion requires.
mechanism: Comprehension is cheaper when a new term arrives attached to something already held in mind. Opening with the unfamiliar term means storing it uninterpreted until its anchor shows up. The passive voice is the correct repair here rather than a fault, because the choice of voice is what controls which term occupies which end.
counter_case: When the new term is the paragraph's topic and will be the subject of the next several sentences, introducing it up front is right even though it is new. Old-before-new is a default that a deliberate topic shift overrides.
source: Williams (rev. Bizup), 'Style: Lessons in Clarity and Grace', 11th ed., Ten Principles 4 and 6, and Lesson 5, 'Diagnosis and Revision: Old Before New' (pp. 68-70, 80-83)

test: Locate the point of syntactic closure in each sentence, meaning where nothing remains but the words being read. Ask whether the material sitting there is the material the author would want a reader to remember. Flag sentences whose final position holds an aside, a citation, a hedge, or a restated given.
cost: The reader emphasises whatever happens to arrive last, so the author loses control of what the sentence is taken to assert.
suggestion: Move the emphasis-worthy phrase to the end and demote the displaced material to a mid-sentence modifier, or split the sentence at a semicolon so the second half gets its own closing slot.
mechanism: Readers exert their greatest interpretive weight at the moment a sentence closes. Filling that slot with something unremarkable leaves no structural clue to what mattered, and the reader has to choose a candidate unaided. Filling it with something that cannot bear emphasis is worse, because the reader emphasises it anyway.
counter_case: A sentence whose whole job is to restate a given before a pivot has nothing emphasis-worthy in it, and manufacturing a stress-worthy ending would overstate a transitional remark.
source: Gopen & Swan, 'The Science of Scientific Writing', American Scientist 78(6), 1990, 'The Stress Position'

test: Count the pieces of information in a sentence that a reader could plausibly take as its point. Compare that count with the number of closing positions the sentence provides, which is one per full stop plus one per correctly used colon or semicolon. Flag any sentence where the first number exceeds the second.
cost: Emphasis-worthy material sits in unmarked interior positions, and the reader has to rank it without any structural signal, which is where two readers diverge.
suggestion: Add a medial closure with a semicolon or colon for each additional point, or split the sentence, rather than cutting words to hit a length target.
mechanism: Length by itself does not make a sentence hard, and a word count is the wrong diagnostic. A hundred-word sentence with a closure before each new stress-worthy item reads easily, and a ten-word sentence carrying three competing points does not. The usable measure is the ratio of candidate points to available closing slots.
counter_case: A summary sentence that deliberately lists parallel items of equal weight needs no internal closures, because the reader is meant to read the list as one undifferentiated set.
source: Gopen & Swan, 'The Science of Scientific Writing', American Scientist 78(6), 1990, 'The Stress Position' (definition of when a sentence is too long)

test: List every main verb in the paragraph. Flag the paragraph if more than half are copulas or light verbs such as is, are, was, has, occurs, exists, is presumed to be, or takes place.
cost: The real actions are buried in nouns where the reader has no structural cue to find them, so the reader must guess what acts on what.
suggestion: Name the actions the paragraph is actually about and promote each to the main verb of its clause, then make the acting character the subject.
mechanism: Readers look for the action of a clause in its verb. When the verbs are all copulas the actions are still present as abstract nouns, but nothing marks them as the actions, so each reader picks a different reading. Promoting the buried action to the verb usually also exposes whether the author knows which entity performs it.
counter_case: Definitions, type declarations, and statements of fact about identity are genuinely copular. Rewriting 'A martingale is a stochastic process such that ...' to force an action verb damages it.
source: Gopen & Swan, 'The Science of Scientific Writing', American Scientist 78(6), 1990, 'Locating the Action', and closing principle 5

test: Scan for abstract nouns ending in -tion, -ment, -ance, -ity, -sis, or -ing that sit as the subject of an empty verb such as have, make, provide, occur, or exist, or that follow one. Flag each occurrence.
cost: The sentence names an action twice over, once as a noun and once as a hollow verb, and the reader has to reassemble who did what from the prepositional debris.
suggestion: Turn the abstract noun back into a verb and make the entity that performs it the subject. If the performer is missing from the sentence, that absence is itself the finding to raise.
mechanism: A nominalisation packages an action as a thing, which frees the verb slot for a placeholder and frees the subject slot from naming any agent. Readers then reconstruct the event from a chain of prepositional phrases. Reversing the nominalisation typically shortens the sentence and forces the agent back into view.
counter_case: A nominalisation is the right choice when it refers back to an action already described, because it then functions as the familiar opening term that links the sentence to the previous one. 'These decisions ...' at the head of a sentence is doing cohesive work, not hiding an agent.
source: Williams (rev. Bizup), 'Style: Lessons in Clarity and Grace', 11th ed., Lesson 3, 'Diagnosis and Revision: Characters', patterns 1-5

test: Read the sentences of a paragraph and ask what single point they jointly make. Flag the paragraph if two candidate points are needed to cover it.
cost: The reader who is tracking one point loses it mid-paragraph, and neither point gets the emphasis of a paragraph-final position.
suggestion: Split at the seam where the second point begins, and give the new paragraph an opening sentence that names its point.
mechanism: Every unit of discourse, from clause to section, carries an expectation of serving one function. A paragraph doing two jobs violates that expectation with no visible error, so the reader blames their own attention rather than the text. Splitting is nearly free and restores one point per unit.
counter_case: A short paragraph that deliberately stages a contrast holds two propositions on purpose, and splitting it would destroy the pivot that is its whole content.
source: Gopen & Swan, 'The Science of Scientific Writing', American Scientist 78(6), 1990, second set of reader expectations ('Each unit of discourse ... is expected to serve a single function, to make a single point')

test: For each numbered item promised in a sentence, check that the following text delivers exactly that many, in that order, with the same labels. Flag any mismatch in count or order.
cost: A reader counting along loses trust in the text and starts re-reading to find the missing item, which costs far more than the announcement saved.
suggestion: Either correct the count and the order, or delete the enumeration and let the items stand as separate paragraphs.
mechanism: An announced count is a promise the reader actively tracks. A flag word such as 'both' or 'three' tells the reader how many pieces of new material to expect in one place. Breaking the count is caught by the reader almost every time, unlike most prose faults.
counter_case: Nothing. A miscounted enumeration is always an error, though the correct repair may be to delete the count rather than to add the item.
source: Gopen & Swan, 'The Science of Scientific Writing', American Scientist 78(6), 1990, 'Perceiving Logical Gaps' (use of the flag word 'both'); Van Buren & Buehler, 'The Levels of Edit', 2nd ed., JPL Publication 80-1 (NASA-CR-162880), 1980, Section VI-H item 6 (language parallelism)

test: For each sentence, count the words between the head of the grammatical subject and its main verb. Flag any sentence where that count exceeds about seven, and any sentence where it exceeds a quarter of the sentence length.
cost: Everything in the gap is read as parenthetical and discounted, so if it mattered the reader has already downgraded it by the time the verb arrives.
suggestion: Either promote the interrupting material to its own clause after a semicolon, or delete it if it is an aside. Choosing between those two is a question for the author, not a silent edit.
mechanism: Readers need the verb to resolve the syntax and cannot assign importance to anything until it arrives. Material that delays the verb is structurally branded as interruptive whatever its content. The longer the delay, the more likely it is that something important has been mislabelled that way.
counter_case: A short qualifying phrase that must bind to the subject rather than the predicate belongs between them. 'Models trained on the paired corpus outperform ...' is correct, and moving the modifier changes the claim.
source: Gopen & Swan, 'The Science of Scientific Writing', American Scientist 78(6), 1990, 'Subject-Verb Separation'; Williams (rev. Bizup), 'Style: Lessons in Clarity and Grace', 11th ed., Ten Principles 5

test: Count the words before the main clause begins. Flag sentences with more than about ten words of introductory phrase or clause, and flag subjects longer than about eight words.
cost: The reader holds an unresolved fragment for the length of the preamble, which uses attention that the content of the sentence then no longer has.
suggestion: Move the introductory material after the main clause, or turn the long abstract subject into a short concrete one by promoting its buried action to the verb.
mechanism: Working memory is spent on unresolved syntax. A long preamble and a long abstract subject both defer the verb, so both drain the same budget. Getting to the verb early leaves the reader with attention to spend on the claim.
counter_case: A preamble that establishes the condition under which the whole claim holds must precede it, since a reader who meets the claim before the condition has to revise it. 'Under the assumptions of Theorem 2, ...' belongs first.
source: Williams (rev. Bizup), 'Style: Lessons in Clarity and Grace', 11th ed., Ten Principles 5 (pp. 145-147)

test: Count consecutive subordinate clauses hanging off one another at the end of a sentence. Flag any chain of more than one, and in particular any 'which ... that ... because ...' tail.
cost: The reader cannot tell what each clause attaches to, and the sentence loses a single identifiable closing emphasis.
suggestion: Replace the second and later links with a resumptive modifier that repeats the key noun, a summative modifier that names what the clause just said, or a free modifier headed by a participle.
mechanism: Each new subordinate clause reopens the question of attachment, and after two the answer stops being recoverable from position. A resumptive or summative modifier extends the sentence without reopening attachment, because it repeats or names its anchor explicitly.
counter_case: Legal and specification prose sometimes needs nested conditions in one sentence so their scope is unambiguous. Splitting can make it unclear which condition governs which clause.
source: Williams (rev. Bizup), 'Style: Lessons in Clarity and Grace', 11th ed., Ten Principles 9 (pp. 151-157)

test: Read each sentence once from left to right and stop at the first point where two parses are open. Flag the sentence if the correct parse is only recoverable from words that come later.
cost: The reader commits to the wrong parse, hits the disambiguating word, and has to back up, which is a cost paid on every reading by every reader.
suggestion: Reorder so the disambiguating word arrives before the ambiguity, or insert the 'that' the sentence needs to signal a clause boundary.
mechanism: Parsing runs incrementally, so a reader commits to a structure before the sentence ends. Garden-path sentences are correct as strings and still expensive, because the cost is the backtrack rather than a misunderstanding. Inserting 'that' after assume, suppose, show, or find is the cheapest available fix.
counter_case: Omitting 'that' is right when another 'that' sits nearby, since two in one clause is harder to parse than the mild ambiguity that dropping one creates.
source: Knuth, Larrabee & Roberts, 'Mathematical Writing', Stanford CS 209 notes, section 1 (Minicourse), points 8 and 17

test: Scan for runs of three or more nouns used as a single modifier chain. Flag each run.
cost: The reader must try every possible bracketing of the chain and choose one without help, which is slow even for a specialist.
suggestion: Unpack the chain with a preposition or an of-phrase so the grouping is explicit, keeping the head noun at the front.
mechanism: English noun stacks carry no marking of internal structure, so a chain of length n has many admissible readings. Specialists resolve them from prior knowledge, which means the chain is transparent only to readers who already know the answer. A single preposition removes the ambiguity at almost no cost in length.
counter_case: An established compound that functions as one name should stay intact. Unpacking 'support vector machine' or 'byte pair encoding' into a prepositional phrase makes it unrecognisable.
source: Knuth, Larrabee & Roberts, 'Mathematical Writing', Stanford CS 209 notes, section 1 (Minicourse), point 26

test: Replace every displayed formula and every inline expression longer than a few symbols with the word 'blah' and read the result aloud. Flag any sentence that stops being grammatical or stops carrying a claim.
cost: Readers skim formulas on a first pass. A sentence that depends on its symbols for grammar leaves the skimming reader with nothing at all.
suggestion: Restate in words what each display asserts, so the prose remains a complete argument with the mathematics as support rather than as syntax.
mechanism: Most readers make a first pass that skips the equations and looks for the shape of the argument. Prose that carries the argument survives that pass and invites a second, closer one. Prose whose clauses are completed by symbols fails the first pass, and there is then no second one.
counter_case: A proof written for verification rather than for reading may legitimately be a chain of displays, provided the surrounding prose says what the chain establishes.
source: Knuth, Larrabee & Roberts, 'Mathematical Writing', Stanford CS 209 notes, section 1 (Minicourse), point 13

test: Check every small number used as an adjective. Flag digits where a spelled word belongs, and spelled words where the number is being named as a value.
cost: Nothing is misunderstood, but the reader's eye stops on the inconsistency and the sentence is read twice.
suggestion: Spell out small numbers used as adjectives and keep digits for numbers referred to as values, then apply the choice uniformly.
mechanism: Numerals in running prose read as data and words read as description, so the choice signals which one is meant. Mixed practice in one paragraph makes the signal noise. The check needs no understanding of the content.
counter_case: Venue style overrides this. Where a journal requires numerals throughout, or where the surrounding text is dense with measurements, uniform numerals read better than a mixture.
source: Knuth, Larrabee & Roberts, 'Mathematical Writing', Stanford CS 209 notes, section 1 (Minicourse), point 18

test: List every claim in the abstract and introduction. For each, name the population it quantifies over and the sample actually evaluated. Flag any claim whose stated population is broader than the sample.
cost: Readers, and later citers, carry forward a claim the experiments never tested, and the overclaim outlives the paper.
suggestion: Narrow the claim to the evaluated sample, naming the datasets, model sizes, and languages in the claim itself, or move the broader statement into a clearly marked discussion of what the result suggests.
mechanism: A claim in an abstract is read as covering whatever population its nouns name. Benchmarks are samples, and a result on a few of them supports a claim about those benchmarks rather than about the construct they were built to probe. The gap is invisible in the abstract and only recoverable by reading the experiments section, which most citers do not do.
counter_case: A claim that is explicitly framed as a conjecture, in a section marked as such, may legitimately range over a population wider than the sample. The requirement is the label, not the narrowing.
source: ACL Rolling Review Reviewer Guidelines, items R2 ('Inappropriate scope of the claims') and R4 ('Misleading or inappropriate framing, overclaiming'); NeurIPS Paper Checklist Guidelines, item 1 (Claims)

test: For each explanatory statement, ask whether it was tested. Flag any statement that has the grammatical form of a finding but rests on intuition, and check whether the paper marks it as speculation anywhere.
cost: A guess acquires the authority of a result, gets cited as fact, and then blocks the work that would have tested it.
suggestion: Keep the intuition and move it into a section explicitly labelled as motivation or conjecture, or add the words that mark its status in place.
mechanism: A paper's typography and register confer authority on every declarative sentence in it equally. Readers cannot distinguish a measured claim from an intuition by looking, so the only available signal is an explicit label. Quarantining speculation in a named section preserves the idea and removes the false authority at the same time.
counter_case: Speculation is not merely permitted but valuable, and a paper with none is often a paper that has hidden its reasoning. The rule constrains where speculation sits, never whether it appears.
source: Lipton & Steinhardt, 'Troubling Trends in Machine Learning Scholarship', arXiv:1807.03341, section 3.1 ('Explanation vs. Speculation'), including the dropout paper's designated Motivation section as the positive example

test: For every claim that a quantity is small, large, close, or bounded, check whether a number, a measurement, or a theorem statement is attached. Flag claims that read as formal but carry neither.
cost: The claim cannot be verified or even pinned down, so a reader who wants to build on it has to guess whether it is a numerical observation or an asymptotic statement.
suggestion: Either state the theorem with its assumptions, or give the measurement with its conditions, or rewrite the sentence as the informal observation it is.
mechanism: Statements that are neither clearly formal nor clearly informal let a weak argument borrow the authority of a proof. A reader cannot tell whether 'the gap is very close to zero' means a measured gap at realistic parameters or a limit as dimension grows. Naming which one is meant is usually a one-sentence repair.
counter_case: An informal statement clearly flagged as intuition needs no theorem, and demanding formality there produces the mathiness the rule exists to prevent.
source: Lipton & Steinhardt, 'Troubling Trends in Machine Learning Scholarship', arXiv:1807.03341, section 3.3 ('Mathiness'), second issue

test: For each theorem, lemma, and formal remark, ask whether the paper's headline claim would change if it were deleted. Apply the author test, which is whether you would rely on this result to make a prediction or to get a system working. Flag any result that fails both.
cost: Pages of the reader's attention go to material that supports nothing, and the apparent rigour disguises where the real evidence is thin.
suggestion: Move the result to an appendix with a sentence saying what it does and does not cover, or cut it, and put the reclaimed space into the analysis that does carry the claim.
mechanism: Equations read as evidence of depth whether or not they bear on the argument. A theorem about the convex case in a paper about non-convex optimisation adds authority without adding support. The reliance test is decidable by the author even when it is not decidable by a reader.
counter_case: A negative or delimiting result that bounds what the method can do belongs in the paper even though the headline claim does not rest on it, because its job is to stop a reader overgeneralising.
source: Lipton & Steinhardt, 'Troubling Trends in Machine Learning Scholarship', arXiv:1807.03341, sections 3.3 and 5.1 (the 'Would I rely on this explanation' test)

test: Find every appeal to a named theorem or general result used as justification. Check that the paper states which hypotheses hold in its setting. Flag appeals where the theorem's conditions are not shown to apply.
cost: The justification is decorative, and a reader who checks it loses confidence in every other citation in the paper.
suggestion: State the hypotheses and why they hold here, or drop the appeal and give the empirical reason for the design choice instead.
mechanism: A named theorem invoked in passing transfers authority without transferring content. The no-free-lunch theorem is routinely cited as licensing heuristics without guarantees even though it formally precludes nothing of the kind. Naming the hypotheses either repairs the appeal or reveals that it never held.
counter_case: A theorem invoked as an orienting analogy, marked as such, is fine. The fault is the pretence of derivation, not the reference.
source: Lipton & Steinhardt, 'Troubling Trends in Machine Learning Scholarship', arXiv:1807.03341, section 3.3 (theory invoked in overly broad ways)

test: Find every comparison to human performance. Check whether the sentence names the task and the conditions, or names a capability. Flag any capability-level comparison.
cost: Readers outside the subfield take the claim as evidence of a general ability, and the correction never travels as far as the claim did.
suggestion: Restate the comparison as a task-and-conditions claim, naming the dataset, the label set, and the fact that the comparison holds under the test distribution only.
mechanism: A phrase such as dermatologist-level conceals that the classifier and the dermatologist perform different tasks under different conditions. The classifier achieves low error on independent and identically distributed test data, while the professional handles open-ended and shifting circumstances. Naming the task is what keeps the two apart.
counter_case: A comparison that is already scoped to the benchmark is correct and useful, and refusing all human baselines removes a genuinely informative reference point.
source: Lipton & Steinhardt, 'Troubling Trends in Machine Learning Scholarship', arXiv:1807.03341, section 3.4.1 (suggestive definitions and human-level claims)

test: Check whether the paper states which of the problems it raises remain open. Flag papers whose discussion presents every question as addressed.
cost: Follow-up work skips a question the paper never actually settled, and the field carries a false belief that it is resolved.
suggestion: Add explicit sentences naming the questions left open, either in the limitations section or at the end of the discussion.
mechanism: Readers infer from silence that nothing remains. Stating what is unresolved costs a few lines and directly invites the follow-up work that a paper wants. The same statement also protects the paper against a later claim that it overreached.
counter_case: A short paper making one narrow, fully settled claim needs no open-problems paragraph, and manufacturing one dilutes a clean result.
source: Lipton & Steinhardt, 'Troubling Trends in Machine Learning Scholarship', arXiv:1807.03341, section 5.1 ('being clear about which problems are open and which are solved')

test: For every proposition asserted, check whether the text says what its status is, meaning proved here, proved elsewhere with a citation, assumed, conjectured, or unknown. Flag propositions with no status marker, and in particular flag negative claims such as 'p does not imply q'.
cost: A reader cannot tell which parts of the paper they are allowed to build on, so a cautious reader rebuilds everything and a careless one builds on sand.
suggestion: Attach the status to the sentence. For an unproved non-implication, say whether a counterexample follows, whether a reference exists, or whether the authors simply do not know.
mechanism: Readers who already knew the status of every statement would not be reading the paper. An unsupported negative claim is the worst case, because it looks like a result and cannot be checked. Confessing that a derivation was attempted and failed costs one clause and is more useful to the field than the ambiguity.
counter_case: Restating a status marker on every sentence of a long proof is noise. A single statement governing a block is enough, and readers infer the scope of the block correctly.
source: Halmos, 'How to Write Mathematics', in How to Write Mathematics (AMS, 1973), pp. 19-48, section 10 ('Honesty is the best policy')

test: For each stated objective, check whether the text names an outcome and a criterion by which its success will be judged. Flag objectives phrased as activities, meaning those whose verb is investigate, explore, study, develop, or examine with no stated endpoint.
cost: The reviewer cannot tell what would count as delivering the objective, so a fundable idea gets scored as a vague one.
suggestion: Rewrite each objective as the outcome plus its assessment criterion, keeping the activity as the method clause that follows.
mechanism: Reviewers are asked directly whether the plan incorporates a mechanism to assess success. An objective phrased as an activity satisfies no such mechanism, because any amount of work discharges it. Naming the endpoint converts an unfalsifiable promise into a checkable one, which is also what makes the risk visible and therefore creditable.
counter_case: An exploratory aim in a high-risk proposal may legitimately have no predefined success metric, provided the text says so and states what will be learned either way. The fault is silence about the criterion, not its absence.
source: NSF Merit Review Criteria, elements considered for both criteria ('Is the plan for carrying out the proposed activities well-reasoned, well-organized and based on a sound rationale? Does the plan incorporate a mechanism to assess success?')

test: For each capability the proposal claims it will have, find the place in the work plan, the resources section, or the applicant's record that supplies it. Flag claims with no such anchor.
cost: The reviewer reads an unanchored capability claim as an assumption rather than a plan, and feasibility is the criterion the proposal then loses on.
suggestion: Add the pointer to the work package, the named resource, or the prior result that supplies the capability, or reduce the claim to what the anchored resources support.
mechanism: Reviewers assess whether adequate resources are available to carry out the proposed activities, and they do that by matching claims to anchors. An unanchored claim is not disbelieved so much as discounted to zero. A one-clause cross-reference converts it back into evidence.
counter_case: Ambition that is explicitly flagged as contingent belongs in a proposal, since the high-risk high-gain framing depends on it. The requirement is that the contingency is stated, not that every claim is de-risked.
source: NSF Merit Review Criteria, elements considered for both criteria (elements considered, resources and plan quality); Van Buren & Buehler, 'The Levels of Edit', 2nd ed., JPL Publication 80-1 (NASA-CR-162880), 1980, Section VI-C item 6 (cross-references must point at something that exists)

test: Build a table of every symbol in the paper with every meaning it carries. Flag any symbol with two meanings and any concept written with two symbols. Include index letters, subscript conventions, and case conventions in the table.
cost: The reader silently merges two things or splits one, and any error that follows is untraceable because the notation hid it.
suggestion: Assign one symbol per concept before revising the mathematics, then apply the assignment everywhere including figures, captions, and appendices.
mechanism: Notation is a promise of identity, so reusing a letter asserts that two things are the same. Reusing an index letter is the common case, where A_j in one place and A_k in another for the same family makes a reader check whether the range changed. Fixing this after drafting is mechanical, and deciding it before drafting is nearly free.
counter_case: A locally scoped reuse inside a single proof, declared at its start and never referenced outside, is acceptable and often clearer than importing a fresh letter from a crowded alphabet.
source: Knuth, Larrabee & Roberts, 'Mathematical Writing', Stanford CS 209 notes, section 1 (Minicourse), point 14; Halmos, 'How to Write Mathematics', in How to Write Mathematics (AMS, 1973), pp. 19-48, section 6 ('Think about the alphabet')

test: Design the symbol assignment before writing, covering every space, function, index, parameter, and set the paper will name. Check that no letter carries a conventional meaning it will contradict, and that no two symbols in one expression are visually confusable.
cost: Ad hoc symbol choices made mid-sentence produce collisions that can only be fixed by renaming across the whole paper, so they usually are not fixed.
suggestion: Reserve conventionally frozen letters for their conventional uses, keep one family of letters per kind of object, and avoid pairs that differ only in case or font when both appear in the same expression.
mechanism: Readers carry strong priors about certain letters, so n for a complex number or epsilon for a positive integer produces a low-level friction that is felt without being localised. Symbol decisions also propagate, since a letter used for one thing is unavailable for another. An hour spent on the alphabet before drafting removes a class of defects that is expensive to remove later.
counter_case: A subfield's entrenched convention beats internal harmony. Where the literature universally writes a particular symbol for a particular object, matching it is right even if it collides with the paper's own scheme.
source: Halmos, 'How to Write Mathematics', in How to Write Mathematics (AMS, 1973), pp. 19-48, section 6 ('Think about the alphabet')

test: For every symbol introduced, count how many times it is used. Flag any symbol used exactly once, and any symbol introduced in a statement whose only purpose is to be referenced inside the following proof.
cost: Every symbol charges the reader a lookup, and a symbol that is never reused charges it for nothing.
suggestion: Delete the symbol and state the sentence in words, accepting an extra half-line in the proof where the name is needed.
mechanism: The best notation is no notation, since a symbol is a name the reader must hold. A name used once carries no information that its referent does not already carry. Introducing it in a theorem statement to save half a line of the proof shifts cost from the author onto every reader of the statement.
counter_case: A symbol introduced in one sentence for reference in the next few sentences of the same paragraph is fine, and the rule is worth bending whenever the alternative is an unwieldy repeated phrase.
source: Halmos, 'How to Write Mathematics', in How to Write Mathematics (AMS, 1973), pp. 19-48, section 16 ('Resist symbols')

test: Find references of the form 'X also satisfies (n)' where the display at (n) is written in terms of a different symbol. Flag each.
cost: The reference is literally false, and the reader has to work out which substitution was intended before continuing.
suggestion: Either say that the numbered relation holds with the new symbol substituted for the old, or name the property and use the name.
mechanism: A numbered display is a specific formula containing specific letters, so a claim that a different object satisfies it is nonsense as written. Readers do reconstruct the intent, and the reconstruction is a real cost paid at a moment when they were following an argument. Naming the property removes the problem permanently.
counter_case: Where the display is explicitly written with a placeholder, and the text says so, referring other objects to it is exactly correct.
source: Halmos, 'How to Write Mathematics', in How to Write Mathematics (AMS, 1973), pp. 19-48, section 16 ('Resist symbols')

test: Check that no sentence begins with a symbol, and that no two symbols are separated only by a comma or a full stop when both belong to different formulas.
cost: An overworked comma or period between two symbols is easy to miss, and the reader parses the pair as one expression and has to back up.
suggestion: Put the appropriate noun in apposition before the symbol at the start of a sentence, and insert a word between symbols belonging to different formulas.
mechanism: Punctuation marks are small and symbols are visually salient, so a period between two symbols is skipped. Beginning a sentence with a symbol removes the capital letter that normally marks the boundary. Naming the object in apposition restores both cues at the cost of one word.
counter_case: Nothing substantive. In a table cell or a display, symbols may of course sit adjacent, since the layout supplies the boundary that prose punctuation would.
source: Knuth, Larrabee & Roberts, 'Mathematical Writing', Stanford CS 209 notes, section 1 (Minicourse), points 1 and 2; Halmos, 'How to Write Mathematics', in How to Write Mathematics (AMS, 1973), pp. 19-48, section 17 ('Use symbols correctly')

test: Check that each relational symbol is read the same way throughout, meaning it always translates into the same words. Flag any sentence where a symbol is used as a preposition in one clause and as a verb in another.
cost: The reader retranslates the symbol on each occurrence and hits a momentary ambiguity at every switch.
suggestion: Fix one reading, translate the symbol into words where the other reading was wanted, and leave the symbol only where the fixed reading fits.
mechanism: A symbol acquires a verbal translation in the reader's head on first use. Switching the translation mid-sentence produces a dissonance that is felt even by readers who could not name the cause. Writing 'for x in A' and reserving the symbol for 'is in' removes it entirely.
counter_case: Displayed mathematics and formal statements in logic use the symbol as an operator with no verbal reading at all, and imposing prose grammar on them is wrong.
source: Halmos, 'How to Write Mathematics', in How to Write Mathematics (AMS, 1973), pp. 19-48, section 17 ('Use symbols correctly')

test: Scan running prose for the logical symbols for implication, universal and existential quantification, and 'such that', and for the abbreviation dots standing in for 'therefore'. Flag each occurrence outside displayed mathematics or a paper on logic.
cost: The reader has to decode a symbol whose expansion is a word, which is slower to read than the word and no more precise.
suggestion: Replace each with the corresponding word or phrase in prose, and keep the symbols for displays and formal statements.
mechanism: Logical symbols in prose save keystrokes for the author and cost decoding for the reader, and the exchange rate is bad. In prose the symbols also lose the visual isolation that makes them legible in a display. Papers on logic are the exception because there the symbols are the subject matter.
counter_case: A paper whose content is formal logic, or a proof written in a formal calculus, uses the symbols correctly in running text and should not be reworded.
source: Knuth, Larrabee & Roberts, 'Mathematical Writing', Stanford CS 209 notes, section 1 (Minicourse), point 3

test: For each named component, method, or phenomenon the paper coins, ask what the name asserts and whether the paper argues it. Flag names that import a claim about cognition, understanding, intent, or emotion.
cost: The name carries a claim past the reader without argument, every later paper must either adopt the claim or fight the name, and the public discussion inherits it.
suggestion: Rename the component after what it computes, and keep the suggestive term as an explicitly labelled analogy in the motivation.
mechanism: A coined term with a colloquial meaning smuggles connotations in without the need to argue for them. Once a suggestive term has a technical definition, every subsequent paper must either embrace the term and confuse its readers or replace it and fragment the literature. Naming after the computation leaves the analogy available and unbinding.
counter_case: A vivid name that genuinely aids memory and makes no substantive claim is a service to readers. The test is whether the name asserts something, not whether it is metaphorical.
source: Lipton & Steinhardt, 'Troubling Trends in Machine Learning Scholarship', arXiv:1807.03341, section 3.4.1 ('Suggestive Definitions')

test: For each technical term, check whether an established definition exists in the literature and whether the paper's usage matches it. Flag terms used in a sense that contradicts or generalises the established one.
cost: Readers who know the established meaning are misled, readers who do not learn the wrong one, and the term becomes unusable for everyone afterwards.
suggestion: Use the correct existing term, or coin a distinct new one and state its relation to the established term in the same sentence.
mechanism: Overloading a precise term makes every subsequent use of it ambiguous, so a reader meeting the word cannot tell which of several meanings applies. Deconvolution now refers to reversing a convolution, to transpose convolution, and to attempts at resolving that confusion. The damage is cumulative and does not decay.
counter_case: Where a subfield has already completed the shift and the original sense has no current users, following the new usage is right and reviving the old one is the confusing choice.
source: Lipton & Steinhardt, 'Troubling Trends in Machine Learning Scholarship', arXiv:1807.03341, section 3.4.2 ('Overloading Technical Terminology')

test: Find every use of a term that packs several distinct meanings, such as interpretability, generalisation, bias, robustness, alignment, reasoning, or understanding. For each occurrence, check whether the surrounding sentence names which sense is meant.
cost: Two papers appear to be in dialogue while addressing different things, and quantitative claims built on the word have no determinate content.
suggestion: Replace the first occurrence in each section with the specific sense, and keep the umbrella term only where the umbrella is the point.
mechanism: A suitcase word packs meanings that share no single cause, so it names a family rather than a quantity. Generalisation covers the train-to-test gap, transfer between populations, and external validity, and conflating them overstates what a system does. Naming the sense once per section is usually enough for the reader to carry it.
counter_case: As an aspirational or organising label the suitcase word is exactly right, and unpacking it would be pedantic. Naming a research programme artificial intelligence is fine. Putting intelligence into an equation as a scalar is not.
source: Lipton & Steinhardt, 'Troubling Trends in Machine Learning Scholarship', arXiv:1807.03341, section 3.4.3 ('Suitcase Words')

test: For each key term the argument depends on, check whether the paper defines it, cites a definition, or leaves it to context. Flag undefined key terms, and flag any term whose meaning shifts between sections.
cost: Reviewers cannot judge whether the results support the claim, because the claim's terms have no fixed content.
suggestion: Define the term on first use and state it twice in complementary ways, once as the formal condition and once as what it amounts to.
mechanism: Readers accumulate a working definition from usage, and a term that is never defined gets a different working definition from each reader. Stating a definition twice, formally and informally, gives readers two chances to converge and lets them check their reading against the author's. All variables should be defined at least informally when first introduced.
counter_case: A term that is standard in the venue's audience needs no definition, and defining it signals that the paper is aimed elsewhere. The judgement is about the venue rather than about the term.
source: ACL Rolling Review Reviewer Guidelines, item G4 ('Key terms too vague and not defined'); Knuth, Larrabee & Roberts, 'Mathematical Writing', Stanford CS 209 notes, section 1 (Minicourse), point 11

test: Check that every abbreviation, acronym, and non-standard symbol is expanded or defined at first use, including first use in the abstract, in each figure caption, and in each table header.
cost: A reader who starts at a figure, which many do, meets an undefined acronym with nothing nearby to resolve it.
suggestion: Expand at first use in the body and again on first use in any caption or table that a reader might reach independently, or add a notation table.
mechanism: Captions and tables are entry points, not continuations, because readers scan figures before reading prose. An acronym defined only in Section 3 is undefined for the reader who arrives at Figure 5. Repeating the expansion in the caption costs a few words and serves the commonest reading path.
counter_case: Field-standard acronyms need no expansion, and expanding them in every caption is clutter. Where the venue's readership universally knows the term, treat it as a word.
source: Van Buren & Buehler, 'The Levels of Edit', 2nd ed., JPL Publication 80-1 (NASA-CR-162880), 1980, Section VI-H item 10 (definition of abbreviations, acronyms, and symbols)
