test: Check every table and figure of main results for error bars, confidence intervals, or a significance test. For each one present, check that the text names what the variability is over, how it was computed, and whether the interval is a standard deviation or a standard error.
cost: A reader cannot tell whether a reported gap is real, and comparing across papers becomes impossible because the intervals mean different things.
suggestion: State the variability source, the number of runs, the estimator, and the multiplier in the caption, and use the same convention in every table.
mechanism: An unlabelled interval is uninterpretable, since a standard deviation over seeds and a standard error over test examples differ by a factor of the square root of the sample size. Readers default to whichever convention their own subfield uses and then compare incomparable numbers. Naming the source in the caption is a one-line fix that survives being read out of order.
counter_case: A single deterministic run of an expensive model may honestly have no error bar, and the correct move is to say so rather than to fabricate one. Reviewers are instructed not to penalise honesty about this.
source: NeurIPS Paper Checklist Guidelines, item 7 (Experiment Statistical Significance); ACL Rolling Review Reviewer Guidelines, item R5

test: For each reported number, check whether the text says it is a single run, a mean, a median, or the best of several. Flag any number whose selection rule is unstated, and any table mixing conventions.
cost: A best-of-many number compared against a baseline's single run is not a comparison, and the reader has no way to see that from the table.
suggestion: State the aggregation for every column in the caption, and use the same aggregation for the method and its baselines.
mechanism: Reporting the maximum over an unstated number of runs inflates the reported result by an amount that grows with the number of runs. Readers assume the convention is uniform across a table because tables signal comparability. Stating the rule makes the comparison auditable and usually reveals whether the baselines got equal treatment.
counter_case: Reporting the best configuration found is correct when the paper's claim is about what the method can reach under tuning, provided the same search budget is reported for the baselines.
source: ACL Rolling Review Reviewer Guidelines, item R1 ('Analysis issues', reporting best-of-unknown-many runs); ACL ARR Responsible NLP Research Checklist, item C3

test: Count the changes the paper introduces relative to the closest prior system. Count the ablation rows that isolate them. Flag any change with no row that removes it while holding everything else fixed.
cost: Readers cannot tell which change produced the gain, so they adopt all of them, and the field builds on a component that does nothing.
suggestion: Add the missing ablation rows, or state explicitly which contributions are not separately attributed and why, so the reader knows the attribution is open.
mechanism: Proposing several changes together and reporting one aggregate gain looks like more work and is in fact less, because the attribution question is left unanswered. Published lineages of architectural improvements have been shown to reduce to better hyperparameter tuning. Where full ablation is impractical, a robustness check or an error analysis can carry the same burden.
counter_case: Ablation is neither necessary nor sufficient and can be genuinely impractical at scale. A paper that says so and substitutes a robustness check or a qualitative error analysis has met the obligation.
source: Lipton & Steinhardt, 'Troubling Trends in Machine Learning Scholarship', arXiv:1807.03341, section 3.2 ('Failure to Identify the Sources of Empirical Gains') and section 5.1

test: For every baseline, check whether the text states the tuning budget it received. Flag baselines tuned less than the proposed method, and flag prompt-based baselines with no reported prompt search.
cost: The headline gap measures tuning effort rather than method quality, and a reader who reproduces the work finds the gap vanishes.
suggestion: Report the search budget per system, or match budgets and rerun, or state plainly that the baseline numbers are taken from the original paper under an unknown budget.
mechanism: A comparison is only informative when the compared systems got comparable effort. Prompt-based baselines are the acute case, since a single unoptimised prompt can cost tens of points. Quoting a number from a prior paper is legitimate, but the reader has to be told that is what happened.
counter_case: Where the baseline is a published state-of-the-art result that the authors cannot rerun, quoting it with a note about the unmatched budget is the honest option and better than omitting the comparison.
source: ACL Rolling Review Reviewer Guidelines, item R1 (baselines 'sufficiently well-tuned for a fair comparison', including prompt tuning)

test: For each dataset, model, and language included in the evaluation, find the sentence that says why it was chosen. Flag selections with no stated rationale, especially where the set looks like a convenience sample.
cost: A reader cannot distinguish a designed evaluation from the subset on which the method happened to work.
suggestion: State the selection criterion, and where the criterion was availability, say so.
mechanism: An unmotivated selection is indistinguishable from a favourable one. Naming the criterion, even when it is simply which datasets have public test labels, converts a suspicion into a stated limitation. Reviewers are asked directly whether the sample is motivated with respect to the claimed contribution.
counter_case: A benchmark suite that is the field's standard needs no per-task rationale, and giving one for each of its forty tasks is noise. Name the suite and why the suite.
source: ACL Rolling Review Reviewer Guidelines, item M4 ('Unmotivated selection')

test: Check that data splits, hyperparameter values, and the procedure by which hyperparameters were chosen appear in the main paper or are pointed at from it. Flag any experiment whose key settings appear nowhere.
cost: The result cannot be reproduced or even interpreted, since the reader cannot tell whether the gain came from the method or the schedule.
suggestion: Put the settings a reader needs in order to appreciate the result in the main text, and the exhaustive list in an appendix with an explicit pointer.
mechanism: Reproducibility failures usually trace to a setting the authors considered obvious. Splitting the details between a main-text summary and an appendix satisfies both the reader following the argument and the reader rebuilding the system. Key settings belong in the main paper to the level of detail needed to appreciate the results.
counter_case: A paper whose contribution is theoretical, or one with no experiments, has nothing to report here and should say so rather than pad.
source: NeurIPS Paper Checklist Guidelines, item 6 (Experimental Setting/Details); ACL ARR Responsible NLP Research Checklist, item C2

test: Check that the number of examples and the train, validation, and test split sizes are reported for every dataset used or created. Flag missing counts, and flag cases where the split procedure is unstated.
cost: A reader cannot judge whether a two-point difference is meaningful, because the test set size that determines the noise floor is unknown.
suggestion: Add a dataset table with per-split counts, and state whether splits are the standard ones or newly drawn.
mechanism: The size of the test set sets the resolution of every comparison made on it. Without counts a reader cannot compute whether a reported gap exceeds sampling noise. The counts are cheap to report and answer several reviewer questions at once.
counter_case: Where the dataset is a fixed public benchmark whose splits are universally known, a citation substitutes for the table, though the counts still help.
source: ACL ARR Responsible NLP Research Checklist, item B6

test: For every third-party metric or tool that produces a reported number, check that the implementation, version, and parameter settings are named. Flag bare metric names.
cost: Two papers report the same metric name with different implementations, and their numbers are compared as if they were the same quantity.
suggestion: Name the package, its version, and the non-default settings alongside the first reported use of the metric.
mechanism: Metric implementations differ in tokenisation, smoothing, and normalisation, and the differences are often larger than the effects being reported. A bare metric name therefore does not identify a quantity. Naming the implementation makes the number comparable and the comparison auditable.
counter_case: Where a metric has one canonical implementation that the field uses without variation, the name alone identifies it and the version note is clutter.
source: ACL ARR Responsible NLP Research Checklist, item C4

test: Check that every table and figure is referred to from the running text, and that the reference says what the reader should see in it rather than only that it exists.
cost: A figure with a bare pointer is either skipped or read against the wrong question, so the evidence it carries does not land.
suggestion: Replace bare pointers with a sentence stating the finding and citing the figure as its support.
mechanism: Readers use the prose to decide which figures to study and what to look for. A bare cross-reference gives no such instruction, so the reader either builds their own question or moves on. Stating the finding first also exposes cases where the figure does not in fact show it.
counter_case: A reference figure that exists for lookup rather than for argument, such as a full hyperparameter table, needs only a pointer.
source: NeurIPS Paper Checklist Guidelines, item 7 (cross-referencing tables and figures in the text); Van Buren & Buehler, 'The Levels of Edit', 2nd ed., JPL Publication 80-1 (NASA-CR-162880), 1980, Section VI-C item 3

test: Scan for doubled pairs such as full and complete, each and every, basic and fundamental, first and foremost, true and accurate, hopes and desires, any and all. Flag each pair.
cost: The reader looks for the distinction the pair implies and finds none, which is a small cost paid every time.
suggestion: Keep one member of the pair, choosing the one whose register matches the surrounding prose.
mechanism: Paired synonyms are a fossil of early English borrowing and now signal only formality. Because coordination normally marks two things, readers begin distinguishing the members before recognising them as one. The check is a fixed list and needs no understanding of the content.
counter_case: A pair whose members genuinely differ must stay. In a legal or specification context 'complete and correct' names two separable properties.
source: Williams (rev. Bizup), 'Style: Lessons in Clarity and Grace', 11th ed., Lesson 9, principle 2 (p. 128)

test: Scan for modifiers whose meaning is already in the word they modify, such as final outcome, future plans, past history, completely revolutionise, true facts, each individual, various different, basic fundamentals. Also scan for category nouns after an adjective, such as pink in colour, large in size, round in shape, during that period of time.
cost: The reader processes a word that adds nothing, and a paper thick with these reads as inflated regardless of its content.
suggestion: Delete the redundant modifier, and for a redundant category convert the adjective into an adverb or a noun so the category word disappears.
mechanism: Every word implies its own category, so naming the category again is pure repetition. These are hard to see while drafting because they are idiomatic, and easy to see against a list. The two patterns have different repairs, which is why they are checked together but fixed differently.
counter_case: Where a contrast is live, the modifier is doing work. 'Past history' is redundant, but 'past performance' against 'projected performance' is not.
source: Williams (rev. Bizup), 'Style: Lessons in Clarity and Grace', 11th ed., Lesson 9, principle 3 (pp. 128-130) and principle 4

test: Find sentences that announce what the paper will do rather than saying what is true. Delete the announcing phrase and read what remains as a claim. Flag the sentence if the remainder is self-evident or is not a claim at all.
cost: The reader is told a topic and given nothing to agree or disagree with, so a paragraph that looked like an argument turns out to contain none.
suggestion: Delete the announcing frame and promote the remainder to a claim. If the remainder is self-evident, the paragraph needs a real claim rather than a rewrite.
mechanism: Metadiscourse that guides a reader is useful, and metadiscourse that substitutes for a claim hides its absence. Stripping the frame is a reliable diagnostic, since a genuine claim survives it and a topic announcement collapses. The diagnostic also tells the author which paragraphs still need thinking.
counter_case: Signposting is legitimate and necessary at section openings and in a paper's contributions list, where the reader needs the map before the argument.
source: Williams (rev. Bizup), 'Style: Lessons in Clarity and Grace', 11th ed., Lesson 9, Quick Tip on metadiscourse (pp. 137-138)

test: Check whether a statement made once is restated later in slightly different words without a marker saying it is the same statement. Flag each unmarked restatement.
cost: The reader stops to work out whether the second version is the same claim or a subtly different one, and either answer costs a re-read of the first.
suggestion: Either delete the restatement, or mark it explicitly as a restatement and repeat the original wording exactly.
mechanism: A reader meeting a familiar-looking statement must decide whether it is identical, which requires retrieving the original. Word-for-word repetition makes the decision instant and is the right form when the purpose is to highlight a small difference. Near-repetition with unexplained variation is the case that costs the most.
counter_case: Deliberate word-for-word repetition is a virtue when the point is a contrast, provided the difference is named. Repeating five conditions and weakening the sixth works only if the text says that is what happened.
source: Halmos, 'How to Write Mathematics', in How to Write Mathematics (AMS, 1973), pp. 19-48, section 12 ('Do and do not repeat')

test: Compare the proofs of successive results. Flag any proof that says 'by the same technique as' or 'see the proof of' and any proof whose steps substantially duplicate an earlier one.
cost: The reader verifies the same reasoning twice and still does not learn what the shared structure was.
suggestion: Extract the shared reasoning as a lemma, state it once, and derive both results from it.
mechanism: Duplicated proof steps are a symptom that a general fact has not been identified. Extracting it shortens the paper, makes both results easier to verify, and often generalises them. A pointer back to an earlier proof asks the reader to do the extraction instead.
counter_case: A short symmetric case may be genuinely faster to restate than to abstract, and a one-line 'the other case is symmetric' is clearer than a lemma nobody needs.
source: Halmos, 'How to Write Mathematics', in How to Write Mathematics (AMS, 1973), pp. 19-48, section 12 ('never repeat a proof')

test: For each numbered or lettered sequence in the document, meaning tables, figures, references, equations, footnotes, sections, and subsections, check for duplicates and for gaps. Check also that each sequence uses one kind of numbering throughout.
cost: A duplicate number makes every reference to it ambiguous, and a gap makes a reader search for the element they assume they missed.
suggestion: Renumber the sequence, and pick one style of numeral or letter per sequence.
mechanism: Numbering is a promise of completeness and uniqueness, and readers check it involuntarily. Duplicates and gaps appear almost exclusively from late insertions and deletions, so they are absent from every draft the authors read carefully. Machine-checkable and never worth an author's manual pass.
counter_case: Nothing. Where a venue's template imposes a numbering scheme, follow it, but duplicates and gaps remain errors under any scheme.
source: Van Buren & Buehler, 'The Levels of Edit', 2nd ed., JPL Publication 80-1 (NASA-CR-162880), 1980, Section VI-C item 4 (a) and (b)

test: Compare the table of contents, or the section list, against the headings in the body, word for word and in mechanical style. Compare figure and table titles in any front list against the captions. Flag every mismatch.
cost: A reader navigating by the contents arrives somewhere whose heading differs and cannot tell whether they are in the right place.
suggestion: Make the two agree in wording, capitalisation, and punctuation, taking the body heading as authoritative unless the author says otherwise.
mechanism: A contents list is an index, and an index whose entries differ from their targets fails at the one job it has. Mismatches arise from renaming a section without regenerating the list. Explanatory material in a caption need not appear in the list, but the title portion must match.
counter_case: A deliberately shortened running head or a truncated contents entry is fine where the template requires it, provided the shortening is systematic rather than an artefact of an edit.
source: Van Buren & Buehler, 'The Levels of Edit', 2nd ed., JPL Publication 80-1 (NASA-CR-162880), 1980, Section VI-C item 1 (Integrity Edit)

test: Compare all figure captions with each other and all table titles with each other. Flag any two that are identical.
cost: A reader who cites or recalls a figure by its caption cannot tell the two apart, and neither can a reader scanning the figure list.
suggestion: Add the distinguishing condition to each caption, since two identical captions almost always mark two conditions of one experiment.
mechanism: A caption is the figure's name, so duplicate captions leave two figures unnamed. The duplication usually happens when a figure is copied to make a variant and the caption is not updated, which means the distinguishing fact is exactly the one missing. Comparing captions pairwise is trivial to automate.
counter_case: Nothing. Continued tables spanning pages carry a repeated title by convention, and those are one table rather than two.
source: Van Buren & Buehler, 'The Levels of Edit', 2nd ed., JPL Publication 80-1 (NASA-CR-162880), 1980, Section VI-C item 5 (Integrity Edit)

test: For every reference to another part of the document, whether by title or by number, check that the target exists and carries the title used. Include references inside figures, slide artwork, and appendices.
cost: The reader follows a pointer to a section that was renamed or merged and cannot tell what was meant.
suggestion: Correct the pointer, and where a referenced element has been absorbed into another, name the new location rather than the old title.
mechanism: Internal cross-references decay under restructuring, and the decay is invisible to authors who know where the material went. Checking by title as well as by number catches the case where the number is right and the name is stale. References embedded in artwork are the commonest survivors of this decay, since figures are edited separately.
counter_case: Nothing. References carried into artwork intended for slides may legitimately be removed rather than corrected, with the author's agreement.
source: Van Buren & Buehler, 'The Levels of Edit', 2nd ed., JPL Publication 80-1 (NASA-CR-162880), 1980, Section VI-C items 6 and 11 (Integrity Edit)

test: For each citation, check that the cited work supports the statement it is attached to. Flag citations whose source states something weaker, something different, or the opposite.
cost: A false attribution propagates, and readers who chase the reference lose trust in every other citation in the paper.
suggestion: Replace the citation with one that supports the statement, or weaken the statement to what the cited work actually establishes.
mechanism: Citations are read as evidence and almost never checked, so a misattribution survives and gets copied. The commonest form is citing a paper that speculated something as though it had shown it, which launders speculation into fact across the literature. Verification requires reading the cited work, which is why the fault survives review.
counter_case: A citation for context or for priority need not support the sentence propositionally. 'This line of work began with [x]' cites an origin rather than a claim.
source: ACL Rolling Review Reviewer Guidelines, item G5 ('Misleading/incorrect citations')

test: For every dataset, model, checkpoint, and code library used, check that the creators are cited, the licence or terms are named, and the version is given with a URL where one exists.
cost: Users of the work cannot tell what they are permitted to do, and the original creators lose the credit that their own funding depends on.
suggestion: Add a table of assets with citation, version, URL, and licence name, and state the licence of anything the paper releases.
mechanism: An asset without a named licence is unusable by anyone with a compliance obligation, which excludes most industrial and much academic reuse. Version matters because benchmark contents change, so a result on an unnamed version is not reproducible. Repackaged datasets carry two licences and both need naming.
counter_case: Where licence information genuinely does not exist, saying so and describing the attempt to obtain it is the correct entry rather than an omission or a guess.
source: NeurIPS Paper Checklist Guidelines, item 12 (Licenses); ACL ARR Responsible NLP Research Checklist, items B1 and B2

test: Check that every opening bracket, brace, and delimiter in every mathematical expression has its match, and that nested delimiters are sized and paired consistently.
cost: An unmatched delimiter makes an expression ambiguous or meaningless, and the reader cannot repair it without guessing the author's intent.
suggestion: Match the fences, and size nested ones so the nesting is visible at a glance.
mechanism: Delimiters carry the grouping structure of an expression, so an unmatched one removes information that nothing else supplies. The defect survives drafting because authors read the intended expression rather than the printed one. Fully machine-checkable.
counter_case: Nothing. Conventional half-open intervals and similar notations use mismatched-looking delimiters by design, and those are matched under their own convention.
source: Van Buren & Buehler, 'The Levels of Edit', 2nd ed., JPL Publication 80-1 (NASA-CR-162880), 1980, Section VI-H item 11 (completeness of fences in mathematical expressions)

test: For each change under consideration, decide whether it is small-scale and non-contentious, meaning spelling, grammar, punctuation, or a factual detail with one right answer. Make those changes. For anything else, raise a query instead, and check that the query names the location and the specific decision the author must make.
cost: A silent change to something the author meant costs the author's meaning, and a vague query costs a round trip that resolves nothing.
suggestion: Convert every non-mechanical finding into a query of the form location, the specific problem, and the decision requested. Make the mechanical corrections without asking.
mechanism: An editor cannot know what the author meant, so a rewrite of an unclear passage is a guess presented as a correction. Querying preserves the author's meaning and costs one exchange. A query that names the exact location and the exact missing item can be answered in one line, while a query saying something is unclear cannot be answered at all.
counter_case: Where the author has explicitly delegated the decision, or where the passage is unambiguously wrong with exactly one correct repair, making the change and noting it is faster and better than querying.
source: CIEP knowledge hub, Philippa Tomlinson, 'What are queries, and how should an author respond?', 19 Jan 2024 (list of query triggers, and examples of author queries); Van Buren & Buehler, 'The Levels of Edit', 2nd ed., JPL Publication 80-1 (NASA-CR-162880), 1980, Section VI-H preamble ('All editorial changes in a Language Edit are made on the basis of specific and identifiable reasons rather than the personal preferences of the editor')

test: Before editing, fix which layer of edit is in scope. When a finding is a contradiction or an inconsistency in meaning between two parts of the document, record it and hand it back rather than resolving it.
cost: An editor who silently reconciles two contradictory statements picks one of them, and if the wrong one survives the error is now invisible and attributed to the author.
suggestion: Report the two locations and the contradiction, and let the author choose which statement is correct.
mechanism: Matching the parts of a document is a mechanical check, while resolving a contradiction in what those parts assert requires knowing which is true. Conflating the two lets an editor make substantive decisions under cover of a mechanical pass. Separating them keeps the author's authority over content and still catches the defect.
counter_case: Where the contradiction is a plain transcription slip, such as a number that disagrees with the same number three lines above and matches everywhere else, correcting it and flagging the correction is proportionate.
source: Van Buren & Buehler, 'The Levels of Edit', 2nd ed., JPL Publication 80-1 (NASA-CR-162880), 1980, Section VI-C ('an Integrity Edit will not resolve any apparent inconsistencies or contradictions in the meaning expressed in different parts of the report')

test: Check whether the paper has a limitations section, and whether it names the assumptions whose violation would change the conclusions, the narrowness of the evaluation, and the factors that affect performance.
cost: Without it, readers cannot tell where the result stops applying, and reviewers substitute their own guesses about what the authors failed to test.
suggestion: Add a limitations section naming the assumptions, the scope of the evaluation, and the sensitivity of the results, in the paper's own voice rather than as a disclaimer.
mechanism: Readers infer scope from silence and infer it generously. A stated limitation converts a weakness a reviewer would find into a scoping decision the authors made, and reviewers are instructed not to penalise honesty about limitations. The section also protects the paper from a later charge of overclaiming.
counter_case: A paper with genuinely no limitations to state should say that rather than invent some, and a limitations section padded with generic caveats is worse than a short honest one.
source: NeurIPS Paper Checklist Guidelines, item 2 (Limitations); ACL ARR Responsible NLP Research Checklist, item A1

test: For every graph in which one plotted quantity was set by the experimenter and the other was measured as a consequence of that setting, check which axis carries the set quantity. Skip any figure whose two axes are both outcome measures, including ROC, precision-recall, calibration, speed-accuracy and other trade-off curves. Skip any figure whose orientation is fixed by a named convention of the field, and skip any figure where the method section does not say which quantity was set.
cost: A reader who has to work out which axis is the input loses the direction of the experiment and re-derives it on every glance back at the figure.
suggestion: Redraw the flagged figure with the set parameter on the horizontal axis and the measured response on the vertical axis, then update the caption and every sentence that names an axis so they still match. Where the method section leaves it open which quantity was set, report the figure to the author instead of choosing.
mechanism: Readers arrive with a convention that cause runs across and effect runs up, and reading against it costs a deliberate correction each time the eye returns to the figure. The exclusion carries the weight here, because a curve of two outcomes has no input axis to move.
counter_case: ROC and precision-recall curves put an outcome on the horizontal axis by settled convention and are correct as drawn, which is why the test excludes them. A sweep with two set parameters, one along the horizontal axis and one distinguished by series, is also already correct.
source: Justin Zobel, Writing for Computer Science, 2nd ed. (Springer, 2004), ch. 6, p. 84: "The horizontal or x-axis should be used for the parameter being varied, or the input; the vertical or y-axis is for the function of the parameter, or the output." and "Plotted lines of discrete data should always have points marked by distinctive marks such as circles, boxes, or triangles."

test: For every series of discrete measurements drawn as a connected line, count the plotted observations. Flag any series of 30 or fewer observations drawn as a bare line with no marker at the measured points. Skip continuous or densely sampled series such as per-step training curves, sampled signals, and any series whose markers would touch at the figure's printed width.
cost: An unmarked line hides how many points were actually measured, so a two-point line reads as a trend and interpolation reads as data.
suggestion: Add one distinct marker, circle, square or triangle, at each measured point of the flagged series, reusing whatever marker set the other figures in the paper already use. Change no plotted value and no axis.
mechanism: Marking the observations is the only way a reader can separate measurement from interpolation. The count threshold in the test is what keeps the fix from turning a dense curve into a solid band.
counter_case: A per-step training curve with thousands of points becomes an ink band once markers are added, so the test excludes it. A scatter plot already carries one marker per observation and needs nothing added.
source: Justin Zobel, Writing for Computer Science, 2nd ed. (Springer, 2004), ch. 6, p. 84: "The horizontal or x-axis should be used for the parameter being varied, or the input; the vertical or y-axis is for the function of the parameter, or the output." and "Plotted lines of discrete data should always have points marked by distinctive marks such as circles, boxes, or triangles."

test: For every table, check whether a horizontal rule separates every pair of adjacent rows or a vertical rule separates every pair of adjacent columns.
cost: Rules between every row substitute ink for the whitespace that would do the grouping, and the reader's eye has to cross a line on every comparison down a column.
suggestion: Report the ruling density together with what the venue style file says about table rules. Where the style file is silent and the table is read down its columns, propose keeping only the rules above the table, below the header and below the last row. Where the style file mandates full ruling, or the table is a wide appendix reference read across, change nothing.
mechanism: Ruling density is a house-style decision before it is a legibility decision, so the sheet outranks the guideline. Zobel's open-table advice applies to a table the reader scans down.
counter_case: A wide appendix reference table read across rather than down is easier to track with a rule under every row. Some journal classes ship table styles that require full ruling, and stripping them fails the submission check.
source: Justin Zobel, Writing for Computer Science, 2nd ed. (Springer, 2004), ch. 6, p. 106: "Tables should be open and uncluttered, with ample white space. Don't have too many horizontal or vertical rules. In particular, there is no need to have a rule between every row or column... In most tables no position should be blank; if there is no applicable value, put in a dash, and explain somewhere what it means... Numbers should be aligned on the decimal point." Unit requirement from ch. 8 checklist, p. 135

test: For every table, list the cells that are empty. Skip cells in a label or grouping column that continue the value in the cell above.
cost: An empty cell is ambiguous between not measured, not applicable, and a genuine zero, and the reader has to guess which.
suggestion: Report each empty cell with its row and column and ask the author which of the three meanings it carries. Propose no filler. A dash asserts inapplicability, a zero asserts a measurement, and neither is recoverable from the blank.
mechanism: The blank is the site of missing information, not the fault itself. Whatever fills it makes a claim the text does not currently make, so the author is the only source.
counter_case: An empty cell that continues a grouping label from the row above is a legitimate ditto and needs no query. A column head already carrying a footnote that defines blank as not run is answered and needs no query either.
source: Justin Zobel, Writing for Computer Science, 2nd ed. (Springer, 2004), ch. 6, p. 106: "Tables should be open and uncluttered, with ample white space. Don't have too many horizontal or vertical rules. In particular, there is no need to have a rule between every row or column... In most tables no position should be blank; if there is no applicable value, put in a dash, and explain somewhere what it means... Numbers should be aligned on the decimal point." Unit requirement from ch. 8 checklist, p. 135

test: For every table column whose entries are all decimal numbers of one quantity, check that the entries are aligned on the decimal point. Skip columns of identifiers, model names, codes, version strings, mixed text, and columns of integers with no decimal point.
cost: A ragged numeric column forces the reader to compare magnitudes by reading digits rather than by seeing column widths.
suggestion: Align the flagged column on the decimal point, for instance with a siunitx S column in LaTeX. Change no digit and add no digit, so a value written to two decimals stays at two decimals with the alignment done by padding whitespace.
mechanism: A table is read down its columns, and decimal alignment is what lets the eye compare magnitudes without reading digits. Restricting the rule to single-quantity decimal columns is what keeps it away from the columns where centring is right.
counter_case: Columns of non-numeric codes or identifiers read better left-aligned or centred, so the test excludes them. Integer-only columns have no decimal point to align on. Padding with trailing zeros to force alignment would be a precision change and is excluded by the suggestion.
source: Justin Zobel, Writing for Computer Science, 2nd ed. (Springer, 2004), ch. 6, p. 106: "Tables should be open and uncluttered, with ample white space. Don't have too many horizontal or vertical rules. In particular, there is no need to have a rule between every row or column... In most tables no position should be blank; if there is no applicable value, put in a dash, and explain somewhere what it means... Numbers should be aligned on the decimal point." Unit requirement from ch. 8 checklist, p. 135

test: For every table column carrying a measured physical or resource quantity, check whether the column head names the unit. Skip columns of dimensionless values, ratios, normalised scores, probabilities, values already marked with a percent sign, and plain counts of things named in the head.
cost: A unitless column of measured values cannot be compared against any other paper, and it is the table fault that most often survives to publication.
suggestion: Recover the unit from the experimental section, the caption, or the released code, and write it into the column head, for instance Time (s). Where no part of the paper states the unit, report the column to the author rather than inferring one, since a wrong unit is worse than a missing one.
mechanism: Zobel's editing checklist asks separately whether units are given for every value. The unit is a fact about the measurement setup, so it is either already somewhere in the paper or only the author has it.
counter_case: A column of normalised scores, a probability column, or an accuracy column already marked % has no unit to add, and writing one in would be wrong. A column headed Documents is a count and already names what it counts.
source: Justin Zobel, Writing for Computer Science, 2nd ed. (Springer, 2004), ch. 6, p. 106: "Tables should be open and uncluttered, with ample white space. Don't have too many horizontal or vertical rules. In particular, there is no need to have a rule between every row or column... In most tables no position should be blank; if there is no applicable value, put in a dash, and explain somewhere what it means... Numbers should be aligned on the decimal point." Unit requirement from ch. 8 checklist, p. 135

test: For every axis label naming a measured physical or resource quantity, check whether the label carries its unit. Skip dimensionless axes, ratios, normalised scores, probabilities, percentages already marked with a percent sign, counts of things the label names, and axes whose unit is stated in the caption instead.
cost: A bare label leaves the reader guessing the unit, so no value read off the figure can be compared with any other paper.
suggestion: Write the unit into the axis label in parentheses, for instance Size (bytes), taking the unit from the experimental section, the caption or the released code. Where no part of the paper states it, report the axis to the author instead of inferring a unit.
mechanism: The unit is a fact about the measurement setup rather than a wording choice, so it is either recorded elsewhere in the paper or only the author holds it. The exclusions carry the safety, since a dimensionless axis has no unit to state.
counter_case: An axis of normalised scores, a probability axis, or a ratio axis correctly has no unit, and writing one in would be wrong. An axis whose caption already gives the unit does not need it duplicated.
source: Justin Zobel, Writing for Computer Science, 2nd ed. (Springer, 2004), ch. 6, p. 113: "Where appropriate, units should be stated in labels. Write \"Size (bytes)\", not just \"Size\"." and "it is helpful to include some representative numbers in the text, because graphs are hard to read with any precision."

test: Flag any axis label containing a scale multiplier such as x 10^3 or 10^-2. Skip scales that the field fixes by convention, for instance training compute quoted at 10^18 FLOPs, and skip labels where the caption already states whether the tick values have been scaled.
cost: A multiplier in the label is genuinely ambiguous about whether it has already been applied, so the reader cannot recover a single number from the figure with confidence.
suggestion: Report the ambiguity and ask the author whether the tick numbers have already been divided by the multiplier. Once the author answers, either restate the axis in a unit that makes the tick numbers plain or spell the scaling out in the caption. Rescale no tick and no plotted value yourself, because the label and the underlying data can already disagree and only the plotting code settles which.
mechanism: Zobel gives the trap directly, noting that readers disagree about whether an axis marked CPU time (seconds x 10^2) has already been scaled. The disagreement is the point, and the text does not contain the answer.
counter_case: Compute axes quoted on a 10^18 scale and memory axes in units of 2^30 bytes are read correctly by the field and need no change. Editing the label to remove the multiplier without knowing which way the scaling ran would silently move every value by three orders of magnitude.
source: Justin Zobel, Writing for Computer Science, 2nd ed. (Springer, 2004), ch. 6, p. 113: "Where appropriate, units should be stated in labels. Write \"Size (bytes)\", not just \"Size\"." and "it is helpful to include some representative numbers in the text, because graphs are hard to read with any precision."

test: For every figure whose reading supports a numeric or comparative claim in the body text, check whether the sentence referencing the figure quotes at least one absolute value. Skip schematics, architecture sketches and other figures carrying no measurements, and skip figures whose values are already tabulated nearby.
cost: A reader cannot recover a number from a graph to better than about one significant digit, so a claim resting only on the figure has no checkable value behind it.
suggestion: Report the figure and the claim, and ask the author for one or two representative absolute values to quote in the referencing sentence. Read no value off the plotted curve yourself, because a number taken from a graph would enter the prose looking like a measurement.
mechanism: Graphs are read to a precision of maybe one significant digit, so any claim needing a number must supply it in prose. The number lives in the results file rather than in the paper, which puts it out of an editor's reach.
counter_case: A schematic or an architecture diagram has no value to quote. A figure that plots exactly the numbers already given in an adjacent table does not need them repeated. An approximate value invented from the curve would be a fabricated measurement, which is why the suggestion forbids reading one off.
source: Justin Zobel, Writing for Computer Science, 2nd ed. (Springer, 2004), ch. 6, p. 113: "Where appropriate, units should be stated in labels. Write \"Size (bytes)\", not just \"Size\"." and "it is helpful to include some representative numbers in the text, because graphs are hard to read with any precision."

test: Group the reported numbers by the quantity they measure. Exclude every value that is exact rather than measured, counts, seeds, byte and parameter sizes, hashes, identifiers, step indices, version numbers, and any figure quoted verbatim from a cited source. Within each remaining group, compare the digits after the decimal point and flag any group whose members differ.
cost: Mixed precision within one quantity invites the reader to believe the longer number was measured more carefully than the shorter one, and that belief is usually false, but harmonising it away can also erase a real difference in measurement error.
suggestion: Report the group and the differing precisions, and ask the author whether the measurement error is the same for every member. Round nothing and pad nothing yourself. Where the error is the same the author picks one precision and applies it in the abstract, the tables and the appendix alike. Where the error genuinely differs, what belongs in the text is a sentence about the two clocks or apparatuses, and the precisions stay apart.
mechanism: Precision is read as a claim about measurement, so both changing it and leaving it inconsistent change what the paper asserts. Zobel's convention for computer science, same absolute precision, holds only when the values came off comparable apparatus, and the text does not say whether they did.
counter_case: A timing from a millisecond clock beside one derived from a nanosecond counter should keep its own precision, with the difference stated. Exact values are excluded outright by the test, since padding a count or a seed to match a neighbour's decimals would corrupt it.
source: Justin Zobel, Writing for Computer Science, 2nd ed. (Springer, 2004), ch. 5 'Mathematics', p. 79: "Numbers of the same units should, for consistency, be represented to the same precision... In computer science, in which values are usually measured to the same absolute precision, it is more logical to represent numbers to the same units." The before/after pair is Zobel's own marked example

test: For every number the text presents as a measurement, compare the reported digits against any stated clock or apparatus resolution. Where no resolution is stated, flag timings carrying more than one digit after the decimal point. Exclude every exact value, counts, seeds, byte and parameter sizes, hashes, identifiers, step indices, and any figure quoted verbatim from a cited source.
cost: Extra digits are an unearned claim of accuracy, and a reader who fails to reproduce the sixth digit loses confidence in the numbers that were solid.
suggestion: Report the number, the digits the stated method does not support, and the missing resolution, then ask the author for the clock or apparatus used. Round nothing yourself. The author either rounds to the digits the measurement supports or adds the description of the timing method that earns them.
mechanism: Digits are how a scientific text encodes confidence, so a rounding decision is a claim-strength decision. Zobel's example is 13.271844 CPU seconds, of which the last four or five digits are meaningless, and he warns that Unix-style timers report nanoseconds while their accuracy below tenths of a second is questionable. Which of the two applies is a fact about the harness rather than about the sentence.
counter_case: Full precision is correct when the digits are exact rather than measured, as with counts, seeds, hash values, byte sizes or a checksum, and rounding those destroys information, so the test excludes them. A figure quoted verbatim from a cited source must keep the source's digits. A paper that already describes a high-resolution timing harness has earned the digits it prints.
source: Justin Zobel, Writing for Computer Science, 2nd ed. (Springer, 2004), ch. 5, p. 79: "Be realistic about accuracy and error. Your system may report that a process required 13.271844 CPU seconds, but in all likelihood the last four or five digits are meaningless. You should not imply accuracy by including spurious numbers." Timing accuracy from ch. 11 'Experimentation', p. 194

test: For every number the text presents bare as a measurement, check whether the same quantity is described anywhere else in the paper as an estimate, a projection, an extrapolation, or a back-of-envelope figure. Flag the mismatch. Do not flag numbers that already carry a hedge.
cost: A projected figure written in the register of a measurement claims a measurement that was never made, and the mismatch only surfaces when a reader tries to reproduce it.
suggestion: Report the mismatch and ask the author to mark the flagged number as an estimate with approximately, about, roughly or over, or to confirm it was measured after all. Add no hedge on your own authority, and never remove or weaken a hedge, an intensifier on a graded absolute, a tentative modal, or a first-person stance marker that is already there, since that wording is the author's claim strength and cutting it lifts the claim past the evidence.
mechanism: Marking an estimate as an estimate is the calibration move Zobel is after, and he gives the reverse subtlety that 0.5 second is not equivalent to half a second, the first implying careful measurement. Both directions turn on what was actually done, which the sentence alone does not report.
counter_case: A number already written as about 13 seconds needs nothing, and tightening it to 13 seconds would assert a measurement. Substituting half a second for 0.5 second, or the reverse, changes the implied care of the measurement, so neither is safe without asking.
source: Justin Zobel, Writing for Computer Science, 2nd ed. (Springer, 2004), ch. 5, p. 79: "Be realistic about accuracy and error. Your system may report that a process required 13.271844 CPU seconds, but in all likelihood the last four or five digits are meaningless. You should not imply accuracy by including spurious numbers." Timing accuracy from ch. 11 'Experimentation', p. 194

test: Find clauses carrying more than one negation, counting negative verbs, negative determiners such as no or none, negative adverbs such as never or hardly, and negative prefixes on the same predicate. Report each clause with the negations marked and the parity you read.
cost: A reader tracking two negations in one clause loses the parity and may take away the opposite of the intended claim, and in a proposal that misreading lands on a review score.
suggestion: Report the clause, the negations, and the reading you arrive at, and ask the author to confirm the intended polarity. Propose no rewrite, because the correct repair depends on which negation carries the point.
mechanism: A negation is processed as an operation on the affirmative, so stacked negations compound the cost and frequently produce a parity error. The parity error is the harm worth surfacing, and surfacing it does not require an editor to choose the polarity, which only the author knows.
counter_case: Litotes and statistical negatives are correct as written and are frequently double-negative in form. 'Not uncommon in low-resource settings' and 'the difference was not non-significant' must survive this check untouched, so this rule reports and stops.
source: Williams (rev. Bizup), 'Style: Lessons in Clarity and Grace', 11th ed., Lesson 9, principle 5 (pp. 130-131)

test: Find single negations of a non-graded lexical verb or preposition that have an established one-word affirmative in the same register, such as 'does not include' for 'excludes', 'did not continue' for 'stopped', 'not before' for 'after'. Exclude any negation of a significance term, an effect size, a probability, a gradable adjective, a modal, a hedge, or an intensifier, and exclude any clause whose point is to deny a reader expectation.
cost: A negated two-word predicate where one affirmative verb says the same thing spends reader effort and page budget with no gain, and in a page-limited proposal the page budget is the scarce one.
suggestion: Offer the affirmative verb as a candidate and mark it for author approval, keeping the negation wherever the denial is the point. Never apply the substitution to a negated hedge, modal, gradable adjective, or statistical term, which this test already excludes.
mechanism: Where a single affirmative lexeme is truth-conditionally equivalent to the negated form, the substitution removes an inversion step with no loss. The equivalence holds only for non-graded predicates, which is why graded and statistical negations are excluded rather than hedged about.
counter_case: 'Not significant' has no affirmative equivalent and must never become 'small'. 'Not yet demonstrated' must not become 'undemonstrated' when the point is that the work is pending, and 'no fewer than three sites' must keep its negation because it sets a floor.
source: Williams (rev. Bizup), 'Style: Lessons in Clarity and Grace', 11th ed., Lesson 9, principle 5 (pp. 130-131)

test: Find evaluative adjectives and self-praise in the proposal's own account of its contributions, such as novel, powerful, elegant, remarkable, groundbreaking, or state-of-the-art used as an adjective. For each, search the same section and the results it cites for a number, a comparison, or a named baseline that would license the word. Keep only the instances where no such support appears anywhere in the proposal.
cost: An unsupported superlative is read as compensation for missing evidence, so the reviewer discounts the surrounding claims rather than the single word.
suggestion: Report the word and the absent support, and offer as a candidate the measurable property the author could state instead, drawn only from material already in the proposal. If no such material exists, report that the claim has no evidence anywhere in the document and let the author decide whether to supply evidence or drop the word.
mechanism: Readers supply their own judgement on results and resist having it supplied for them. Where the proposal holds the licensing number, moving the judgement to the number is strictly better. Where it holds no number, the defect is the missing evidence, and deleting the adjective would hide it.
counter_case: An adjective that is a term of art rather than praise stays. 'Novel object recognition task', 'state-of-the-art hardware' as a procurement fact, and 'significant' in its statistical sense are not self-praise and are excluded by the evaluative-use condition.
source: Knuth, Larrabee & Roberts, 'Mathematical Writing', Stanford CS 209 notes, section 1 (Minicourse), point 12 ('be humble and don't use superlatives of praise'); Williams (rev. Bizup), 'Style: Lessons in Clarity and Grace', 11th ed., Lesson 9, 'Intensifiers'

test: Find evaluative adjectives about the proposal's own contributions that DO have a supporting number, comparison, or named baseline stated in the same passage. Report the pairing of word and evidence.
cost: Nothing is wrong here, and the cost of acting is real. Cutting a licensed adjective removes accurate wording and can flatten the one sentence a reviewer would have quoted.
suggestion: Report the pair and propose nothing. Note only whether the evidence sits close enough to the word that a reviewer skimming the passage will meet both.
mechanism: The superlative guidance targets unearned judgement. Once the licensing evidence is present and adjacent, the adjective is a summary of it, and an editor removing it is destroying correct text. The only remaining question is placement, which is the author's call.
counter_case: Adjacency is not the same as support. If the nearby number measures something other than the property the adjective claims, the instance belongs to the unsupported rule instead, and this rule must not certify it.
source: Knuth, Larrabee & Roberts, 'Mathematical Writing', Stanford CS 209 notes, section 1 (Minicourse), point 12 ('be humble and don't use superlatives of praise'); Williams (rev. Bizup), 'Style: Lessons in Clarity and Grace', 11th ed., Lesson 9, 'Intensifiers'

test: Find priority claims about the proposal's own work, such as 'the first to', 'the only', 'no previous study has'. For each, check whether the claim is bounded enough to be checkable and whether the proposal states the bound.
cost: An unbounded priority claim is the one sentence a reviewer will try to falsify, and a single counterexample discredits the section it sits in.
suggestion: Report the claim and the bound it would need to be checkable, such as the population, the measure, or the date. Never delete a priority claim and never hedge it into vagueness, because a bounded priority claim is information a reviewer wants.
mechanism: Priority is a factual assertion rather than praise, so the repair is bounding rather than removal. A checkable bound turns the reviewer's falsification attempt into a confirmation, which is the opposite of what an unbounded claim invites.
counter_case: An already bounded claim needs nothing. 'The first published evaluation on all 40 languages of the suite' states its population and measure, and rewriting it as 'one of the first evaluations' loses information and weakens correct text.
source: Knuth, Larrabee & Roberts, 'Mathematical Writing', Stanford CS 209 notes, section 1 (Minicourse), point 12 ('be humble and don't use superlatives of praise'); Williams (rev. Bizup), 'Style: Lessons in Clarity and Grace', 11th ed., Lesson 9, 'Intensifiers'

test: In a journal or conference paper with more than one author, find passive constructions whose only apparent purpose is to avoid naming the authors as agent, where the sentence's own topic chain would put the authors in the subject slot and the agent is the authors.
cost: A passive built to dodge a pronoun hides who acted, so the reader cannot separate this paper's work from prior work.
suggestion: Offer the active form with 'we' as a candidate for the author to accept, and leave the passive wherever the agent is unknown, irrelevant, already established, or where the cohesive order needs the object in the opening slot.
mechanism: The passive controls which term opens and which closes a sentence, and spending it as a politeness device wastes it. 'We now prove' is shorter, says whose result it is, and preserves the topic chain.
counter_case: Some venues and some house styles bar first person outright, and methods sections often use the passive by convention so that procedure rather than actor is the topic. Neither is a defect, and this rule is scoped to papers precisely so it never touches grant text.
source: Knuth, Larrabee & Roberts, 'Mathematical Writing', Stanford CS 209 notes, section 1 (Minicourse), point 6; Williams (rev. Bizup), 'Style: Lessons in Clarity and Grace', 11th ed., Lesson 4 and Lesson 5 (on when the passive is correct)

test: In an NIH application, check the Project Summary/Abstract and Specific Aims for first-person pronouns introduced by an editing pass. Report them against NIH's third-person convention for the Project Summary.
cost: A summary rewritten into first person departs from the convention reviewers and NIH staff expect in that specific attachment, which reads as unfamiliarity with the mechanism.
suggestion: Report the pronouns and the convention, and propose no conversion in either direction without the author's decision. Never apply a 'prefer we' rule to an NIH Project Summary.
mechanism: NIH's Project Summary is written about the project rather than by a narrator, so the third-person convention there is a funder convention rather than a style preference. A general first-person preference inverts it and damages a correct application.
counter_case: The convention is attachment-specific. Research Strategy and biosketch personal statements are routinely first person in NIH applications, so this rule must not spread beyond the Project Summary and Specific Aims.
source: Knuth, Larrabee & Roberts, 'Mathematical Writing', Stanford CS 209 notes, section 1 (Minicourse), point 6; Williams (rev. Bizup), 'Style: Lessons in Clarity and Grace', 11th ed., Lesson 4 and Lesson 5 (on when the passive is correct)

test: In a UKRI application, find first-person singular in the applicant's own narrative sections and check whether an editing pass has converted it to 'we' or to the passive where the applicant is the sole named agent.
cost: Converting a sole applicant's 'I' to 'we' invents a team, and a reviewer weighing the applicant's own capability can no longer tell which claims are theirs.
suggestion: Report any such conversion and restore the applicant's own voice as the default. Propose no move toward 'we' or the passive in these sections.
mechanism: UKRI narrative sections are read as statements by the applicant about their own track record and plan, so first-person singular is the correct register for a sole applicant. The general technical-writing preference against 'I' does not transfer to this document type.
counter_case: Genuinely collective work stays collective. Where a section describes what the applicant and named co-investigators will do together, 'we' is accurate and must not be forced back to 'I'.
source: Knuth, Larrabee & Roberts, 'Mathematical Writing', Stanford CS 209 notes, section 1 (Minicourse), point 6; Williams (rev. Bizup), 'Style: Lessons in Clarity and Grace', 11th ed., Lesson 4 and Lesson 5 (on when the passive is correct)

test: In a Wellcome application, find first-person singular in the applicant's own sections and check whether an editing pass has replaced it with 'we' or with an agentless passive where the applicant is the sole agent.
cost: Wellcome reads the applicant's sections as their own account, so an imposed 'we' or passive obscures what the applicant personally will do and who is accountable for it.
suggestion: Report the change and restore the applicant's first-person singular. Propose no conversion away from it.
mechanism: The applicant's voice carries the accountability signal these sections are assessed on. A general preference for 'we' removes that signal, so the rule here is protective rather than corrective.
counter_case: Team sections and joint applications are collective by design, and 'we' there is correct. This rule covers only sections where the applicant is the sole named agent.
source: Knuth, Larrabee & Roberts, 'Mathematical Writing', Stanford CS 209 notes, section 1 (Minicourse), point 6; Williams (rev. Bizup), 'Style: Lessons in Clarity and Grace', 11th ed., Lesson 4 and Lesson 5 (on when the passive is correct)

test: In an ERC B1 or B2 with a single Principal Investigator, find places where the PI's first-person singular or 'the PI' has been replaced by 'we' or by a passive that hides the PI.
cost: ERC evaluates the PI alongside the project, and a 'we' in a single-PI proposal makes it unclear whether the PI or an unnamed team holds the expertise being assessed.
suggestion: Report the substitution and restore the PI's own voice. Propose no move to 'we' in a single-PI ERC proposal.
mechanism: The PI-centred evaluation criterion makes agency load-bearing in ERC text, so the choice between 'I', 'the PI', and 'we' is a content decision rather than a style one and belongs to the author.
counter_case: Team-execution passages legitimately use 'we' or name team members, and Synergy proposals have several PIs. Neither is in scope here.
source: Knuth, Larrabee & Roberts, 'Mathematical Writing', Stanford CS 209 notes, section 1 (Minicourse), point 6; Williams (rev. Bizup), 'Style: Lessons in Clarity and Grace', 11th ed., Lesson 4 and Lesson 5 (on when the passive is correct)

test: Enumerate every in-text pointer to a table, figure, equation, reference, footnote, section, or appendix, and find the pointers whose target does not exist, is numbered outside the existing range, or names an element of a different type from the one at that number.
cost: A reader following a pointer to nothing stops mid-argument and has to reconstruct where they were, and a reviewer doing that on a page-limited proposal registers it as carelessness about evidence.
suggestion: Correct the pointer to the element the surrounding sentence describes when exactly one existing element matches that description. When two or more could match, or none does, report the broken pointer with the candidates and change nothing. Never resolve a broken pointer by deleting the sentence that carries it.
mechanism: The pointer and its target are checkable against each other mechanically, and where the sentence's own description singles out one existing element the repair is determined. Where it does not, guessing a target silently redirects the argument, which is worse than leaving the break visible.
counter_case: Off-by-one breaks often come in runs after a late insertion, and renumbering one pointer to match a neighbouring pointer's guess can shift a whole run onto the wrong elements. If the same document has several broken pointers of the same type, report the set rather than repairing them one at a time.
source: Van Buren & Buehler, 'The Levels of Edit', 2nd ed., JPL Publication 80-1 (NASA-CR-162880), 1980, Section VI-C item 3 (Integrity Edit)

test: Enumerate every table, figure, equation, footnote, appendix, and reference-list entry, and find those that no in-text pointer cites. Report each with the place in the text where its content would be used.
cost: An element the text never invokes is either page budget spent for nothing or a sign that a paragraph meant to use it was cut or never written, and the second case is the expensive one.
suggestion: Report the uncited element and propose the in-text citation that would connect it, naming the sentence it belongs with. Propose no deletion. Never delete a figure, table, appendix, reference-list entry, publication entry, or CV item on the strength of this check.
mechanism: Uncited and broken are different defects with different repairs. Absence of a pointer is evidence about the text, not about the element, and the element may be required by the funder's forms or cited from another element rather than from prose.
counter_case: Many elements are legitimately uncited in running prose. Reference-list entries in numeric styles are reached through the numbered citations, funder-mandated tables such as a Gantt chart or budget justification appear because the call requires them, and a decorative or cover figure is cited by its caption alone. None of these is a defect.
source: Van Buren & Buehler, 'The Levels of Edit', 2nd ed., JPL Publication 80-1 (NASA-CR-162880), 1980, Section VI-C item 3 (Integrity Edit)

test: In author-written running prose only, find terms appearing in two or more surface forms across spelling variety, hyphenation, capitalisation of defined terms, and number formatting. Exclude quoted material, reference-list entries and cited titles, proper names of datasets, models, software, corpora, genes, and organisations, URLs and DOIs, code and identifiers, funder-mandated headings and form field labels, and text copied verbatim from the call. Report each term with its variants and the count of each.
cost: A term in two forms briefly raises the question of whether a difference is meant, and a reader who has stopped trusting the surface stops trusting the numbers.
suggestion: Report the variants and their counts and propose nothing. Which form is correct depends on the author's style sheet, the venue, and the funder's own spelling in the call, none of which this check can read.
mechanism: Consistency lets a reader stop attending to surface form, but the choice of which form to standardise on is not recoverable from the document. Reporting the variant set gives the author a decision they can make once and apply, which is what a style sheet is for.
counter_case: A quotation keeps its source's spelling and hyphenation, and normalising it is a misquotation rather than a fix. A dataset or model name keeps its published capitalisation even where it clashes with the surrounding prose, so 'fastText' and 'ImageNet' are not inconsistencies. Reference titles keep the original spelling variety of their publication.
source: CIEP fact sheet, 'The role and purpose of the editorial profession', 16 Dec 2025 (the five c's, and evidence on reader trust); Van Buren & Buehler, 'The Levels of Edit', 2nd ed., JPL Publication 80-1 (NASA-CR-162880), 1980, Section VI-G (Mechanical Style Edit)

test: Find every percentage that expresses a change (increase, decrease, reduction, improvement, speed-up). Flag it only when neither the sentence nor the immediately preceding sentence states the value that the percentage is taken of. Do not flag a percentage that reports a level rather than a change (accuracy of 82%), a percentage-point difference already labelled as such, or a change whose two absolute values are given.
cost: A 30% decrease denotes a different number depending on whether the base is the old value or the new, so the size of the result stays undetermined and the reader cannot reconstruct either endpoint.
suggestion: Report the sentence and ask the author which value is the 100% base, then have the base named in the sentence, by convention the starting value ('a 30% reduction relative to the 4.0 GB baseline'). Do not supply or infer the missing number.
mechanism: Zobel gives the convention that 100% is the starting point and requires the reader to be told what is a percentage of what. The base value lives in the experiment, not in the sentence, so an editor can detect the gap but cannot close it.
counter_case: A percentage change needs no restatement when the two absolute values are already in the same sentence or the sentence before, since the base is then recoverable; flagging those produces noise. Percentages that report a level, not a change, are outside this rule entirely.
source: Justin Zobel, Writing for Computer Science, 2nd ed. (Springer, 2004), ch. 5, p. 78: "Avoid the phrase \"orders of magnitude\"... In this example, is the unit of magnitude binary or decimal? It would be better to be explicit." and pp. 79-80: "When stating a percentage, ensure that the reader knows what is a percentage of what... The convention is to use 100% as the starting point"

test: Flag every occurrence of the phrase 'orders of magnitude' (and 'an order of magnitude') in the abstract, in a results or contributions sentence, or in any sentence reporting the paper's own measurements. Do not flag it in related-work or background prose that characterises a line of work rather than a measured result.
cost: Two orders of magnitude means 100 to a decimal reader and 4 to a binary one, so a headline claim about the paper's own result carries a factor-of-25 ambiguity.
suggestion: Report the occurrence and ask the author for the measured multiplier in figures ('at least a hundred times faster'). Propose no substitution, because the factor is not present in the text and any figure an editor chooses would be invented.
mechanism: Zobel is prescriptive about the phrase, since the unit of magnitude may be binary or decimal, and his marked repair converts 'at least two orders of magnitude faster' to 'at least a hundred times faster'. The repair depends on the underlying measurement, which is why the rule can only ask.
counter_case: The phrase is acceptable, and this rule deliberately does not reach it, in a related-work sentence where the base is established by surrounding text and the looseness is the point. It stays flaggable in an abstract or a results sentence even when the surrounding text is loose.
source: Justin Zobel, Writing for Computer Science, 2nd ed. (Springer, 2004), ch. 5, p. 78: "Avoid the phrase \"orders of magnitude\"... In this example, is the unit of magnitude binary or decimal? It would be better to be explicit." and pp. 79-80: "When stating a percentage, ensure that the reader knows what is a percentage of what... The convention is to use 100% as the starting point"

test: Flag a decimal magnitude below one written without its leading zero (.3 Kb) when the quantity is not bounded by one. Exclude quantities that cannot exceed one and whose house style drops the zero, in particular P values, correlation coefficients, and proportions under AMA style, and exclude anything inside math mode, code, a filename or a version string.
cost: A bare decimal point is lost against surrounding punctuation, so '.3' can be read as '3' and a tenfold error passes unseen.
suggestion: Insert the leading zero (.3 -> 0.3) in the excluded-free cases only. Where the venue style sheet dictates the opposite for bounded statistics, record the venue rule and leave the value untouched.
mechanism: Zobel: never omit the leading 0 in numbers whose magnitude is less than 1. AMA reverses this for statistics that cannot exceed 1, which is why the test carves them out rather than the suggestion hedging.
counter_case: 'P = .04' is correct AMA and must not be changed to 0.04; the same is true of r = .61. Both are the exact cases the parent rule would have damaged.
source: Justin Zobel, Writing for Computer Science, 2nd ed. (Springer, 2004), ch. 5, pp. 77-81. Marked pairs quoted verbatim: "X There were between four and 32 processors in each machine. / There were between 4 and 32 processors in each machine."; "X There were 14 512-Kb sets. [check] There were fourteen 512-Kb sets."; "X About 1/3 of the data was noise. [check] About one-third of the data was noise."; "Never omit the leading 0 in numbers whose magnitude is less than 1"; "Put white space between values and units."

test: Flag a numeric value written hard against its unit in running prose (11.2Kbytes, 50ms). Exclude symbols that are by convention closed up (percent sign, degree sign, currency), unit strings inside code, filenames, identifiers or math mode, and any venue whose style sheet requires closed-up unit symbols.
cost: Without the space the value and unit fuse into one token, so the eye has to segment it before reading, and '11.2Kbytes' is easy to misread as a single opaque label.
suggestion: Insert a space between value and unit, non-breaking where the typesetting allows it, changing no digits.
mechanism: Zobel: put white space between values and units. SI agrees except for the closed-up symbols named in the exclusions.
counter_case: '95%' and '37degC' style closed-up symbols are correct as written; inserting a space there is the damage. A style sheet demanding '11.2KB' also overrides, and the choice should be recorded.
source: Justin Zobel, Writing for Computer Science, 2nd ed. (Springer, 2004), ch. 5, pp. 77-81. Marked pairs quoted verbatim: "X There were between four and 32 processors in each machine. / There were between 4 and 32 processors in each machine."; "X There were 14 512-Kb sets. [check] There were fourteen 512-Kb sets."; "X About 1/3 of the data was noise. [check] About one-third of the data was noise."; "Never omit the leading 0 in numbers whose magnitude is less than 1"; "Put white space between values and units."

test: Flag two numerals separated only by a space where the first is a count and the second begins a compound modifier (14 512-Kb sets). Restrict to cases where the first number is a whole number below twenty-one, so that it can be spelt out without clumsiness. Report, but do not repair, cases where the first number is larger or is an exact reported value.
cost: Adjacent numerals read as one number, so '14 512-Kb sets' briefly looks like 14,512 and the reader has to back up.
suggestion: Spell out the first number in words (14 512-Kb sets -> fourteen 512-Kb sets), leaving the second in figures.
mechanism: Zobel's marked pair: 'X There were 14 512-Kb sets. / There were fourteen 512-Kb sets.' Spelling the first number breaks the collision without touching either value.
counter_case: '2048 512-Kb sets' must not become 'two thousand and forty-eight'; the boundary at twenty-one keeps the rule from producing that. A recast ('sets of 512 Kb, 2048 of them') is the author's call, so those cases are reported only.
source: Justin Zobel, Writing for Computer Science, 2nd ed. (Springer, 2004), ch. 5, pp. 77-81. Marked pairs quoted verbatim: "X There were between four and 32 processors in each machine. / There were between 4 and 32 processors in each machine."; "X There were 14 512-Kb sets. [check] There were fourteen 512-Kb sets."; "X About 1/3 of the data was noise. [check] About one-third of the data was noise."; "Never omit the leading 0 in numbers whose magnitude is less than 1"; "Put white space between values and units."

test: Flag a sentence whose first word is a numeral in figures. Do not propose a rewrite; only report.
cost: A sentence-initial figure gives the reader no capital-letter cue that a sentence has started, so the boundary between the previous sentence and this one is momentarily invisible.
suggestion: Report the sentence and ask the author to choose: spell the number out, or recast so the sentence opens on a word. Propose no specific recast, since both fixes rewrite the author's sentence and one of them changes emphasis.
mechanism: Zobel's rule is that a sentence should not open on a numeral, but he offers two remedies. Choosing between them is an authorial decision about emphasis, and mechanically spelling out '512 experiments were run' produces prose the author did not write.
counter_case: Spelling out is wrong for a large or exact opening value ('2048 shards were resharded'), and recasting can bury a number the author put first on purpose. That is why nothing is proposed automatically.
source: Justin Zobel, Writing for Computer Science, 2nd ed. (Springer, 2004), ch. 5, pp. 77-81. Marked pairs quoted verbatim: "X There were between four and 32 processors in each machine. / There were between 4 and 32 processors in each machine."; "X There were 14 512-Kb sets. [check] There were fourteen 512-Kb sets."; "X About 1/3 of the data was noise. [check] About one-third of the data was noise."; "Never omit the leading 0 in numbers whose magnitude is less than 1"; "Put white space between values and units."

test: Flag a coordinated pair or range of the same kind of quantity where one side is spelt out and the other is in figures (between four and 32 processors; from 8 to twelve runs). Both members must denote the same kind of thing; do not flag a spelt-out number sitting beside an unrelated figure.
cost: Mixed modes inside one range make the two endpoints look like different kinds of quantity, so the reader checks whether the range is really a range.
suggestion: Put both sides in figures (between 4 and 32 processors), unless the venue style sheet requires numbers up to ten in words, in which case put both sides in words and record the choice.
mechanism: Zobel's marked pair: 'X There were between four and 32 processors in each machine. / There were between 4 and 32 processors in each machine.' The requirement is one mode per construction, which both branches satisfy.
counter_case: Venues that spell out numbers up to ten would want 'between four and thirty-two', so the rule fixes the mode mismatch without hard-coding figures. A sentence like 'four of the 32 processors' is a different construction, not a range, and is left alone.
source: Justin Zobel, Writing for Computer Science, 2nd ed. (Springer, 2004), ch. 5, pp. 77-81. Marked pairs quoted verbatim: "X There were between four and 32 processors in each machine. / There were between 4 and 32 processors in each machine."; "X There were 14 512-Kb sets. [check] There were fourteen 512-Kb sets."; "X About 1/3 of the data was noise. [check] About one-third of the data was noise."; "Never omit the leading 0 in numbers whose magnitude is less than 1"; "Put white space between values and units."

test: Flag a slashed fraction used as an abbreviation in running prose (1/3 of the data). Exclude anything inside math mode, an equation, a table cell, code, a filename, a ratio or aspect specification, a date, and any fraction that is part of an exact reported value or a unit expression (1/s, 1/e).
cost: A slashed fraction in prose reads as arithmetic, so the reader parses a division before recognising a quantity word.
suggestion: Spell the fraction out with a hyphen (1/3 -> one-third), changing the value not at all.
mechanism: Zobel's marked pair: 'X About 1/3 of the data was noise. [check] About one-third of the data was noise.' Fractions are not to be used as abbreviations in prose; in mathematics they are the notation, which is why math mode is excluded.
counter_case: 'a 4/3 aspect ratio', 'the 1/s in the denominator' and any fraction inside displayed mathematics must stay in figures; rewriting those breaks notation rather than prose.
source: Justin Zobel, Writing for Computer Science, 2nd ed. (Springer, 2004), ch. 5, pp. 77-81. Marked pairs quoted verbatim: "X There were between four and 32 processors in each machine. / There were between 4 and 32 processors in each machine."; "X There were 14 512-Kb sets. [check] There were fourteen 512-Kb sets."; "X About 1/3 of the data was noise. [check] About one-third of the data was noise."; "Never omit the leading 0 in numbers whose magnitude is less than 1"; "Put white space between values and units."

test: Flag a number-plus-unit compound used as an adjective before a noun where the unit is spelt out and the compound is unhyphenated (a 10 millisecond delay, a 3 gigabyte index). Exclude compounds whose unit is a symbol or abbreviation (10 ms delay, 3 GB index), where SI practice keeps the space and no hyphen.
cost: Without the hyphen the reader cannot tell whether the number modifies the unit or the noun, so 'a 3 gigabyte index' hesitates between one index of three gigabytes and three gigabyte-sized indexes.
suggestion: Hyphenate the spelt-out compound (a 10-millisecond delay), leaving the number and unit words unchanged.
