mechanism: Standard English compound-modifier practice, applied only where the unit is a word. SI style forbids hyphenating a value to a unit symbol, so symbol forms are excluded by the test instead of being repaired.
counter_case: 'a 10 ms delay' is correct as written and must not become '10-ms'; that is the case the parent rule would have broken. Predicative uses ('the delay was 10 milliseconds') take no hyphen either and are not matched.
source: Justin Zobel, Writing for Computer Science, 2nd ed. (Springer, 2004), ch. 5, pp. 77-81. Marked pairs quoted verbatim: "X There were between four and 32 processors in each machine. / There were between 4 and 32 processors in each machine."; "X There were 14 512-Kb sets. [check] There were fourteen 512-Kb sets."; "X About 1/3 of the data was noise. [check] About one-third of the data was noise."; "Never omit the leading 0 in numbers whose magnitude is less than 1"; "Put white space between values and units."

test: Build a table of quantities appearing in more than one figure, table or axis label. Flag any pair of labels that use two different names for what the text treats as one quantity. Report only; do not unify.
cost: One quantity under two names reads as two quantities, so a reader comparing Figure 2 with Table 3 cannot tell whether the same measurement is on both.
suggestion: Report the pair and ask the author whether the two labels denote one quantity or two. If one, they choose the surviving name; if two, the fix is to sharpen the distinction, and an editor cannot tell which case holds from the labels alone.
mechanism: Zobel's editing checklist asks whether x axes measuring the same units carry the same label, but whether two names are synonyms or a real distinction is a fact about the measurements, not about the manuscript.
counter_case: 'Latency' in one figure and 'CPU time' in another may be wall-clock and CPU cost, genuinely different measurements; unifying them silently erases the distinction. Automatic unification is exactly the damage this rule refuses to do.
source: Justin Zobel, Writing for Computer Science, 2nd ed. (Springer, 2004), ch. 8 'Editing', p. 135: "Has \"megabyte\" been written as \"Mb\" in some places and \"Mbyte\" in others?"; "Are the graphs all the same size? Are the axis units always given?"; "Are all tables in the same format?... do all tables have the same orientation?"

test: Flag any quantity whose unit is written with two different spellings or abbreviations across figures, tables and text (Mb in one place, Mbyte in another; sec and s; MiB and MB).
cost: Two spellings of one unit force the reader to decide whether the unit itself differs, and Mb against Mbyte can mean a factor of eight.
suggestion: Report the variants and ask the author which unit is actually meant, since Mb (megabit) and Mbyte (megabyte) are different units and the labels do not settle it. Once the author confirms one unit, fix a single spelling in the style sheet and apply it to text, tables and the labels inside figure images.
mechanism: Zobel asks directly whether megabyte has been written as Mb in some places and Mbyte in others. Figure labels drift because they live in image files and plotting scripts, so the rename has to reach the plotting code, not only the manuscript.
counter_case: Mb and MB may both be correct in a paper that reports bandwidth in megabits and storage in megabytes; unifying the spelling there would falsify one of them. MiB against MB is likewise a real distinction, not a typo.
source: Justin Zobel, Writing for Computer Science, 2nd ed. (Springer, 2004), ch. 8 'Editing', p. 135: "Has \"megabyte\" been written as \"Mb\" in some places and \"Mbyte\" in others?"; "Are the graphs all the same size? Are the axis units always given?"; "Are all tables in the same format?... do all tables have the same orientation?"

test: Flag any figure axis or table column that reports a dimensioned quantity with no unit given anywhere in the label, header, caption or table note.
cost: A column headed 'size' with no unit is unusable, since the reader cannot compare it with anything or judge whether a difference is large.
suggestion: Report the missing unit and ask the author to supply it. Do not infer a unit from neighbouring tables or from the magnitude of the values, since the guess would silently rescale every number in the column.
mechanism: Zobel's checklist asks whether the axis units are always given. The unit is a fact about the measurement, absent from the manuscript by construction whenever this rule fires.
counter_case: Dimensionless quantities (accuracy, F1, a ratio, a count of items) correctly have no unit and are not matched. Inferring 'MB' because a sibling table uses MB is the failure mode this rule avoids.
source: Justin Zobel, Writing for Computer Science, 2nd ed. (Springer, 2004), ch. 8 'Editing', p. 135: "Has \"megabyte\" been written as \"Mb\" in some places and \"Mbyte\" in others?"; "Are the graphs all the same size? Are the axis units always given?"; "Are all tables in the same format?... do all tables have the same orientation?"

test: Flag pairs of tables that present the same kind of comparison in opposite orientations, one with methods as rows and the other with methods as columns. Restrict to pairs of comparable size, and do not flag a pair where the two tables have very different numbers of rows or columns.
cost: Flipping orientation between two tables of the same comparison makes the reader re-learn the layout, and a cell-by-cell comparison across the pair becomes a transposition exercise.
suggestion: Report the pair and propose one orientation for both, noting that the transposed table must still fit the column or page width. Leave the transposition to the author or to a build that can check the fit, since whether the wider form fits is not visible in the source.
mechanism: Zobel asks whether all tables are in the same format and whether all tables have the same orientation. Page fit is a typesetting fact that the manuscript source does not carry.
counter_case: Orientation may legitimately differ when one table has far more rows than the page can take in the other layout, which is why lopsided pairs are excluded from the test rather than argued away in the suggestion.
source: Justin Zobel, Writing for Computer Science, 2nd ed. (Springer, 2004), ch. 8 'Editing', p. 135: "Has \"megabyte\" been written as \"Mb\" in some places and \"Mbyte\" in others?"; "Are the graphs all the same size? Are the axis units always given?"; "Are all tables in the same format?... do all tables have the same orientation?"

test: Flag any figure that encodes a continuous quantitative variable with a rainbow or jet colour map (heatmap, surface, density, colour bar). Exclude figures whose field convention fixes the map and says so in the caption or the venue guidance, for instance certain meteorological and medical-imaging displays, and exclude figures whose stated task is locating a boundary rather than ordering values.
cost: A rainbow scale is not monotonic in lightness and its two ends look alike, so the reader misreads the extremes and sees banding where the data is smooth.
suggestion: Replace the map with a perceptually monotonic sequential map, or a diverging map when the variable is deviation from a meaningful midpoint. Data values and their ordering are untouched, only the colour lookup changes.
mechanism: Rougier and colleagues require colour to be chosen by type, sequential for low-to-high, diverging for deviation from a midpoint, and advise against rainbow or jet unless there is an explicit reason. Nguyen and colleagues name the specific failure that the colours at the beginning and the end are almost equivalent.
counter_case: A rainbow map is defensible where a field convention has fixed it and readers are trained on it, and where the task is finding a boundary rather than ranking values, so those figures are excluded by the test rather than overridden case by case.
source: Rougier, Droettboom & Bourne, 'Ten Simple Rules for Better Figures', PLoS Computational Biology 10(9):e1003833 (2014), DOI 10.1371/journal.pcbi.1003833, Rule 6 ('Use Color Effectively'): avoid rainbow and jet "unless there is an explicit reason to do so". Numeric limits from Nguyen, Jung & Gupta, 'Examining data visualization pitfalls in scientific publications', Visual Computing for Industry, Biomedicine, and Art 4:27 (2021), DOI 10.1186/s42492-021-00092-y, section M1: "five to seven well-chosen colours pre-attentively" and qualitative scales "three to five different colored categories". Nature mandates a named palette: research-figure-guide.nature.com, 'Colour and accessibility', requires "An accessible colour palette to be used (for example Wong, B. Points of view: Colour blindness. Nature Methods 8, 441 (2011))", published as eight hex values #000000 #e69f00 #56b4e9 #009e73 #f0e442 #0072b2 #d55e00 #cc79a7; Wong reports colour-vision deficiency in "as many as 8 percent of men and 0.5 percent of women" of Northern European ancestry and warns that "any color with components of red and green can cause trouble". Krzywinski, 'Points of view: Color coding', Nature Methods 7(8):573 (2010), caps categorical use: "we can define a group of 6-8 colors. Beyond this number, the task of picking distinctive colors becomes difficult"

test: Flag any figure in which category identity is carried by hue alone, with no redundant marker shape, dash pattern, direct label or position cue.
cost: In greyscale printing or with red-green colour-vision deficiency, hue-only encoding erases the category distinction entirely, so up to eight percent of male readers cannot read the figure at all.
suggestion: Add a redundant channel to every series, marker shape, dash pattern or an end-of-line label, and use a colourblind-safe palette such as Wong's eight values. Add cues; remove no series and merge no categories.
mechanism: Redundant encoding is what makes a figure survive greyscale printing and colour-vision deficiency. Nature requires an accessible palette and cites Wong, who reports deficiency in as many as 8 percent of men and 0.5 percent of women of Northern European ancestry and warns that any colour with components of red and green can cause trouble.
counter_case: A figure with a single series, or one where position already identifies each mark (a labelled bar chart), needs no redundant cue and is not matched. Dash patterns are also a poor second channel on dense scatter marks, where shape or direct labels should be chosen instead.
source: Rougier, Droettboom & Bourne, 'Ten Simple Rules for Better Figures', PLoS Computational Biology 10(9):e1003833 (2014), DOI 10.1371/journal.pcbi.1003833, Rule 6 ('Use Color Effectively'): avoid rainbow and jet "unless there is an explicit reason to do so". Numeric limits from Nguyen, Jung & Gupta, 'Examining data visualization pitfalls in scientific publications', Visual Computing for Industry, Biomedicine, and Art 4:27 (2021), DOI 10.1186/s42492-021-00092-y, section M1: "five to seven well-chosen colours pre-attentively" and qualitative scales "three to five different colored categories". Nature mandates a named palette: research-figure-guide.nature.com, 'Colour and accessibility', requires "An accessible colour palette to be used (for example Wong, B. Points of view: Colour blindness. Nature Methods 8, 441 (2011))", published as eight hex values #000000 #e69f00 #56b4e9 #009e73 #f0e442 #0072b2 #d55e00 #cc79a7; Wong reports colour-vision deficiency in "as many as 8 percent of men and 0.5 percent of women" of Northern European ancestry and warns that "any color with components of red and green can cause trouble". Krzywinski, 'Points of view: Color coding', Nature Methods 7(8):573 (2010), caps categorical use: "we can define a group of 6-8 colors. Beyond this number, the task of picking distinctive colors becomes difficult"

test: Count the distinct colours encoding categories in each figure. Flag any figure using more than about seven, or more than five on a qualitative scale. Report only.
cost: Beyond a handful of colours the reader stops distinguishing categories pre-attentively and has to consult the legend for every mark, so the figure becomes a lookup table.
suggestion: Report the count and propose de-emphasis rather than deletion: keep every series, colour the few the text discusses, draw the rest as thin grey lines with direct labels, and ask the author which series are focal. Never merge categories into an 'other' group and never drop a series, since both discard reported per-category values.
mechanism: Nguyen and colleagues give the perceptual limits, five to seven well-chosen colours pre-attentively and three to five categories on a qualitative scale, and Krzywinski caps categorical use at six to eight colours because beyond that picking distinctive colours becomes difficult. The limit is on how many colours can be told apart, not on how many series may be shown, so the repair is de-emphasis.
counter_case: A large categorical palette is acceptable in a figure whose point is diversity rather than per-category comparison. And merging the tail into 'other' destroys data a reader may cite, which is why this rule proposes greying out instead of grouping.
source: Rougier, Droettboom & Bourne, 'Ten Simple Rules for Better Figures', PLoS Computational Biology 10(9):e1003833 (2014), DOI 10.1371/journal.pcbi.1003833, Rule 6 ('Use Color Effectively'): avoid rainbow and jet "unless there is an explicit reason to do so". Numeric limits from Nguyen, Jung & Gupta, 'Examining data visualization pitfalls in scientific publications', Visual Computing for Industry, Biomedicine, and Art 4:27 (2021), DOI 10.1186/s42492-021-00092-y, section M1: "five to seven well-chosen colours pre-attentively" and qualitative scales "three to five different colored categories". Nature mandates a named palette: research-figure-guide.nature.com, 'Colour and accessibility', requires "An accessible colour palette to be used (for example Wong, B. Points of view: Colour blindness. Nature Methods 8, 441 (2011))", published as eight hex values #000000 #e69f00 #56b4e9 #009e73 #f0e442 #0072b2 #d55e00 #cc79a7; Wong reports colour-vision deficiency in "as many as 8 percent of men and 0.5 percent of women" of Northern European ancestry and warns that "any color with components of red and green can cause trouble". Krzywinski, 'Points of view: Color coding', Nature Methods 7(8):573 (2010), caps categorical use: "we can define a group of 6-8 colors. Beyond this number, the task of picking distinctive colors becomes difficult"

test: Flag any reported uncertainty carrying more than two significant digits: a plus-or-minus term, a standard error, a standard deviation, a confidence-interval half-width, or a stated margin of error. Match only the uncertainty itself. Never match a point estimate, a count, a seed, a byte or parameter size, a hash, an identifier, a step or epoch index, a version number, a hyperparameter value, or any interval endpoint that is itself a reported value.
cost: An uncertainty carries no information beyond its leading digits, and printing more implies the uncertainty was itself measured precisely, which overstates what the experiment establishes.
suggestion: Round the uncertainty to two significant digits (+/- 0.4173 -> +/- 0.42) and leave every other number in the table exactly as written.
mechanism: Higham states the precision convention for errors, that when reporting errors you report at most two significant digits. The convention applies to the error term alone, which is why the test enumerates what must not be touched.
counter_case: '+/- 0.4173' becomes '+/- 0.42', but 'seed 1729', '7B parameters', 'step 24000' and an accuracy of '82.417' are not uncertainties and must survive untouched. A point estimate's precision is a separate question this rule does not answer.
source: N. J. Higham, Handbook of Writing for the Mathematical Sciences, 2nd ed. (SIAM), p. 91, as quoted in the Proceedings of ANZIAM submission guidelines, https://journal.austms.org.au/ojs/index.php/ANZIAMJ/about/submissions: "Only essential information should be included in a table" and "when reporting errors, report at most two significant digits". Column-cutting corroborated by Zobel, Writing for Computer Science, 2nd ed. (2004), p. 106

test: For every table, list the columns and mark any column that no sentence in the paper refers to, directly or by implication. Report the list. Do not propose deletion of any column.
cost: Every unreferenced column widens the table, shrinks the type, and lengthens the distance the eye travels to the column that matters, so the useful comparison gets harder in proportion to the unused data.
suggestion: Report the unreferenced columns and ask the author which are load-bearing for readers rather than for the prose. Where the author agrees, move them to an appendix table at full width; never delete a column, since a reader may cite a cell the prose never mentions.
mechanism: Higham states that only essential information should be included in a table, and Zobel advises two tables, or better, being selective, rather than cramming in many columns. Whether a column is essential depends on how the paper will be used, which the manuscript does not record.
counter_case: A wide table is right when it is the paper's reference artefact, a full per-language or per-benchmark results table whose completeness is the contribution and whose individual cells others cite. Deleting columns there removes published results, so relocation, agreed with the author, is the strongest move available.
source: N. J. Higham, Handbook of Writing for the Mathematical Sciences, 2nd ed. (SIAM), p. 91, as quoted in the Proceedings of ANZIAM submission guidelines, https://journal.austms.org.au/ojs/index.php/ANZIAMJ/about/submissions: "Only essential information should be included in a table" and "when reporting errors, report at most two significant digits". Column-cutting corroborated by Zobel, Writing for Computer Science, 2nd ed. (2004), p. 106

test: For each figure that encodes a one-dimensional quantity with a two- or three-dimensional mark (circle area, bubble diameter scaled with the value, a pictogram scaled in both directions, a 3-D bar or a pie with depth), compute Tufte's lie factor as the drawn effect measured in the rendered figure divided by the effect in the underlying numbers, measuring the drawn effect on the visual dimension the reader compares. Flag the figure when the ratio falls outside 0.95 to 1.05. This test does not look at axis range or baseline choices.
cost: Scaling both width and height by the value squares the difference, so a 1.5x difference is drawn as a 2.25x one. The reader takes their sense of magnitude from the mark rather than from the axis label, and the inflated version is what gets remembered and cited.
suggestion: Re-encode the quantity on a single length or position dimension, a bar length or a dot position on a shared scale, so one unit of data is one unit of drawn extent, then recompute the ratio and confirm it sits inside the band. Leave the axis range exactly as the author set it.
mechanism: The lie factor turns the vague charge of a misleading graph into arithmetic with a published tolerance. Tufte states the band explicitly, that lie factors greater than 1.05 or less than 0.95 indicate substantial distortion far beyond minor inaccuracies in plotting, and dimensional inflation is the one cause of a high ratio that has a single correct repair. A linear quantity has a linear encoding available, and moving to it changes no number and no axis.
counter_case: Area encoding is correct where the quantity is itself an area or a count of a two-dimensional thing, a patch of land or a receptive-field footprint, and bubble size legitimately carries a third variable in a scatter where the reader is asked to rank rather than to measure. In those figures state the scaling law in the caption rather than re-encoding.
source: Edward R. Tufte, The Visual Display of Quantitative Information, 2nd ed., 'Graphical Integrity', p. 57: "Lie Factor = size of effect shown in graphic / size of effect in data" and "Lie Factors greater than 1.05 or less than 0.95 indicate substantial distortion, far beyond minor inaccuracies in plotting." Page verified against the running head 'GRAPHICAL INTEGRITY 57' on the page carrying the text

test: For each figure whose caption or surrounding text makes a claim about the size of a difference, and whose value axis neither starts at zero nor spans the full range of the scale, compute Tufte's lie factor from the rendered panel and the underlying numbers, state which convention was used for size of effect (difference of values or ratio of values), and report the ratio together with the axis range. Flag only where the ratio exceeds 1.05.
cost: A truncated axis under a magnitude claim can draw a 1.2-point gap as a doubling, and the reader carries away the drawn magnitude. Reporting the ratio and the range puts the mismatch in front of the author while leaving the presentation decision with the person who knows what effect size the field treats as material.
suggestion: Report the ratio, the axis range and the convention used, and propose no change to the axis. Ask the author to choose between widening the axis and stating the numeric difference with its interval in the caption.
mechanism: Tufte's band is arithmetic, but the repair for a truncated axis is not. Whether a zoomed range is the correct presentation depends on the smallest difference that matters in the field, which is nowhere in the figure. Tufte's own example is contested on this point, a thread on his site recomputing the 14.8 as 5.78 by dividing ratios rather than percentage changes, so the convention has to be stated alongside the number.
counter_case: Loss curves, accuracy panels near ceiling and calibration plots are routinely and correctly drawn on a narrow range, where a zero baseline would compress the whole result into one row of pixels. A high ratio there is a signal to check the caption wording rather than evidence of distortion.
source: Edward R. Tufte, The Visual Display of Quantitative Information, 2nd ed., 'Graphical Integrity', p. 57: "Lie Factor = size of effect shown in graphic / size of effect in data" and "Lie Factors greater than 1.05 or less than 0.95 indicate substantial distortion, far beyond minor inaccuracies in plotting." Page verified against the running head 'GRAPHICAL INTEGRITY 57' on the page carrying the text

test: Count the cells in the data matrix a figure plots, meaning underlying numbers rather than marks on the page. Flag the figure only where the count is twenty or fewer, the marks are categorical bars or grouped bars with no connecting line and no fitted trend, and no numeral for a plotted value appears in the panel.
cost: A grouped bar chart over sixteen numbers spends a full column to convey what a compact table gives exactly, and it withholds the values a reader needs in order to compare against their own run.
suggestion: Print the exact plotted values as numerals, either as labels on the bars or by moving the same numbers into a table. Change no value and add no mark that was not already plotted.
mechanism: Tufte states the crossover directly, that tables usually outperform graphics in reporting on small data sets of twenty numbers or less and the special power of graphics comes in the display of large data sets. Restricting the flag to unconnected categorical bars keeps the shape-carrying figures out, since a bar grid asserts no shape and loses nothing by carrying its numbers.
counter_case: Bars without printed values are right where the panel is read from a projected slide, and where error bars are drawn and their overlap is the message, in which case put the interval bounds in the caption rather than crowding the panel with two numbers per bar.
source: Edward R. Tufte, The Visual Display of Quantitative Information, 2nd ed., p. 56: "Tables usually outperform graphics in reporting on small data sets of 20 numbers or less. The special power of graphics comes in the display of large data sets."

test: Count the cells in the data matrix a figure plots. Where the count is twenty or fewer and the figure occupies more than a third of a column, report the count and the area used, and note whether the marks are connected, fitted, or ordered along a continuous axis.
cost: Page area in a paper is fixed, and a third of a column spent on five numbers is a third of a column taken from a result that needed the room. Reporting the count and the area lets the author make that trade with the numbers in view.
suggestion: Report the count and the area and propose no replacement. Ask the author whether the shape of the marks or their values is the claim, since that is settled by the argument rather than by the panel.
mechanism: Tufte's twenty-number crossover is about where graphics gain power over tables, and it does not say a small graphic is wrong. The information that decides the case, whether linearity or a trend or a qualitative pattern is being asserted, sits in the author's argument, so the rule can only surface the count.
counter_case: Four points falling on a line where linearity is the claim, a scaling curve over five model sizes, and a qualitative example grid are all correct at this count, and a table would destroy the reading in each. A sixteen-cell heatmap whose point is a block structure is likewise correct while being smaller than its table.
source: Edward R. Tufte, The Visual Display of Quantitative Information, 2nd ed., p. 56: "Tables usually outperform graphics in reporting on small data sets of 20 numbers or less. The special power of graphics comes in the display of large data sets."

test: Search for the plus-minus sign and for the form 'mean (value)' in results text, tables and captions. Flag every occurrence where neither the sentence, the caption, the table header nor the methods text names the second term as a standard deviation, a standard error, a confidence interval half-width, a range or an inter-percentile range.
cost: An unnamed second term leaves the reader guessing between a spread that describes the data and an interval that describes the mean, and those differ by a factor of the square root of n, so the same digits can read as a tight result or a noisy one.
suggestion: Ask the author which quantity the term is, then name it at first use and in every caption and table header that carries it. Do not infer the term from its magnitude, and do not alter the digits.
mechanism: SAMPL fixes the notation as mean (SD) rather than mean plus-or-minus SD precisely because the plus-minus form is what lets the ambiguity persist unnoticed. Naming the term is the part that needs no arithmetic and no n, and it is the part the text can be missing entirely, so it stands alone as a rule.
counter_case: A venue template or a shared results macro may define the convention once, in which case the naming belongs at that one site and the individual sentences are already covered. A term named in a table header does not need repeating in every cell.
source: Lang & Altman, 'Basic statistical reporting for articles published in clinical medical journals: the SAMPL Guidelines', in Science Editors' Handbook (EASE, 2013), https://www.equator-network.org/wp-content/uploads/2013/07/SAMPL-Guidelines-6-27-13.pdf, 'Reporting descriptive statistics' and 'Reporting hypothesis tests': "Do NOT use the standard error of the mean (SE) to indicate the variability of a data set... (The SE is an inferential statistic -- it is about a 68% confidence interval -- not a descriptive statistic.)" and "Use the form: mean (SD), not mean +/- SD." Items are unnumbered in SAMPL and are cited by heading

test: Flag every sentence where a term is named as a standard error, SE, SEM or s.e.m. and the surrounding claim is about how variable the data are, how consistent the runs were, or how stable the method is, rather than about how precisely the mean is estimated.
cost: The standard error is an interval on the mean rather than a description of the data, so quoting it as spread understates the variability by a factor of the square root of n and makes a noisy result read as tight.
suggestion: Ask the author for n and for the standard deviation and add the spread alongside the existing term, or leave the standard error in place and reword the claim so it speaks about the precision of the mean. Never relabel the printed number as a standard deviation, since the digits would then assert a spread the data does not have.
mechanism: SAMPL bans the substitution twice and for two different reasons, once against using the standard error to indicate the variability of a data set because it is an inferential statistic about a 68% interval, and separately against using it to indicate the precision of an estimate. Conversion between the two needs n, which the sentence often omits, so the flag can be automatic while the fix cannot.
counter_case: The plus-minus form over seeds is entrenched in machine learning and a venue may expect it, in which case keep the notation and add n so a reader can convert. A stability claim backed by the standard error is also fine where the run-to-run spread is stated separately in the same paragraph.
source: Lang & Altman, 'Basic statistical reporting for articles published in clinical medical journals: the SAMPL Guidelines', in Science Editors' Handbook (EASE, 2013), https://www.equator-network.org/wp-content/uploads/2013/07/SAMPL-Guidelines-6-27-13.pdf, 'Reporting descriptive statistics' and 'Reporting hypothesis tests': "Do NOT use the standard error of the mean (SE) to indicate the variability of a data set... (The SE is an inferential statistic -- it is about a 68% confidence interval -- not a descriptive statistic.)" and "Use the form: mean (SD), not mean +/- SD." Items are unnumbered in SAMPL and are cited by heading

test: Flag every p value printed as 0, 0.0, 0.00, 0.000, .000 or any all-zero decimal string, in text, tables and figure captions.
cost: No test returns exactly zero, so the reader learns only that the print format truncated the value. The claim cannot be pooled, re-analysed or checked against a reported statistic.
suggestion: Replace the zero with the floor form the venue uses, p < 0.001 under SAMPL or P<.001 under JAMA, keeping the leading-zero convention already in force in the document. Where the analysis output is at hand and the value is exponentially small, report it in exponent form instead of at the floor.
mechanism: SAMPL sets the smallest reportable value at P < 0.001 and JAMA prescribes P<.001 below that threshold, so the floor exists in both schemes and an all-zero string is unreachable in either. The replacement is entailed by the printed string alone and needs no access to the analysis.
counter_case: In high-multiplicity settings a genuine 3e-17 is better reported in exponent form than at the floor, so a zero produced by rounding an exponentially small value belongs in the exponent rather than at p < 0.001. A literal 0 in a column of exact combinatorial or simulated counts is not a p value at all, so confirm the column header before touching it.
source: Lang & Altman, 'Basic statistical reporting for articles published in clinical medical journals: the SAMPL Guidelines', in Science Editors' Handbook (EASE, 2013), https://www.equator-network.org/wp-content/uploads/2013/07/SAMPL-Guidelines-6-27-13.pdf: "P values should be reported as equalities when possible and to one or two decimal places... Do NOT report 'NS'; give the actual P value. The smallest P value that need be reported is P < 0.001, save in studies of genetic associations." Decimal scheme from JAMA Instructions for Authors, 'Reporting Standards and Data Presentation', https://jamanetwork.com/journals/jama/pages/instructions-for-authors. Leading-zero divergence: APA Publication Manual, 7th ed., section 6.36, conditions the zero on whether the statistic can exceed 1

test: Flag every place where a test result is reported as 'NS', 'ns' or 'not significant' with no p value anywhere in the same sentence, table cell, row or caption.
cost: An unreported p value cannot be pooled, re-analysed or checked, and the reader cannot tell 0.06 from 0.83, which are different results with the same label.
suggestion: Ask the author for the value from the analysis output and report it as an equality. Do not substitute a bound such as p > 0.05, since the bound is not what the analysis produced and it carries no more information than the label it replaced.
mechanism: SAMPL forbids 'NS' outright and requires the actual P value. The value itself is not in the document, so the rule can find the label automatically and can never supply the replacement.
counter_case: A table whose caption or adjacent column gives the values and whose cells carry 'NS' as a reading aid is already reporting them, so the flag belongs on the caption-less case. Where the value is genuinely unrecoverable, a figure re-used from a prior paper for instance, say so in the text rather than inventing a bound.
source: Lang & Altman, 'Basic statistical reporting for articles published in clinical medical journals: the SAMPL Guidelines', in Science Editors' Handbook (EASE, 2013), https://www.equator-network.org/wp-content/uploads/2013/07/SAMPL-Guidelines-6-27-13.pdf: "P values should be reported as equalities when possible and to one or two decimal places... Do NOT report 'NS'; give the actual P value. The smallest P value that need be reported is P < 0.001, save in studies of genetic associations." Decimal scheme from JAMA Instructions for Authors, 'Reporting Standards and Data Presentation', https://jamanetwork.com/journals/jama/pages/instructions-for-authors. Leading-zero divergence: APA Publication Manual, 7th ed., section 6.36, conditions the zero on whether the statistic can exceed 1

test: Flag every p value reported as an inequality other than a bound the venue's scheme defines, for example p > 0.05, p < 0.05 or p < 0.01. Do not flag the floor forms p < 0.001 and P<.001, do not flag JAMA's top bound P>.99, do not flag exponent-form values, and do not flag inequalities inside a quotation or attributed to another paper's reported result.
cost: An inequality discards the value that a meta-analysis or a replication check needs, and a threshold-shaped bound such as p > 0.05 also imports a significance cutoff the author may not have intended to claim.
suggestion: Ask the author for the exact value from the analysis output and report it as an equality, keeping the floor form for anything below it. Where the value cannot be recovered, leave the inequality as printed and state in the text that the exact value is unavailable.
mechanism: SAMPL requires P values as equalities where possible while also setting a floor at P < 0.001, and the two only conflict if the floor is not excluded from the equality rule. Excluding the venue's own defined bounds resolves that, and what remains, an undefended threshold bound, is repairable only from the analysis output.
counter_case: Genetic association studies are exempted from the floor by SAMPL and routinely report far below it, and JAMA defines P>.99 as a legitimate top bound, so both are correct as printed. An inequality quoted from another paper is also correct, since the exact value was never in this author's hands.
source: Lang & Altman, 'Basic statistical reporting for articles published in clinical medical journals: the SAMPL Guidelines', in Science Editors' Handbook (EASE, 2013), https://www.equator-network.org/wp-content/uploads/2013/07/SAMPL-Guidelines-6-27-13.pdf: "P values should be reported as equalities when possible and to one or two decimal places... Do NOT report 'NS'; give the actual P value. The smallest P value that need be reported is P < 0.001, save in studies of genetic associations." Decimal scheme from JAMA Instructions for Authors, 'Reporting Standards and Data Presentation', https://jamanetwork.com/journals/jama/pages/instructions-for-authors. Leading-zero divergence: APA Publication Manual, 7th ed., section 6.36, conditions the zero on whether the statistic can exceed 1

test: Collect every p value in the document and compare its leading-zero treatment against the venue convention recorded on the style sheet. Flag the document only where both forms appear for p values and a convention has been recorded or can be read off a clear majority of the p values present.
cost: Two leading-zero forms in one results section read as two hands on the manuscript and draw a copy-editing query on every occurrence, which costs a revision round for a difference that carries no meaning.
suggestion: Add or remove the single character before the decimal point so every p value follows the recorded convention, and change no digit and no decimal place. Where no convention is recorded, adopt the form used by the majority of the document's p values and write that choice onto the style sheet.
mechanism: The leading zero is house style and both forms are correct, so the only defect available is inconsistency inside one document. Because the repair touches one character before the decimal point, it cannot alter a reported value, which is what separates it from the decimal-place question that was bundled with it.
counter_case: APA conditions the zero on whether the statistic can exceed 1, stripping it for p and r while keeping it for t and F, so a document writing .03 for p and 0.98 for a t statistic is consistent rather than mixed. Values inside quoted material keep the source's form.
source: Lang & Altman, 'Basic statistical reporting for articles published in clinical medical journals: the SAMPL Guidelines', in Science Editors' Handbook (EASE, 2013), https://www.equator-network.org/wp-content/uploads/2013/07/SAMPL-Guidelines-6-27-13.pdf: "P values should be reported as equalities when possible and to one or two decimal places... Do NOT report 'NS'; give the actual P value. The smallest P value that need be reported is P < 0.001, save in studies of genetic associations." Decimal scheme from JAMA Instructions for Authors, 'Reporting Standards and Data Presentation', https://jamanetwork.com/journals/jama/pages/instructions-for-authors. Leading-zero divergence: APA Publication Manual, 7th ed., section 6.36, conditions the zero on whether the statistic can exceed 1

test: Search the page-limited narrative for http, https, www., doi.org and for outward phrases (see our website, available online, full details at). Flag a hit only where the load-bearing element of that sentence, a number, a method name, a dataset name or an artefact identifier, appears nowhere in the narrative and the link is its only carrier.
cost: NSF states reviewers are under no obligation to view linked sites and ERC states linked and embedded material will be disregarded, with experts having no access to supporting documentation during evaluation. The claim is therefore scored as unsupported rather than as supported elsewhere.
suggestion: Ask the author for the fact and state it in the sentence, then keep the link exactly where it is as a citation. Delete no URL under this rule.
mechanism: A reviewer working an assigned pile has no browser tab open for this proposal and, at ERC, is reading inside a closed evaluation system. A link reads as a promise that the evidence exists somewhere, which is the shape of an unsupported claim. Adding the fact removes the defect without touching the citation, and the fact itself is outside the document, so the rule can find the gap and cannot fill it.
counter_case: A DOI beside a claim whose number is already in the text is a citation and passes untouched. Where the support is a whole results table that cannot fit the page limit, the correct move is one summary statistic in the narrative with the link kept as the pointer to the table.
source: NSF, Proposal & Award Policies & Procedures Guide (PAPPG) 24-1, Chapter II.D.2.d(ii) Page Limitations and Inclusion of URLs ('the Project Description must be self-contained, and that URLs must not be used'); ERC (European Research Council), Information for Applicants to the Starting and Consolidator Grant Calls, Version 11.0 (22 July 2026), section 2.2 supporting documentation ('any hyperlinks to other documents, embedded material, and any other documents ... will be disregarded. Experts will not have access to any supporting documentation during the evaluation.'). URLs: NSF PAPPG 24-1 ch. II — https://www.nsf.gov/policies/pappg/24-1/ch-2-proposal-preparation; ERC Information for Applicants V11.0 — https://ec.europa.eu/info/funding-tenders/opportunities/docs/2021-2027/horizon/guidance/information-for-applicants_he-erc-stg-cog_en.pdf

test: Where the funder is NSF and the document is the Project Description, inventory every URL and report it against the call's own text on URLs. Where the funder is ERC, check whether the call specifies an exception to the disregard rule, then report the inventory with that clause attached.
cost: NSF requires the Project Description to be self-contained and states URLs must not be used, and a non-conforming proposal is returned without review, so the exposure is the whole submission rather than one sentence.
suggestion: Report the inventory and the clause it is being read against, and propose no deletion or rewrite. Put the conformance decision to the author, since only the text of that competition's call settles it.
mechanism: ERC's disregard rule is prefixed 'Unless specified in the call', and NSF's prohibition sits in a chapter that is revised between PAPPG editions and applies to one named document rather than the whole package. The governing sentence is therefore outside the narrative, which makes an automatic deletion a guess with the submission at stake.
counter_case: Some calls explicitly permit links, so the same URL can be permitted and load-bearing in one competition and fatal in another. Data-availability statements, biosketches and facilities documents sit outside the Project Description page limit and are not covered by this test.
source: NSF, Proposal & Award Policies & Procedures Guide (PAPPG) 24-1, Chapter II.D.2.d(ii) Page Limitations and Inclusion of URLs ('the Project Description must be self-contained, and that URLs must not be used'); ERC (European Research Council), Information for Applicants to the Starting and Consolidator Grant Calls, Version 11.0 (22 July 2026), section 2.2 supporting documentation ('any hyperlinks to other documents, embedded material, and any other documents ... will be disregarded. Experts will not have access to any supporting documentation during the evaluation.'). URLs: NSF PAPPG 24-1 ch. II — https://www.nsf.gov/policies/pappg/24-1/ch-2-proposal-preparation; ERC Information for Applicants V11.0 — https://ec.europa.eu/info/funding-tenders/opportunities/docs/2021-2027/horizon/guidance/information-for-applicants_he-erc-stg-cog_en.pdf

test: In References Cited, flag any entry whose author list is abbreviated (et al., 'and others', a trailing ellipsis) or shorter than the author list printed on the published item.
cost: NSF states it will return without review proposals that are not consistent with the preparation instructions, and the reference-entry field list is one of those instructions. A malformed bibliography is a compliance finding reached before any reviewer reads the science.
suggestion: Replace the abbreviated list with every author in the order the publication prints them, taken from the publisher record or the DOI landing page rather than from a search snippet. Change no other field of the entry.
mechanism: A truncated author list removes the reader's ability to see whether the cited work is the applicant's own, which is the fact a panel most often wants from that entry. It is also the one defect an administrator can find without reading the science, so it is checked early and cheaply.
counter_case: Some items are bylined to a collaboration or consortium (LIGO Scientific Collaboration, BIG-bench authors) or run to hundreds of names. Reproduce the byline as printed, including the collaboration name, instead of expanding it into individuals.
source: NSF, Proposal & Award Policies & Procedures Guide (PAPPG) 24-1, Chapter II.D.2.e References Cited ('the names of all authors (in the same sequence in which they appear in the publication), the article and journal title, book title, volume number, page numbers, and year of publication'); Chapter II.A.1 (return without review). URLs: NSF PAPPG 24-1 ch. II — https://www.nsf.gov/policies/pappg/24-1/ch-2-proposal-preparation

test: For every References Cited entry that is a journal article, a book or a book chapter, flag a missing journal or book title, volume, page range or year. Entries of any other item type are outside this test.
cost: NSF states it will return without review proposals that are not consistent with the preparation instructions, and the reference-entry field list is one of those instructions. A malformed bibliography is a compliance finding reached before any reviewer reads the science.
suggestion: Fill each missing field from the publisher record or the DOI landing page for that item. If a field does not exist for the item at hand, the item is not a journal article, book or chapter and this rule does not apply to it.
mechanism: Reference checking is the one part of a proposal a reader can audit without expertise, so it is where a sceptical reviewer starts and where an administrator finishes. For these three item types every listed field genuinely exists, so the gap is a transcription failure and the fix is mechanical lookup.
counter_case: Online-first articles carry an article number instead of a page range, and several journals have dropped volume numbering. Give the DOI and the article number exactly as printed instead of reconstructing a volume.
source: NSF, Proposal & Award Policies & Procedures Guide (PAPPG) 24-1, Chapter II.D.2.e References Cited ('the names of all authors (in the same sequence in which they appear in the publication), the article and journal title, book title, volume number, page numbers, and year of publication'); Chapter II.A.1 (return without review). URLs: NSF PAPPG 24-1 ch. II — https://www.nsf.gov/policies/pappg/24-1/ch-2-proposal-preparation

test: For every References Cited entry that is a preprint, dataset, software release, standard or technical report, flag the entry only when it carries no persistent identifier (DOI, arXiv ID, ISO or RFC number, or a version tag with a repository URL). Absent volume and page fields are not a defect for these item types.
cost: NSF states it will return without review proposals that are not consistent with the preparation instructions, and the reference-entry field list is one of those instructions. A malformed bibliography is a compliance finding reached before any reviewer reads the science.
suggestion: Add the identifier the item actually has, copied character for character, and leave the volume and page fields absent. Never supply a volume, issue or page range for these item types.
mechanism: These item types have no volume or pages to transcribe, so a field checker that demands them pushes the author into fabrication. What the reader needs instead is a handle that resolves to the exact thing cited, which is what the funder asks for in place of the missing fields.
counter_case: A dataset or software item with a versioned identifier needs the version actually used, because a concept DOI resolves to the latest release and can silently change what the citation points at. Copy the identifier verbatim and do not normalise or shorten it.
source: NSF, Proposal & Award Policies & Procedures Guide (PAPPG) 24-1, Chapter II.D.2.e References Cited ('the names of all authors (in the same sequence in which they appear in the publication), the article and journal title, book title, volume number, page numbers, and year of publication'); Chapter II.A.1 (return without review). URLs: NSF PAPPG 24-1 ch. II — https://www.nsf.gov/policies/pappg/24-1/ch-2-proposal-preparation

test: Render the counted parts of the proposal at the layout the funder mandates (for ERC A4, Times New Roman or Arial or similar, at least 11 point, single spacing, 2 cm side and 1.5 cm bottom margins) and locate the page cut for each part. Report every claim, objective, figure or definition in a counted part that falls after its own cut. Sections that sit outside the page count by rule (References Cited, the ERC Funding ID and time-commitment sections, ethics and security annexes) are outside this test.
cost: ERC states only the material presented within the limits will be evaluated and that peer reviewers will be asked to read within the limits only, with no obligation to read beyond. NSF enforces the 15-page Project Description strictly. Text past the cut is not weakly scored, it is not scored.
suggestion: Report the part, the size of the overflow and the items that fall past the cut, and name candidate donor paragraphs without touching them. Propose no cut. Which paragraph is expendable depends on what the panel already knows and on the science, neither of which can be read off the page.
mechanism: Overflow happens at the end, which is where objectives, criteria and the risk statement usually sit, so the material lost is the material the evaluation form asks about. Detecting the cut is a rendering question and fully decidable. Choosing which correct paragraph dies is not, and an automatic cut destroys text the author needs.
counter_case: A figure whose caption straddles the cut is only partly lost, and material placed in an uncounted section is not lost at all. Report the item and the part it sits in, and never count an uncounted section as overflow.
source: ERC (European Research Council), Information for Applicants to the Starting and Consolidator Grant Calls, Version 11.0 (22 July 2026), section 2.2 layout and page limits ('In fairness to all applicants, the page limits will be strictly applied. ... Only the material that is presented within these limits will be evaluated.'); NSF, Proposal & Award Policies & Procedures Guide (PAPPG) 24-1, Chapter II.D.2.d(ii) ('Conformance to the 15-page limit will be strictly enforced'). URLs: ERC Information for Applicants V11.0 — https://ec.europa.eu/info/funding-tenders/opportunities/docs/2021-2027/horizon/guidance/information-for-applicants_he-erc-stg-cog_en.pdf; NSF PAPPG 24-1 ch. II — https://www.nsf.gov/policies/pappg/24-1/ch-2-proposal-preparation

test: Compare the rendered font family, point size, line spacing and margins of the counted parts against the minimums the funder states, and flag any body-text value below them.
cost: ERC states only the material presented within the limits will be evaluated and that peer reviewers will be asked to read within the limits only, with no obligation to read beyond. NSF enforces the 15-page Project Description strictly. Text past the cut is not weakly scored, it is not scored.
suggestion: Restore each value to the stated minimum and re-render. Never take body text below the minimum to recover space, because the promise to read to the limit is conditional on the layout instructions being respected. If restoring the layout pushes material past the page cut, that overflow is a separate finding for the author to resolve.
mechanism: Shrinking the font to fit voids the protection the page limit carries, because ERC conditions the read-to-the-limit promise on the font instructions being met. The mandated minimum is a single stated value, so restoring it changes appearance and pagination while leaving every word intact.
counter_case: Figure captions, table bodies and footnotes are often allowed a smaller size than body text. A 9-point caption under an 11-point body is not a violation, so check the call's own wording before changing anything outside the body text.
source: ERC (European Research Council), Information for Applicants to the Starting and Consolidator Grant Calls, Version 11.0 (22 July 2026), section 2.2 layout and page limits ('In fairness to all applicants, the page limits will be strictly applied. ... Only the material that is presented within these limits will be evaluated.'); NSF, Proposal & Award Policies & Procedures Guide (PAPPG) 24-1, Chapter II.D.2.d(ii) ('Conformance to the 15-page limit will be strictly enforced'). URLs: ERC Information for Applicants V11.0 — https://ec.europa.eu/info/funding-tenders/opportunities/docs/2021-2027/horizon/guidance/information-for-applicants_he-erc-stg-cog_en.pdf; NSF PAPPG 24-1 ch. II — https://www.nsf.gov/policies/pappg/24-1/ch-2-proposal-preparation

test: For every portal text box with a character maximum, count the characters in a counter outside the portal and report any box at or over the cap, naming the sentence the cap falls inside and the claim that sentence carries.
cost: ERC states the description of resources will be truncated once it exceeds the maximum allowed characters. The panel then reads a sentence that stops mid-clause, and the claim it carried is gone with no error message anywhere.
suggestion: Report the box, the count, the cap, the sentence the cap cuts and whether the claim it carries appears anywhere else in the submission. Propose no trim. Which claim is sacrificed, and whether it moves into the scientific proposal instead, is the author's decision.
mechanism: Silent truncation is the only failure mode in a proposal where the applicant, the office and the reviewer all see something different, and the reviewer's copy is the truncated one. Counting characters is mechanical and worth doing every time. Deciding which required fact to give up is not in the text, and a trim to the last full sentence can drop the one fact the box existed to carry.
counter_case: Portals differ on whether line breaks, non-ASCII characters and pasted formatting count toward the cap, so a count within a few dozen characters of the limit is not proof of safety. Report near-cap boxes as at risk rather than as clear.
source: ERC (European Research Council), Information for Applicants to the Starting and Consolidator Grant Calls, Version 11.0 (22 July 2026), Resources and Time Commitment section note ('description of resources will be truncated once it exceeds the maximum allowed characters'). URLs: ERC Information for Applicants V11.0 — https://ec.europa.eu/info/funding-tenders/opportunities/docs/2021-2027/horizon/guidance/information-for-applicants_he-erc-stg-cog_en.pdf

test: Where the proposal states that its contribution is a claim about the field's understanding (a mechanism, an explanation, a bound, a model), search the non-specialist part for a sentence whose subject is the field's current understanding and whose verb is a change verb (change, open, challenge, overturn, replace, alter, rule out). Flag the proposal if no such sentence exists, or if the only candidate is about the project's activity rather than about the field.
cost: ERC asks the panel at both steps whether the project will advance the frontier of knowledge, and the Information for Applicants tells applicants Part I should explain what may be changed, opened or challenged. With no such sentence the generalist has to construct the answer, and the score reflects the construction they manage in one reading.
suggestion: Add one sentence naming the belief, method or bound that stops being true if the project succeeds, and place it where the objectives begin rather than in the closing paragraph. Take that belief from the proposal's own related-work section, so the sentence reports a claim the proposal already defends.
mechanism: A generalist panel member cannot infer the size of a contribution from the size of the effort, because the effort is legible and the contribution is not. The change sentence is the only place the proposal converts work into consequence in terms the reviewer can repeat at the panel meeting. Its absence is scored as absence of ambition rather than as an omission.
counter_case: Where the belief only falls under one of two possible outcomes, name both. A change sentence that quietly assumes the favourable branch reads as overclaiming to a reviewer who has just read the risk section.
source: ERC (European Research Council), Information for Applicants to the Starting and Consolidator Grant Calls, Version 11.0 (22 July 2026), section 2.2 Part I ('what may be changed, opened, challenged or how the results of the work will alter the current understanding of the field'); ERC (European Research Council), ERC Work Programme 2027 (Commission Decision C(2026)4907), section 1.6.5 Evaluation Elements. URLs: ERC Information for Applicants V11.0 — https://ec.europa.eu/info/funding-tenders/opportunities/docs/2021-2027/horizon/guidance/information-for-applicants_he-erc-stg-cog_en.pdf; ERC Work Programme 2027 — https://ec.europa.eu/info/funding-tenders/opportunities/docs/2021-2027/horizon/wp-call/2027/wp_horizon-erc-2027_en.pdf

test: Where the proposal states that its contribution is a capability (a device, a measurement technique, a corpus, a dataset, a method or a piece of software), search the non-specialist part for a sentence naming what becomes measurable or possible that was not, and who gains it. Flag the proposal if no such sentence exists.
cost: ERC asks the panel at both steps whether the project will advance the frontier of knowledge, and the Information for Applicants tells applicants Part I should explain what may be changed, opened or challenged. With no such sentence the generalist has to construct the answer, and the score reflects the construction they manage in one reading.
suggestion: Add one sentence naming the capability, the question it makes answerable and the community that inherits it. Do not add a claim about the field's beliefs changing, because that is not what this proposal is offering and the reviewer can check it against the work plan.
mechanism: A capability proposal loses the same way a theory proposal does, by leaving the generalist to convert effort into consequence unaided. The consequence here is that a question becomes askable, which is a statement the reviewer can repeat at the panel. Forcing it into the vocabulary of overturned beliefs produces a claim the work plan cannot support.
counter_case: A capability proposal can also carry a genuine theory claim, and where the related-work section already names a belief the capability puts to the test, that belief belongs in the sentence too. What is forbidden is manufacturing such a claim, not reporting a real one.
source: ERC (European Research Council), Information for Applicants to the Starting and Consolidator Grant Calls, Version 11.0 (22 July 2026), section 2.2 Part I ('what may be changed, opened, challenged or how the results of the work will alter the current understanding of the field'); ERC (European Research Council), ERC Work Programme 2027 (Commission Decision C(2026)4907), section 1.6.5 Evaluation Elements. URLs: ERC Information for Applicants V11.0 — https://ec.europa.eu/info/funding-tenders/opportunities/docs/2021-2027/horizon/guidance/information-for-applicants_he-erc-stg-cog_en.pdf; ERC Work Programme 2027 — https://ec.europa.eu/info/funding-tenders/opportunities/docs/2021-2027/horizon/wp-call/2027/wp_horizon-erc-2027_en.pdf

test: Where the non-specialist part carries no sentence whose subject is the field's current understanding and also does not state whether the contribution is a claim about understanding or a new capability, report the ambiguity.
cost: ERC asks the panel at both steps whether the project will advance the frontier of knowledge, and the Information for Applicants tells applicants Part I should explain what may be changed, opened or challenged. With no such sentence the generalist has to construct the answer, and the score reflects the construction they manage in one reading.
suggestion: Report that the contribution type cannot be read off the text, quote the two closest candidate sentences and stop. Propose no change sentence, because a claim about understanding and a claim about capability need different sentences and only the author knows which project this is.
mechanism: The two contribution types are repaired by different sentences, and the text that triggers this rule does not say which applies. Writing either one guesses, and the guess that manufactures a theory claim is the expensive direction because a reviewer will test it against the work plan.
counter_case: Some proposals genuinely offer both a result about the field and a lasting resource, and a report that forces one type is wrong about the project. Say which passages point each way and leave the choice open.
source: ERC (European Research Council), Information for Applicants to the Starting and Consolidator Grant Calls, Version 11.0 (22 July 2026), section 2.2 Part I ('what may be changed, opened, challenged or how the results of the work will alter the current understanding of the field'); ERC (European Research Council), ERC Work Programme 2027 (Commission Decision C(2026)4907), section 1.6.5 Evaluation Elements. URLs: ERC Information for Applicants V11.0 — https://ec.europa.eu/info/funding-tenders/opportunities/docs/2021-2027/horizon/guidance/information-for-applicants_he-erc-stg-cog_en.pdf; ERC Work Programme 2027 — https://ec.europa.eu/info/funding-tenders/opportunities/docs/2021-2027/horizon/wp-call/2027/wp_horizon-erc-2027_en.pdf

test: List every passage that labels a step high-risk, exploratory, speculative or uncertain and whose text locates the risk in the outcome (the effect may not hold, the method may not work, the data may not carry the signal). For each, read the outcome sentence for that step and flag it if its verb is unconditional (will show, will establish, will demonstrate, will prove).
cost: ERC states proposals are expected to take risks but that the risk and its management must be well thought through and addressed. A certainty verb over an acknowledged risk gives the reviewer a contradiction inside the proposal, which they resolve against the more confident sentence.
suggestion: Rewrite the outcome sentence as a measurement and name what is learned on each branch, so the risk label and the outcome sentence describe the same uncertainty. Keep the risk label, and keep every hedge and modal already in the passage.
mechanism: Applicants label risk in the risk section because the form asks for it, then write the science sections in the confident register the rest of the proposal uses. The reviewer reads both and has to decide which one the applicant believes. Stating what is learned on the failure branch converts the contradiction into the risk management the funder asked for.
counter_case: Where the failure branch teaches nothing, naming it exposes a real gap in the work plan rather than a prose defect. Report that gap instead of writing a branch sentence the plan cannot support.
source: ERC (European Research Council), Guide for Peer Reviewers to the ERC Starting and Consolidator Grant Calls, Version 6.0 (30 September 2025, 2026 calls), section 1 Evaluation of ERC Starting and Consolidator Grant Proposals ('The ERC research proposals are expected to take risks. It remains important, however, that the risk and its management are well thought through and addressed in the proposal.'). URLs: ERC Guide for Peer Reviewers V6.0 — https://ec.europa.eu/info/funding-tenders/opportunities/docs/2021-2027/experts/guide-for-peer-reviewers_he-erc-stg-cog_en.pdf

test: List every passage that labels a step high-risk, exploratory, speculative or uncertain and whose text locates the risk in schedule, access or resources (a delivery date, a data access agreement, recruitment, a compute allocation, a dependency on another work package). Flag the risk label only. The outcome sentence for such a step is outside this test whatever its verb.
cost: ERC states proposals are expected to take risks but that the risk and its management must be well thought through and addressed. A certainty verb over an acknowledged risk gives the reviewer a contradiction inside the proposal, which they resolve against the more confident sentence.
suggestion: Keep the label and say which kind of risk it is, then add the mitigation that applies to timing (a buffer, a fallback source, a reordered dependency). Leave the unconditional outcome verb as it stands, because what is uncertain is when the step happens rather than what it shows.
mechanism: A schedule risk and an outcome risk read identically once both are compressed into the word high-risk, and the reviewer resolves the ambiguity against the applicant. Naming the kind of risk removes the apparent contradiction without weakening a result the applicant is entitled to assert.
counter_case: A delay severe enough to lose the data entirely is an outcome risk wearing a schedule label, and then the outcome sentence does need conditioning. The dividing question is whether failure changes what is learned or only when it is learned.
source: ERC (European Research Council), Guide for Peer Reviewers to the ERC Starting and Consolidator Grant Calls, Version 6.0 (30 September 2025, 2026 calls), section 1 Evaluation of ERC Starting and Consolidator Grant Proposals ('The ERC research proposals are expected to take risks. It remains important, however, that the risk and its management are well thought through and addressed in the proposal.'). URLs: ERC Guide for Peer Reviewers V6.0 — https://ec.europa.eu/info/funding-tenders/opportunities/docs/2021-2027/experts/guide-for-peer-reviewers_he-erc-stg-cog_en.pdf

test: List every passage that labels a step high-risk, exploratory, speculative or uncertain without saying whether the risk is in the outcome or in the schedule, and whose outcome sentence carries an unconditional verb (will show, will establish, will demonstrate, will prove). Report the label and the outcome sentence together.
cost: ERC states proposals are expected to take risks but that the risk and its management must be well thought through and addressed. A certainty verb over an acknowledged risk gives the reviewer a contradiction inside the proposal, which they resolve against the more confident sentence.
suggestion: Report the pair and ask which kind of risk was meant. Propose no rewrite, because conditioning an outcome that is merely late corrupts a correct claim, and leaving an outcome risk unconditioned leaves the contradiction the reviewer scores against.
mechanism: The repair depends on a fact the passage withholds, namely whether failure changes the result or only its date. Both wrong guesses are expensive in opposite directions, so the useful output is the question rather than an edit.
counter_case: A passage reading 'high-risk, high-gain' is the funder's own call language and may carry no specific risk claim at all. Report it as call language rather than as an unspecified risk.
source: ERC (European Research Council), Guide for Peer Reviewers to the ERC Starting and Consolidator Grant Calls, Version 6.0 (30 September 2025, 2026 calls), section 1 Evaluation of ERC Starting and Consolidator Grant Proposals ('The ERC research proposals are expected to take risks. It remains important, however, that the risk and its management are well thought through and addressed in the proposal.'). URLs: ERC Guide for Peer Reviewers V6.0 — https://ec.europa.eu/info/funding-tenders/opportunities/docs/2021-2027/experts/guide-for-peer-reviewers_he-erc-stg-cog_en.pdf

test: Restrict to the parts a generalist scores, the ERC Part B1 extended synopsis and the NSF Project Summary. Take the published descriptor and keyword list for the panel or programme selected on the form. Extract every technical noun phrase from those parts and flag any phrase absent from the descriptor and not glossed in the same or the previous sentence.
cost: At ERC Step 1 panel members are asked to act as generalists, and NSF requires the Project Summary be understandable to a broad audience within the scientific domain. In these two parts an off-descriptor unglossed term is read as noise and the sentence carrying it does not score.
suggestion: Gloss on first use with a five-to-ten word apposition, or substitute the phrase the descriptor already uses. Propose the gloss and let the author approve it, because the shortest honest gloss depends on what the work actually claims and the descriptor does not supply that.
mechanism: Panel descriptors are the funder's own statement of the vocabulary the panel shares, which makes them a checkable substitute for guessing what a reviewer knows. A generalist meeting an unglossed term carries on and loses the clause. Because Step 1 decides whether any specialist reads you at all, a term only a specialist can parse costs you the specialist.
counter_case: ERC Part B2 and the NSF Project Description go to specialist remote reviewers and this rule does not reach them. Glossing 'residual stream' for an interpretability reviewer spends B2 page budget and reads as condescension to the scorer who decides Step 2.
source: ERC (European Research Council), Information for Applicants to the Starting and Consolidator Grant Calls, Version 11.0 (22 July 2026), section 1.6 Evaluation Process ('The panel members are asked to act as generalists when evaluating the proposals.'); ERC (European Research Council), Guide for Peer Reviewers to the ERC Starting and Consolidator Grant Calls, Version 6.0 (30 September 2025, 2026 calls), Annex 2 Primary Panel Structure (published panel descriptors); NSF, Proposal & Award Policies & Procedures Guide (PAPPG) 24-1, Chapter II.D.2.b Project Summary ('understandable to a broad audience within the scientific domain'). URLs: ERC Information for Applicants V11.0 — https://ec.europa.eu/info/funding-tenders/opportunities/docs/2021-2027/horizon/guidance/information-for-applicants_he-erc-stg-cog_en.pdf; ERC Guide for Peer Reviewers V6.0 — https://ec.europa.eu/info/funding-tenders/opportunities/docs/2021-2027/experts/guide-for-peer-reviewers_he-erc-stg-cog_en.pdf; NSF PAPPG 24-1 ch. II — https://www.nsf.gov/policies/pappg/24-1/ch-2-proposal-preparation

test: Restrict to the parts specialist remote reviewers score, the ERC Part B2 and the NSF Project Description. Flag every technical noun phrase that is absent from the published panel descriptor and carries no gloss.
cost: An off-descriptor term in B2 is a fork rather than a fault. It is either standard in the assigned reviewer's sub-field, where a gloss wastes page budget, or outside it, where the clause is lost. The text does not say which reviewer was assigned.
suggestion: Report the term, the page and the descriptor it is missing from. Propose nothing, because whether the assigned specialist already knows the term is knowledge the proposal does not contain.
mechanism: Assignment of remote reviewers happens after submission and is not visible to the author, so the same term can be free or expensive depending on who opens the file. A list of off-descriptor terms lets the author make that bet deliberately once, instead of a checker making it silently on every line.
counter_case: 'Residual stream' in B2 needs no gloss for the interpretability reviewer the panel will pick, and adding one costs half a line on a hard page limit. The same phrase in a B2 sent to a panel whose descriptor covers only cognitive neuroscience does need one, and only the author can guess which panel read it.
source: ERC (European Research Council), Information for Applicants to the Starting and Consolidator Grant Calls, Version 11.0 (22 July 2026), section 1.6 Evaluation Process ('The panel members are asked to act as generalists when evaluating the proposals.'); ERC (European Research Council), Guide for Peer Reviewers to the ERC Starting and Consolidator Grant Calls, Version 6.0 (30 September 2025, 2026 calls), Annex 2 Primary Panel Structure (published panel descriptors); NSF, Proposal & Award Policies & Procedures Guide (PAPPG) 24-1, Chapter II.D.2.b Project Summary ('understandable to a broad audience within the scientific domain'). URLs: ERC Information for Applicants V11.0 — https://ec.europa.eu/info/funding-tenders/opportunities/docs/2021-2027/horizon/guidance/information-for-applicants_he-erc-stg-cog_en.pdf; ERC Guide for Peer Reviewers V6.0 — https://ec.europa.eu/info/funding-tenders/opportunities/docs/2021-2027/experts/guide-for-peer-reviewers_he-erc-stg-cog_en.pdf; NSF PAPPG 24-1 ch. II — https://www.nsf.gov/policies/pappg/24-1/ch-2-proposal-preparation

test: Treat each attachment as a document on its own, so ERC Part B1 and Part B2, and each separate NIH attachment, are checked independently. Within one attachment, find the first occurrence of each acronym and flag it where that occurrence is bare and an expansion of the same acronym appears later in the same attachment.
cost: NSF's own proposal-writing guide states the rule, and NSF returns proposals that are not consistent with its preparation instructions. A reader who has to reconstruct an expansion mid-page loses the sentence it sat in.
suggestion: Move the existing expansion up to the first occurrence in that attachment, keeping the acronym in parentheses, and reduce the later occurrence to the bare acronym. Re-run after any reordering.
mechanism: Reordering paragraphs is the last edit most proposals get, and it silently moves the first use of an acronym after a later one. The expansion is already in the attachment, so the fix is a move rather than an invention, and nothing about the meaning is at stake.
counter_case: Where the later expansion sits in a figure caption, a table cell or a heading, leave it. Captions are read out of sequence and an expansion there is doing its own job, so moving it strips the caption of a term its reader met nowhere else.
source: NSF, A Guide for Proposal Writing (NSF 04-016), Step 3, Little Things That Can Make a Difference ('The first time you use an acronym, write out what it stands for and put the acronym in parentheses.'). URLs: NSF 04-016 — https://nsf-gov-resources.nsf.gov/pubs/2004/nsf04016/nsf04016.pdf?VersionId=_pFLVguJ41PzvWwyThPBaqnSFad20hao

test: Within one attachment, taken alone, find each acronym for which no expansion appears anywhere in that attachment. Exclude forms that are proper names rather than initialisms, such as GPT-4, BERT, SQuAD and CUDA, and exclude the funder's own form codes.
cost: NSF's guide asks for the expansion at first use, and an acronym expanded nowhere in the attachment leaves a generalist with a token instead of a concept. Per-attachment reading means an expansion living in a sibling attachment does not help.
suggestion: Supply the expansion at the first occurrence with the acronym in parentheses. Propose the expansion for the author to confirm, because the correct expansion is not in the attachment and several near-identical acronyms exist across fields.
mechanism: Authors drop expansions for terms that are house vocabulary in their own group, so the missing expansion is exactly the one they cannot see. The expansion has to come from outside the text, which is why this is a question rather than a substitution.
counter_case: 'EEE' expands one way in the applicant's own lab and another in an unrelated literature, so a checker guessing from context can insert a wrong expansion into a compliance-checked attachment. Contrast a form code such as 'PHS 398', which is the funder's own name for the document and must stay unexpanded.
source: NSF, A Guide for Proposal Writing (NSF 04-016), Step 3, Little Things That Can Make a Difference ('The first time you use an acronym, write out what it stands for and put the acronym in parentheses.'). URLs: NSF 04-016 — https://nsf-gov-resources.nsf.gov/pubs/2004/nsf04016/nsf04016.pdf?VersionId=_pFLVguJ41PzvWwyThPBaqnSFad20hao

test: Within one attachment, taken alone, flag any acronym expanded two or more times in running prose. Do not compare across attachments, so an expansion in Part B1 and another in Part B2 is not a hit. Ignore expansions in figure captions, table cells, headings and the abstract.
cost: A second expansion in the same running text tells the reader they missed the first one, and on a hard page limit it spends a line the argument needed. NIH and ERC both count pages rather than words.
suggestion: Keep the expansion at the first occurrence in that attachment and reduce every later occurrence in running prose to the bare acronym.
mechanism: Multiple authors drafting different sections each expand the acronym they own, and the duplicates survive the merge because each one reads correctly in isolation. Removing a duplicate inside one attachment cannot cost a reader anything, since they have already met the expansion in the same file.
counter_case: NIH is read attachment by attachment, so the Specific Aims and the Research Strategy each need their own first-use expansion and a second expansion across that boundary is required rather than redundant. The same holds for ERC Part B1 and Part B2 as separate PDFs.
source: NSF, A Guide for Proposal Writing (NSF 04-016), Step 3, Little Things That Can Make a Difference ('The first time you use an acronym, write out what it stands for and put the acronym in parentheses.'). URLs: NSF 04-016 — https://nsf-gov-resources.nsf.gov/pubs/2004/nsf04016/nsf04016.pdf?VersionId=_pFLVguJ41PzvWwyThPBaqnSFad20hao

test: Find every passive clause describing work the project will do where the agent is not recoverable from the sentence. Keep only clauses whose work already appears against a named owner in the proposal's own work-package table, Gantt chart or staffing list. Exclude any clause whose work is performed by a core facility, a commercial service, a consortium partner outside the budget, or a procedure that is deliberately agentless, such as randomisation, blinding or automated scoring.
cost: NIH instructs applicants to write in the active voice and gives the reason, that active voice clarifies who will take which actions. Factor 3 asks whether the investigators have the expertise to conduct the proposed work, and an agentless clause supplies no one to attach that judgement to.
suggestion: Rewrite with the owner already named in the work-package table as the grammatical subject. Propose the rewrite with the table row quoted beside it, because promoting a table entry into prose is a staffing commitment the author has to confirm.
mechanism: Researchers write in the passive because journals trained them to, and the habit carries into a document whose whole purpose is to say who will do what. Requiring the owner to be in the table first means the rewrite reuses a commitment the author has already made, so no new promise is invented.
counter_case: 'Samples will be sequenced at the core facility' has no owner in the work-package table and must stay passive, since naming the WP2 postdoc implies effort the budget does not fund. 'Participants will be randomised to arm A or B' is agentless on purpose, and naming a randomiser misstates the method rather than the staffing.
source: NIH, General Grant Writing Tips (grants.nih.gov/grants-process/write-application/general-grant-writing-tips), Tip 3 ('Write in the active voice: "We will develop an experiment." Active voice clarifies who will take which actions. Avoid using passive voice: "An experiment will be developed."'); NIH, Simplified Review Framework, Factor 3 Expertise and Resources. URLs: NIH General Grant Writing Tips — https://grants.nih.gov/grants-process/write-application/general-grant-writing-tips

test: Find every passive clause describing work the project will do where the agent is not recoverable from the sentence and the work appears against no owner in any work-package table, Gantt chart or staffing list.
