Exclude clauses whose work is done by a core facility, a commercial service, a partner outside the budget, or a deliberately agentless procedure.
cost: Factor 3 is answered by matching tasks to people, so project work with no owner anywhere is a gap in the plan rather than a defect in the sentence. Rewriting the clause hides the gap behind a fluent active verb.
suggestion: Report the clause and the fact that no work-package row owns the work. Propose nothing, because the proposal does not say who will do it and supplying a name fabricates a commitment the reviewer will price.
mechanism: An unowned passive is usually the trace of work that was never staffed, so the sentence is the symptom and the missing table row is the fault. Handing the author the list lets them either assign the work or cut it, both of which a checker inventing a subject would foreclose.
counter_case: 'The annotation guidelines will be validated' with no annotator, no month and no work-package row is a genuine hole, and rewriting it as 'We will validate the annotation guidelines' makes an unfunded promise read as a plan. Contrast the same clause where WP3 already lists a research assistant for validation, which the sibling rule rewrites instead.
source: NIH, General Grant Writing Tips (grants.nih.gov/grants-process/write-application/general-grant-writing-tips), Tip 3 ('Write in the active voice: "We will develop an experiment." Active voice clarifies who will take which actions. Avoid using passive voice: "An experiment will be developed."'); NIH, Simplified Review Framework, Factor 3 Expertise and Resources. URLs: NIH General Grant Writing Tips — https://grants.nih.gov/grants-process/write-application/general-grant-writing-tips

test: Build a list of every concept the proposal names more than once and every surface form used for it, counting only forms that appear in the author's own running prose. Exclude quoted matter, the reference list, the titles of cited works, the proper names of datasets, software, benchmarks, tasks and metrics as their authors spell them, and any label reproduced from figure-generating code, a table header or an axis. Flag any concept carrying two or more forms with no sentence equating them.
cost: NIH instructs applicants to be consistent with terms, references, and writing style. A reviewer who cannot tell whether two names denote one thing has to decide, and Factor 2 asks whether the design is rigorous, which no one can judge while the referents are unsettled.
suggestion: Choose one form as canonical, equate the others once at first use, and replace the remaining occurrences in running prose only. Propose the canonical choice rather than applying it, because which form the panel recognises is not recoverable from the proposal.
mechanism: Synonym variation is a habit trained by prose style advice and by multiple authors drafting different sections. Each new name for a known thing costs a reader a decision they cannot verify. Confining the replacement to running prose keeps the fix away from the strings that are correct because someone else chose them.
counter_case: An axis reading 'vocab_overlap' comes from the plotting code, so renaming it in the caption alone desynchronises caption and image and the reviewer sees the mismatch. A cited title such as 'Vocabulary Overlap in Multilingual Transfer' keeps its own wording even when the canonical term is shared-subword fraction, and rewriting it makes the reference unfindable.
source: NIH, General Grant Writing Tips (grants.nih.gov/grants-process/write-application/general-grant-writing-tips), Tip 3 ('Be consistent with terms, references, and writing style.'). URLs: NIH General Grant Writing Tips — https://grants.nih.gov/grants-process/write-application/general-grant-writing-tips

test: Flag any single surface form used in the proposal for two distinct concepts. Ignore forms whose sense is fixed in the same noun phrase by a modifier, such as a statistical model against a trained model.
cost: One name for two things is the harder half of the consistency fault, because the reader cannot even detect it. Factor 2 rigour claims collapse when a quantity in the aims turns out to be a different quantity in the approach.
suggestion: Report both sites, the two senses and the pages. Propose nothing, because deciding which concept keeps the shared name and what the other becomes needs the author's intent and the field's usage, neither of which is in the text.
mechanism: Collisions arise when two sections were drafted by different authors who each owned one sense, so both uses look right locally and only the pair is wrong. A rename touches the aims, the figures and the budget narrative together, which makes it an author decision rather than a substitution.
counter_case: 'Overlap' meaning subword sharing in the aims and speaker-population sharing in WP3 is a real collision worth a rename. 'Model' for a trained checkpoint in one clause and for a regression in the next is disambiguated by its modifier and needs no change, so flagging it burns the author's attention.
source: NIH, General Grant Writing Tips (grants.nih.gov/grants-process/write-application/general-grant-writing-tips), Tip 3 ('Be consistent with terms, references, and writing style.'). URLs: NIH General Grant Writing Tips — https://grants.nih.gov/grants-process/write-application/general-grant-writing-tips

test: Restrict to the NIH Project Summary/Abstract attachment of an NIH or other PHS application. Flag first-person pronouns and sentences reporting work the applicant team has already completed. Do not apply to any other summary box, and in particular not to a UKRI summary, a Wellcome plain-English summary, or any field whose own instructions ask for first person or plain language.
cost: NIH's binding instruction for the Project Summary/Abstract is to avoid both descriptions of past accomplishments and the use of the first person. It is a formatting instruction in a section NIH publishes if the award is made, so the fault outlives the review.
suggestion: Propose a third-person recast that carries every hedge, modal and quantity across unchanged, and propose moving the past-accomplishment sentence to the Research Strategy where prior work belongs. Apply only once the author confirms, because the recast has to pick a new subject and that choice can shift what is being claimed.
mechanism: The abstract is usually the last section written and is often adapted from a paper abstract or a progress report, both of which carry the first person and the past tense. Naming the one attachment the instruction binds keeps the check from reaching boxes where first person is what the funder asked for.
counter_case: A Wellcome plain-English summary and a UKRI summary both invite 'we', so the same scan run there converts compliant text into a fabricated violation and strips the voice the reviewer was told to expect. Inside the NIH abstract, a recast that turns 'we expect a modest gain' into 'the project delivers a gain' deletes the hedge and overclaims, which is why the recast is proposed rather than applied.
source: NIH, Application Guide FORMS-I, General Instructions for NIH and Other PHS Agencies, section 7 Project Summary/Abstract ('Avoid both descriptions of past accomplishments and the use of the first person. Please be concise.'). URLs: NIH Application Guide FORMS-I — https://grants.nih.gov/grants/how-to-apply-application-guide/forms-i/general-forms-i.pdf

test: In any project summary or abstract other than the NIH Project Summary/Abstract, flag sentences whose main clause reports work the applicant team has already completed. Leave first-person pronouns entirely alone under this rule.
cost: Space in a summary box is the scarcest in the application, and a track-record sentence there is either the strongest thing in the box or the weakest, depending on what the funder asked for. Guessing wrong in either direction costs the box.
suggestion: Report the sentence and the share of the box it occupies. Propose nothing, because several funders invite a track-record sentence in the summary and only the instructions printed against that field decide.
mechanism: Summary boxes are reused across submissions, so a sentence that was compliant on one form travels to another where it is not. Reporting the past-work sentences and their cost in words lets the author check them against the one instruction that governs, rather than against a rule imported from NIH.
counter_case: An ERC B1 synopsis can legitimately open on completed pilot work that establishes feasibility, and cutting it removes the evidence the panel needs at Step 1. The same sentence in the NIH abstract is an instruction violation, which the sibling rule handles.
source: NIH, Application Guide FORMS-I, General Instructions for NIH and Other PHS Agencies, section 7 Project Summary/Abstract ('Avoid both descriptions of past accomplishments and the use of the first person. Please be concise.'). URLs: NIH Application Guide FORMS-I — https://grants.nih.gov/grants/how-to-apply-application-guide/forms-i/general-forms-i.pdf

test: For each background or literature paragraph, check whether any later sentence refers back to it - an aim, a method choice, a risk, or a capability claim. Flag paragraphs that no later sentence uses.
cost: NIAID states the cost directly: trim the fat, omit all information not needed to make your case, and if you try to wow reviewers with your knowledge they'll find flaws and penalize you heavily. Every non-load-bearing paragraph adds surface for an objection and removes space from the argument.
suggestion: Add one clause to the paragraph naming the aim, method choice or gap it orients, and move the paragraph next to that claim. Do not delete it - the same paragraph may be the orientation a non-specialist reviewer needs.
mechanism: An unlinked background paragraph is invisible to a reviewer writing strengths and weaknesses, because nothing in the argument points at it. Adding the link makes it load-bearing without betting on how specialist the panel is, and the operation is reversible from the text.
counter_case: NIAID says the farther removed reviewers are from your field, the more information you must provide, and that a key point should be repeated. A paragraph a specialist would skip can be exactly what the third, generalist reviewer needs - so the link is added and the text stays.
source: NIAID (NIH), Write Your Research Plan, Approach ('Trim the fat—omit all information not needed to make your case. If you try to wow reviewers with your knowledge, they'll find flaws and penalize you heavily. Don't give them ammunition by including anything you don't need.'); Add Emphasis ('if it's a key point, repeat it, then repeat it again'); Significance, Innovation, and Approach ('Don't skimp—the farther removed your reviewers are from your field, the more information you'll need to provide'). URLs: NIAID Write Your Research Plan — https://www.niaid.nih.gov/grants-contracts/write-research-plan

test: In an NIH application at or near the page limit, list the background paragraphs that no later sentence depends on and report their length as a fraction of the Research Strategy.
cost: NIAID states the cost directly: trim the fat, omit all information not needed to make your case, and if you try to wow reviewers with your knowledge they'll find flaws and penalize you heavily. Every non-load-bearing paragraph adds surface for an objection and removes space from the argument.
suggestion: Report the paragraphs and the space they occupy, alongside both halves of NIAID's advice - trim the fat, and supply more background the farther reviewers are from your field. Propose no deletion; only the applicant knows how specialist the study section is.
mechanism: The length judgement turns on the breadth of the panel, which is not in the document. Reporting the measurement lets the applicant weigh it, while an automatic cut silently bets that every reviewer is a specialist.
counter_case: NIAID's Add Emphasis section tells applicants to repeat a key point and repeat it again, so measured redundancy is deliberate there. A rule that deletes on the length signal alone would cut the repetition NIAID asked for.
source: NIAID (NIH), Write Your Research Plan, Approach ('Trim the fat—omit all information not needed to make your case. If you try to wow reviewers with your knowledge, they'll find flaws and penalize you heavily. Don't give them ammunition by including anything you don't need.'); Add Emphasis ('if it's a key point, repeat it, then repeat it again'); Significance, Innovation, and Approach ('Don't skimp—the farther removed your reviewers are from your field, the more information you'll need to provide'). URLs: NIAID Write Your Research Plan — https://www.niaid.nih.gov/grants-contracts/write-research-plan

test: List the two or three groups whose published results are closest to the proposal's aims, including likely reviewers, and check each is cited in the narrative.
cost: NIAID's checkpoints are to cite the literature thoroughly but not excessively, to cite all papers important to the field including those from potential reviewers, and to keep the count under about 100. NIAID states the consequence. If you leave out an important work, reviewers may assume you're not aware of it.
suggestion: Cite the closest prior result in the sentence that states its limit, so the citation carries an argument. Add entries only - never trade one against an existing entry to hold a count.
mechanism: Reviewers are selected for expertise in the applicant's area, so an omitted closest result is disproportionately likely to be a reviewer's own, and the omission reads as ignorance rather than as an editorial choice. Presence of a named work is countable.
counter_case: A page-limited proposal cannot cite everything, and where a body of work is genuinely out of scope one clause saying so beats a citation dump. The closest published result to the aims is never out of scope, which is why this rule is limited to it.
source: NIAID (NIH), Write Your Research Plan, Referencing Publications ('References show your breadth of knowledge of the field. If you leave out an important work, reviewers may assume you're not aware of it.') and its Checkpoint ('I cite all papers important to my field, including those from potential reviewers.'; 'I include fewer than 100 citations (if possible).'). URLs: NIAID Write Your Research Plan — https://www.niaid.nih.gov/grants-contracts/write-research-plan

test: For each bibliography entry, check whether any narrative sentence cites it. Report entries with no citing sentence.
cost: NIAID's checkpoints are to cite the literature thoroughly but not excessively, to cite all papers important to the field including those from potential reviewers, and to keep the count under about 100. NIAID states the consequence. If you leave out an important work, reviewers may assume you're not aware of it.
suggestion: Report the uncited entries and stop. Propose no removal - NIAID treats the reference list as evidence of breadth of the field, some funders require the list in full, and an uncited orientation entry can be correctly present.
mechanism: An uncited entry has two indistinguishable causes from inside the text: padding, or deliberate orientation the funder asked for. The count is decidable, the cause is not, so the measurement is reportable and the edit is not.
counter_case: NIAID says to cite all papers important to the field, including those from potential reviewers, whether or not a sentence needs them. Deleting such an entry to tidy the list removes exactly the paper NIAID told the applicant to include.
source: NIAID (NIH), Write Your Research Plan, Referencing Publications ('References show your breadth of knowledge of the field. If you leave out an important work, reviewers may assume you're not aware of it.') and its Checkpoint ('I cite all papers important to my field, including those from potential reviewers.'; 'I include fewer than 100 citations (if possible).'). URLs: NIAID Write Your Research Plan — https://www.niaid.nih.gov/grants-contracts/write-research-plan

test: In an NIH application, count the bibliography entries and report the count against NIAID's checkpoint of fewer than 100 citations, if possible.
cost: NIAID's checkpoints are to cite the literature thoroughly but not excessively, to cite all papers important to the field including those from potential reviewers, and to keep the count under about 100. NIAID states the consequence. If you leave out an important work, reviewers may assume you're not aware of it.
suggestion: Report the count and the checkpoint. If the count runs far over, propose merging duplicate entries for the same work, and nothing else - do not propose deleting reference entries.
mechanism: The under-100 checkpoint is an NIH-specific number carrying NIAID's own 'if possible' qualifier, so it is a signal to surface rather than a limit to enforce. Merging duplicates lowers the count without losing a work.
counter_case: ERC and Horizon Europe set no such ceiling, and ERC explicitly counts preprints that other funders exclude, so a list that is over-long for NIAID is unremarkable elsewhere. A proposal reviewing a large literature can exceed 100 without fault.
source: NIAID (NIH), Write Your Research Plan, Referencing Publications ('References show your breadth of knowledge of the field. If you leave out an important work, reviewers may assume you're not aware of it.') and its Checkpoint ('I cite all papers important to my field, including those from potential reviewers.'; 'I include fewer than 100 citations (if possible).'). URLs: NIAID Write Your Research Plan — https://www.niaid.nih.gov/grants-contracts/write-research-plan

test: In an NIH application, flag any narrative sentence that carries a full bibliographic reference (journal, volume, pages, year) for a work that also has an entry in Bibliography and References Cited.
cost: NIH requires published experimental details be cited in the Research Strategy with the full reference in the Bibliography, and states not to use hyperlinks in that section unless specified in the funding opportunity. Both are instructions, so non-compliance is found before the science is read.
suggestion: Replace the inline full reference with the bracketed citation key, keeping the experimental detail in the narrative and the full entry in Bibliography and References Cited, as the NIH Application Guide instructs. Leave any DOI or link in the entry untouched.
mechanism: NIH instructs that published experimental details be cited in the Research Strategy with the full reference in Bibliography and References Cited, so the duplicated inline entry is both non-compliant and a charge against the page budget. One correct destination exists, which makes the move safe.
counter_case: Where the work has no bibliography entry - a personal communication, or an in-press manuscript identified only in the narrative - the inline detail is the only reference and must stay. ERC Part B, which carries its own inline reference style inside the page count, is outside this rule.
source: NIH, Application Guide FORMS-I, General Instructions for NIH and Other PHS Agencies, Research Strategy ('Cite published experimental details in the Research Strategy attachment and provide the full reference in G.220 - R&R Other Project Information Form, Bibliography and Reference Cited.'); NIH, Advice on Application Sections, Bibliography & References Cited ('Do not use hyperlinks in this section unless specified in the funding opportunity.'). URLs: NIH Application Guide FORMS-I — https://grants.nih.gov/grants/how-to-apply-application-guide/forms-i/general-forms-i.pdf; NIH advice on application sections — https://grants.nih.gov/grants-process/write-application/advice-on-application-sections

test: List the hyperlinks, DOIs and permanent identifiers in the reference or output list, and report which funder's instructions govern that section.
cost: NIH requires published experimental details be cited in the Research Strategy with the full reference in the Bibliography, and states not to use hyperlinks in that section unless specified in the funding opportunity. Both are instructions, so non-compliance is found before the science is read.
suggestion: Report each link with the instruction that governs it - NIH bars hyperlinks in Bibliography and References Cited unless the funding opportunity specifies them, while ERC asks for DOIs or permanent links to listed outputs. Propose removal only where the notice governing that specific section bans links.
mechanism: A link in a reference list is either required, permitted or barred depending on the section and the funder, and the document itself does not say which. Reporting the link next to the governing instruction keeps the identifier while surfacing the compliance question.
counter_case: ERC's track record asks for the DOI or permanent link of each selected output and counts preprints that other funders exclude, and NIH data management and sharing sections permit links. A blanket strip destroys a required identifier and cannot be reconstructed from the remaining text.
source: NIH, Application Guide FORMS-I, General Instructions for NIH and Other PHS Agencies, Research Strategy ('Cite published experimental details in the Research Strategy attachment and provide the full reference in G.220 - R&R Other Project Information Form, Bibliography and Reference Cited.'); NIH, Advice on Application Sections, Bibliography & References Cited ('Do not use hyperlinks in this section unless specified in the funding opportunity.'). URLs: NIH Application Guide FORMS-I — https://grants.nih.gov/grants/how-to-apply-application-guide/forms-i/general-forms-i.pdf; NIH advice on application sections — https://grants.nih.gov/grants-process/write-application/advice-on-application-sections

test: In a Horizon Europe proposal at or near the Part B page limit, list the paragraphs that no published Horizon Europe award criterion asks for and total their length as a fraction of the limit.
cost: Horizon Europe states it plainly: do not consider the page limit as a target, it is in your interest to keep your text as concise as possible, since experts rarely view unnecessarily long proposals in a positive light. Each criterion is scored out of 5 with an individual threshold of 3, so an unfavourable disposition is expressed as a score.
suggestion: Report the total and name the paragraphs, quoting Horizon Europe's own statement that the page limit is not a target. Propose no deletion - a cut paragraph is not recoverable from the text, and the same material may be what an implementation or impact question demands.
mechanism: Horizon Europe says experts rarely view unnecessarily long proposals positively, and each criterion is scored out of 5 with a threshold of 3, so length costs goodwill that shows up as a score. Whether a given paragraph answers a criterion is a reading of the criterion, not a property of the paragraph, so the measurement reports and the applicant cuts.
counter_case: A large-consortium implementation section that must quantify every task legitimately fills the limit. Under ERC or UKRI the criteria and the page and word accounting differ - ERC excludes references from its limit while UKRI counts them inside the word count - so a paragraph unrequested here is requested there.
source: European Commission, Horizon Europe Application Form (HE RIA and IA), Part B technical description template, V5.1 (22 January 2026), Page limit ('Please, do not consider the page limit as a target! It is in your interest to keep your text as concise as possible, since experts rarely view unnecessarily long proposals in a positive light.'); European Commission, Horizon Europe Work Programme 2026-2027, 15. General Annexes (Commission Decision C(2025) 8493 of 11 December 2025), Annex A (admissibility) and Annex D (award criteria, scores and weighting), Annex D Scores and weighting ('each criterion will be scored out of 5. The threshold for individual criteria will be 3. The overall threshold ... will be 10.'). URLs: Horizon Europe application form HE RIA/IA part B — https://ec.europa.eu/info/funding-tenders/opportunities/docs/2021-2027/horizon/temp-form/af/af_he-ria-ia_en.pdf; Horizon Europe general annexes — https://ec.europa.eu/info/funding-tenders/opportunities/docs/2021-2027/horizon/wp-call/2026-2027/wp-15-general-annexes_horizon-2026-2027_en.pdf

test: In an ERC Starting or Consolidator application, for each output in the selected-outputs list of the CV and track record, check the text states the applicant's role in producing it and how it demonstrates capacity to carry out the proposed project.
cost: ERC asks for a short explanation of the significance of the selected outputs, the role of the applicant in producing each of them, and how they demonstrate the applicant's capacity to carry out the proposed project. Wellcome asks which outputs are most relevant and what your role was. UKRI says to choose only past contributions that best evidence the ability to deliver this work.
suggestion: Add one clause of role and one clause naming the part of the work plan the output makes deliverable. Leave every listed entry in place - ERC asks for the explanation, not for a shorter list.
mechanism: ERC asks explicitly for the significance of each selected output, the applicant's role in producing it, and how it demonstrates capacity for the proposed project. A multi-author output tells a reviewer nothing about the applicant until the role is stated, and the fix is additive so nothing required can be lost.
counter_case: Where the field's convention makes the role unambiguous - sole authorship, or alphabetical ordering with the norm stated - one sentence covering the whole list satisfies ERC without a clause per entry. ERC also counts preprints as outputs, so a preprint entry is not a candidate for removal.
source: ERC (European Research Council), Information for Applicants to the Starting and Consolidator Grant Calls, Version 11.0 (22 July 2026), section 2.2 Curriculum Vitae and Track Record ('A short explanation of the significance of the selected outputs, the role of the applicant in producing each of them, and how they demonstrate the applicant's capacity to successfully carry out their proposed project'); Wellcome Trust, How to write an application for funding, section 'Make your application easy to read and understand' and 'Make sure your proposal is competitive' ('Which of your research outputs is most relevant to your proposed research and what was your role in developing these outputs?'); UKRI/EPSRC, New Investigator Award (applicant-led mode) opportunity page, sections Vision and Approach, Applicant and team capability to deliver, and Summary ('only choose past contributions that best evidence their ability to deliver this work'). URLs: ERC Information for Applicants V11.0 — https://ec.europa.eu/info/funding-tenders/opportunities/docs/2021-2027/horizon/guidance/information-for-applicants_he-erc-stg-cog_en.pdf; Wellcome how to write an application — https://wellcome.org/research-funding/guidance/prepare-to-apply/how-to-write-wellcome-grant-application; EPSRC New Investigator Award opportunity — https://www.ukri.org/opportunity/epsrc-new-investigator-award-applicant-led-mode/

test: In a Wellcome application, check the research-outputs section says which outputs are most relevant to the proposed research and what the applicant's role in developing them was.
cost: ERC asks for a short explanation of the significance of the selected outputs, the role of the applicant in producing each of them, and how they demonstrate the applicant's capacity to carry out the proposed project. Wellcome asks which outputs are most relevant and what your role was. UKRI says to choose only past contributions that best evidence the ability to deliver this work.
suggestion: State relevance and role in the applicant's own first-person voice, which Wellcome's guidance uses, and add the clauses to the existing entries rather than shortening the list.
mechanism: Wellcome asks which outputs are most relevant and what the applicant's role was, and addresses the applicant directly. Supplying both in the first person answers the question in the register the funder wrote it in, and adding text cannot remove a required entry.
counter_case: NIH's third-person Project Summary convention breaks here - a Wellcome outputs section written as 'the applicant designed' reads as lifted from another application. The inversion also holds, so this first-person phrasing must not be carried into an NIH summary.
source: ERC (European Research Council), Information for Applicants to the Starting and Consolidator Grant Calls, Version 11.0 (22 July 2026), section 2.2 Curriculum Vitae and Track Record ('A short explanation of the significance of the selected outputs, the role of the applicant in producing each of them, and how they demonstrate the applicant's capacity to successfully carry out their proposed project'); Wellcome Trust, How to write an application for funding, section 'Make your application easy to read and understand' and 'Make sure your proposal is competitive' ('Which of your research outputs is most relevant to your proposed research and what was your role in developing these outputs?'); UKRI/EPSRC, New Investigator Award (applicant-led mode) opportunity page, sections Vision and Approach, Applicant and team capability to deliver, and Summary ('only choose past contributions that best evidence their ability to deliver this work'). URLs: ERC Information for Applicants V11.0 — https://ec.europa.eu/info/funding-tenders/opportunities/docs/2021-2027/horizon/guidance/information-for-applicants_he-erc-stg-cog_en.pdf; Wellcome how to write an application — https://wellcome.org/research-funding/guidance/prepare-to-apply/how-to-write-wellcome-grant-application; EPSRC New Investigator Award opportunity — https://www.ukri.org/opportunity/epsrc-new-investigator-award-applicant-led-mode/

test: In a UKRI applicant-and-team-capability section, report each listed past contribution that carries no statement of how it evidences the ability to deliver this work.
cost: ERC asks for a short explanation of the significance of the selected outputs, the role of the applicant in producing each of them, and how they demonstrate the applicant's capacity to carry out the proposed project. Wellcome asks which outputs are most relevant and what your role was. UKRI says to choose only past contributions that best evidence the ability to deliver this work.
suggestion: Report those entries and propose adding the delivery link to each. Leave the selection itself to the applicant, and never propose deleting a contribution - UKRI counts references inside the word count but the CV attachment may still require entries listed in full.
mechanism: UKRI asks applicants to choose only past contributions that best evidence the ability to deliver this work, so the judgement is a selection the applicant makes, not a deletion derivable from the text. The delivery link is addable; the selection is not decidable from inside the document.
counter_case: A narrative-CV style section wants a small set of contributions, while the same publication list under ERC or Wellcome must appear in full. Cutting here to satisfy a word count can strip an entry another attachment requires.
source: ERC (European Research Council), Information for Applicants to the Starting and Consolidator Grant Calls, Version 11.0 (22 July 2026), section 2.2 Curriculum Vitae and Track Record ('A short explanation of the significance of the selected outputs, the role of the applicant in producing each of them, and how they demonstrate the applicant's capacity to successfully carry out their proposed project'); Wellcome Trust, How to write an application for funding, section 'Make your application easy to read and understand' and 'Make sure your proposal is competitive' ('Which of your research outputs is most relevant to your proposed research and what was your role in developing these outputs?'); UKRI/EPSRC, New Investigator Award (applicant-led mode) opportunity page, sections Vision and Approach, Applicant and team capability to deliver, and Summary ('only choose past contributions that best evidence their ability to deliver this work'). URLs: ERC Information for Applicants V11.0 — https://ec.europa.eu/info/funding-tenders/opportunities/docs/2021-2027/horizon/guidance/information-for-applicants_he-erc-stg-cog_en.pdf; Wellcome how to write an application — https://wellcome.org/research-funding/guidance/prepare-to-apply/how-to-write-wellcome-grant-application; EPSRC New Investigator Award opportunity — https://www.ukri.org/opportunity/epsrc-new-investigator-award-applicant-led-mode/

test: Applies only to a Horizon Europe proposal (RIA/IA Part B or an ERC Part B drafted on the Commission application form). If any part of the narrative was drafted with a generative AI tool, check whether the Part B contains a statement naming which tools were used and for which sections. Flag the absence of that statement. Do not fire on proposals to any other funder.
cost: Horizon Europe's guidance on generative AI requires applicants to be transparent about which AI tools were used and how, and makes the applicant fully responsible for content produced by the tool. An undisclosed use is an integrity failure against an explicit instruction in the funder's own template.
suggestion: Report that the Horizon Europe form asks for a disclosure of AI tool use and that none is present, and ask the author to write the statement naming the tools and the sections they touched. Draft nothing about tools or sections yourself, since only the author knows what was used.
mechanism: The obligation lives in the Commission's own template guidance, so an evaluator reading a Horizon Europe Part B has a stated expectation to check against. The applicant carries responsibility for text they did not compose, which makes the omission theirs rather than the tool's.
counter_case: UKRI states that assessors must not take into account or speculate about whether generative AI was used, and permits its use with caution. This rule must not fire on a UKRI, NIH or Wellcome application, where an unprompted disclosure volunteers information the funder never asked for and cannot use.
source: European Commission, Horizon Europe Application Form (HE RIA and IA), Part B technical description template, V5.1 (22 January 2026), Guidance on the use of generative AI tools for the preparation of the proposal ('must be transparent in disclosing which AI tools were used and how they were utilized'; 'Verify the accuracy, validity, and appropriateness of the content and any citations generated by the AI tool'; 'Provide a list of sources used to generate content and citations, including those generated by the AI tool. Double-check citations to ensure they are accurate and properly referenced.'); UKRI/EPSRC, New Investigator Award (applicant-led mode) opportunity page, sections Vision and Approach, Applicant and team capability to deliver, and Summary, Using generative AI in expert review. URLs: Horizon Europe application form HE RIA/IA part B — https://ec.europa.eu/info/funding-tenders/opportunities/docs/2021-2027/horizon/temp-form/af/af_he-ria-ia_en.pdf; EPSRC New Investigator Award opportunity — https://www.ukri.org/opportunity/epsrc-new-investigator-award-applicant-led-mode/

test: For any funder, list every citation in the narrative that the author cannot confirm they have opened, and check the author, venue, year and the claim it is attached to against the original record. Flag each citation whose fields do not match the source, and each citation the author cannot confirm having read. Do not infer AI use from a mismatch.
cost: A citation whose authors, venue or year do not match the record is an accuracy failure in every funder's frame, and Horizon Europe states explicitly that citations must be double-checked to ensure they are accurate and properly referenced. One reference an evaluator cannot resolve turns every other reference into a thing to be verified.
suggestion: Report each unverifiable or mismatched citation with the field that fails, and ask the author to correct it against the original or replace it. Never delete a reference entry, and never change the claim the citation supports, since the intended source may be a different paper the author can identify.
mechanism: A wrong citation is plausible in exactly the fields a reader checks first, and the writer who did not compose it has no memory of the paper to catch the error. Verification is mechanical against the record, so the check is available before any reader sees the document.
counter_case: A preprint, a dataset, a standards document or an in-press paper may legitimately have no matching journal record, and ERC explicitly counts preprints that other funders exclude. A field that does not resolve in one index is not evidence of fabrication, and an author-supplied DOI settles it.
source: European Commission, Horizon Europe Application Form (HE RIA and IA), Part B technical description template, V5.1 (22 January 2026), Guidance on the use of generative AI tools for the preparation of the proposal ('must be transparent in disclosing which AI tools were used and how they were utilized'; 'Verify the accuracy, validity, and appropriateness of the content and any citations generated by the AI tool'; 'Provide a list of sources used to generate content and citations, including those generated by the AI tool. Double-check citations to ensure they are accurate and properly referenced.'); UKRI/EPSRC, New Investigator Award (applicant-led mode) opportunity page, sections Vision and Approach, Applicant and team capability to deliver, and Summary, Using generative AI in expert review. URLs: Horizon Europe application form HE RIA/IA part B — https://ec.europa.eu/info/funding-tenders/opportunities/docs/2021-2027/horizon/temp-form/af/af_he-ria-ia_en.pdf; EPSRC New Investigator Award opportunity — https://www.ukri.org/opportunity/epsrc-new-investigator-award-applicant-led-mode/

test: Applies only to a UKRI or NIH application. If the narrative contains a statement disclosing generative AI use, report it and check the opportunity text for whether that funder requests such a statement.
cost: UKRI states that assessors must not take into account or speculate about whether generative AI was used. A disclosure that the funder does not request adds text a reviewer is instructed to disregard, inside a page or word limit that is scored.
suggestion: Report that this funder does not request an AI-use statement and that the sentence spends limited space on something assessors are told to disregard. Propose no edit and remove nothing, since the author may have a local, institutional or co-applicant obligation the opportunity text does not carry.
mechanism: Disclosure norms were set by one funder and copied across applications by writers reusing a Part B. The receiving funder's instruction to its reviewers is public, so whether the sentence earns its space is checkable in the opportunity text rather than guessable.
counter_case: An institution, a sponsor or a specific UKRI or NIH opportunity may require its own AI statement, and some NIH notices address AI use in peer review materials. The presence of any such requirement makes the sentence correct as written, so this rule reports and never removes.
source: European Commission, Horizon Europe Application Form (HE RIA and IA), Part B technical description template, V5.1 (22 January 2026), Guidance on the use of generative AI tools for the preparation of the proposal ('must be transparent in disclosing which AI tools were used and how they were utilized'; 'Verify the accuracy, validity, and appropriateness of the content and any citations generated by the AI tool'; 'Provide a list of sources used to generate content and citations, including those generated by the AI tool. Double-check citations to ensure they are accurate and properly referenced.'); UKRI/EPSRC, New Investigator Award (applicant-led mode) opportunity page, sections Vision and Approach, Applicant and team capability to deliver, and Summary, Using generative AI in expert review. URLs: Horizon Europe application form HE RIA/IA part B — https://ec.europa.eu/info/funding-tenders/opportunities/docs/2021-2027/horizon/temp-form/af/af_he-ria-ia_en.pdf; EPSRC New Investigator Award opportunity — https://www.ukri.org/opportunity/epsrc-new-investigator-award-applicant-led-mode/

test: Applies to an NIH research plan. Count the bold spans and measure the share of body text they cover. Flag the document where bold exceeds a few per cent of body text, and list the bold spans that are not the hypothesis, an objective or a key result. Exclude from the list every bold span that is notation rather than emphasis, including bold vectors, matrices, tensors and other bold mathematical symbols, and bold that is part of a figure or table label, a heading, or a required form field name.
cost: NIH instructs applicants to use bold judiciously to highlight key concepts so reviewers can scan the pages and retrieve information quickly. Bold spread across a page destroys the retrieval function it was added for, and the reviewer scanning for the hypothesis finds no signal.
suggestion: Report the bold density and the list of rhetorical bold spans, and ask the author which one or two items the argument turns on. Unbold only the spans the author confirms, and leave every notation span bold, since bold there is part of the symbol and not emphasis.
mechanism: Bold accumulates one locally justified edit at a time until no unmarked text is left to contrast against. Emphasis works by scarcity, and its purpose in an application is to let a scanning reader retrieve one thing. The density is mechanical, so the failure is visible before any reviewer sees it.
counter_case: NIAID notes that many applicants bold the hypothesis or rationale deliberately and advises repeating a key point, so sparse bold on exactly those items is the intended use. In a methods or theory section, bold lower-case letters are vectors and bold capitals are matrices, and unbolding them changes the mathematics.
source: NIH, General Grant Writing Tips (grants.nih.gov/grants-process/write-application/general-grant-writing-tips), Tip 2: Be Organized ('Use bold text judiciously to highlight key concepts, allowing reviewers to scan the pages and retrieve information quickly.'); NIAID (NIH), Write Your Research Plan, Write a Narrative and Add Emphasis ('Many people use bold or italics to emphasize items they want to bring to the reviewers' attention, such as the hypothesis or rationale.'). URLs: NIH General Grant Writing Tips — https://grants.nih.gov/grants-process/write-application/general-grant-writing-tips; NIAID Write Your Research Plan — https://www.niaid.nih.gov/grants-contracts/write-research-plan

test: List every italic span in the narrative and classify each as notation or rhetorical emphasis. Notation includes species binomials and other taxonomic names, gene and allele symbols, mathematical variables and parameters, non-English words and phrases, cited work titles, and legal case names. Report the count of rhetorical italics and the share of body text they cover.
cost: Italics in a scientific proposal carry meaning far more often than they carry emphasis, so a density figure computed over all italics measures nothing. Reporting the two classes separately is what lets an author judge whether rhetorical emphasis has lost its scarcity.
suggestion: Report the two counts and the rhetorical spans, and propose nothing. Any decision about italics belongs to the author, because whether a given italic is a gene symbol, a variable, a loanword or emphasis is settled by the field's convention and not by the document.
mechanism: Italic markup is one code carrying several unrelated conventions at once, so no automatic reading of an italic span recovers its function. A rule that acts on the markup rather than on the confirmed function will unitalicise a species name or a variable, which is an error of fact in the science.
counter_case: Escherichia coli, the gene TP53, the variable n, in vivo and de novo are all correctly italic and none of them is emphasis. A document whose italics are entirely notation has no emphasis problem however high the raw italic count.
source: NIH, General Grant Writing Tips (grants.nih.gov/grants-process/write-application/general-grant-writing-tips), Tip 2: Be Organized ('Use bold text judiciously to highlight key concepts, allowing reviewers to scan the pages and retrieve information quickly.'); NIAID (NIH), Write Your Research Plan, Write a Narrative and Add Emphasis ('Many people use bold or italics to emphasize items they want to bring to the reviewers' attention, such as the hypothesis or rationale.'). URLs: NIH General Grant Writing Tips — https://grants.nih.gov/grants-process/write-application/general-grant-writing-tips; NIAID Write Your Research Plan — https://www.niaid.nih.gov/grants-contracts/write-research-plan

test: For each section, find the sentence carrying its central claim and count the sentences of general background that precede it. Flag any section where the claim arrives after more than two sentences of background that a reader does not need in order to parse the claim. Do not flag a section whose opening sentences define a term or notation used in the claim sentence, and do not examine or relocate any qualifier.
cost: The Social Science Research Council's guidance is explicit that you should say what you have to say immediately, crisply and forcefully. Cronan and Deckard describe the buried lede as inverting the journalist's pyramid so the reviewer must read lengthy general background before learning what is proposed.
suggestion: Move the existing claim sentence, verbatim and with every qualifier it already contains, to the opening of the section, and keep the displaced background after it. Change no wording, and in particular do not lift, split or relocate any condition inside the claim sentence.
mechanism: Academic training teaches the opposite order, because a paper earns its claim through the argument that precedes it. A proposal is read by someone deciding whether to keep reading, so a claim that arrives late may not arrive at all. Reordering whole sentences leaves the truth conditions of each sentence untouched, which is what makes this the safe half of the ordering problem.
counter_case: A claim that would be misread without a prior definition needs the definition first, so a section opening on notation or on a stipulated term is correct as written. A narrative section deliberately built as a story with a delayed reveal is a style choice the author owns.
source: [name] Przeworski and Frank Salomon, On the Art of Writing Proposals, Social Science Research Council, section 'Capture the Reviewer's Attention?' ('So, say what you have to say immediately, crisply, and forcefully.'; 'This is the moment to overstate, rather than understate, your point or question. You can add the conditions and caveats later.'); Mike Cronan and Lucy Deckard (Academic Research Funding Strategies, formerly Texas A&M Office of Research Development and Grant Writing), New Faculty Guide to Competing for Research Funding, 2nd ed. 2022 (copy hosted by Loyola University New Orleans Office of Academic Affairs), 'Don't Bury the Lede: Get to the Point Quickly'. URLs: SSRC, On the Art of Writing Proposals — https://s3.amazonaws.com/ssrc-cdn1/crmuploads/new_publication_3/the-art-of-writing-proposals.pdf; Cronan & Deckard, New Faculty Guide — https://academicaffairs.loyno.edu/sites/default/files/new_faculty_guide_to_competing_for_research_funding502_0.pdf

test: Find every qualifier that precedes the claim it attaches to, whether a leading subordinate clause, a prepositional frame or a sentence of caveat. For each, classify it as a scope restriction that changes what the claim asserts, or as a hedge that expresses doubt without changing the claim's truth conditions. Report both classes with the classification.
cost: A leading caveat is read as the writer's doubt about a claim they have not yet made, which is the failure the SSRC guidance targets. A leading scope restriction is doing the opposite work, bounding a claim that would be false without it, and the two are not distinguishable by position.
suggestion: Report each leading qualifier with its classification and propose nothing. Whether a phrase bounds the claim or merely softens it depends on what the author is asserting, so the author decides. Never move, delete or weaken a hedge, a modal or an intensifier on this rule.
mechanism: Position is the only cue an automatic pass has, and position does not separate the two functions. Acting on position alone converts a bounded true statement into an unbounded false one, which is a worse defect than the ordering it was meant to fix and one no later reader can detect from the text.
counter_case: 'For the 40 languages with Wikipedia dumps above 100MB, coverage is complete' cannot have its opening clause moved after the claim without asserting complete coverage of every language. 'Although this has been shown only at small scale, vocabulary sharing explains most of the transfer' has a leading clause that can safely follow, because the claim's truth conditions do not depend on it.
source: [name] Przeworski and Frank Salomon, On the Art of Writing Proposals, Social Science Research Council, section 'Capture the Reviewer's Attention?' ('So, say what you have to say immediately, crisply, and forcefully.'; 'This is the moment to overstate, rather than understate, your point or question. You can add the conditions and caveats later.'); Mike Cronan and Lucy Deckard (Academic Research Funding Strategies, formerly Texas A&M Office of Research Development and Grant Writing), New Faculty Guide to Competing for Research Funding, 2nd ed. 2022 (copy hosted by Loyola University New Orleans Office of Academic Affairs), 'Don't Bury the Lede: Get to the Point Quickly'. URLs: SSRC, On the Art of Writing Proposals — https://s3.amazonaws.com/ssrc-cdn1/crmuploads/new_publication_3/the-art-of-writing-proposals.pdf; Cronan & Deckard, New Faculty Guide — https://academicaffairs.loyno.edu/sites/default/files/new_faculty_guide_to_competing_for_research_funding502_0.pdf

test: In the work plan and methodology, find each tentative frame whose grammatical object is an action by the applicant team rather than a result, specifically 'we plan to', 'we hope to', 'it might be interesting to', 'one could', 'X can be done', and 'it would be possible to' applied to a task that appears in the deliverables, milestones, budget or Gantt chart. Flag only these. Do not flag any modal, hedge or tentative frame attached to a finding, an outcome, an effect size or a prediction, and do not flag a modal inside a stated conditional branch or contingency plan.
cost: Cronan and Deckard name the failure and its consequence. A research plan peppered with these words reads as if the PI is not sure what he will do if he wins the grant, and 'we will do x' is always more convincing than 'we plan to, might, could, would do x'. The mismatch is checkable, because the same task is already committed in the deliverables.
suggestion: Rewrite the action as a committed future for exactly the tasks the plan already commits to elsewhere, and leave every statement about what the work will find exactly as written, including its modals and hedges. If the task is not in the deliverables, milestones or budget, report the mismatch instead and ask the author whether it is in scope.
mechanism: Hedging is the reflex of a discipline that punishes overclaiming and it survives the move from paper to proposal, where the reader is assessing commitment rather than truth. The distinction that matters is between uncertain actions, which are a problem, and uncertain outcomes, which are the point. Anchoring the test to the deliverables makes that distinction evidential rather than a guess.
counter_case: 'The effect may not persist at 70B' is a claim about an outcome and must keep its modal, since a committed future there promises a result the project cannot deliver. 'If the 512-GPU allocation is granted we could extend to 70B' is a declared contingency and the modal is carrying the condition.
source: Mike Cronan and Lucy Deckard (Academic Research Funding Strategies, formerly Texas A&M Office of Research Development and Grant Writing), New Faculty Guide to Competing for Research Funding, 2nd ed. 2022 (copy hosted by Loyola University New Orleans Office of Academic Affairs), 'Avoid Irritating Your Reviewer' ('The tentative or uncommitted proposal. ... The research plan is peppered with words like "might," "could," "would," "it might be interesting to," "X can be done," etc. This kind of tentative wording weakens your proposal'; 'Wording such as, "We will do x" is always more convincing than, "We plan to/might/could/would do x."'); Derek Abbott, Guide to technical writing, School of Electrical and Electronic Engineering, University of Adelaide, 'How to annoy the hell out of a PhD examiner' ('Use the word "hope" or "hopeful". These types of words are meaningless in scientific writing and are completely banned.'). URLs: Cronan & Deckard, New Faculty Guide — https://academicaffairs.loyno.edu/sites/default/files/new_faculty_guide_to_competing_for_research_funding502_0.pdf; Abbott technical writing guide, Adelaide — https://www.eleceng.adelaide.edu.au/personal/dabbott/wiki/index.php/Guide_to_technical_writing

test: Find every tentative modal or hedge attached to a result, an effect, a prediction or an interpretation, and check whether the same uncertainty is acknowledged in the risk section or the contingency plan. Report modals whose uncertainty appears nowhere else in the proposal.
cost: An outcome the applicant is genuinely unsure about is the reason the work is worth funding, and the reviewer needs to see that the plan survives either result. A hedged prediction with no matching entry in the risk or contingency section leaves the reviewer unable to tell whether the applicant has thought the branch through.
suggestion: Report each hedged outcome that has no matching risk or contingency entry, and ask the author whether to add one. Propose no change to the hedged sentence, and never delete, weaken or replace the modal, since the hedge is an accurate statement about what is not yet known.
mechanism: The hedge and the risk section are two views of the same uncertainty, so their disagreement is a gap in the plan rather than a defect in the prose. Editing the prose to remove the hedge hides the gap instead of closing it and leaves the proposal promising an outcome nobody can guarantee.
counter_case: A hedge on a result that is already covered in the risk table is complete as written and needs nothing. A field where the negative result is the standard publishable outcome may need no contingency entry at all, and the author is the one who knows that.
source: Mike Cronan and Lucy Deckard (Academic Research Funding Strategies, formerly Texas A&M Office of Research Development and Grant Writing), New Faculty Guide to Competing for Research Funding, 2nd ed. 2022 (copy hosted by Loyola University New Orleans Office of Academic Affairs), 'Avoid Irritating Your Reviewer' ('The tentative or uncommitted proposal. ... The research plan is peppered with words like "might," "could," "would," "it might be interesting to," "X can be done," etc. This kind of tentative wording weakens your proposal'; 'Wording such as, "We will do x" is always more convincing than, "We plan to/might/could/would do x."'); Derek Abbott, Guide to technical writing, School of Electrical and Electronic Engineering, University of Adelaide, 'How to annoy the hell out of a PhD examiner' ('Use the word "hope" or "hopeful". These types of words are meaningless in scientific writing and are completely banned.'). URLs: Cronan & Deckard, New Faculty Guide — https://academicaffairs.loyno.edu/sites/default/files/new_faculty_guide_to_competing_for_research_funding502_0.pdf; Abbott technical writing guide, Adelaide — https://www.eleceng.adelaide.edu.au/personal/dabbott/wiki/index.php/Guide_to_technical_writing

test: Find every comparative or superlative formed on a non-quantifier absolute that has no gradations, specifically more or most or less applied to unique, optimal, optimum, exhaustive, universal or complete, and constructions such as 'an improved level of optimality' or 'a more complete solution'. Flag only these ungradable comparatives. Do not flag an approximator on a quantifier, including almost all, nearly none, fairly complete, largely universal, or virtually always.
cost: Adelaide's guide gives the rule and the reason. Words such as unique and optimum do not have gradations, so something is unique or it is not, and 'an improved level of optimality' is literally incoherent. A reviewer who notices one starts checking whether the rest of the quantitative language is as loose.
suggestion: Replace the whole phrase with the bounded comparative the evidence supports, naming the comparison set, the metric and the condition. Do not repair the phrase by deleting the comparative and leaving the bare absolute, since that asserts more than the original did.
mechanism: An ungradable comparative comes from wanting emphasis without wanting commitment, and it yields a phrase with no truth conditions at all. The repair has to supply the comparison the writer was reaching for, because the two available deletions both fail. Dropping the comparative promotes the claim, and dropping the absolute empties it.
counter_case: A scoped absolute is precise rather than overclaimed, so 'optimal under the stated loss' and 'complete for the 40 languages listed' are correct as written. An approximated quantifier such as 'almost all' or 'fairly complete' is a hedged true claim, and deleting its approximator manufactures a false absolute out of it.
source: Derek Abbott, Guide to technical writing, School of Electrical and Electronic Engineering, University of Adelaide, 'How to annoy the hell out of a PhD examiner' ('Treat singular concepts as if they have gradations. "The parameters have an improved level of optimality." Words such as "unique", "optimum", etc. do not have gradations. Something is unique or it is not.'); Purdue University, Purdue OWL, Grant Writing in the Sciences and Specificity in Writing, Specificity in Writing ('Claiming an absolute usually has to do with using "absolute terms," such as: all, none, every, never, always, and the like.'). URLs: Abbott technical writing guide, Adelaide — https://www.eleceng.adelaide.edu.au/personal/dabbott/wiki/index.php/Guide_to_technical_writing; Purdue OWL — https://owl.purdue.edu/owl/subject_specific_writing/professional_technical_writing/grant_writing/grant_writing_specificity_in_writing.html

test: Find every ungraded absolute term (all, none, never, always, every, first, unique, optimal, complete, exhaustive, universal) and check whether the sentence or its immediate context states the scope over which the absolute holds, meaning the comparison set, the metric, the condition or the time window. Report each absolute with no stated scope.
cost: Purdue names the fault, that absolute terms and generalisations claim more than the evidence carries. An unscoped 'first' or 'complete' is the kind of claim a reviewer who works in the area will test against one counterexample they happen to know, and the whole paragraph then reads as unchecked.
suggestion: Report each unscoped absolute and ask the author for the scope that makes it true, or for the bounded claim they intended. Propose no wording, and never remove an approximator, a hedge or an intensifier in the course of this check, since 'almost all' and 'fairly complete' are already scoped claims and are correct as written.
mechanism: Whether an absolute is supportable depends on evidence outside the document, so the text alone cannot decide it and the author is the only source. Reporting keeps the two failure modes apart, because the unsupported absolute needs evidence added and the hedged claim needs nothing at all.
counter_case: 'The first corpus of its kind' may be exactly true and worth stating plainly, and some absolutes are the finding. 'Almost all languages in the sample' is scoped by 'in the sample' and already carries its approximator, so it must not be reported as an unscoped absolute or altered.
source: Derek Abbott, Guide to technical writing, School of Electrical and Electronic Engineering, University of Adelaide, 'How to annoy the hell out of a PhD examiner' ('Treat singular concepts as if they have gradations. "The parameters have an improved level of optimality." Words such as "unique", "optimum", etc. do not have gradations. Something is unique or it is not.'); Purdue University, Purdue OWL, Grant Writing in the Sciences and Specificity in Writing, Specificity in Writing ('Claiming an absolute usually has to do with using "absolute terms," such as: all, none, every, never, always, and the like.'). URLs: Abbott technical writing guide, Adelaide — https://www.eleceng.adelaide.edu.au/personal/dabbott/wiki/index.php/Guide_to_technical_writing; Purdue OWL — https://owl.purdue.edu/owl/subject_specific_writing/professional_technical_writing/grant_writing/grant_writing_specificity_in_writing.html

test: For each entry in the CV, track record or publication list, record whether it carries a status word (published, in press, accepted, submitted, preprint, in preparation) and whether it names a venue or archive and a date. Report every entry missing a status, a venue or a date. Do not report entries that already carry all three.
cost: Kraicer warns that most granting agencies will not accept a manuscript in preparation, and Reid's submission checklist asks as a yes-or-no item whether all articles in the CV are actually published. An entry with no status leaves the reviewer to guess which of the two it is, and the guess goes against the applicant.
suggestion: Report the incomplete entries to the applicant as a list, with the missing field named for each one. Propose no edit and delete nothing. Only the applicant knows whether an unstatused item is a live submission, an archived preprint or an unfinished draft, and those three cases need three different repairs.
mechanism: Status, venue and date are per-entry fields, so their presence or absence is decidable by inspection without any judgement about the work. What the missing field should be filled with is not decidable from the document, which is why this rule stops at reporting.
counter_case: An entry reading 'submitted to ACL 2027' is complete and must not be reported. An entry the applicant then upgrades to a preprint with a DOI is stronger, not weaker, so a report that pushed toward deletion would have been the wrong advice.
source: Jacob Kraicer (Director of Research Grants, Human Frontier Science Program), The Art of Grantsmanship, published by HFSP, section 2 Before You Start to Write ('Do this well in advance so that the work can appear in your application as "published", "in press" or "a submitted manuscript". Most granting agencies will not accept a manuscript "in preparation".'); C.P. Patrick Reid (University of Arizona), Handbook for Preparing and Writing Research Proposals, IUFRO-SPDC, 2000 (ISBN 3-901347-23-2), Appendix III Preparation and Submission Checklist, category E ('Are all of the articles in your curriculum vitae actually published (not just in preparation)?'). URLs: HFSP, The Art of Grantsmanship — https://www.hfsp.org/sites/default/files/webfm/Communications/The%20Art%20of%20Grantsmanship.pdf; IUFRO-SPDC proposal handbook — https://www.iufro.org/media/fileadmin/publications/manuals/research-proposal-writing-en.pdf

test: ERC Part B only. For each track-record entry marked in preparation, in progress or unstatused, check whether the same work exists as a preprint with a DOI or a stable link. Report the ones that do.
cost: ERC counts a preprint as evidence when it carries a DOI or link, so an ERC applicant who writes 'in preparation' over work that is already on arXiv is discarding admissible evidence and inviting the in-preparation objection at the same time.
suggestion: Report the entry together with the DOI or link found, and ask the applicant to confirm the preprint is the same work so the entry can be restated as a preprint with its identifier. Never remove the entry, and never apply this to a funder whose rules exclude preprints.
mechanism: The admissibility of preprints is funder-specific, which is why the test names ERC. Within ERC the check is a lookup, because either an identifier exists for the work or it does not.
counter_case: Under a funder that excludes preprints from the track record, the same restatement is wrong and the entry should stay as it is. A preprint of a different but similarly titled paper is not the same work, which is why confirmation is asked for rather than assumed.
source: Jacob Kraicer (Director of Research Grants, Human Frontier Science Program), The Art of Grantsmanship, published by HFSP, section 2 Before You Start to Write ('Do this well in advance so that the work can appear in your application as "published", "in press" or "a submitted manuscript". Most granting agencies will not accept a manuscript "in preparation".'); C.P. Patrick Reid (University of Arizona), Handbook for Preparing and Writing Research Proposals, IUFRO-SPDC, 2000 (ISBN 3-901347-23-2), Appendix III Preparation and Submission Checklist, category E ('Are all of the articles in your curriculum vitae actually published (not just in preparation)?'). URLs: HFSP, The Art of Grantsmanship — https://www.hfsp.org/sites/default/files/webfm/Communications/The%20Art%20of%20Grantsmanship.pdf; IUFRO-SPDC proposal handbook — https://www.iufro.org/media/fileadmin/publications/manuals/research-proposal-writing-en.pdf

test: Find each claim in the proposal body whose only support is a citation to the applicant's own unpublished or in-preparation work. Report the claim and the entry it leans on.
cost: A reviewer who cannot reach the evidence treats the claim as unsupported, so a load-bearing claim resting on a future paper is read as weaker than one resting on a figure the reviewer can see on the page.
suggestion: Report the pairing of claim and unreachable citation to the applicant, and ask whether the underlying data can be shown in the proposal instead. Propose no wording and remove neither the claim nor the citation, because whether the data can be disclosed and whether it fits the space are the applicant's calls.
mechanism: Locating the pairing is mechanical, because the citation target is either reachable by a reviewer or it is not. Choosing between showing the data, softening the claim and leaving it as is depends on facts outside the document.
counter_case: A background claim that is not load-bearing needs no such treatment, and a claim citing someone else's unpublished work raises a different question that this rule does not cover.
source: Jacob Kraicer (Director of Research Grants, Human Frontier Science Program), The Art of Grantsmanship, published by HFSP, section 2 Before You Start to Write ('Do this well in advance so that the work can appear in your application as "published", "in press" or "a submitted manuscript". Most granting agencies will not accept a manuscript "in preparation".'); C.P. Patrick Reid (University of Arizona), Handbook for Preparing and Writing Research Proposals, IUFRO-SPDC, 2000 (ISBN 3-901347-23-2), Appendix III Preparation and Submission Checklist, category E ('Are all of the articles in your curriculum vitae actually published (not just in preparation)?'). URLs: HFSP, The Art of Grantsmanship — https://www.hfsp.org/sites/default/files/webfm/Communications/The%20Art%20of%20Grantsmanship.pdf; IUFRO-SPDC proposal handbook — https://www.iufro.org/media/fileadmin/publications/manuals/research-proposal-writing-en.pdf

test: Within one list, one set of same-level headings, or one table stub column, compare the grammatical construction of the items that are present. Report any item whose part of speech or construction differs from its siblings. Do not apply this test to enumerator labels or to the completeness of the sequence.
cost: The reader reads the difference in form as a difference in kind and looks for a distinction that is not there.
suggestion: Recast the odd item into the construction its siblings share, changing wording only and leaving the content untouched. Where it will not recast without changing what the item says, report it instead as a possible structural mismatch for the applicant to resolve.
mechanism: Parallel form signals parallel status, so a break in form signals a break in status. Comparing constructions among siblings needs no understanding of the content, which makes it the cheapest reliable check available.
counter_case: Where the items genuinely are not parallel in kind, forcing the wording hides a real structural problem, so the report route is the correct outcome. A deliberate final item that breaks form for emphasis, such as a one-word summary row closing a table, is not an error.
source: Van Buren & Buehler, 'The Levels of Edit', 2nd ed., JPL Publication 80-1 (NASA-CR-162880), 1980, Section VI-H item 6 (language parallelism), including the (a)-without-(b) test

test: Check every enumerated sequence for an orphan label, meaning an (a) with no (b), an (i) with no (ii), or a numbered first item with no second. Report each orphan with its location.
cost: An orphan label reveals a level of the outline that was planned and never filled, and a reviewer who sees it reads the section as unfinished.
suggestion: Report the orphan label and its surrounding sentence. Propose nothing, because the two repairs are opposite in effect. Either a missing sibling item is supplied, which only the applicant can write, or the enumeration is dropped and the text runs on, which changes the emphasis of the passage.
mechanism: Detecting a lone label is a pure sequence check. Choosing between supplying the missing item and removing the label needs the content that was never written, so the rule stops at reporting.
counter_case: A single item deliberately labelled to be cross-referenced later, such as a lone condition (a) that a proof calls back to, is not an orphan and must not be reported as one.
source: Van Buren & Buehler, 'The Levels of Edit', 2nd ed., JPL Publication 80-1 (NASA-CR-162880), 1980, Section VI-H item 6 (language parallelism), including the (a)-without-(b) test

test: For each displayed equation, read the lead-in text ending at the display. Report a colon only where the lead-in is not a complete sentence on its own, meaning the display supplies the grammatical completion. Ignore the punctuation inside or after the display.
cost: A reader who treats the display as a clause is given the wrong signal about where the sentence ends, which forces a re-read of the surrounding prose.
suggestion: Delete the colon. Leave the lead-in words and the display exactly as they are, so the sentence runs into the display as its own grammar requires.
mechanism: A colon announces that a complete sentence has ended and a specification follows. Where the sentence runs into the display, the colon mislabels the boundary, and removing it restores the boundary the grammar already sets. Whether the lead-in stands alone is decidable by reading it without the display.
counter_case: A colon is right when the lead-in is complete and the display specifies or enumerates, as in 'The update rule has two terms:' followed by a display, and such cases are outside this test. A lead-in ending in 'as follows' or 'the following' is complete and keeps its colon.
source: Knuth, Larrabee & Roberts, 'Mathematical Writing', Stanford CS 209 notes, section 1 (Minicourse), point 23; Halmos, 'How to Write Mathematics', in How to Write Mathematics (AMS, 1973), pp. 19-48, section 17

test: For each displayed expression, check whether the sentence containing it ends at the display and whether the display carries the comma or full stop that sentence would need. Report displays where the punctuation is absent or inconsistent with the other displays in the same document.
cost: A display read as a clause needs the punctuation of a clause, and a document that punctuates some displays and not others leaves the reader resolving the sentence boundary by guesswork.
suggestion: Report the displays and the pattern the document currently follows. Propose no inserted character, because a comma or full stop placed inside mathematics can be read as part of the expression, and because punctuating displays is a house style that the venue or the applicant sets document-wide.
mechanism: Halmos and the Stanford notes treat a display as a clause needing clause punctuation, but the mark has to sit where it cannot be mistaken for notation, and that placement depends on the expression. Reporting the inconsistency is decidable, inserting the mark is not.
counter_case: A document that consistently omits terminal punctuation on displays, as many venues require, is internally correct and the report should say so rather than push toward insertion. A display ending in a set brace, a matrix or an ellipsis is exactly where an added mark is most likely to be misread.
source: Knuth, Larrabee & Roberts, 'Mathematical Writing', Stanford CS 209 notes, section 1 (Minicourse), point 23; Halmos, 'How to Write Mathematics', in How to Write Mathematics (AMS, 1973), pp. 19-48, section 17

test: Within a single sentence, find hedging words and phrases such as may, might, appear, seem, suggest, indicate, somewhat, possibly and in some respects, and report sentences where several of them modify the same claim so that the level of commitment cannot be recovered. Report the hedges found and where they sit.
cost: Over-hedging makes the reader unable to find the claim, so a defensible result reads as an author unwilling to say what was found.
suggestion: Report the sentence with its hedges listed, and ask the applicant which single level of commitment the evidence supports. Delete no hedge and rewrite nothing, because each hedge that goes strengthens the claim, and only the applicant knows whether the stronger claim is one the evidence will carry.
mechanism: Counting the hedges in a sentence is a surface test. Choosing which to keep is a claim about the strength of the underlying evidence, which lives outside the document, so the rule reports and asks.
counter_case: A sentence whose hedges modify different claims is not stacked and must not be reported, as in a sentence saying one effect is established and a second may follow. A statement of what was done rather than what it means carries no hedge at all, and 'we trained three models' must never become 'we appear to have trained three models'.
source: Williams (rev. Bizup), 'Style: Lessons in Clarity and Grace', 11th ed., Lesson 9, 'Hedges and Intensifiers' (pp. 135-137)

test: Find each paragraph whose main claim is stated without any hedge while the evidence named in the same paragraph is a single experiment, a single dataset or a single run. Report the claim and the evidence it names.
cost: Under-hedging invites a reader to reject a defensible claim because it was stated indefensibly, and a reviewer who finds one such claim rereads the rest looking for others.
suggestion: Report the mismatch between the flat claim and the single piece of evidence named, and ask the applicant whether further evidence exists that is not cited here. Add no hedge, because adding one asserts a limit on the evidence that the document does not establish.
mechanism: Detecting a flat claim next to a single named result is a surface test over the paragraph. Whether the claim is actually under-supported depends on evidence the applicant may hold outside the text, so the rule asks rather than edits.
counter_case: A statement of procedure or of what the work did carries no hedge by design and is not a target. A claim supported elsewhere in the document by other results is correctly flat, and the report exists so the applicant can say so.
source: Williams (rev. Bizup), 'Style: Lessons in Clarity and Grace', 11th ed., Lesson 9, 'Hedges and Intensifiers' (pp. 135-137)

test: Scan for obviously, clearly, of course, undoubtedly, it is clear that, needless to say and trivially. Report each occurrence with the statement it introduces. Make no judgement about whether the statement is supported.
cost: Readers reflexively suspect the opposite of whatever these words introduce, so the intensifier can cost the author credibility on exactly the sentences that needed it most.
suggestion: Report the occurrences as a list with their statements. Propose no deletion, because the same word is doing one of two opposite jobs, either marking a step a specialist reader may skip or marking a spot where an argument was declined, and telling them apart needs the author's knowledge of the step.
mechanism: Finding the words is a literal string test. Their effect depends on whether the following step really is standard for the intended reader, which is a fact about the field and the audience rather than about the text.
counter_case: Halmos allows 'obvious' as a signal to a novice that a step is standard and can be skipped, provided the author has verified it still looks obvious months later and that a reader who questioned it was answered rather than intimidated. Blanket deletion destroys that signal, which is why nothing here is deleted.
source: Williams (rev. Bizup), 'Style: Lessons in Clarity and Grace', 11th ed., Lesson 9, Quick Tip (p. 137); Halmos, 'How to Write Mathematics', in How to Write Mathematics (AMS, 1973), pp. 19-48, section 10 ('Honesty is the best policy')

test: For each statement introduced by obviously, clearly, of course, undoubtedly, it is clear that, needless to say or trivially, search the document for a proof, a citation, an appendix pointer or a figure that supports it. Report the statements for which no such support is found anywhere in the document.
cost: An unsupported statement marked as evident is where a sceptical reviewer stops, because the marker tells them the author knew support was expected and did not give it.
suggestion: Report the statement and the fact that no supporting pointer was found in the document. Ask the applicant whether support exists to point at. Add no pointer and invent no reference, and leave the intensifier alone, because the fix may be a citation the applicant holds rather than any change to this sentence.
mechanism: Searching the document for a nearby proof, citation or pointer is mechanical and its negative result is reliable within the document. Whether the support exists outside the document is knowledge only the applicant has.
counter_case: A statement that already carries a pointer, such as 'the estimator is unbiased, by the argument in Appendix A.2', is supported and must not be reported even though it keeps a marker word. A step that is standard textbook material may legitimately have no in-document proof, which the applicant can answer in one line.
source: Williams (rev. Bizup), 'Style: Lessons in Clarity and Grace', 11th ed., Lesson 9, Quick Tip (p. 137); Halmos, 'How to Write Mathematics', in How to Write Mathematics (AMS, 1973), pp. 19-48, section 10 ('Honesty is the best policy')
