test: For every theorem statement, list the hypotheses it carries and check which ones the proof visibly invokes. Flag any hypothesis that no step of the proof appears to use, and report it alongside the steps that would need it.
cost: An unused hypothesis makes the reader hunt for where it mattered, and a hypothesis that is used only through a cited lemma looks unused to any surface check.
suggestion: Report the hypothesis together with the proof steps that appear not to need it, and propose no edit. Only an author who can rule out implicit use, such as a hypothesis consumed inside a cited lemma or a background convention, can decide whether it goes.
mechanism: A theorem statement is a contract and readers audit it against the proof, so an extra hypothesis costs a search for its role. The finding is worth surfacing, but the check that produces it reads only the visible steps. Implicit use through a lemma, a standing convention, or an unstated appeal to a structure theorem leaves no trace in the proof text, so a deletion driven by the check can turn a true theorem into a false one.
counter_case: In 'if R is a commutative semisimple ring then x^2 - y^2 = (x-y)(x+y)', semisimplicity really is idle, but commutativity is invoked only by the silent step that rewrites xy as yx, so a check reading operator names alone would flag it too and deleting it falsifies the theorem.
source: Knuth, Larrabee & Roberts, 'Mathematical Writing', Stanford CS 209 notes, section 1 (Minicourse), point 5; Halmos, 'How to Write Mathematics', in How to Write Mathematics (AMS, 1973), pp. 19-48, section 11 ('Down with the irrelevant and the trivial'); NeurIPS Paper Checklist Guidelines, item 3 (Theory, Assumptions and Proofs)

test: For every theorem statement, check for an assumption the proof uses that the statement does not carry and that no visible standing convention supplies for that statement.
cost: A theorem missing an assumption its proof relies on is false as stated, and a reader who cites it out of context imports the error.
suggestion: Add the used assumption to the statement, or make the standing convention that supplies it visible and say which statements it governs. Remove nothing in the same edit.
mechanism: Adding an assumption the proof already relies on cannot break the theorem, since it only narrows a scope the proof never had. The two repairs are different in kind, which is why this rule carries only the additive one. The choice between writing the assumption into the statement and pointing at a section-level convention depends on how many statements in the section need it, so the fix site is an author decision even though the finding is not.
counter_case: A standing convention declared once at the top of a section, such as 'all spaces are separable', may be omitted from every statement inside it, provided the declaration is visible and the section boundary is clear. Repeating it in each statement is then noise, and the right repair is to make the declaration harder to miss.
source: Knuth, Larrabee & Roberts, 'Mathematical Writing', Stanford CS 209 notes, section 1 (Minicourse), point 5; Halmos, 'How to Write Mathematics', in How to Write Mathematics (AMS, 1973), pp. 19-48, section 11 ('Down with the irrelevant and the trivial'); NeurIPS Paper Checklist Guidelines, item 3 (Theory, Assumptions and Proofs)

test: Check every numbered display for a reference elsewhere in the manuscript. Flag the numbered displays that no reference in the manuscript points to.
cost: An unused number draws attention and spends a moment of the reader's search for why it exists.
suggestion: Report the unreferenced numbers and propose no unnumbering. A label may be the target of a reference outside the file being checked, and some venues require every display numbered, so only the author knows whether the number can go.
mechanism: A label signals that an expression will be needed again, so an unreferenced label promises something the text never delivers. The finding is cheap and reliable within one file. Acting on it is not, because cross-references live in appendices, rebuttals, companion papers, and slide decks that the check never sees, and a removed label silently breaks all of them.
counter_case: Numbering every display uniformly is right when reviewers or co-authors need to cite lines during revision, and some venues require it. A label may also be referenced from a rebuttal, an appendix in a separate file, or an earlier published version, none of which the manuscript itself shows.
source: Halmos, 'How to Write Mathematics', in How to Write Mathematics (AMS, 1973), pp. 19-48, section 16 ('Resist symbols'); Knuth, Larrabee & Roberts, 'Mathematical Writing', Stanford CS 209 notes, section 1 (Minicourse), point 16

test: Flag every reference to a numbered display whose number first appears later in reading order than the reference, then check whether the display depends on definitions, notation, or results that sit between the reference and the display's current position.
cost: A forward reference to a number not yet on the page costs the reader a page-turn, and a display moved ahead of the definitions it uses costs a full rereading.
suggestion: Where the display depends on nothing between the two points, move it to its first reference. Where it depends on intervening material, leave the order alone and make the pointer explicit, naming the section or page where the display appears.
mechanism: Forward references are a real cost, but the repair is only available when the display is order-independent. A derivation's dependency order is content, and a display promoted above the definition of its own symbols reads as nonsense. Splitting on the dependency check gives one branch a move and the other branch a pointer, and both branches leave a correct manuscript.
counter_case: A display may use a weight function defined only after its first mention, so moving it forward would make it read before its own terms exist. A display in a numbered proof environment may also be unmovable without renumbering everything around it.
source: Halmos, 'How to Write Mathematics', in How to Write Mathematics (AMS, 1973), pp. 19-48, section 16 ('Resist symbols'); Knuth, Larrabee & Roberts, 'Mathematical Writing', Stanford CS 209 notes, section 1 (Minicourse), point 16

test: Flag a set that is introduced as an explicit indexed list and whose subsets are then written with a second level of index, and only where no later text uses an inner index on its own, the enumeration order, or an induction over the index. Do not flag matrix entries, doubly indexed families, or any expression whose two index positions are independent coordinates.
cost: An index of an index makes the reader hold two levels of bookkeeping for a set that may carry no order at all.
suggestion: Report the expression together with every place the inner index is used, and propose no rewrite. Set-membership form is equivalent only when the enumeration carries no content, and whether an index is later used for counting, ordering, or induction is not visible at the site of the flag.
mechanism: Introducing a set as an explicit list forces its subsets into indices of indices, and set-membership notation says the same thing with one level. The saving is real where the enumeration is decorative. It is destructive where it is not, because the index is often the object the later argument manipulates, so the rule reports and the author rewrites.
counter_case: Where the ordering of elements is part of the content, as in a sequence, a sorted list, or an induction on the index, the explicit indexed form is correct and the indices carry meaning. Two-level subscripts such as a matrix entry a_{i,j} or a family x_{n,k} indexed by two independent parameters are correct as written and must never be de-nested.
source: Knuth, Larrabee & Roberts, 'Mathematical Writing', Stanford CS 209 notes, section 1 (Minicourse), point 15

test: For every graph, check that each axis names the quantity it plots, and that each axis carrying a dimensional quantity also gives its unit. Flag axes with no quantity name and dimensional axes with no unit. Do not flag a dimensionless axis for lacking a unit.
cost: An unlabelled axis makes a figure uninterpretable without the caption, and a dimensional axis without a unit makes the numbers on it unreadable at any distance.
suggestion: Add the quantity name, and the unit where the quantity is dimensional, taking both from the surrounding text or the data description. Where the text nowhere states the unit, report the gap and ask the author rather than inferring one. Change no plotted value and no table in the same edit.
mechanism: Axis labels are the figure's version of the discipline that a table's column heads provide, and a reader who has to reconstruct them from the caption has lost the figure's advantage over prose. The label text is recoverable from the manuscript in most cases and guessable in none, so the rule supplies it from the text and stops where the text is silent.
counter_case: A dimensionless axis, such as a ratio, a probability, an accuracy, or a normalised score, correctly carries no unit, and appending one would be wrong. An axis on a log scale also needs the scale said, and adding a bare unit without it misleads.
source: Gopen & Swan, 'The Science of Scientific Writing', American Scientist 78(6), 1990, opening table example; Van Buren & Buehler, 'The Levels of Edit', 2nd ed., JPL Publication 80-1 (NASA-CR-162880), 1980, Section VI-D item 6 (ordinates and abscissas labelled)

test: For a table that carries one varying condition and one outcome, check whether the condition runs down the left and the outcome to the right. Flag reversed tables, excluding any table sorted on the outcome, any table whose reader's task is ranking, and any table whose transpose would not fit the page.
cost: A reversed table makes the reader search for the pattern instead of seeing it, because the payoff sits where the familiarisation belongs.
suggestion: Transpose the table so the context variable runs down the left in its natural order and the outcome to the right. Change no cell value, no heading wording, and no unit in the same edit.
mechanism: Reading runs left to right, so a reader familiarises on the left and looks for the payoff on the right. A table with the outcome on the left presents identical information and is measurably harder to read. The transpose is safe only once ranking tables and page-fit constraints are excluded, since in those cases the current shape is the content or the only shape available.
counter_case: Where the outcome is the sort key and the reader's task is ranking, as in a leaderboard, putting the score first is right because ranking is the content. A table of many conditions against two outcomes also runs off the page when transposed, and the wide form is then correct.
source: Gopen & Swan, 'The Science of Scientific Writing', American Scientist 78(6), 1990, opening table example; Van Buren & Buehler, 'The Levels of Edit', 2nd ed., JPL Publication 80-1 (NASA-CR-162880), 1980, Section VI-D item 6 (ordinates and abscissas labelled)

test: Scan only for actually, basically, really, and kind of. Delete each and check whether the sentence's meaning changed. Flag every deletion that changed nothing. Do not extend the scan to hedges, near-quantifiers, or intensifiers.
cost: Each of these costs a word of the reader's attention and returns nothing, and in aggregate they make a confident paper read as padded.
suggestion: Delete them. Keep 'actually' where it marks a contrast with an expectation the text has just raised, and keep 'really' where it is contrastive in the same way.
mechanism: These four are drafting tics with no truth-conditional load in the ordinary case, so the deletion test is sound for them and runs mechanically over a closed list. The list is deliberately short. The words dropped from it hedge or approximate, which makes their deletion a change of claim rather than a change of wording, so they are handled by a report-only rule instead.
counter_case: 'Actually' can be contrastive, as in 'the effect looks small, and actually it reverses at low temperature', where deleting it loses the contradiction the sentence exists to state. The same holds for 'really' in 'the gain is real, and really it compounds'.
source: Williams (rev. Bizup), 'Style: Lessons in Clarity and Grace', 11th ed., Lesson 9, 'Six Principles of Concision', principle 1 (pp. 127-128)

test: Scan for virtually, practically, generally, quite, particular, certain, various, individual, and given. Report each with its full sentence and name the role it plays there, hedge, approximate quantifier, forward pointer to a set the text later specifies, or empty filler.
cost: A reader who meets several of these in a paragraph cannot tell padding from a stated limit on the claim, and neither can a mechanical scan.
suggestion: Report each occurrence with its sentence and its apparent role, and propose no deletion. Removing one of these words changes what the sentence claims, upgrading a hedged statement to an absolute one or dropping a restriction the argument depends on, so the author decides every case.
mechanism: These words fail the deletion test for the opposite reason to the fillers. Deleting them does change meaning, and the change is invisible in the sentence's grammar while being decisive in its content. A report that names the role each one plays gives the author the same list without letting an automatic pass strengthen a claim past its evidence.
counter_case: 'Virtually all' is a genuine hedge distinct from 'all', and deleting it strengthens a claim beyond the evidence. 'Certain conditions' is empty when the text never says which and load-bearing when it does, and only the surrounding argument decides which case is in front of you. 'Quite' before a graded absolute similarly grades a claim rather than decorating it.
source: Williams (rev. Bizup), 'Style: Lessons in Clarity and Grace', 11th ed., Lesson 9, 'Six Principles of Concision', principle 1 (pp. 127-128)

test: A passage in someone else's file has a gap the editor cannot fill (a missing derivation step, an unwritten paragraph, a wording the editor is unsure of, a link not yet minted) and the editor's change is a labelled in-place marker -- \todo{}, an owner macro, a commented plan line, or a bracketed 'fill in from X' -- rather than prose. Trigger for a check: the draft contains a spot where the editor's own edit stops mid-thought with no marker naming what is owed and who owes it.
cost: An unmarked gap is invisible: the coauthor who could fill it never learns it exists, and the gap surfaces at submission as a missing number, an empty \ref, or a sentence that stops. An unowned marker is nearly as bad -- everyone reads it as someone else's job.
suggestion: Leave the gap as a marker at the exact site, and put two things in it: what is needed and who has the material ('fill in from Rickard's equations', '\todo{dense evaluation}', '% add a link for github before the final version'). Use the project's owner macro when one exists so the marker carries an addressee.
mechanism: In multi-author drafts the scarce resource is attention pointed at the right line. A marker at the site converts private knowledge that something is missing into shared, locatable state, and it survives handoffs that memory and chat messages do not. Naming the owner turns the marker from a complaint into an assignment. The site matters as much as the text: a to-do list at the top of the file loses the coupling to the sentence that needs it.
counter_case: Camera-ready and reviewer-facing versions, where a surviving marker leaks internal deliberation to reviewers or ships literal '\todo' into the PDF. Also when the editor does have the knowledge -- then a marker is procrastination dressed as process, and writing the sentence is strictly better. And in a file being read by an external collaborator for the first time, dense owner macros can read as accusation rather than assignment.
source: corpus discovery, 6 instances in 50 sampled edits (discovered1.jsonl)

test: An inline query macro or comment asks for something ('should we start with the leaderboard results?', 'add link to the video', 'how is this rephrasing?') and the surrounding text now supplies it -- often with the reply visible in the same macro chain ('\mss{agree added new subsection}'). Checkable: a query macro whose request is satisfied by text within a paragraph or two of it.
cost: Live-looking queries in a settled passage make every reader re-adjudicate a decision that is already made, and a reader who trusts the query starts arguing with a version of the text that no longer exists. Near submission the residue is also a leak risk.
suggestion: When the text answers a query, delete the query and the whole reply chain in the same pass that lands the answer -- not just the question. If the decision needs a record, it belongs in the commit message or the PR description, not in the file.
mechanism: A query macro is a request for state change; once the state changed, it is stale metadata that costs a reader the same attention as live content. Leaving the answered thread as a record confuses two audiences, since the coauthor needs the decision and the reader needs only the text. Deleting the reply along with the question is what marks the thread closed -- half-deleted threads read as still open.
counter_case: When the answer landed in a way the asker has not seen yet -- deleting the question then hides that their point was addressed, and they will raise it again. Keep the thread through one round of their review. Also on contested points where the query records a disagreement that is only provisionally resolved.
source: corpus discovery, 4 instances in 50 sampled edits (discovered1.jsonl)

test: An empirical sentence rests on a bare head noun -- 'examples', 'models', 'feedback', 'a single aggregate performance score' -- where which members are meant changes whether the sentence is true or checkable. Trigger: a plural or mass noun inside a claim that a reader could satisfy with a different set than the authors measured.
cost: The reader either over-reads the claim (all models, all feedback) or cannot check it at all, and a reviewer who picks the wrong set finds a counterexample the authors never claimed to cover.
suggestion: Add the discriminating qualifier at the noun, not in a later sentence: 'examples that are all challenging in a similar manner', '5-7 recent, highly capable models', 'feedback on model performance and outputs'.
mechanism: A head noun sets the quantification domain of the whole sentence, so a vague one makes every downstream number ambiguous. The author knows the domain and so does not feel the gap, which is why this is almost always caught by the second reader rather than the writer. Fixing it at the noun rather than in a follow-up sentence keeps the claim and its scope in one parse.
counter_case: When the sentence is deliberately general -- a background or framing statement where the broad noun is the claim, and a qualifier would falsely narrow a genuinely universal point. Also in abstracts under a hard length limit, where the qualifier is better spent once in the setup than repeated at every noun, and where over-qualification makes the contribution read as narrow.
source: corpus discovery, 4 instances in 50 sampled edits (discovered1.jsonl)

test: A sentence says the work measures or agrees with the target construct itself, where the evidence only supports a proxy or a subset -- 'measuring theory of mind', 'this is in line with our results'. Trigger: a claim of measurement or agreement with no named proxy and no named subset.
cost: A reviewer who tests the literal claim finds it false, and the paper loses credit for the narrower result it actually established.
suggestion: Downgrade the object to what was shown: 'measuring progress towards theory of mind', 'in line with our results for the large improver'. Insert the proxy or the subset rather than adding a hedging adverb.
mechanism: Overclaiming usually comes from a missing noun rather than a missing hedge, so the repair is to name the proxy or the population instead of softening the verb. A named restriction is checkable and still counts as a result, while 'may' or 'suggests' weakens the sentence without making it verifiable. The person who did not run the experiment is the one who notices, because they read the sentence literally.
counter_case: Where the restriction is already established a line earlier and repeating it makes the paragraph read as retreating from its own finding. Also in a general-audience abstract, where naming the proxy at every step can hide the contribution behind machinery -- state the construct once with the proxy fixed nearby.
source: corpus discovery, 2 instances in 50 sampled edits (discovered1.jsonl)

test: A criterion, baseline, or count is named but the number or procedure needed to act on it is absent: 'statistically similar in performance' with no threshold, a GloVe baseline with no pooling rule, submission counts with no accepted counts. Checkable: a decision word ('similar', 'we use X representations', 'received N submissions') with no operational constant attached.
cost: A replicator has to guess, and two guesses give two different tables. A reviewer reads the unquantified criterion as a hidden degree of freedom.
suggestion: Attach the constant at the point of first use -- the inequality and its z, the pooling rule for the embedding baseline, the accepted counts alongside the submission counts -- rather than deferring to an appendix.
mechanism: Unquantified criteria are the cheapest place for a result to become unreproducible, because the missing constant is usually one the author fixed without deliberating. Placing it inline binds the number to the claim it licenses, so later edits to one cannot silently orphan the other. The incoming editor catches these precisely because they lack the tacit default the author was carrying.
counter_case: Standard settings under a length limit where inlining every constant buries the argument -- there the appendix plus one pointer is better than an inline dump. And where the constant is genuinely swept rather than fixed, pinning one value misrepresents the protocol; state the range.
source: corpus discovery, 3 instances in 50 sampled edits (discovered1.jsonl)

test: A figure or table can be read off the page but its caption omits the conditions under which it was produced (training-set size, dev split, number of seeds) or the source of a redrawn image. Trigger: caption text that describes only what is plotted, on an exhibit whose interpretation depends on settings or whose design came from another paper.
cost: A reader who skims exhibits -- most readers -- draws a conclusion from a single seed or a borrowed diagram as if it were a many-seed result or original work. Missing provenance on an adapted figure is a credit failure, not just a gap.
suggestion: Put the reading conditions in the caption ('single seed', '15\% of the dev set for validation') and, for any exhibit derived from published work, a one-clause credit ('Image based off Fig. 1 from \citet{...}').
mechanism: Captions are read out of order and quoted out of context, so they are the only place a condition reliably travels with the exhibit. The author remembers the settings and so writes the caption for themselves; the coauthor writes it for the skimming reader. Provenance in the caption also protects the borrowed figure from being cited back to the wrong paper.
counter_case: Venues with hard caption-length caps or figure-heavy papers where the same conditions repeat on every exhibit -- there one settings paragraph plus short captions reads better, and stuffing captions makes the page unreadable. Also do not add a seed count to a caption when the count is disputed or you are guessing it.
source: corpus discovery, 2 instances in 50 sampled edits (discovered1.jsonl)

test: The paper promises artifacts -- code, models, data, demos -- but no sentence says where they are or when they will appear. Checkable: the abstract or intro mentions released resources with no URL, no anonymized-link block, and no release footnote.
cost: A reviewer who cannot find the artifact discounts the reproducibility claim, and readers who would have used the release never get to it.
suggestion: Add the availability line at the end of the abstract or as a first-page footnote: a project URL for a non-anonymous version, a labelled '\textbf{Anonymized Links:}' block under review, or an explicit 'All code and data will be released upon publication'.
mechanism: Availability is a claim about the paper's own conduct, so it belongs where the claims are, not buried in an appendix a reviewer reaches last. A labelled block is what makes it survive the anonymization pass instead of being deleted with the URLs. The person taking over the file adds it because the original author is optimizing the prose and treating release as logistics.
counter_case: When release is not actually approved -- an unclearable dataset, licence or institutional review pending -- a promise added for reviewer goodwill is a commitment the project may have to break. And a bare project URL in a double-blind submission de-anonymizes the paper; use the anonymized form or nothing.
source: corpus discovery, 3 instances in 50 sampled edits (discovered1.jsonl)

test: The document still carries submission apparatus that is unfinished: template placeholder author blocks ('Author 1 \\ Address line'), an affiliation missing for a listed author, a section file that no \input reaches, or a venue-mandated statement (impact, ethics, related work) that is absent. All four are mechanically detectable from the source tree.
cost: Desk rejection or a lost section. An unwired \input silently drops written work from the PDF, and no reader or author notices because the file still exists.
suggestion: Before each submission, diff the section files against the \input list, replace every template block with real front matter, and add the venue's required statements verbatim from its call. Treat this as a pass over the source, not a read of the PDF.
mechanism: These failures are invisible in the rendered document, which is the only artefact the authors actually review, so prose-level care does not catch them. They also concentrate at handoff, when the person who created a file is not the person assembling the submission. A single source-level sweep costs minutes and removes a class of failures no amount of rereading finds.
counter_case: Mid-project drafts, where a related-work file is deliberately unwired to keep compiles short and a boilerplate impact statement would be premature. Also, adding a generic impact statement to a paper with real societal stakes is worse than leaving it out -- the template sentence signals the authors did not think about it.
source: corpus discovery, 4 instances in 50 sampled edits (discovered1.jsonl)

test: A named prior phenomenon or result is asserted with no citation ('catastrophic forgetting, where learning a new task ... results in dramatic degradation'), or a list of subareas omits one that is now standard in the field. Trigger: a factual claim about prior work with no \cite, or an enumeration of a literature that a specialist would call incomplete.
cost: An uncited background fact reads as the authors' own assertion or as carelessness, and an incomplete list tells the reader whose work the authors do not know -- often a reviewer's.
suggestion: Add the citation at the asserted fact, and top up survey-style lists with the missing subarea and its canonical reference rather than leaving the list as first drafted.
mechanism: Background sentences are written from memory at speed, and the author's certainty about the fact is exactly what suppresses the citation. Lists of subareas date fast, so the first draft's coverage becomes wrong without anyone editing it. The coauthor who works in the adjacent literature is the only person who can see both gaps, which is why these edits arrive on handoff.
counter_case: Sentences where the fact is definitional and citing it implies the field is unsettled, and paragraphs already dense with citations where one more turns prose into a bibliography. Do not lengthen a list to look comprehensive if the added entry is not load-bearing for the argument -- that is padding.
source: corpus discovery, 3 instances in 50 sampled edits (discovered1.jsonl)

test: A term or component first appears inside a result, contrast, or evaluation, with no sentence saying what it is or which already-known thing it corresponds to -- 'max-confidence' and 'confidence-weighted majority vote' used before their relation to Best-of-N and weighted majority vote is stated; 'pretrained model' used against 'intertraining' with no definition; a prompt-injection classifier evaluated before it is described. Checkable: a named object whose first occurrence is in a claim rather than in a definition.
cost: Readers who know the standard method cannot tell whether the paper renamed it or changed it, and readers who do not know it cannot follow the contrast at all. Both suspect novelty inflation.
suggestion: At first use, add one anchoring sentence that either defines the term with a concrete instance ('a standard pre-trained LM, e.g., vanilla BERT') or states the correspondence explicitly ('analogous to Best-of-N and weighted majority vote respectively, with reward scores replaced by confidence estimates').
mechanism: A new name over a known mechanism forces the expert reader to reverse-engineer the mapping while also tracking the argument, and they often resolve the ambiguity as overclaiming. Stating the equivalence costs one sentence and converts the name into shorthand the reader can carry. The definition also fixes the contrast set, so later sentences comparing the term against a baseline become checkable.
counter_case: When the correspondence is only partial -- naming an analogy that does not hold in the regime that matters trains the reader on a wrong model, which is worse than no anchor. And in a venue where the mapping is common knowledge, spelling it out reads as condescension and spends a sentence you need elsewhere.
source: corpus discovery, 3 instances in 50 sampled edits (discovered1.jsonl)

test: A roadmap or contribution list where some items carry a pointer to where they are delivered ('(\S\ref{sec:auto_extraction})', 'in Fig. X') and a sibling item carries none. Also a results subsection that opens directly on figures with no lead-in naming what the reader is about to be shown. Purely checkable: pointer present on n-1 of n parallel items.
cost: The reader treats the unpointed item as a claim with no delivery, which is the same signal as a promise the paper does not keep. In a figure block with no lead-in, the reader has to guess which figure carries which conclusion.
suggestion: Give every item in the parallel list its own pointer, and open a figure-heavy subsection with one sentence that names the interpretation to come and refers to the first exhibit.
mechanism: Parallel structures set an expectation, so a missing element reads as absence of the thing rather than absence of the pointer. Pointers are also what let a skimming reader convert the contribution list into a reading plan, which is how most reviewers use it. The asymmetry is easy for the author to miss because they know where each contribution lives, and trivial for the next reader to spot.
counter_case: Abstracts and one-paragraph summaries, where section references are noise and the venue may forbid them. Also a list whose items all live in one section -- repeating the same \S\ref on each line is clutter, and one pointer for the group is better.
source: corpus discovery, 2 instances in 50 sampled edits (discovered1.jsonl)

test: An editor working on a co-author's draft meets a spot that needs a decision they cannot make from the text alone (an unstated audience, a symbol's contents, a title choice, a figure that omits models the text names, a section that exists only as a heading). Trigger: the problem's fix requires facts, authority, or a choice that lives with another person.
cost: The two failure modes both cost the reader. A silent rewrite by someone who does not own the fact puts a confident wrong statement in the paper. A comment parked in email or a global TODO list detaches from the sentence it is about, so the person who could fix it never sees it at the site and the defect ships.
suggestion: Leave an owner-tagged query inline at the exact site, in the project's comment macro (\name{...}, \todo{...}) or a % comment, phrased as the specific question or the specific missing content, and addressed to the person who owns it. Then run a sweep for those tags before every submission so none survives into the PDF.
mechanism: In a multi-author draft the knowledge needed to fix a defect is usually not in the same head as the eye that spots it. An inline owner-tagged query is the only channel that keeps the defect and its location and its owner together, which is why experts writing on someone else's text produce these instead of edits. The cost of the practice is debris, and the data shows the debris being swept in a later pass by a third person.
counter_case: When the defect has exactly one correct answer visible in the text - a broken \ref, a duplicated word, a wrong figure number - a query is worse than a fix. It spends a co-author's attention on something no one needed to decide, and it risks surviving into the camera-ready. Also worse on deadline day when the addressee is offline and the sentence must simply be made true or cut.
source: corpus discovery, 8 instances in 50 sampled edits (discovered2.jsonl)

test: A sentence makes an absolute-scope claim - 'first to', 'no existing X', 'prevents/maintains Y', 'no cohesive standardized platform' - about a component or a literature that the person drafting the sentence did not build or does not own, and no citation or measurement sits adjacent to it.
cost: The one reader who knows the field will name the counterexample, and once one absolute claim breaks, every other claim in the paper is read as loose. Where the claim is about the authors' own system ('prevents capability degradation'), a reviewer who reads the appendix and finds degradation treats it as misreporting rather than as an overstatement.
suggestion: Route the claim to the person who owns the component or the literature before it is stated flatly. Either attach the evidence (a measurement, a citation, the scope it holds within) or narrow it to the scope that is actually defended: 'the first to merge PEFT adapters at this scale', 'no benchmark evaluates multi-agent play across time'.
mechanism: Absolute claims are written by whoever is drafting the framing and are usually about someone else's part of the work, so the drafter cannot check them. This is why they are the single most contested item in cross-author revision here: the challenge always comes from the owner, never from the writer. Treat any absolute-scope claim as unverified until the owner signs it off.
counter_case: Competition reports, systems papers and proposals are often judged on a flatly stated novelty, and hedging the registered contribution to 'one of the first' reads as no confidence in it. If the owner has already established the claim in the paper, do not soften the sentence - point it at the evidence instead.
source: corpus discovery, 3 instances in 50 sampled edits (discovered2.jsonl)

test: A uniform series - table rows, list items, per-person bios, a colour or macro legend - has one member missing or left empty while every sibling is filled, and the missing member is referred to or used elsewhere in the document.
cost: A reader does not read a gap as unfinished, they read it as content. An empty bio slot next to full ones says this person has no standing; a tool list missing two tools says the agent cannot do those things; a legend without a colour for a category that appears in a figure makes the figure unreadable at that point.
suggestion: Fill the slot to the same template and depth as its siblings, or remove the slot entirely so no gap is visible. Where the content is not yours to write, name the owner in an inline query at the slot rather than leaving it blank.
mechanism: Parallel structure sets a reader expectation of coverage, so absence inside it carries meaning the authors never intended. This is a cross-author failure by construction: each contributor fills their own row and no one owns the empty ones, so it is normally the next editor who sees it. It is also cheap to detect mechanically, since siblings give the template.
counter_case: Some gaps are the finding. A comparison table deliberately shows that one condition has no counterpart, an ablation cell is legitimately not applicable, an author bio is withheld for anonymous review. Filling those either fabricates content or destroys the point the layout is making - mark them explicitly as '--' or 'n/a' instead of populating them.
source: corpus discovery, 4 instances in 50 sampled edits (discovered2.jsonl)

test: A sentence names prior work or a class of prior work and either enumerates several items with \citep for each except one, or announces the acknowledgement ('it is essential to acknowledge the related work on X') and cites nothing.
cost: The reader takes an uncited item in a cited list as the authors' own coinage, and a promise of acknowledgement with no reference reads as a gap the authors hoped not to fill. Both invite a reviewer to supply the missing reference as a criticism instead of as background.
suggestion: Give every enumerated component its own citation, and convert any 'we acknowledge related work on X' sentence into the actual citations. If the list is uneven because the missing reference is unknown, ask the co-author who owns that subfield rather than leaving the slot bare.
mechanism: Citation gaps in enumerations survive because the writer of the list knows which reference belongs where and does not notice the one they skipped. A second reader sees the ragged edge immediately. The fix needs knowledge outside the text, which is why it lands as a cross-author edit rather than a self-revision.
counter_case: At the head of a related-work section a signposting sentence is meant to be uncited because everything below it is the citation; adding references there duplicates the section. Anonymity periods and venue reference limits are also real reasons a specific citation is deliberately absent.
source: corpus discovery, 3 instances in 50 sampled edits (discovered2.jsonl)

test: A sentence that ends in a citation group carries an appended clause specifying a mechanism, a purpose or a narrower application ('both through direct memorization and through learning co-occurrence patterns', 'for feedback collection') that the cited works do not themselves establish or cover.
cost: The rider borrows the citation's authority without being covered by it. A reader who follows the reference finds it does not say that, which is the cheapest kind of credibility loss, and in the narrowing case the citations are silently misdescribed as being about a subfield they are not about.
suggestion: Cut the rider back to what the citations support, or split it into its own sentence with its own evidence. Where the mechanism is the paper's own claim, state it as such and point to the section that shows it, rather than letting it ride on someone else's reference.
mechanism: Scope creep at the end of a cited sentence is invisible to the writer, who knows the mechanism is true and treats the reference as decoration. It is highly visible to a co-author who knows the cited literature. The fix is subtractive and does not need new evidence, which is why these appear as clean deletions.
counter_case: When the mechanism clause is the paper's contribution and is demonstrated later, deleting it removes the thesis from the place where the reader needs it. The same holds when the rider exists to separate the paper's sense of a term from a rival sense in the cited work - there, cutting it reintroduces the ambiguity the author was avoiding.
source: corpus discovery, 2 instances in 50 sampled edits (discovered2.jsonl)

test: The source contains authoring scaffolding whose job is done: a placeholder standing where text now exists ('fill in in the end', a red TODO for a dataset that is now described), or a review comment whose issue has been addressed.
cost: Scaffolding that outlives its purpose ships. A placeholder inside an abstract or a red TODO in a submitted PDF tells reviewers the draft was not read end to end, and live-looking comments make later readers re-litigate settled decisions.
suggestion: Delete the marker once the content it stood for exists or the comment it carried is resolved, in the same pass that resolves it. Keep an explicit sweep for the project's comment macros and TODO strings as the last step before any submission.
mechanism: Comment tags are addressed to a person, not to the file, so once the person has acted no one is responsible for the tag any more. That leaves removal to whoever next edits the region, usually a different author. The deletion carries no meaning risk when the replacement content is visibly present, which is what makes it batchable.
counter_case: If the marker is the only record of genuinely unfinished work, deleting it silently converts a known hole into an unknown one - the missing standard deviations flagged in this same corpus are a deliberate durable flag, not debris. Verify the content exists before removing the marker, and never clear another person's open comment merely to tidy the file.
source: corpus discovery, 3 instances in 50 sampled edits (discovered2.jsonl)

test: A result is stated as a finding with no mention of the obvious deflating context a reader will supply: that the winner was already known to be the winner, or that a stronger class of systems was excluded from the comparison.
cost: The reader who knows the deflating fact stops trusting the framing and starts looking for what else was left out. Volunteering it costs one sentence; having a reviewer raise it costs the claim.
suggestion: Add the concession at the claim, with a bound rather than a shrug: 'the best was MNLI, which was already known as such', 'these models perform better than the open-source models we describe but are still below humans'. State the comparison and where the numbers are.
mechanism: Authors under-report facts that seem to weaken their result, and co-authors reading fresh restore them because they can see the reviewer's objection forming. A concession that comes with a bound converts a vulnerability into evidence of care, and it takes the objection off the table before review.
counter_case: When the excluded comparison is genuinely out of scope - a different training budget, a closed system with unknown data - the concession invites a demand for an experiment you cannot run. And a results section thick with concessions reads as no confidence; put a scope statement in the limitations rather than a hedge on every claim.
source: corpus discovery, 2 instances in 50 sampled edits (discovered2.jsonl)

test: A formal object's verbal gloss does not match its definition. Either a symbol or macro appears with no words attached ($o_t$ with no statement of what it contains, a measure introduced only as \stabilitymeasure{}), or it carries a friendly interpretive gloss that the model does not license ('$\theta_i$, signifying some skill level').
cost: An unglossed symbol forces every later reader to rebuild the formalism, and a wrong gloss is worse: a reader who is told a fitted latent parameter means skill will read every downstream result as being about skill, which is a claim the paper never tested.
suggestion: At first use give each symbol and each macro-named construct a gloss that is checkable against its definition, and no wider. If the interpretation is a hypothesis rather than a definition, mark it as one and cite the evidence, or cut it and let the definition stand alone.
mechanism: The person who wrote the formalism cannot see the gap between the symbol and its meaning because both are in their head. Gloss errors run in both directions, which is the part that gets missed: reviewers demand missing definitions but rarely warn that a helpful semantic label on a latent or fitted quantity is itself an untested claim. Both are caught by the co-author who has to use the notation.
counter_case: In interpretability work the interpretation of a latent quantity is the contribution, and deleting the gloss deletes the finding. There the correct move is to keep the gloss and attach the evidence for it, not to retreat to the bare definition.
source: corpus discovery, 3 instances in 50 sampled edits (discovered2.jsonl)

test: A claim or conclusion sentence sits next to the material that licenses it without naming the link: an illustrative example followed by no statement of the general point, a conclusion that silently rests on two separate findings, a headline result stated without the training condition that makes it surprising.
cost: The reader has to reconstruct the inference, and may reconstruct a different one or none. Where the surprise depends on a condition stated pages earlier - the model never saw those explanations - a reader who does not recall it reads a strong result as routine.
suggestion: Insert the bridging clause that names the warrant at the point of the claim: 'So X defines types as the change in surface forms', 'Combining with the ...', 'Despite never seeing Jabberwocky explanations, ...'. One clause, carrying the licence, before the claim.
mechanism: Authors omit these bridges because the inference is obvious from inside the work, so the omission is invisible in self-revision and obvious to the next reader. The bridge is also where a paper's contribution actually lands - the example without its point is decoration, and the result without its condition is a number.
counter_case: If the two findings come from different setups or populations, a 'combining' connective manufactures a joint claim neither experiment supports, and an explicit 'therefore' asserts causation where the data is correlational. Name the link only as strongly as the design allows, and where it cannot be named, keep the findings apart.
source: corpus discovery, 3 instances in 50 sampled edits (discovered2.jsonl)

test: A float is committed to the draft with an empty or placeholder caption - \caption{}, \caption{.}, \caption{Caption.} - while the figure file itself is final and referenced.
cost: Captions are the most-read text after the abstract, and a reader who meets a figure with no caption gets an image with no claim. Worse, the caption is where the finding would have been written down, so the finding stays unwritten and later drafts inherit a figure nobody can defend.
suggestion: Write the caption in the same edit that adds the float, stating what the panel shows and what the reader should conclude from it, not just what is plotted. If the result is not yet settled, say so in the caption and mark the float as provisional rather than leaving the caption blank.
mechanism: Floats are added when the plot is produced, which is a data-pipeline act, and captions are a writing act, so the two get separated and only the first happens. In collaborative drafts the plot's owner and the section's author are often different people, so no one closes the loop. An empty caption is a one-line mechanical trigger, which makes this cheap to catch.
counter_case: When the float is a stand-in for an experiment still running, a confident caption commits the paper to a result it does not have. Comment out the float or caption it as pending instead - an assertive caption on a placeholder figure is a worse failure than a blank one.
source: corpus discovery, 3 instances in 50 sampled edits (discovered2.jsonl)

test: A comparison or ranking is asserted in the body text or a results table with point estimates only - win rates, means, 'superiority is consistent across nearly all benchmarks' - and no dispersion, no test, and no pointer to where either lives.
cost: The reader cannot tell whether a 63% versus 54% gap is a finding or noise, and a ranking that is actually within error becomes the paper's headline. If the statistics do exist in an appendix, a claim with no pointer to them is read as a claim with none.
suggestion: Attach the dispersion to the numbers, or cross-reference the analysis that carries it - '(see App. X for detailed statistical analysis)' - at the sentence that makes the comparative claim, not only at the top of the section. Where a table's standard deviations are genuinely missing, flag the hole explicitly rather than shipping bare means.
mechanism: Point estimates are what the pipeline emits, so the table is written from the pipeline and the significance work happens later or elsewhere. The claim sentence and its statistical support then live in different files and often different authors' heads. Pointing the claim at its support costs a parenthetical and is what lets a reader check the ranking at all.
counter_case: With one run per cell by design - a single-seed sweep chosen to buy more conditions - inventing an interval or running a test on n=1 misleads more than the bare number does. State the n and the reason for it, and mark the ranking as provisional instead of dressing it in statistics.
source: corpus discovery, 2 instances in 50 sampled edits (discovered2.jsonl)

test: An incoming editor hits a spot in someone else's draft where the right fix depends on a fact only the original author has (is this list complete? where did these spans come from? is this claim new?). Trigger: the edit would require inventing a fact, and no addressed inline note (\name{...}, \todo, bracketed owner tag) sits at that spot.
cost: The reader of the next draft gets either a guessed fact presented as the authors' own, or a defect that stays invisible because the only person who noticed it left no trace at the site. Both are silent; the second costs a whole revision round when a reviewer finds it instead.
suggestion: Leave the text as it stands and insert an addressed note at the exact character position of the problem, phrased as the question you cannot answer, e.g. \raj{is the models listed all?} beside the figure caption whose model list you doubt. Address it to the person who can answer, and put it inside the caption/paragraph it concerns rather than in a separate comment block.
mechanism: On a shared .tex the manuscript is also the coordination channel, and position carries information a message elsewhere cannot: the note's location says which of nine sentences is wrong. Editors in this corpus reach for a note precisely when the deficit is knowledge rather than prose, so the note marks the boundary between what the editor could verify and what they could not. Deleting the doubt instead, or fixing it by guess, launders an unverified claim into the authors' voice. The notes also stack into a visible thread: three of these rows are a second editor replying to or querying an earlier note at the same site.
counter_case: Any file about to leave the collaboration compiled: a rebuttal, a camera-ready, a grant PDF uploaded to a portal. There the note prints, and a visible \lil{...} in a reviewer's copy costs more than the ambiguity it flags, so the question goes to chat and the text ships as-is. Also skip it when the answer is already elsewhere in the draft, or when the disagreement is taste; a note that only says 'I would have written this differently' turns into work for the next editor with nothing decidable at the end.
source: corpus discovery, 8 instances in 50 sampled edits (discovered3.jsonl)

test: A \name{...} note, bracketed owner tag, or %-TODO addressed to a person is deleted. Check whether the surrounding text changed in the same edit. Trigger for the violation: the note vanishes and the sentence, caption, or block it pointed at is byte-identical.
cost: The asker cannot tell a satisfied request from a dropped one. They either re-raise it (a wasted round) or assume it was handled and let a real defect through. Ownership tags are worse: deleting '[[name] [name]]' from an unwritten subsection erases who owes the section, not the debt.
suggestion: Delete the note in the same edit as the change it asked for, so the diff itself is the acknowledgement. When declining, keep the note and append a reply rather than removing it. When you are the named owner clearing your own placeholder, delete it only once the content exists.
mechanism: These notes are the only record of a request in a corpus with no issue tracker, so the delete is a speech act, not tidying. Coupling removal to the fix makes the version history answer 'was this addressed?' without anyone remembering. The clean case here is [name].[name] deleting the vague phrase 'argumentative contexts' together with the query that asked what it meant, which resolves and closes in one motion. The failure mode is asymmetric: an over-kept note is visible clutter, a wrongly-deleted note is invisible loss.
counter_case: A request you deliberately refused. Silently deleting the note there erases a disagreement the asker still holds and will discover at submission, when it is expensive; the note must survive with a reply attached. Also do not enforce this on the pre-submission sweep, where every note is stripped on purpose regardless of resolution and the coupling would block the sweep.
source: corpus discovery, 4 instances in 50 sampled edits (discovered3.jsonl)

test: A run of prose changes topic (new resource type, new experiment, new subtopic) with no sectioning command at the seam, or a sectioning command exists but its argument is empty or it carries no \label while the document \refs sections elsewhere. Observable: paragraph N and paragraph N+1 share no content words and sit under one heading.
cost: A skimming reader, and every reviewer is one, cannot see that the block exists or what job it does; the block's function has to be reconstructed from its first sentence. Without a \label, coauthors write 'as described above' instead of \ref, and those phrases silently go wrong on the next reorder.
suggestion: Insert a heading at the seam naming the block by its content, at the smallest level that fits (\paragraph for a resource category, \subsection for a plan item), and put a \label immediately after it. Name the block by what it contains ('Educational resources'), not by its role ('Additional data').
mechanism: The most frequent structural move of an incoming editor in this corpus is to name and anchor a block the previous author left running, five times in fifty. This is the reader's table of contents being built after the fact, by the first person who reads the draft cold and gets lost. The \label half is not cosmetic: it converts a positional reference into a symbolic one, so structure can be reordered later without silently corrupting the prose.
counter_case: A two-or-three-paragraph argument whose steps depend on each other. A heading in the middle tells the reader they may enter there, and they will, arriving without the premise. Also under a hard page limit, where a \paragraph costs a line and a half that a result could occupy, and where a strong first sentence does the same signposting for free.
source: corpus discovery, 5 instances in 50 sampled edits (discovered3.jsonl)

test: A sentence attributes a finding, a performance level, or the existence of a resource to the world outside the paper ('X showed that...', 'reaching close to human performance', a named language resource in a list) and contains no \cite/\citep covering that specific item.
cost: The reader cannot separate what this paper establishes from what it inherits, and cannot check the inherited part. In a related-work paragraph an uncited attribution reads as either an unverifiable assertion or an unacknowledged borrowing.
suggestion: Attach the citation to the specific item it supports, inside the list or clause, not at the end of the sentence. In an enumeration where several items each have their own source, cite item by item, as in '..., Chinese~\citep{liu2024zhoblimp...}, Dutch, ..., Japanese~\citep{someya-oseki-2023-jblimp}, ...'.
mechanism: An editor arriving on a foreign paragraph reads it as a reviewer would and finds the provenance gaps first, because those are the only defects checkable without the authors' knowledge. Placing the reference beside its item rather than at the sentence end keeps the mapping unambiguous when a list carries mixed provenance, which is the case a trailing citation group destroys.
counter_case: A result the paper itself proves. Adding a citation there implies the finding is borrowed and quietly hands the contribution to someone else. Likewise a definitional statement every reader of the venue already holds; the citation adds a line of bibliography and signals insecurity rather than rigor.
source: corpus discovery, 3 instances in 50 sampled edits (discovered3.jsonl)

test: Commented-out source that is no longer live: a %-prefixed \input for a section that was dropped, template boilerplate shipped by the conference class ('You may include other additional sections here.'), or a commented URL, name, or affiliation sitting beside its anonymized replacement.
cost: Ranges from clutter that makes the next editor guess which of two \input lines is real, to a live anonymity breach: a commented real repository URL beside \url{https://anonymized} is in the .tex that coauthors, and sometimes the submission's source bundle, get.
suggestion: Delete the dead line rather than leaving it commented. When the content might come back, move it to a scratch file or rely on version control, which is what the history is for. Anonymity-relevant residue (real URLs, names, affiliations) is deleted, never commented, in any file that leaves the group.
mechanism: A comment marker hides text from the compiler and from nobody else. It survives every copy of the source, so the source, not the PDF, becomes the leak surface, and de-anonymizing residue is invisible to anyone proofreading the built document. The clutter cost compounds separately: parallel commented and live \input lines make the document's real structure unreadable at exactly the moment a new editor needs it.
counter_case: [name].[name] commenting out a whole intro sentence in the same corpus is the legitimate use: an editor parks text where a coauthor can see and restore it, deliberately keeping it visible rather than burying it in history. Sweeping those away destroys a shared undo mid-negotiation. Distinguish by age and adjacency - a commented line the current editor just created is a proposal, one orphaned from a dropped section is residue.
source: corpus discovery, 3 instances in 50 sampled edits (discovered3.jsonl)

test: A phrase whose deletion leaves the sentence's information intact: a modal or ability stack ('need to be able to compare' where nothing depends on need or ability), a light noun plus relative pronoun ('process that guide'), a paired nominal where the second term subsumes the first.
cost: Words the reader must parse and discard. Under a page limit they also displace content, and the stacked-modal form specifically blurs whether the sentence states a requirement or an action.
suggestion: Cut to the load-bearing verb: 'need to be able to compare' becomes 'to compare'. Cut the light noun and its relative: 'a process that guides' becomes 'guides'. For paired nominals, keep both terms only if the paper measures both.
mechanism: Empty words survive first drafts because the author is thinking about the claim, not the phrasing, and they are invisible to that author on reread. A second reader sees them immediately, which is why they show up as cross-editor deletions. The gain is small per instance and real in aggregate, since these phrases cluster in the sentences an author found hardest to write.
counter_case: The paired-nominal case in this very corpus is the risk: deleting 'understanding and' from 'table understanding and reasoning capabilities' narrows what the benchmark claims to cover, and if its ten datasets do test both, the trim understates the contribution to save two words. Also keep the modal when the modality is the point ('models need to be able to X' as a stated requirement, not a description of what the paper does).
source: corpus discovery, 2 instances in 50 sampled edits (discovered3.jsonl)

test: A contribution bullet, closing paragraph, or call-to-action sentence asserts reach the paper never measured: applicability to domains not tested ('likely useful to multiple domains, and can be adopted for ... other fields'), or a comprehensiveness adjective over the artifact ('comprehensive dataset and standardized schema'). Trigger: no section of the paper reports evidence for the asserted breadth.
cost: A reviewer prices the whole paper on its weakest claim, and an untested breadth claim in a contributions list is the cheapest thing to attack. It also crowds out the claim the paper can defend, which usually sits in the neighbouring sentence.
suggestion: Delete the sentence when its content is a hope rather than a result, and let the adjacent defensible sentence carry the paragraph; in these two rows the following sentence already made the point without the overreach. When the breadth claim must stay, demote it to an explicitly labelled expectation with the concrete adjacent domain named.
mechanism: Overclaims are written by the person who knows how the method works and can feel it generalizing; that feeling is not evidence and is unavailable to the reader. A senior editor arriving on the draft is reading as the reviewer will and deletes the claim rather than hedging it, because a hedged unsupported claim still occupies the line without earning it. The evidence for the cut is that both rows leave a strictly stronger paragraph behind.
counter_case: Grant proposals and workshop or competition proposals, where breadth is a scored criterion and the reviewer form asks for exactly this claim. Deleting the transfer-to-other-fields bullet from an ERC or NSF-style section removes something the panel is required to rate, so the fix there is to substantiate the claim, never to cut it.
source: corpus discovery, 2 instances in 50 sampled edits (discovered3.jsonl)

test: A method or technique is described with no indication of whether it operates at training time or inference time, and the distinction changes what the reader must assume about cost and deployment. The mirror trigger: a scope qualifier ('during inference') appears in a clause whose sentence already fixed the scope.
cost: The reader mis-prices the method. A preprocessing step at inference costs per-query latency and needs the parser at deploy time; the same step at training costs nothing at deployment. Repeating the qualifier instead makes the reader look for a second scope that does not exist.
suggestion: Pin the scope once, at the first mention where the reader could get it wrong, attached to the verb that does the work: 'proposed UCCA based preprocessing in inference time, splitting sentences to different events'. Then drop it from later clauses in the same sentence or paragraph that the first mention already covers.
mechanism: Train-versus-inference is the axis that decides whether an ML contribution is cheap or expensive, and authors omit it because for them the method has only ever run one way. Both directions of this pair appear in the corpus, an editor adding the qualifier to a prior-work description and another deleting it where the sentence already said 'inference under an early exit strategy', which shows the norm being enforced is placement rather than presence. Exactly once, at the first point of doubt, is what keeps the reader from re-deriving the scope at every mention.
counter_case: Methods that genuinely run in both regimes: forcing one scope statement makes the sentence false, and the honest form names both. And in an abstract or opening paragraph of a paper whose entire framing is inference-time, restating the scope is worth the redundancy, because a reader who arrives there without having read the body has no earlier mention to inherit it from.
source: corpus discovery, 2 instances in 50 sampled edits (discovered3.jsonl)

test: An editor working in someone else's file hits a word or claim whose intended meaning cannot be recovered from the draft, and the file already defines per-author comment macros.
cost: A silent rewrite guesses at the other author's meaning and can install a claim the data does not support, and the original author never learns that the passage stopped a reader.
suggestion: Wrap the doubt in your own comment macro next to the exact span and leave the text untouched, naming the specific thing you could not verify.
mechanism: In a shared draft the person who can settle a vague scope word is usually the person who ran the experiments. An inline question keeps the doubt pinned to the span, so it survives until that one person reads it. Rewriting instead erases the evidence that a reader stumbled, and the guess enters the paper under the original author's name. All four observed cases target a word whose extent or referent the editor had no way to check.
counter_case: Where the editor does hold the missing knowledge, a comment is worse than a fix, because the co-author then pays a round trip for an edit the editor could have made. It is also wrong on a draft hours from the deadline, where an unresolved marker either ships in the PDF or forces a scramble.
source: corpus discovery, 4 instances in 50 sampled edits (discovered4.jsonl)

test: A comment macro sits beside text that already satisfies what it asked for, such as a citation it called missing now present, a notation it questioned now changed, or a camera-ready todo whose task is done.
cost: Stale markers make the draft look unread, bury the live comments among dead ones, and sometimes compile into the submitted PDF.
suggestion: Delete the marker in the same edit that satisfies it rather than leaving it for a cleanup pass nobody schedules.
mechanism: A comment is state with a lifecycle, and it carries signal only while unresolved. Once satisfied it charges every later reader a re-check of whether the request still stands. In one observed case the citation the note called missing is visible in the surrounding text, so the note had become pure noise. The editors here close somebody else's request at the moment the fix lands.
counter_case: Where the fix answers only part of the comment, deleting it drops the unaddressed half silently and no trace remains. Where the commenter asked for a judgement rather than an edit, only the commenter can close it, and a co-author deleting it removes their vote from the decision.
source: corpus discovery, 4 instances in 50 sampled edits (discovered4.jsonl)

test: An editor is about to leave inline comments in a file whose preamble defines one comment macro per collaborator, and no macro exists for them.
cost: Comments left in a borrowed macro get attributed to the wrong person, so answers go to the wrong author, and comments left in raw color survive the pass that strips the macro family.
suggestion: Add one \newcommand for yourself in the preamble beside the existing ones, following their pattern and taking an unused color, before writing the first comment.
mechanism: Per-person markup is the addressing scheme of a shared draft. Attribution is what makes a comment answerable, and a uniform macro family is what lets the whole channel be switched off in one line at camera-ready. Two different editors joining two different papers each made this their edit, which suggests it is a recognised entry ritual rather than a coincidence.
counter_case: On a draft with no such convention, adding a personal macro imposes a system nobody else uses and the comments go unread by co-authors who never see the color. Strict venue templates also break when extra definitions land in the preamble.
source: corpus discovery, 2 instances in 50 sampled edits (discovered4.jsonl)

test: The source carries commented-out prose or layout that duplicates or contradicts what the live text now says.
cost: The next editor cannot tell which version is intended, and uncommenting the shadow copy silently reverts a decision that was already taken.
suggestion: Delete the commented block once the live text supersedes it instead of keeping it as a private undo.
mechanism: A commented-out sentence reads as a live alternative to everyone except the person who commented it out. In one observed case a commented thank-you sat directly above a rewritten live version of the same sentence, so a reader had to compare two drafts of one line. Version control already holds the history, so the shadow copy buys nothing and charges a decision on every read.
counter_case: A commented block holding a variant kept for a specific venue, such as an alternate table sizing for a page limit, is working material and deleting it forces someone to rebuild it under deadline. The same holds for a block a co-author explicitly parked with a note.
source: corpus discovery, 2 instances in 50 sampled edits (discovered4.jsonl)

test: A sentence contains a word or clause fragment that no longer parses, sitting where an earlier edit removed part of a phrase or a macro name.
cost: Readers stall on garbled text, and a broken macro name can silently swallow the words that follow it in the compiled PDF.
suggestion: Read the full sentence around every earlier deletion and remove the orphaned fragment.
mechanism: Partial deletion is the standard failure mode of editing prose that lives inside markup. The damage hides in plain sight, because the leftover looks like unchanged context in a diff of the deleted span. Both observed cases are an author returning to their own file after a day and finding wreckage from their own previous pass, which is exactly when a fresh read catches it.
counter_case: In a file a co-author is editing right now, half-finished phrasing can be work in progress, and tidying it destroys a sentence somebody is mid-way through building.
source: corpus discovery, 2 instances in 50 sampled edits (discovered4.jsonl)

test: The text names a table, an artifact, a platform, or a caveat handled elsewhere, with no \ref, \cite, or \Cref attached.
cost: Readers who want the underlying material have to hunt for it, and reviewers read an uncited named system as an unsupported claim of novelty.
suggestion: Attach the pointer at the first mention, inside the same sentence.
mechanism: Every named thing in a paper has a home, either in the document or in the literature. The mention is where the reader forms the intention to check, so that is where the pointer has to sit. Three separate editors each added exactly one pointer to someone else's sentence, once a table, once an appendix, once the platform the work runs on.
counter_case: A mention that is deliberately generic gains weight without gaining clarity, and the second and third mention of the same table do not need the number again. Repeating pointers inside a short passage reads as padding.
source: corpus discovery, 3 instances in 50 sampled edits (discovered4.jsonl)

test: Results are displayed or listed with no sentence saying what to conclude, or a sentence names a table without saying what the table shows.
cost: The reader supplies their own conclusion, which is usually weaker or narrower than the one the authors earned.
suggestion: Add one sentence giving the aggregate reading, naming the comparison and the direction of the result.
mechanism: A table reports numbers and a claim reports a finding, and only the authors can bridge the two. In all three observed cases the inserted sentence opens on the overall pattern and then names the specific conditions, which is the order a reader needs to absorb it. The move showed up in a discussion, in an ablation passage, and in an introduction summary, so it is not tied to one section type.
counter_case: Where the caption and the section opener already state the same takeaway, a third statement is filler. Adding a takeaway the numbers only weakly support turns a fair display into an overclaim that a reviewer will target.
source: corpus discovery, 3 instances in 50 sampled edits (discovered4.jsonl)

test: A takeaways sentence or a bolded claim carries a second finding, with its own figure reference, stacked onto the first.
cost: Two findings in one summary sentence dilute both, and numbers repeated from the table make the summary read as a second results section.
suggestion: Keep the headline finding in the summary and let the table or figure carry the supporting numbers and the secondary result.
mechanism: Summary passages accrete findings, because every co-author wants their result in the takeaways. Both observed deletions cut the trailing clause together with its pointer and left the leading claim standing, which suggests the editors were holding one summary sentence to one claim. In both cases the cut clause was also the weaker of the two, which is where a reviewer would push first.
counter_case: Where the second finding is the one that qualifies the first, such as a scope limit or a failure case, cutting it leaves an overclaim alone in the summary. In a paper whose contribution is the pair of findings together, splitting them across sections hides the contribution.
source: corpus discovery, 2 instances in 50 sampled edits (discovered4.jsonl)

test: A sentence or clause announces what the text is about to do, and the announced material follows immediately.
cost: The reader spends a sentence learning what the next sentence shows, and the announcement goes stale the moment the structure changes.
suggestion: Delete the announcement and let the material stand, keeping a forward pointer only where the reader must wait several pages.
mechanism: Announcements are written for the writer, who needs the outline while drafting. Once the material exists the outline is visible in the material. One observed cut dropped a section pointer from the front of a claim in an introduction, the other dropped a stand-alone announcing sentence from a response letter, and in both the following text ran on unchanged.
counter_case: In a long proposal or a rebuttal that reviewers read out of order, the explicit roadmap is the only navigation available, and cutting it costs more than it saves. Reviewer-facing documents in particular reward telling the reader where each answer lives.
source: corpus discovery, 2 instances in 50 sampled edits (discovered4.jsonl)

test: A prescription, a general claim, or an unexplained methodological restriction stands with no condition or reason attached.
cost: A reader who does not share the unstated condition reads the sentence as false, and a reviewer reads the unexplained restriction as an unforced weakness.
suggestion: Add the short condition or purpose clause in place, naming the situation in which the sentence holds or the constraint that forced the choice.
mechanism: Most claims in a paper hold inside a scope the authors never wrote down. Three editors each added a few words to somebody else's sentence, one giving the reason a method was restricted, one naming the setting where a prescription applies, one adding the priority under which a recommendation flips. The clause is cheap and it closes the obvious objection at the point where the reader raises it, rather than in a limitations section they may never reach.
counter_case: Loading conditions onto a claim the evidence fully supports weakens it for nothing, and a proposal that qualifies every ambition reads as unconfident to a funder. A condition that repeats one already set at the top of the section is noise.
source: corpus discovery, 3 instances in 50 sampled edits (discovered4.jsonl)

test: A block of text runs with no heading while its neighbours have them, or a heading carries only a generic process word such as Methodology or Approach.
cost: Readers who scan headings get no map of the paper, and a generic heading spends a line of the most prominent text in the document without narrowing anything.
suggestion: Add a heading that names the specific object or phenomenon covered, and drop a heading whose whole content is a process label.
mechanism: Headings are the one part of a paper every reader reads. Three of the four observed edits added a specific title over material already written, naming the dataset, the non-idealities, or the benchmarks under discussion. The fourth deleted a bare Methodology subsection heading, which is the same standard applied in the other direction, and that pairing is what makes the pattern a rule rather than a habit of adding headings.
counter_case: Venues and funders that require named sections make the generic heading mandatory, and deleting it costs a compliance point that no amount of specificity recovers. Adding headings inside a short passage also fragments an argument that reads better continuous.
source: corpus discovery, 4 instances in 50 sampled edits (discovered4.jsonl)

test: A body sentence points at a float or a run of examples and only describes what is shown ("Figure X illustrates that M predicts Y", "scores are high across the board", a list of qualitative cases) with no following sentence stating the claim the reader should take away.
cost: The reader has to invent the finding, and two readers invent different ones. A number that is high for a boring reason gets credited to the method, and a run of examples reads as decoration rather than evidence.
suggestion: Append one sentence that names the conclusion, and where the number has a mundane cause, name the cause in the same breath. Say what the result licenses the reader to believe and what it does not.
mechanism: Authors read their own floats with the finding already in mind, so the pointer feels complete to them and incomplete to everyone else. Three separate incoming editors here added the missing takeaway rather than any new data, which shows the gap is invisible from inside the draft. The added sentence is also where the contrast with prior work and the practical consequence get stated, so its absence costs the paper its framing, not just clarity.
counter_case: A results walkthrough where every row supports the same conclusion turns into a chant if each pointer gets its own takeaway sentence. Worse, on a qualitative sample grid whose point is that behaviour varies case by case, an appended takeaway manufactures a finding the figure does not support.
source: corpus discovery, 3 instances in 50 sampled edits (discovered5.jsonl)

test: A float carries no caption at all, or a caption that names the quantity plotted without saying what the axes or the sorted columns are, so the float cannot be read without hunting for the paragraph that produced it.
cost: A reviewer who skims floats first reads nothing. Axis units and log scaling get guessed wrong, which makes a modest gain look enormous or the reverse.
suggestion: Give every float a caption, and inside it define each axis with its scale, say what one point aggregates over, and state the column ordering when it is inherited from another table.
mechanism: Floats move during typesetting, so the paragraph that defines the axes may end up a page away from the picture. The caption is the only text guaranteed to travel with the figure, which makes it the place where the reading instructions belong.
