Both instances here are an incoming editor supplying axis definitions or a caption slot the previous author never filled.
counter_case: An appendix table that repeats a main-paper table with identical axes does not need the definitions restated, and under a hard page limit a caption that duplicates the body paragraph can push the float onto a later page, separating it from the discussion it serves.
source: corpus discovery, 2 instances in 50 sampled edits (discovered5.jsonl)

test: You are editing a passage written by someone else and your objection depends on knowledge you do not have (whether the experiment exists, why a design was chosen, whether a later section already answers it). The draft shows either a silent rewrite of that passage or the objection recorded somewhere outside the file.
cost: A silent rewrite destroys the information the original author had and the reason they had it, and the author often reverts it without knowing why it changed. An objection raised in chat or a review call detaches from the sentence that caused it and dies there.
suggestion: Insert a named note at the exact site, addressed to the person who can resolve it, stating the objection and the decision it needs. Leave the author's text intact underneath so the choice is theirs, and sweep the notes as a separate deliberate pass.
mechanism: Twenty percent of the changes in this sample are an incoming editor writing an addressed note rather than touching the prose, which makes annotation the single most common cross-editor move in the data. The pattern holds because placement, motivation strength and definition scope all depend on knowledge the author holds and the reader does not, so a rewrite is a guess while a note is a question with an address. Standard writing guidance covers how to fix prose, not what to do when you are the wrong person to fix it.
counter_case: For a defect with exactly one correct fix (a missing package, a truncated URL, an absent citation key you know) a note costs a round-trip and the fix costs nothing, so annotating there just slows the draft. The other failure mode is not sweeping. Notes left in a file that reaches camera-ready ship inside the PDF, so the annotate move only works if someone owns the deletion pass.
source: corpus discovery, 10 instances in 50 sampled edits (discovered5.jsonl)

test: A passage would sit equally well in two sections (a survey of prior approaches inside the motivation, a definition inside the method or the related work), or a sequence of analyses is ordered on an axis different from the one the paper says it studies.
cost: The reader builds a map of the paper from the section names and then keeps finding material where the map says it should not be, so nothing can be relocated by memory. Content in the wrong section also gets read with the wrong expectation and is judged as a failure of that section.
suggestion: Decide placement by the function the passage performs for the reader at that moment, not by the topic it names, and move it whole. Where the analyses could be grouped either way, group them on the axis the contribution claims, so the organization argues for the paper.
mechanism: Placement is the most frequent structural objection in this sample and it is close to invisible to the author, because a passage written in flow feels like it belongs wherever the flow put it. The second reader arrives without that flow and sees only the section label, which is exactly the reader's position. Three different projects show the same move, each raised by the incoming editor rather than the author.
counter_case: Where section order was fixed by the venue or the call (related work last, a mandated work-package ordering, an ERC structure), a placement objection reopens a decision that is not the paper's to make. And pulling all motivation out of the intro into related work leaves the intro with no stake in the problem, which is a worse read than a slightly digressive intro.
source: corpus discovery, 3 instances in 50 sampled edits (discovered5.jsonl)

test: A motivating premise or a design decision has an obvious cheap counterargument that the draft never names (older benchmarks being abandoned is fine rather than a problem, a demonstration whose chosen case cannot separate the effect from a confound, a comparison the reader will immediately ask to see split).
cost: The reader supplies the counterargument themselves and then discounts everything the premise supports, including results that would survive on their own. A reviewer who finds the hole first treats it as evidence the authors did not think about it.
suggestion: Name the counterargument in one clause and answer it in the next, or change the premise to one that does not invite it. Where the objection is about a demonstration case, pick the case that isolates the mechanism even if it is less attractive.
mechanism: A motivating premise gets far less scrutiny from its author than a result does, because it is not the thing being defended, and that is exactly why it is the easiest place to attack the paper. The two instances here are incoming readers naming the objection the author had not considered, one of them explicitly as a prediction about what a reviewer will ask. Answering the objection in place costs a clause and buys the whole downstream argument.
counter_case: Raising an objection in the abstract, where there is no room to answer it, converts a confident claim into a visible weakness. And pre-empting an objection that only one collaborator would ever raise adds a defensive paragraph that plants the doubt it was meant to settle.
source: corpus discovery, 2 instances in 50 sampled edits (discovered5.jsonl)

test: The draft reports material whose own conclusion is that nothing was concluded (a sweep with no clear choice), describes an experiment that is not present, or lists a contribution in the abstract that no section develops.
cost: Every inconclusive passage the reader crosses lowers their estimate of the parts that do hold, and an abstract promise with nothing behind it reads as overclaiming even when the rest of the paper is exact.
suggestion: Cut the passage rather than hedging it, and cut the abstract line rather than softening it. Where the material is the only record of a real decision, move it to an appendix with the decision stated plainly instead of dressing it as a result.
mechanism: Hedging keeps the reader's attention on material that cannot pay for it, so the honest move and the persuasive move point the same way here. All three instances are the incoming editor deleting, not qualifying, which suggests experienced co-authors treat weak secondary material as a cost to the strong claims rather than as extra credit. The abstract case matters most because a promise there sets the contract the whole paper is read against.
counter_case: When the deleted passage is the only justification for a setting that is reported elsewhere, cutting it leaves an unexplained hyperparameter and a reader who cannot reproduce the run. The row-26 deletion does exactly this to a 30-epoch choice, so the correct move there was relegation with the reasoning kept, not removal.
source: corpus discovery, 3 instances in 50 sampled edits (discovered5.jsonl)

test: A term of art carries a claim before it has been defined, or a noun phrase leaves out the specifier that fixes its scope (which metrics, set by whom, between which two things), and the missing piece cannot be recovered from the sentence.
cost: The reader either stops to guess or carries an approximate meaning forward and misreads every later use. Ambiguity in a relational word is worse than a missing definition because it silently changes what the method is claimed to do.
suggestion: Define the term at its first load-bearing use in the same sentence that first asserts something about it, and attach the specifier to the noun rather than leaving it to context. Where you are the wrong person to know the intended scope, mark the word and ask.
mechanism: The author cannot see the gap because the specifier is present in their head while they write, and a term they use daily does not feel like jargon. Three unrelated projects show the same repair, once as a definition folded into the opening claim and twice as a missing specifier on a noun. The cost lands on the reader who is closest to the paper's actual audience, the one who reads carefully enough to notice the ambiguity.
counter_case: Defining a term the venue's readers use every day spends the intro's most valuable sentences telling them what they know. And pinning a deliberately open scope, where any metric really is meant, narrows the contribution to the examples you happened to name.
source: corpus discovery, 3 instances in 50 sampled edits (discovered5.jsonl)

test: The file holds scaffolding that its question has outlived, a TODO whose task is done, prose commented out during a rewrite that has since settled, or a template placeholder still sitting under the real content.
cost: Co-authors re-open resolved questions and redo finished work, because a live TODO is indistinguishable from an open one. Commented prose also competes with the live sentence during the next edit, and a placeholder that survives to submission ships inside the PDF.
suggestion: Delete the scaffolding in the same pass that resolves it, and where you are not the person who resolved it, delete only what the surrounding text visibly satisfies. Keep the sweep as a named pre-submission step so nothing depends on memory.
mechanism: Collaborative drafts accumulate notes far faster than they lose them, because inserting one is cheap and deleting one needs the knowledge that it is done. Four instances here are the deletion side of that ledger, including a template author block still sitting under real author names. No writing guide addresses comment hygiene, yet in a shared LaTeX tree it is the difference between a note that coordinates and a note that misinforms.
counter_case: A TODO can look satisfied because nearby text changed while the actual task is still open, and deleting it drops the task with no trace. Commented prose deliberately kept as a rollback point for a contested rewrite should also stay until the rewrite is agreed, so a blanket sweep before the argument settles destroys the fallback.
source: corpus discovery, 4 instances in 50 sampled edits (discovered5.jsonl)

test: A borrowed term or an empirical claim sits next to an empty or partial citation group, including the case where the group cites recent work on a phenomenon while the paper that originated it is absent.
cost: The reader cannot check the claim, and worse, an incomplete cluster reads as unawareness of the line of work rather than as an omission. A reviewer who is one of the missing authors reads it as a slight.
suggestion: Fill the key at the site rather than in a to-do list, and when a cluster names a phenomenon, check that the originating paper is inside it and not only the recent follow-ups. Where you do not know the right reference, park the candidate titles at that exact spot.
mechanism: Four instances here are an incoming co-author adding a key into an existing group, not building a bibliography, which shows the failure is a cluster that looks finished while missing its anchor. Citing the follow-up without the origin is invisible to the drafter, since the follow-up is the paper they read most recently, and highly visible to anyone who knows the area. The repair is cheap and only the person who knows the literature can make it, which is why it keeps falling to the second reader.
counter_case: Where the sentence is deliberately about the recent line only, adding the originating work mis-attributes the claim to it. And under a page limit, padding a group toward completeness costs a line and reads as citation stuffing, so the anchor plus one representative beats five keys.
source: corpus discovery, 4 instances in 50 sampled edits (discovered5.jsonl)

test: A clause restates what the sentence has just said with different words, or a coordinated pair names one activity twice (experimentation and exploration, tagged with tags).
cost: The reader looks for the distinction the second term promises, finds none, and trusts the next distinction less. Under a page limit the words also displace content that carries information.
suggestion: Keep the more specific member of the pair and drop the other, and cut a trailing clause whose content is already in the subject. Read the sentence aloud once after cutting to check that the rhythm still lands where the emphasis belongs.
mechanism: Doublets enter because the writer was choosing between two words and kept both, so the redundancy is a fossil of drafting rather than a decision. Two projects here show the incoming editor removing exactly that fossil, in one case a clause that repeated the noun immediately before it. The cost is small per instance and compounds over a paper into prose that feels padded.
counter_case: A pair sometimes names two genuinely different activities, so collapsing running the trials and scanning the space into one word loses a real distinction. In a license or ethics statement, redundancy is also load-bearing, because the second phrasing closes an interpretation the first leaves open.
source: corpus discovery, 2 instances in 50 sampled edits (discovered5.jsonl)

test: A sentence spends its opening on the paper's own procedure or intentions before reaching content ("Let us recall that our main research question is about", "Moreover, we are interested in understanding").
cost: The reader waits through a frame that carries no information to reach the claim, and the claim then arrives in a subordinate position where it reads as an aside rather than as the point.
suggestion: Delete the frame and promote the content to the main clause, keeping the tense and the actor the frame supplied. Where the frame was doing a navigational job across a long gap, replace it with a concrete pointer to the section rather than a reminder of intent.
mechanism: Frames are written for the author, who needs to remind themselves where they are in the argument, and they survive into the draft because they read as courtesy. Both instances here are an incoming editor deleting the frame and letting the following sentence stand alone, one of them adopting a co-author's suggested replacement in the same edit. The direct sentence is shorter and states the same thing, which is why the move is close to free.
counter_case: After ten pages of derivation a genuine reminder saves the reader a hunt, so removing it forces them backwards. In a grant proposal, restating the research question at each section head is also the reviewer's navigation aid rather than metadiscourse, and cutting it makes the proposal harder to score.
source: corpus discovery, 2 instances in 50 sampled edits (discovered5.jsonl)

test: The paper presents a usable artifact (tool, dataset, demo) and gives no pointer a reader can follow, or gives one that cannot resolve, such as a URL whose identifier is truncated.
cost: A reader who wanted to try the thing cannot, and a reviewer reads the artifact claim as unverifiable. A broken link is worse than none, because it converts an invitation into a dead end in front of the reviewer.
suggestion: Put the pointers where the artifact is claimed, and give the reader the shortest path to seeing it work rather than only the repository root. Check each URL resolves in a fresh session before submission.
mechanism: Both instances here are the incoming editor adding or completing the pointer, one adding a demo and a video next to a bare repository link, the other restoring a cut-off notebook identifier. The artifact is the strongest evidence a tool paper has, and it is worthless unless a stranger can reach it in one click. Truncation in particular is invisible to the author, whose editor renders the link as text they already know works.
counter_case: Under double-blind review a live demo or a personal repository link deanonymizes the submission, so the pointer belongs in the camera-ready and not in the draft. Linking a repository that is not yet public also produces a 404 in front of the reviewer, which reads worse than a promise to release.
source: corpus discovery, 2 instances in 50 sampled edits (discovered5.jsonl)

test: A venue-mandated slot is blank or partial, such as a checklist justification that names the assets it reuses without their license terms, or a paper with funding and support to declare and no acknowledgments section.
cost: The blank is a compliance failure rather than a style problem, so it can cost a desk rejection independently of the paper's quality. A partial asset statement also leaves the reuse rights of the work undetermined for anyone who wants to build on it.
suggestion: Fill the slot with the specific fact, naming the license by version and the support by grant, and route it to the person who actually holds that fact rather than approximating it. Track the slots as a submission gate rather than as prose.
mechanism: These slots fall between authors, because each of them is knowable by exactly one person and interesting to none, which is why both instances here were filled by the second editor rather than the first. The information is also not derivable from the paper, so no amount of careful reading substitutes for asking. Treating the slots as a checklist rather than as writing is what gets them done.
counter_case: Under anonymous review the acknowledgments must stay empty, since filling them in deanonymizes the submission and can itself be a desk reject. And a license asserted from memory rather than from the upstream terms is a false statement, which is worse than an admitted gap.
source: corpus discovery, 2 instances in 50 sampled edits (discovered5.jsonl)

test: A stretch of draft covers two distinguishable regimes or topics with no heading between them, or a heading exists with its title or its cross-reference label left unfilled.
cost: The reader cannot locate anything by memory and cannot be sent anywhere by reference, so every mention of an earlier result costs a linear scan. An untitled unit also hides the paper's organization from the one reader who skims the headings first.
suggestion: Cut at the topic boundary, title the unit by the claim it establishes rather than by the material it contains, and attach a label so later sections can point at it. Name the unit before writing into it so the boundary drives the content.
mechanism: Three projects here show the incoming editor adding structure rather than prose, once as a full section skeleton, once as a supplied subsection title, once as a label on a heading that had none. The pattern reflects that a draft's structure is obvious to the person who wrote it in order and opaque to anyone arriving later. A titled and labelled unit is also the unit a co-author can be handed, which is why the structural pass tends to precede the writing pass.
counter_case: Empty placeholder headings compile into a contents list of nothing and disguise missing content as present structure, which is dangerous close to a deadline. Headings finer than the argument's joints, a subsection for every paragraph, also break one line of reasoning into fragments that each look self-contained.
source: corpus discovery, 3 instances in 50 sampled edits (discovered5.jsonl)

test: A spot in someone else's draft where the text is wrong or unsupported and the fix needs information only another author has, with no marker sitting at that spot.
cost: One macro call inline. It has to be swept before submission, and a stale marker that outlives its problem misleads the next reader.
suggestion: Leave the question in an author-initialled macro at the exact word that triggered it, phrased as the one thing you need answered, and delete the macro the moment the answer lands in the prose. Example forms seen here are \[name]{is it ok to say that without explaining there are adverse affect, what it affects etc.?} and \dtc{who is them}, and the closing move is the plain deletion of \[name]{not clear} once the passage was rewritten.
mechanism: A cross-author editor who cannot resolve a problem has two bad options and one good one. Silently rewriting invents content the owner may not stand behind, and saying nothing loses the observation. The site-anchored query keeps the defect attached to its coordinates so the only person who can close it sees it in context, and the deletion of the marker is the receipt that it was closed.
counter_case: On a shared draft inside 48 hours of a deadline the markers stop being a channel and become debris, because nobody will read them in time and any that survive the sweep print in the PDF. At that point an editor who can make a defensible guess should make the edit and say so out of band.
source: corpus discovery, 4 instances in 50 sampled edits (discovered6.jsonl)

test: An inline marker already sits at the passage and you are the person it was aimed at, or you disagree with it.
cost: Nothing in the built document. The thread grows, so it must be collapsed into prose eventually or it becomes a private conversation embedded in a public file.
suggestion: Answer inside or immediately beside the existing marker instead of editing the prose it points at, so the exchange stays anchored to the sentence under dispute. Seen as \[name]{Could you point what don't you like? so we can fix it.} placed directly after \[name]{not sure if I like the following argument}, and as a clause written into the interior of an existing \[name]{...} comment.
mechanism: An inline query is treated in practice as a channel, not a flag. The second author writes back at the same coordinates rather than in chat, which keeps the disagreement legible to whoever opens the file next and prevents two people editing the same sentence from opposite premises. The thread only ends when one of them converts the agreement into prose and removes the markers.
counter_case: Where the objection is about taste rather than fact and both authors are equally entitled, the thread deadlocks and the sentence stalls for weeks. One person should take the pen, write a version, and let the other revert.
source: corpus discovery, 2 instances in 50 sampled edits (discovered6.jsonl)

test: You want to change another author's sentence and the change is a matter of wording rather than fact.
cost: A visible substitution is uglier than a clean edit and needs a second pass to absorb, and readers of the source see two candidate texts.
suggestion: Insert the replacement wording marked as yours, either wrapped in your initials macro inline or parked as a commented alternative next to the live sentence, so the owner accepts or rejects rather than discovers the change by diff. Seen as \FT{. These} inserted to break a run-on, and as a commented restatement of a sentence placed immediately before the live version.
mechanism: Silent restyling of a co-author's sentence is the change most likely to be reverted, because the owner reads it as loss of control rather than as help. Marking the substitution converts it into a proposal that costs the owner one glance. It also preserves the original wording so that a rejected suggestion does not require reconstruction from memory.
counter_case: For a mechanical fix with exactly one right answer, a missing article or a broken \ref, the marked proposal wastes the owner's attention and slows the fix. Those go in silently.
source: corpus discovery, 2 instances in 50 sampled edits (discovered6.jsonl)

test: You hold raw material for a passage, notes, measurements, a comparison you made, and the prose that must absorb it is not written yet.
cost: Comment bulk in the source. Anything parked and forgotten silently drops out of the paper, since a comment never fails a build.
suggestion: Commit the material as a LaTeX comment at the exact place the prose will use it, close enough that the writer cannot miss it. Seen as a commented block of per-tool observations placed directly above the \paragraph{Prodigy} that must state them, and a commented note recording which two conditioning modes were tested placed at the head of the failure-mode analysis.
mechanism: Between having the facts and having the sentences there is a gap where knowledge lives only in one person's head. Parking it in the file at the point of use moves the knowledge into the shared artifact without forcing whoever holds it to also be the one who writes the prose. The location is the whole point, since the same note filed in a separate document is never retrieved at the moment it is needed.
counter_case: Material that will never be written up, discarded pilot runs and superseded configurations, should not be parked. It reads to a later collaborator as an unmet obligation and produces work that reinstates something already rejected.
source: corpus discovery, 2 instances in 50 sampled edits (discovered6.jsonl)

test: Scaffolding in the source that has been overtaken by the real text, a stub subsection describing what should go there, a submission checklist whose items are done, template test content from a copied figure.
cost: Low, but deleting is irreversible in a live shared editor with no branch, so fencing is the cheaper form.
suggestion: Either wrap the dead block so the compiler skips it, as with the \end{comment} added to close an obsolete checklist, or delete it outright, as with the removed stub \subsection{"algorithm"} placeholder and the leftover \filldraw ... {test 1\\is aligned left} node from a template dependency figure.
mechanism: Scaffolding is written to be read by the authors and is invisible to them once it has served, which is why template test nodes and finished checklists survive into late drafts. A cross-author editor is the first person who reads it cold and is therefore the one who notices. Fencing rather than deleting is what the same editors do when they are unsure the block is really dead.
counter_case: A checklist that looks finished may be the only record of what still has to happen at camera-ready. Fence it, do not delete it, unless every item is verifiably done.
source: corpus discovery, 3 instances in 50 sampled edits (discovered6.jsonl)

test: A float or cross-reference whose key slot is empty or truncated, an \includegraphics with no path, a \label with no key, a caption that is a placeholder, a \ref naming a key no label defines.
cost: Minutes. The risk is guessing a key or a file that means something different from what the author intended.
suggestion: Fill the slot from the object's own identity, the source filename or the caption subject, and keep every \ref in step with the key it names. Seen as :TD_distribution completing a bare \label{tab, static_benchmarks completing an empty table label, and figures/errors/figure2_failure_depth.pdf completing an open \includegraphics brace.
mechanism: An empty brace is the one unfinished state in a LaTeX draft that produces no visible complaint at the site of the error. The build either fails somewhere else or prints a bold ?? in a place nobody rereads, so the defect travels between authors intact. The same handoff produces both directions of the fault, one author emptying a graphics path mid-swap and another filling one in, which is why it is worth a standing check rather than an ad hoc fix.
counter_case: Where the intended figure genuinely does not exist yet, filling the path with a plausible nearby PDF makes a wrong exhibit compile cleanly, which is worse than a broken build. Leave it empty and mark it.
source: corpus discovery, 6 instances in 50 sampled edits (discovered6.jsonl)

test: Two versions of the same passage live in the compiled document at once, a sentence whose two halves come from different drafts, or an \input of a rewritten section sitting beside the \input of the section it replaced.
cost: Deciding which version survives usually needs the rewriter, so this is a query rather than a silent cleanup.
suggestion: Retire the superseded version in the same edit that introduces the new one, and if the rewrite has to be staged, comment out the old \input rather than leaving both wired in. The failure shows here as a spliced sentence reading "This is because the weights between the models This often occurs when the weights at a given between models transform information in similar ways." and as \input{method_v2} added directly after \input{method}.
mechanism: Rewriting in place inside a shared editor has no atomic commit, so the intermediate state where both versions are live is a normal state of the file rather than an accident. Nobody rereads their own rewrite from the top, so the residue survives, and the person who finds it is the next author. The distinguishing symptom is grammatical impossibility, a sentence that no single writer would produce, which makes the fault easy to spot and impossible to fix without knowing which half was intended.
counter_case: Keeping both versions live is correct while two authors are deliberately comparing framings for a section, as long as one is commented out. Cutting the loser early destroys the comparison the co-author set up.
source: corpus discovery, 3 instances in 50 sampled edits (discovered6.jsonl)

test: A noun phrase carrying a tag about the authors' relation to the thing rather than about the thing, "which are deemed useful" on a list of features, "we find in this work" inside a definition.
cost: None. The deletion is determinate and leaves the sentence grammatical.
suggestion: Delete the authorial tag and let the term be defined by its content. "we provide the following useful features which are deemed useful" becomes "we provide the following features", and "the mergeability of weights we find in this work, describing the degree to which..." becomes "mergeability, describing the degree to which...".
mechanism: Provenance tags get written when the author is still arguing for the contribution rather than stating it, and they double up with the surrounding claim, since a feature presented in a features section is already offered as useful. The tag also weakens a definition by making the defined object depend on this paper rather than on its own criteria. A cross-author reader notices because the tag adds nothing to their understanding of the term.
counter_case: Where a term already exists in the literature with a different sense, the provenance marker is doing real work and must stay, which is why the same corpus shows an editor inserting "in our model," to keep a borrowed idea from being read as a claim about the original.
source: corpus discovery, 2 instances in 50 sampled edits (discovered6.jsonl)

test: A number stated with no unit, or a sample size stated with no statement of the precision it permits.
cost: Adding the precision figure requires computing it, and stating it invites reviewers to apply it to every comparison in the paper.
suggestion: Attach the unit at the site the number appears, as with the axis label extended to "budget ($\times$ full MMLU evaluations)", and where an n is given, state what that n buys, as with "With n = 100 trials, a typical 95\% confidence Wilson half-width is about pm 9 percentage points when the success rate is in the 0.6-0.8 range."
mechanism: A bare quantity is read against whatever scale the reader already has in mind, which for compute budgets and for benchmark sizes is usually the wrong one. The unit and the implied error bar are both facts the author knows and the reader cannot recover. Placing the translation at the site of the number, rather than in a methods paragraph, is what makes it reach the reader who only looks at the figure.
counter_case: In a paper whose claims rest on ranking rather than on absolute margins, volunteering a per-cell half-width invites a precision objection to a claim that never depended on that precision. State the aggregate test instead.
source: corpus discovery, 2 instances in 50 sampled edits (discovered6.jsonl)

test: A sentence true of a wider or narrower case than the one it names, where the mismatch sits on a single word.
cost: Near zero, and the patch is reversible. Overuse turns the sentence into a chain of parentheses.
suggestion: Patch the scope at the exact word rather than recasting the sentence, widening with a parenthetical as in "some prompt formats (or examples) with a very low number of evaluations", or narrowing with an inserted phrase as in "Specifically, in our model, we take inspiration".
mechanism: A scope error is usually not an error of thought, it is a sentence written while the author had one case in view. The minimal in-place patch is preferred by these editors over rewriting because it leaves the other author's sentence recognisably theirs, which makes it likely to survive. It also confines the change to the word that was actually wrong, so a later reader can see what was in doubt.
counter_case: Where three or more scope patches accumulate in one sentence, the parentheses hide the structure and a full recast is the honest fix. A sentence that needs qualifying twice was making two claims.
source: corpus discovery, 2 instances in 50 sampled edits (discovered6.jsonl)

test: A sentence that positions the work against cited prior work but names no axis of difference, saying it extends, expands, or improves on them.
cost: Naming the axis commits you to it, and a reviewer who owns the cited work will check whether the stated shortcoming is real.
suggestion: State the respect, not the relation. "expands the works of X and Y" becomes "expands the works of X and Y by extending inference-time logical thinking in the form of belief graphs into training", and a bare "but their methods" becomes an enumeration of the three specific respects, orthogonal designs, no extrapolation, no statistical guarantee.
mechanism: A relation word to prior work reads as a claim of novelty while carrying no content, so the reader cannot check it and the reviewer supplies the missing axis themselves, usually unfavourably. The authors always know the axis, since it is why they cited that work. Writing it down converts an assertion of standing into a testable difference.
counter_case: For a paper whose contribution is engineering scale rather than a conceptual delta, forcing a stated axis of difference produces an invented one and hands the reviewer a weak claim to attack. Say plainly that the difference is scale.
source: corpus discovery, 2 instances in 50 sampled edits (discovered6.jsonl)

test: A block of results or a section that starts straight into detail with no label for what this block covers, especially where several such blocks follow one another.
cost: Headings and lead clauses take space, and a wrong label misdirects the reader more than no label does.
suggestion: Put the scope label at the top of the block, either as a paragraph heading such as \paragraph{General Results} inserted above an undifferentiated results run, or as a lead clause such as "Our first instantiation focused on the classification use case, where".
mechanism: The author knows which of several cases each block covers and therefore does not feel the absence of the label. A reader arriving from the section head has no way to tell whether a paragraph is the general result or one of the special ones until they have read it. Both moves here were made by an author taking over someone else's section, which is exactly the position the reader occupies.
counter_case: In a short section with one result, a heading over the only block implies siblings that do not exist and makes the reader hunt for them.
source: corpus discovery, 2 instances in 50 sampled edits (discovered6.jsonl)

test: A relational noun or verb appears with its argument missing - a 'subset', 'throughput', 'effect', 'variant', 'the 4 highest', or a verb like 'assess' or 'generalizes' with no of-what or to-what attached. Flag every relational head whose complement is not recoverable from the same sentence.
cost: The reader silently fills the slot with the nearest plausible noun and often fills it wrong, so a scoping error looks like a comprehension failure. Reviewers read 'generalizes' as unbounded and score the claim as unsupported.
suggestion: Insert the complement in place, as a short prepositional phrase, taken from the surrounding sentences rather than invented - 'only a small subset of evaluations', 'Throughput of serving compressed LoRAs', 'assess the effect of a practical decision', 'generalizes to variants of the training problem'.
mechanism: Drafters hold the referent in working memory while writing and never notice the slot is empty, which is why this survives self-revision and is caught by the next person. Five of the fifty changes here are exactly this insertion, each a three-to-six word prepositional phrase and each made by the incoming editor rather than the author. The repair is local and the correct filler is almost always present within one or two sentences of context, which is why the incoming reader can supply it and the author cannot see the gap.
counter_case: Row 36 inserts 'of serving compressed LoRAs' into what reads as a table or axis label 'Throughput{...}'. In a plot axis or a narrow table header the complement will not fit and belongs in the caption instead, so expanding the header there would break the table layout while adding nothing the caption did not already carry.
source: corpus discovery, 5 instances in 50 sampled edits (discovered7.jsonl)

test: A change to someone else's draft that the editor cannot make correctly without a decision only the author or a coauthor can take - an invented acronym, a subsection whose result may be null, a design choice with no stated reason. Detect the site by asking whether the edit needs information the file does not contain.
cost: Silently guessing writes a wrong fact into the paper under someone else's name, and silently doing nothing loses the finding entirely, because the next reader has no way to know the spot was ever inspected.
suggestion: Leave a named, addressed note at the exact character position of the problem, phrased as a question with the proposed answer attached - '\[name]{why pearson is important? why not call it correlation from now on? ... then we can just use $r$}' or '\mss{i think we should remove this subsection, especially if it at the end shows 0}'.
mechanism: The site carries the information the question needs, so moving the question to email or a comment thread strips its context and it dies unanswered. Both instances here attach a proposed resolution to the question rather than only raising a doubt, which lets the author answer with a yes instead of re-deriving the problem. Row 13 shows the supporting habit - a new editor first defines a colored macro under their own name before touching the prose, so authorship of every query is visible.
counter_case: Row 24's query sits in sections/04-results.tex of an ICML submission. Past the camera-ready freeze the same note ships inside the PDF, and row 48 is the cleanup of exactly that failure, a leftover '\gal{was here}' marker found in a thesis chapter. A query is correct only while a closing pass is still scheduled.
source: corpus discovery, 2 instances in 50 sampled edits (discovered7.jsonl)

test: Scaffolding in the file whose task is visibly finished or whose question is visibly settled - a commented-out alternative paragraph, a truncated fragment with a \todo in it, todo items whose work now appears in the results, a meta-note debating a section that now exists, a bare presence marker.
cost: Live and dead notes look identical, so the closing pass either re-reads settled questions on every sweep or starts skipping notes altogether and misses the live ones. Dead scaffolding also leaks into camera-ready PDFs and into shared overleaf views seen by funders.
suggestion: Delete the settled item outright rather than marking it done, and delete it in the same pass that settles it. Keep the deletion narrow - remove '\mg{Maybe also that our experiments cover only English data.}' or '\gal{was here}' and leave every neighbouring note that still names an open task untouched.
mechanism: Six of the fifty changes are this deletion, spread over five projects and five editors, which makes it the most frequent single act in the shard. Deletion is preferred over a done-marker because the value of the note channel is that its length equals the amount of open work. Commented-out prose behaves the same way - row 4 removes a motivation sentence that had been parked behind a percent sign, which no longer had any owner.
counter_case: Row 15's own ctx_after contains '\todo{Brian + Mubashara: review Limitations section}'. That note names two people and an unfinished review, so sweeping the neighbourhood by pattern would delete a live assignment and the review would never happen. Only items whose task is verifiably complete in the same file may go.
source: corpus discovery, 6 instances in 50 sampled edits (discovered7.jsonl)

test: An abstract category asserted without its concrete member - 'a bottom-line evaluation metric' with no metric named, 'gaining popularity' with no adopter named, a claim about gains with no number, a paragraph heading asserting a property with no measurement under it.
cost: The reader cannot check the claim and cannot tell whether the authors have a specific case in mind or are generalising from none. In a discussion section this reads as the paper declining to state its own effect size.
suggestion: Append the smallest concrete member that already exists in the work - ', such as BLEU.' after the metric category, or the measured figures, 'the average gain for the smallest labeled data examined was $62\%$ (and $77\%$ when considering the most difficult cases of more than $10$ classes)'.
mechanism: The author knows the instance and treats naming it as redundant, while the incoming reader is the first person for whom the category is genuinely empty. Four changes here are this insertion and all four are additive, none replaces the abstract statement, so the pattern is instantiation rather than substitution. The numbers inserted in row 10 come from a table already in the paper, which is why this is a surfacing move and not new analysis.
counter_case: Row 38 is the deletion of exactly such a concreteness addition - a passage naming NLLB as the source that 'did not meet the required level of quality' was cut on self-revision, because the named instance carried a judgment about a third party that the paper had no measurement for. Instantiate only from evidence the paper itself reports.
source: corpus discovery, 4 instances in 50 sampled edits (discovered7.jsonl)

test: A paragraph in an abstract or introduction that moves from background straight to detail with no sentence naming the consequence - a posed question with no statement of what answering it buys, a prescription with no statement of the harm it avoids, a setup with no 'in this paper we', an opening question with no premise before it.
cost: The reader reaches the method with no criterion for judging it and has to reconstruct the motivation backwards from the experiments. Panel readers of proposals stop at the first paragraph that has no stated payoff.
suggestion: Insert one sentence at the joint, naming the consequence in the paper's own terms - 'Answering this question might assist us in understanding how to obtain a more mergeable models', or the harm before the remedy, 'Relying on blindly translated datasets risks overindexing evaluations of'.
mechanism: Four changes here are this insertion, in four projects by four different editors, always at a paragraph joint and never as a rewrite of the surrounding sentences. Three of the four are visibly unpolished, with typos left in place, which shows the editors treated the missing link as more urgent than the prose. The author cannot see the gap because the consequence is the reason they started writing, so it feels stated.
counter_case: Row 20's abstract already opened with two direct questions, so under a hard word cap the added framing clause competes with the sentence reporting the result. In a grant template that mandates a separate motivation section, as in row 4's full.tex, repeating the payoff at every paragraph joint reads to a panel as padding.
source: corpus discovery, 4 instances in 50 sampled edits (discovered7.jsonl)

test: Cross-reference machinery that does not resolve - a \ref or \citep with empty braces, a \ref key that no \label defines, a sectioning command that other text points at but which carries no \label.
cost: The compiled paper shows a bold question mark or a stray bracket where a table or section number belongs, which reviewers read as a draft submitted without a final compile.
suggestion: Supply the missing half at the site - write the key into the empty \ref, as in '~\ref{tab:eval_results}' and 'Fig.~\ref{fig:benchmark_release}', or add the anchor to the referenced heading, '\label{app:language-specific}'.
mechanism: Three changes here are this repair, in three projects by three editors, and in each the intended target is fixed by the surrounding sentence - the sentence says which table it shows, or the appendix heading repeats the key's wording. That determinacy is what makes it a mechanical fix rather than a question. The defect survives because the author sees their own intent when reading the sentence and never reads the compiled number.
counter_case: In a scratch file like row 37's ICML2024/sections/todo.tex, refs point at sections nobody has written yet. Supplying a label there fabricates an anchor for absent content and converts a visible question mark into an invisible wrong pointer, so scratch and planning files get a query instead.
source: corpus discovery, 3 instances in 50 sampled edits (discovered7.jsonl)

test: A table or figure whose caption does not let it be read alone - no caption at all, or a caption that names the content but never says what a visual channel encodes, with colors, panels or line styles unexplained.
cost: Readers who skim by figure, which includes most reviewers, get nothing from the display and either ignore the result or misread the grouping. A color that is never keyed makes a multi-series plot unreadable.
suggestion: State the content and then the encoding, in the caption itself - '\caption{\small VQA Performance change between LiveXiv and a manually curated subset.}' and, for the encoding, one appended sentence, 'Different colors indicate different submissions.'
mechanism: Both instances are the incoming editor adding what the figure's author could see without help, which is the signature of display blindness rather than carelessness. The encoding sentence is separable and short, appended after the existing caption text rather than rewritten into it. Captions are also the last thing regenerated when a display changes, so the gap tends to appear at exactly the point where the display was recently rebuilt.
counter_case: Row 42's added sentence keys colors to submissions. If that figure is later regenerated in grayscale, reordered, or recolored by approach rather than by submission, the caption sentence becomes a confident false statement, which is worse than the original silence. Encoding sentences must be re-checked on every figure rebuild.
source: corpus discovery, 2 instances in 50 sampled edits (discovered7.jsonl)

test: A results claim stated over a population wider than the one measured - 'the comparison reveals that X' where X held for most but not all conditions, or 'we show that language models Y' where only models trained a particular way were tested.
cost: One counterexample a reviewer can name turns an unqualified sentence into a false statement and puts the rest of the section's claims in doubt. The qualified version costs three words and is unfalsifiable.
suggestion: Narrow the claim at the verb or at the subject noun rather than adding a sentence of caveats - 'The comparison reveals that in most cases ...', or restrict the population, 'language models which have been fine-tuned on the same dataset'.
mechanism: Both instances are short insertions by the incoming editor into a claim the author wrote unqualified, and in both the narrowing matches the experiment section rather than softening the claim in general. The author overreaches because they remember the aggregate result and not the exception rows. The scope word goes inside the claim so a reader cannot pick up the broad version without the qualifier.
counter_case: Row 17's 'in most cases' sits in supplementary material where the exact table follows. Carried into an abstract, an unquantified 'in most cases' is both weaker and less informative than the fraction itself, so the right repair there is the number rather than the hedge.
source: corpus discovery, 2 instances in 50 sampled edits (discovered7.jsonl)

test: A sentence-initial discourse connective that names the wrong relation to the sentence before, or an unmarked shift in scope where the relation has to be guessed - a second sibling example introduced by 'For instance,', or a jump from a specific case to a general claim with no marker.
cost: A mislabeled relation makes the reader subordinate a parallel item to the previous one and rebuild the list halfway through the paragraph. An unmarked widening makes a general claim look like it is still about the single case just discussed.
suggestion: Set the marker to the relation that actually holds. Delete 'For instance,' from the second item of a list of sibling examples, and open the widening sentence with 'More generally'.
mechanism: Both changes here are by the same editor, in two different projects, and both act on the first two words of a sentence without touching its content, which is what separates this from ordinary rewriting. The defect appears because paragraphs get their sentences reordered late, and the connectives keep the relations of the old order. The check is cheap because only the first clause of each sentence has to be compared against the previous sentence.
counter_case: The same surface string is right in one place and wrong in the other - row 8 deletes a leading 'For instance,' while a genuinely subordinate example needs it. A checker that flags all sentence-initial connectives, or that adds one at every unmarked boundary, will fight the author on every paragraph.
source: corpus discovery, 2 instances in 50 sampled edits (discovered7.jsonl)

test: A structural slot that the document already promises but that has no heading - a roadmap sentence naming three parts where the first has no \section, or an enumerated paragraph marker like 'i)' with no title after it.
cost: Readers navigating by heading cannot find the unit the roadmap sent them to, and in a survey list an unnamed item cannot be cited or skimmed. The document's outline and its text disagree, which reads as an unfinished draft.
suggestion: Create the anchor with the wording the promise already used - add '\section{Experience}' where the roadmap said this section elaborates on teaching experience, and name the numbered slot, '\paragraph{i) Scattered evolution and the need for consolidation.}'.
mechanism: Both instances are incoming edits that add only a heading and change no prose, so the content was already there and only its handle was missing. The promise itself supplies the wording, which is why the repair does not need the author. Headings are typed last and enumerated paragraph titles are typed after their bodies, so this is where drafting order leaves a hole.
counter_case: Row 19 is the opposite case - an editor inserting an empty '\begin{itemize} \item \end{itemize}' under \section{Analysis} as a deliberate placeholder. Naming or filling a slot that the drafter has just opened as a plan for themselves pre-empts their outline, so an empty slot created in the current pass is left alone.
source: corpus discovery, 2 instances in 50 sampled edits (discovered7.jsonl)

test: Does an inline note aimed at a co-author (a \name{} macro, a colored-text aside, a commented question) still sit in the file after the thing it asked about was answered, fixed, or cut?
cost: One deletion, no prose risk. The real cost is misjudging closure and erasing the only record of an open problem.
suggestion: Close notes in the same edit that resolves them: delete your own flag together with the text you cut in response to it, delete a question together with the answer once the answer has been read, and delete another person's request once you have actually made the change it asked for. If you cannot verify the issue is closed, leave the note and list it instead.
mechanism: In a shared .tex the note macro is the only place an unresolvable problem can be parked, so an open note is a live claim on someone's attention. The closing deletion is therefore load-bearing rather than cosmetic: it is how the file reports that the claim is discharged. All five instances here are closures, and they come from every role in the exchange - the asker sweeping after being answered, the answerer sweeping his own answer with the question, and a third party sweeping a request after acting on it.
counter_case: Row 30 deletes 'I don't like it that the caption hides the curves'. If the caption spacing had not in fact been changed, that deletion silently drops a real layout bug that only one co-author had noticed - a reworded sentence is not the same as an answered evidence question, and sweeping on 'looks handled' is how open problems disappear.
source: corpus discovery, 5 instances in 50 sampled edits (discovered8.jsonl)

test: Is what you are adding to a co-author's file for the reader, or for the co-author? If it is for the co-author (why you moved something, the phrasing you rejected, a topic banner organising a shared section), is it in the comment channel at the site of the change rather than in the prose?
cost: Free while drafting. Accumulated author-facing comments make diffs noisier and must be swept before camera-ready.
suggestion: Write author-facing material as a comment or note macro placed exactly where the change is, including the variant you discarded, and sweep dead comment traffic (template boilerplate, superseded alternatives) as you pass it. Never smuggle author-facing explanation into the reader-facing sentence.
mechanism: With several people in one file, an unexplained restructuring reads as damage and gets reverted; a comment at the site converts it into a decision the next person can accept. The same channel carries the rejected phrasing, so a later editor can see what was already tried, and topic banners that tell co-authors where their paragraph belongs. Because the channel is invisible to the reader, its only maintenance pressure is other authors, which is why stale template lines survive for months until someone sweeps them.
counter_case: Row 22 keeps two rejected conditions as trailing comments while the condition is still being settled between two authors. Sweeping those as 'dead comments' before the co-author has seen them destroys the record of an open decision, so the sweep half of this rule only applies to comments whose question is already settled.
source: corpus discovery, 3 instances in 50 sampled edits (discovered8.jsonl)

test: Are there slots in the document with nothing behind them - an empty \subsection, a bold run-in label followed by the literal word 'Text', a bullet list of candidate experiments, a figure whose \label is commented out so nothing references it?
cost: Insertion is free. Deletion can drop a co-author's plan that exists only as that slot.
suggestion: When you want a co-author to write something, insert the empty heading or labelled slot and name what belongs in it - that is a clearer handoff than prose asking for it. When a slot is still empty as the deadline approaches, delete the slot rather than writing filler, and say in the handoff which slots you removed.
mechanism: The section skeleton doubles as a to-do list between authors: an empty \subsection{Result} or a '\textbf{Base models for more exploration.} Text' stub states scope and implicit ownership without anyone writing a note. This is the same open/close cycle as the inline-note channel, but it leaves no note, so the only trace of the request is structural. The closing move is the deletion of a slot that was never filled, including placeholder figures whose \label was commented out precisely so that the unfilled slot would not break the build.
counter_case: Row 46 deletes \subsection{Notation} from a roadmap-following methodology section. If the notation table was sitting in a co-author's uncommitted copy, the deletion removes the agreed place for it and the table comes back mid-Methodology or not at all. An empty slot near a deadline is a question for the owner, not a cleanup.
source: corpus discovery, 5 instances in 50 sampled edits (discovered8.jsonl)

test: Does the claim say over what range it holds - which models, which data, which language, which assumption is being made - or does it read as unconditional?
cost: A clause. It narrows the apparent reach of the result and needs a fact the editor may not have.
suggestion: Add the boundary at the site of the claim ('as long as behavioral drift remains limited', 'implicitly assuming', 'uses English as the default language, and provides infrastructure to add more'), not a modal verb. If you do not know the bound, ask the author for it rather than inserting 'may' or 'often'.
mechanism: Not one of these four insertions adds a hedge; each names a condition, an assumption, or a default. The difference matters because a hedge keeps the sentence's full reach while making it unfalsifiable, whereas a condition tells the reader exactly where the result stops and invites the obvious test. The editor supplying the bound is typically the person who owns that part of the system or the analysis, which is why this shows up as a cross-author edit rather than self-revision.
counter_case: For a genuinely unbounded empirical observation, inventing a crisp condition is worse than hedging: writing 'holds for models above 7B' when only three models were run is a fabricated boundary, and 'we observe this in our three settings' is the honest form. Word-budgeted abstracts are also a legitimate place where only a hedge fits.
source: corpus discovery, 4 instances in 50 sampled edits (discovered8.jsonl)

test: Does a phrase pre-announce in abstract terms what the very next sentence spells out concretely?
cost: Trivial; risk is stranding the reader if the concrete version is far away.
suggestion: Delete the abstract pre-announcement and keep the concrete spelling-out, including the framing preamble that only restates the sentence's obvious job ('As our data source we use X' becomes 'We use X').
mechanism: Multi-author drafts double-state constantly because two people describe the same mechanism from different distances and neither deletes the other's version. The editors here keep the version that carries the operational detail and cut the one that only gestures at it. The cut is safe exactly when the concrete statement is adjacent.
counter_case: Row 34 works only because the next sentence immediately defines empirical difficulty as the fraction of systems that solve an instance. If that definition sat three paragraphs later, deleting 'using observed outcomes from a pool of systems' leaves the reader with an undefined 'difficulty-ordered split' for a page - keep the summary when the detail is not next.
source: corpus discovery, 3 instances in 50 sampled edits (discovered8.jsonl)

test: Is there a parenthetical pointer to visual apparatus - '(see Figure N)', an inline colour-key - inside an overview sentence or a heading, where the reader has no context yet for what they would look at?
cost: A deleted parenthetical; the reference must exist somewhere the claim is actually argued.
suggestion: Drop the pointer from contribution summaries and heading-adjacent text and place it at the sentence that argues the claim. If nothing later points at the figure, that is the real problem to fix.
mechanism: Overview sentences are read for the shape of the argument, and a pointer there asks for a page jump the reader cannot cash in yet. Both instances are senior editors removing pointers from a junior author's summary text, one to a figure in an intro contribution list, one to a colour legend attached to a subsection heading. The information is not lost, only relocated to where the reader is already looking at the thing.
counter_case: A teaser Figure 1 designed to be read with the intro's first paragraph is the opposite case: there the pointer in the opening sentence is the whole point, and removing it leaves a full-width figure that no sentence ever invites the reader into.
source: corpus discovery, 2 instances in 50 sampled edits (discovered8.jsonl)

test: Does every entry in the front matter resolve - each affiliation key defined, each email linked, no leftover template lines - and is your own entry correct?
cost: Minutes, mechanical. Late changes to author macros can renumber or reorder the author list.
suggestion: Patch your own affiliation and contact entry yourself rather than asking whoever set up the template, and check the block for undefined keys and template leftovers before each build. Say in the handoff that you touched the author block, since it is the one place where a silent edit changes another person's name in print.
mechanism: The author block is written once by whoever instantiated the venue template and then quietly patched by everyone else, so nobody owns it and errors survive until the person they misrepresent fixes them. All three edits are metadata repairs by someone other than its author: a missing \icmlaffiliation key, author-separator macros with explanatory comments attached, and a co-author wrapping another author's bare email in a mailto link. The pattern is ownership-by-subject, not ownership-by-file.
counter_case: Redefining \Authands or adding affiliation keys at camera-ready can silently reorder or renumber the author list, and a key the venue style does not define breaks the build outright. When the block is wrong but consistent, waiting for the venue's own checker is safer than an unannounced fix.
source: corpus discovery, 3 instances in 50 sampled edits (discovered8.jsonl)
